title: Chinese HSK 1
description: Mandarin Chinese from your first sentences to the new HSK 1 (HSK 3.0, in force from July 2026). Grammar lessons cover 是 and 有, questions with 吗, 呢 and question words, numbers, dates and time, measure words, position words, 在 and 正在, the modal verbs 会, 能, 想, 要 and 可以, serial verbs, double objects and 了 for completed actions and change. All 300 words of the level (25 of them from the pinyin course) are learned through typed review cards with tone numbers, and all 246 characters are learned through notecards, inside words and by tracing them stroke by stroke, with pinyin you can turn off and a switch to traditional characters. The last lessons practise reading signs and menus, listening and the exam format. Requires Chinese: Pinyin and Tones.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Names and 是: who are you?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the pinyin course you learned the sounds and tones of Mandarin, your first 21 characters and
greetings such as {你好|nǐ hǎo} and {谢谢|xiè xie}. This lesson turns them into conversation. By the
end you can say who you are and what your name is, ask other people the same, say "no, I'm not",
ask yes-or-no questions, and say how you are. You'll also learn 13 new characters.

## How the lessons work

Every lesson has the same parts:

- **Explanations and examples.** Chinese is written in characters, with **[[pinyin]]** (the official
  spelling of Mandarin in the Latin alphabet) above each one: {老师|lǎo shī}. The Pinyin
  switch hides it. Try it from time to time on words you know, because in real life there is no
  pinyin. The Tone colours switch colours each syllable by its **[[tone]]**, the pitch pattern that
  is part of every syllable: first tone red, second green, third blue, fourth purple, neutral grey.
- **Characters.** Each lesson teaches the **[[characters]]** its words use: what they mean, how they
  sound, which **[[radical]]** they're filed under in a dictionary, and how many strokes they have.
  You trace each one stroke by stroke on a writing pad, in the standard **[[stroke order]]**. A
  notecard for every character joins your notecard deck.
- **Script.** The course is written in simplified characters, the standard in mainland China. A
  Traditional switch shows the same text in traditional characters, as used in Taiwan and
  Hong Kong: {={学生|xué sheng}=} becomes {+{学生|xué sheng}+}. The words stay mainland Mandarin.
- **Words.** The new words are listed at the end and join your vocabulary reviews when you finish
  the lesson. When the app asks for Chinese, type pinyin with tone numbers (`ni3 hao3` becomes
  nǐ hǎo; `v` stands for ü; 5 or nothing for the neutral tone) or type characters with your
  device's keyboard. Tones count: *ni hao* without them is marked wrong.

The 25 words of the pinyin course ({你|nǐ}, {我|wǒ}, {是|shì}, {不|bù}, {中国|Zhōng guó}, the numbers
and the rest) are already in your reviews and are used freely here.

## Pronouns: I, you, he, she

| Chinese | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | I, me | |
| {你|nǐ} | you | to one person: friends, classmates, children, anyone your age |
| {您|nín} | you (polite) | to an older person, a teacher, a customer, a stranger |
| {他|tā} | he, him | |
| {她|tā} | she, her | |

These are **[[pronouns]]**, words that stand in for a person's name. Chinese pronouns never change
form: {我|wǒ} is both "I" and "me", {他|tā} both "he" and "him".

{他|tā} and {她|tā} sound exactly the same, *tā*. Only writing shows the difference: 他 has the
"person" radical 亻 on the left, 她 the "woman" radical 女. Writing used to make no difference at
all; 她 was coined about a hundred years ago to match "she" in European languages. When you
listen, the context tells you who is meant.

{您|nín} is {你|nǐ} with a heart (心) underneath. Use it for people you show respect to: a
teacher, an older person, someone you serve in a shop or office. Among friends and people your
age {你|nǐ} is normal, and {您|nín} would sound stiff. {您好|nín hǎo} is the polite form of
{你好|nǐ hǎo}.

## The basic sentence: A {是|shì} B

{是|shì} links two nouns, like English "am", "is", "are":

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — I'm a student.
{他|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — He's a teacher.
{您|nín}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。 — You're Teacher Wang.

{王|Wáng} is a common family name. The family name comes first, so {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī} is "Teacher
Wang", the normal way to address or talk about a teacher. Notice that there's no word for "a" or
"the", and that {是|shì} never changes: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}, {你|nǐ}{是|shì}, {他|tā}{是|shì}. Chinese verbs have
no endings for person or tense at all. That alone makes Chinese grammar much smaller than you
might fear.

In grammar terms, the **[[subject]]** is who or what the sentence is about ({我|wǒ}), and the
**[[predicate]]** is what is said about it ({是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}). {是|shì} is a **[[verb]]**; {学生|xué sheng}
and {老师|lǎo shī} are **[[nouns]]**, words for people and things. The order is the English one:
subject, verb, object.

## Saying "is not": {不|bú}{是|shì}

Put {不|bù} before the verb to make it negative. Before a fourth tone, {不|bù} is said and written
*bú*, so {不|bú}{是|shì} is *bú shì*:

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — I'm not a teacher.
{她|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}，{她|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — She isn't a student, she's a teacher.

{不|bù} always goes right before the word it negates, never at the end of the sentence.

## Names: {叫|jiào} and {什么|shén me}

{叫|jiào} means "to be called". It's the usual way to give your name:

{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。 — My name is Anna. (I am called Anna.)
{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。 — His name is Li Ming.

{安娜|Ān nà} is Anna in Chinese; {李明|Lǐ Míng} has the family name {李|Lǐ}. {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{安娜|Ān nà}
("I'm Anna") is fine too, especially when you introduce yourself to a group or answer the phone.

To ask someone's name, use {什么|shén me}, "what", and {名字|míng zi}, "name":

{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ — What's your name? (You are called what name?)
{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}？ — What's he called?

Here is the key rule of Chinese questions: **the question word stays where the answer goes**.
English moves "what" to the front; Chinese doesn't move anything. Ask the question, then answer
it by replacing {什么|shén me} (or {什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}) with the answer:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}**{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}**？ | {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}**{安娜|Ān nà}**。 |
| {她|tā}{是|shì}**{什么|shén me}**{老师|lǎo shī}？ (what kind of teacher?) | {她|tā}{是|shì}**{汉语|Hàn yǔ}**{老师|lǎo shī}。 (a Chinese teacher) |

{汉语|Hàn yǔ}, "Chinese", is a word from the next lesson. With a teacher or an older stranger,
{您|nín}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ is fine; the honors lesson on Chinese names shows a
still politer way to ask.

## Yes-or-no questions with {吗|ma}

Put {吗|ma} at the end of a statement and it becomes a yes-or-no question. Nothing else changes:

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — You're a student.
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{吗|ma}？ — Are you a student?

{吗|ma} is a **[[question particle]]**: a small word, always in the neutral tone, that turns a
sentence into a question. Never add it to a question that already has a question word:
{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ has no {吗|ma}.

Chinese has no single word for "yes" or "no". You answer with the verb of the question, alone or
in a full sentence:

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？ — Are you a teacher?
{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — Yes, I am (a teacher).
{不|bú}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — No, I'm a student.

## How are you? {很|hěn} and adjectives

{你好|nǐ hǎo} is a greeting, "hello". {你|nǐ}{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？ is a real question, "are you well?",
used with someone you haven't seen for a while or who might be unwell. It isn't the automatic
"how are you?" of English. The usual answer:

{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。 — I'm fine, thanks.

Look at what's missing: no {是|shì}. {好|hǎo} (good, well), {大|dà} (big) and {小|xiǎo} (small) are
**[[adjectives]]**, words that describe, and a Chinese adjective is a predicate by itself. ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{好|hǎo}~~
is wrong. Instead, an adjective in a plain statement normally takes {很|hěn} in front:

{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — I'm fine.
{中国|Zhōng guó}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 — China is big.

{很|hěn} is an **[[adverb]]**, a word placed before a verb or adjective to say how or how much. Its
dictionary meaning is "very", but here it's usually unstressed and means little: {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}
is "I'm fine", not "I'm very well". Without {很|hěn}, {我|wǒ}{好|hǎo} sounds like half of a contrast
("I'm fine, but..."). Stress {很|hěn} when you really mean "very". You'll meet more adjectives in
Module 3.

## Dialogue: the first class

Anna ({安娜|Ān nà}) and David ({大卫|Dà wèi}) are at their first Chinese class with Teacher Wang
({王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}).

```dialogue
# The first class
王老师: {你们|nǐ men}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。
= Hello, everyone! I'm Teacher Wang.
安娜: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, Teacher Wang!
王老师: {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= What's your name?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。
= My name is Anna.
王老师: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, are you a student?
安娜: {是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
= Yes, I'm a student.
王老师: {他|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}？{他|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？
= What's his name? Is he a teacher?
安娜: {不|bú}{是|shì}，{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}。
= No, he isn't a teacher. His name is David.
大卫: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, Teacher Wang!
王老师: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？
= David, how are you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。
= I'm fine, thank you.
```

Some things to notice. {你们|nǐ men}{好|hǎo} is "hello" to a group; {你们|nǐ men}, "you" plural,
is a word from the next lesson. {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{好|hǎo} is how students greet a teacher: name or
title + {好|hǎo}. David uses {您|nín} for his teacher; the teacher uses {你|nǐ} for her students.

## Introducing yourself

> {你好|nǐ hǎo}！
>
> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}，{不|bú}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。
>
> {谢谢|xiè xie}！

Hello! My name is Anna. I'm a student, not a teacher. Thank you! Put in your own name, written
in pinyin or in a Chinese name if you have one (the honors lesson on names helps you choose).

```speak
{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。
= Hello! My name is Anna.
{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= What's your name?
{您|nín}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？
= Are you a teacher?
{不|bú}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
= No, I'm a student.
{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。
= I'm fine, thank you.
{老师|lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, teacher!
```

## Pronunciation

- {什么|shén me}: *sh* is retroflex (tongue tip curled up), and the second syllable is in the
  **[[neutral tone]]**, short and light with no mark: *shén me*. The same goes for {名字|míng zi}, with
  *z* like the "ds" in "beds", and for {学生|xué sheng}, where the second syllable is light too.
- {是|shì} and {老师|lǎo shī}: the *-i* after *sh* isn't an "ee". It's a buzz with the tongue still
  curled back.
- {叫|jiào}: *j* is a soft "j" with the tongue flat behind the lower teeth; *iao* glides through
  i-a-o in one syllable.
- {您|nín} ends in *-n* (tongue at the top teeth), not *-ng*: *nín*, not *níng*.
- Two third tones in a row: the first becomes a second tone. This **[[tone sandhi]]** is never
  written, so {你好|nǐ hǎo} is said *ní hǎo* and {很好|hěn hǎo} is said *hén hǎo*. In {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}
  the {我|wǒ} is usually a short, low "half third" tone (in quick speech you may hear it rise too).
- {不|bù} changes to *bú* before a fourth tone. This course writes the change: {不|bú}{是|shì}.

In pinyin terms, a syllable is an **[[initial]]** (the consonant at the start: *sh*, *j*, *n*) and a
**[[final]]** (the rest: *-en*, *-iao*, *-in*), with a tone over the final.

## Characters
{=

The 13 characters of this lesson. 学 and 生 in {学生|xué sheng} are taught in the next lesson;
they have pinyin like everything else. The character sections always show the simplified forms,
with the traditional form beside each new character; with the Traditional switch on, the
tracing pads and notecards show the traditional forms.

| Character | Traditional | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 是 | same | to be; yes | shì | 日 | 9 | {是|shì}, {不|bú}{是|shì} |
| 他 | same | he, him | tā | 亻 | 5 | {他|tā}, {他们|tā men} (lesson 2) |
| 她 | same | she, her | tā | 女 | 6 | {她|tā}, {她们|tā men} (lesson 2) |
| 您 | same | you (polite) | nín | 心 | 11 | {您|nín}, {您好|nín hǎo} |
| 叫 | same | to be called; to call | jiào | 口 | 5 | {叫|jiào} |
| 什 | same | (part of "what") | shén | 亻 | 4 | {什么|shén me} |
| 么 | 麼 | (word ending) | me | 丿 | 3 | {什么|shén me}, {怎么|zěn me} (lesson 18) |
| 名 | same | name | míng | 口 | 6 | {名字|míng zi} |
| 字 | same | character, word | zì; zi in {名字|míng zi} | 子 | 6 | {名字|míng zi}, {汉字|hàn zì} (lesson 19) |
| 吗 | 嗎 | (question particle) | ma | 口 | 6 | {吗|ma} |
| 很 | same | very | hěn | 彳 | 9 | {很|hěn}, {很好|hěn hǎo} |
| 老 | same | old | lǎo | 老 | 6 | {老师|lǎo shī} |
| 师 | 師 | teacher, master | shī | 巾 | 6 | {老师|lǎo shī} |

The radicals are as the app's stroke data files them. Printed dictionaries mostly agree; 么 is
under 丿 in some and under 厶 in others.

### Radicals: 口, 亻 and 女

Most characters are built from smaller parts, called **[[components]]**. One component, the
**[[radical]]**, is the part a dictionary files the character under, and it often hints at the
meaning. Three radicals cover a lot of this course:

- **口 "mouth"** ({口|kǒu}, *kǒu*): 38 of the characters in this track are filed under it. Many
  are words of speaking or sound: {叫|jiào} (to call), {吗|ma} (a spoken particle). 名 is under
  口 too. On the left, 口 is drawn smaller and narrower: compare 口 with the 口 in 叫 and 吗.
- **亻 "person"** ({人|rén} standing at the side, called {单人旁|dān rén páng}, "single-person
  side"): 19 characters. It's the form 人 takes on the left of a character: {你|nǐ}, {他|tā},
  {什|shén}. Characters with 亻 are often about people.
- **女 "woman"** (*nǚ*): 13 characters, among them {好|hǎo} and {她|tā}, and many words for female
  relatives you'll meet in lesson 3.

Two other radicals here: 心 "heart" at the bottom of 您, and 子 "child" at the bottom of 字.

Memory notes (our own pictures, not the history of the characters):

- 您 is 你 with 心, heart, underneath: "you", said with feeling and respect.
- 名: at night (夕, *evening*) you can't see who's there, so you call out your name with your
  mouth (口). This is the traditional explanation found in old dictionaries; take it as a
  memory aid.
- 字: a child (子) under a roof (宀): children learn to write characters at home.
- 很 starts with 彳, "step", which has nothing to do with the meaning here.

### Stroke order

- 女 in 她: three strokes, the bent one first (like く: down to the left, then down to the right),
  then the left-falling stroke, then the horizontal. On the left side of a character the last
  stroke rises to the right instead of lying flat, to make room.
- 也 in 他 and 她: three strokes: the horizontal that turns down with a hook, the short vertical,
  then the long vertical that bends right with a hook at the end, written last.
- 是: the 日 on top first (4 strokes), then the long horizontal, then the vertical, the short
  horizontal, the left-falling and the right-falling strokes.
- 么: left-falling stroke, the bent stroke, then the dot.

```trace
是他她您叫什么
```

```trace
名字吗很老师
```

Write it: 是 他 她 叫 什 么 名 字 吗 很. These are characters the HSK expects learners to write
by hand by level 2. Write each three times from memory, on paper or the pad, then check.

=}

## Common mistakes

- {是|shì} before an adjective: ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}~~. Adjectives don't need {是|shì}: {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
- Moving the question word to the front: ~~{什么|shén me}{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}？~~ The question word stays where
  the answer goes: {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
- {吗|ma} on a question that already has {什么|shén me}: ~~{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}{吗|ma}？~~
- {不|bù} in the wrong place: ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{不|bù}{老师|lǎo shī}~~. It goes before the verb:
  {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。
- Answering "yes" with {好|hǎo}. {好|hǎo} agrees to a suggestion ("OK"); to answer
  {是|shì}{吗|ma}, use {是|shì} or {不|bú}{是|shì}.
- {你|nǐ} to a teacher you've just met. Use {您|nín}, or the title: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}。

## Key points

- A {是|shì} B: "A is B". {是|shì} never changes; negative {不|bú}{是|shì} (*bú* before the fourth tone).
- {叫|jiào} + name: "to be called". {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ — What's your name?
- Question words stay where the answer goes.
- {吗|ma} at the end makes a yes-or-no question; answer with the verb ({是|shì} / {不|bú}{是|shì}).
- Adjectives work without {是|shì} and usually take an unstressed {很|hěn}: {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
- {他|tā} and {她|tā} are both *tā*; {您|nín} is the polite "you".
- Third tone + third tone: the first is said as a second tone (*ní hǎo*), but written as a third.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Countries and languages: 哪国人, 也, 都, 呢
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 1 you said who you are with {是|shì} and {叫|jiào} and asked questions with {吗|ma} and
{什么|shén me}. Now you'll say where you're from and which languages you speak, talk about
groups of people ("we", "they", "all of us"), and say "me too". By the end you can hold a short
first conversation with a new classmate.

## We, you, they: the plural 们

Add {们|men} (neutral tone) to a pronoun for more than one person:

| One | More than one |
|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} I | {我们|wǒ men} we, us |
| {你|nǐ} you | {你们|nǐ men} you (plural) |
| {他|tā} he | {他们|tā men} they (men, or a mixed group) |
| {她|tā} she | {她们|tā men} they (all women) |

{们|men} is a **[[plural suffix]]**, and it's the only one Chinese has. It's used for people only.
A noun on its own can be one or many: {学生|xué sheng} is "a student" or "students", and context
decides. {们|men} can go after a noun for people when you mean a particular group,
{老师们|lǎo shī men} ("the teachers"), and {老师们|lǎo shī men}{好|hǎo}！ greets a room of teachers.
It's never used with a number: "three students" is {三|sān}{个|gè}{学生|xué sheng}, with no {们|men}
({个|gè} is lesson 3's word).

{他们|tā men} covers a group of men and also any mixed group; {她们|tā men} is for women only. Both
sound the same. {你们好|nǐ men hǎo}！ is "hello, everyone".

## Where are you from? 哪国人

Add {人|rén} (person) to the name of a country, and you have the nationality:

| Country | Person | Language |
|---|---|---|
| {中国|Zhōng guó} China | {中国人|Zhōng guó rén} Chinese | {汉语|Hàn yǔ}, {中文|Zhōng wén} Chinese |
| {美国|Měi guó} the US | {美国人|Měi guó rén} American | {英语|Yīng yǔ} English |
| {英国|Yīng guó} the UK | {英国人|Yīng guó rén} British | {英语|Yīng yǔ} English |
| {加拿大|Jiā ná dà} Canada | {加拿大人|Jiā ná dà rén} Canadian | {英语|Yīng yǔ}, {法语|Fǎ yǔ} French |
| {澳大利亚|Ào dà lì yà} Australia | {澳大利亚人|Ào dà lì yà rén} Australian | {英语|Yīng yǔ} |
| {日本|Rì běn} Japan | {日本人|Rì běn rén} Japanese | {日语|Rì yǔ} Japanese |
| {德国|Dé guó} Germany | {德国人|Dé guó rén} German | {德语|Dé yǔ} German |

Only {中国|Zhōng guó}, {国|guó} and the languages {汉语|Hàn yǔ} and {中文|Zhōng wén} are words of
this course; the other names are here so you can talk about yourself. Many end in {国|guó},
"country". Others are sound loans: {加拿大|Jiā ná dà} is "Canada" said with Chinese syllables.

To ask, use {哪|nǎ}, "which": {哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}, "which-country person":

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}？ — Where are you from? (What nationality are you?)
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。 — I'm American.

The question word stays where the answer goes, as in lesson 1: {哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén} is replaced
by {美国人|Měi guó rén}. Be careful with the tones: {哪|nǎ} (third tone) asks "which", while
{那|nà} (fourth tone), which you'll meet in lesson 3, points: "that".

## Languages: 汉语 and 中文

Many language names end in {语|yǔ}, "language": {汉语|Hàn yǔ}, {英语|Yīng yǔ}, {日语|Rì yǔ}. Chinese
has two everyday words for its own language:

- {汉语|Hàn yǔ}, "the language of the Han", the majority people of China. It's the usual word in
  teaching: textbooks, classes and the HSK ("{汉语|Hàn yǔ} Proficiency Test").
- {中文|Zhōng wén}, "Chinese writing", used for the language in general and especially for written
  Chinese: a menu or a website "in Chinese", the language setting on your phone.

In conversation the two are interchangeable: {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} and
{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{中文|Zhōng wén} both mean "I speak Chinese". The standard spoken language you're
learning, Mandarin, is called {普通话|pǔ tōng huà} ("the common speech") in mainland China.

## Speaking languages: 说 and 会

{说|shuō} means "to speak" or "to say": {说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}, to speak Chinese.

{会|huì} before a verb means "can", for a skill you've learned: speaking a language, swimming,
driving.

{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}。 — I can speak English.
{他|tā}{不|bú}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — He can't speak Chinese.
{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？ — Can you speak Chinese? — {会|huì}。 Yes. / {不|bú}{会|huì}。 No.

As with {是|shì}, you answer with the verb: {会|huì} or {不|bú}{会|huì} (bú, before the fourth tone
of huì). Lesson 19 compares {会|huì} with the other two words for "can".

## Follow-up questions with 呢

After you've said something about yourself, {呢|ne} turns the same question back on someone
else: "and you?", "what about...?"

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{加拿大人|Jiā ná dà rén}，{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？ — I'm Canadian. And you?
{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}。{他|tā}{呢|ne}？ — I speak English. What about him?

{呢|ne} is another **[[question particle]]**, in the neutral tone like {吗|ma}. The difference: {吗|ma}
turns a whole statement into a yes-or-no question; {呢|ne} goes after just a noun or pronoun and
means "and the same question about this one?" It needs the earlier sentence to make sense.

## Also and all: 也 and 都

{也|yě}, "also, too", and {都|dōu}, "all, both", are adverbs, so they go **after the subject and
before the verb**, never at the end like English "too":

{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — I'm a student too.
{她|tā}{也|yě}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — She can speak Chinese too.
{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。 — We're all Americans. (or: We're both Americans.)
{他们|tā men}{都|dōu}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}。 — They can all speak English.

{都|dōu} sums up the plural subject before it, so the subject must come first: never
~~{都|dōu}{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}…~~ for "all of us are...". With two people it means "both".

Together, the order is always {也|yě}{都|dōu}, never {都|dōu}{也|yě}:

{我们|wǒ men}{也|yě}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — We're all students too.

With a negative, the adverbs still come first, and {不|bù} sits right before the verb:

{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{不|bú}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — I'm not a teacher either.
{他们|tā men}{都|dōu}{不|bú}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — None of them can speak Chinese.

English uses "either" and "none" here; Chinese keeps {也|yě} and {都|dōu}.

## Dialogue: a new classmate

Anna meets Li Ming ({李明|Lǐ Míng}), a Chinese student, at a language exchange. David is with her.

```dialogue
# At the language exchange
李明: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= Hello! My name is Li Ming. What's your name?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。
= My name is Anna.
李明: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}？
= Anna, where are you from?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm American. And you?
李明: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{中国人|Zhōng guó rén}。{他|tā}{呢|ne}？{他|tā}{也|yě}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}{吗|ma}？
= I'm Chinese. And him? Is he American too?
安娜: {不|bú}{是|shì}，{他|tā}{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}。{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}。
= No, he's British. His name is David.
李明: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？
= David, can you speak Chinese?
大卫: {会|huì}！{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{学生|xué sheng}。
= Yes! We're both students of Chinese.
李明: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}。
= I'm a student too. I can speak English.
大卫: {太好了|tài hǎo le}！
= Great!
```

Notice David's answer: {会|huì}！ alone is "Yes (I can)!" {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{学生|xué sheng} is "a student of
Chinese": the describing word comes first. {太好了|tài hǎo le}, "great!", is a set phrase you'll
take apart in lesson 12.

## Introducing yourself, part two

> {你们好|nǐ men hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}，{也|yě}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。{谢谢|xiè xie}！

Hello, everyone! My name is David. I'm British. I speak English, and I speak Chinese too. I'm a
student. Thank you! Notice the second sentence: the subject isn't repeated after the comma, and
{也|yě} still comes right before the verb.

```speak
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}？
= Where are you from?
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}，{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm American. And you?
{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？
= Can you speak Chinese?
{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
= I'm a student too.
{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{中文|Zhōng wén}。
= We can all speak Chinese.
{你们好|nǐ men hǎo}！
= Hello, everyone!
```

## Pronunciation

- {说|shuō}: *sh* (retroflex) + *uo*, a round "w-o". Don't let it slide into "shoe".
- {会|huì}: pinyin *ui* is short for *uei*, so it sounds like "hway", with the tone mark on the
  *i*.
- {都|dōu}: *ou* as in "dough", high and level.
- {汉语|Hàn yǔ}: a fourth tone, then a third. *yu* is the ü sound (say "ee" with rounded lips);
  after *y*, *j*, *q* and *x* the dots aren't written.
- {我|wǒ}{也|yě}: two third tones, so the first rises: *wó yě*. Longer runs of third tones change
  according to how the words group; for now, say each word clearly and let listening do the rest.
- {哪|nǎ} vs {那|nà}: dip and rise for "which", a short fall for "that".
- {们|men} and {呢|ne} are in the neutral tone: short, light, no mark.


## Characters
{=

| Character | Traditional | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 学 | 學 | to study, learning | xué | 子 | 8 | {学生|xué sheng}, {大学|dà xué} (lesson 5) |
| 生 | same | life, to be born | shēng; sheng in {学生|xué sheng} | 生 | 5 | {学生|xué sheng}, {医生|yī shēng} (lesson 5) |
| 们 | 們 | (plural for people) | men | 亻 | 5 | {我们|wǒ men}, {你们|nǐ men}, {他们|tā men} |
| 国 | 國 | country | guó | 囗 | 8 | {国|guó}, {中国|Zhōng guó} |
| 哪 | same | which | nǎ | 口 | 9 | {哪|nǎ}, {哪儿|nǎr} (lesson 9) |
| 汉 | 漢 | Han (Chinese) | hàn | 氵 | 5 | {汉语|Hàn yǔ}, {汉字|hàn zì} (lesson 19) |
| 语 | 語 | language | yǔ | 讠 | 9 | {汉语|Hàn yǔ} |
| 文 | same | writing, script | wén | 文 | 4 | {中文|Zhōng wén} |
| 说 | 說 | to speak, to say | shuō | 讠 | 9 | {说|shuō}, {说话|shuō huà} (lesson 10) |
| 会 | 會 | can (a skill) | huì | 人 | 6 | {会|huì} |
| 呢 | same | (question particle) | ne | 口 | 8 | {呢|ne} |
| 也 | same | also, too | yě | 乚 | 3 | {也|yě} |
| 都 | same | all, both | dōu | 阝 | 10 | {都|dōu} |

Two filing notes: 也 is under 乚, which many dictionaries treat as a form of 乙; 会 is under 人,
the roof on top.

### Radicals: 氵, 讠 and 心

- **氵 "water"** ({三点水|sān diǎn shuǐ}, "three drops of water"): the form {水|shuǐ} (water) takes on
  the left. 19 characters of this track are filed under it, many of them words for water, liquids and rivers. 汉
  has it because it began as the name of a river, the Han; the Han dynasty took its name from that
  region, and "Han" came to mean the Chinese people and their language. 没 in {没关系|méi guān xi}
  has it too (lesson 3).
- **讠 "speech"** ({言字旁|yán zì páng}, "the side form of 言"): the simplified side form of
  {言|yán}, "speech", which keeps its full shape 訁 in traditional characters (說, 語). 19 characters,
  most of them about speaking and language: {语|yǔ}, {说|shuō}, and 谢 in {谢谢|xiè xie}. It has two
  strokes: a dot, then a horizontal that turns down and flicks up.
- **心 "heart"** ({心|xīn}): 13 characters of this track are filed under it, among them {您|nín}
  from lesson 1 and {想|xiǎng} (to want, to think) in lesson 9, both with 心 at the bottom. Many are about thinking and feeling. On the
  left it takes another shape, 忄, taught in lesson 21.

Memory notes:

- 们 is 亻 (person) + 门 ({门|mén}, door). 门 gives the sound *men*: a true sound clue. You'll see
  this "meaning part + sound part" pattern in most characters.
- 哪 is 口 + {那|nà}: "that", asked with the mouth, becomes "which?". 那 gives the sound.
- 语 is 讠 (speech) + 吾 (*wú*, an old word for "I"), which once gave the sound.
- 呢 is 口 + 尼 (*ní*), the sound part.
- 国: in the simplified form, 玉 ({玉|yù}, jade) inside an enclosure 囗: a treasure inside the
  borders. The traditional form, 國, has 或 inside instead.
- 生: the oldest forms show a plant growing out of the ground, hence "life, to be born". A
  {学生|xué sheng} is "one who learns" and a {医生|yī shēng} (lesson 5) "one who heals".

### Stroke order

- 国: "close the box last". Write the left side and the top-and-right side of 囗 first, then 玉
  inside (王, then the dot), and the bottom stroke of 囗 last. The same rule applies to 四 and 日.
- 学: the three short strokes at the top first (dot, dot, left-falling), then the cover 冖, then
  子.
- 文: dot, horizontal, left-falling, right-falling.
- 生: left-falling stroke, horizontal, horizontal, vertical, and the long bottom horizontal last.
- 都: the left part 者 first, then 阝 on the right: a turning stroke with a curved hook, then a
  vertical.

```trace
学生们国哪汉语
```

```trace
文说会呢也都
```

Write it: 学 生 们 国 汉 语 文 说 会 也. Three times each from memory, then check.

## Common mistakes

- {也|yě} at the end, as in English: ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{也|yě}~~. It goes before the
  verb: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
- {都|dōu} before the subject: ~~{都|dōu}{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}~~. Subject first:
  {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
- {都|dōu}{也|yě} instead of {也|yě}{都|dōu}.
- {们|men} after a number or for things: ~~{三|sān}{个|gè}{学生|xué sheng}{们|men}~~.
- {吗|ma} and {呢|ne} mixed up: {你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？ alone means "and you?"; ~~{你|nǐ}{吗|ma}？~~ means nothing.
- {哪|nǎ} said with a fourth tone, which turns "which" into "that".
- {会|huì} left out: {我|wǒ}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} is "I speak Chinese" (now, or as a habit); "I can
  speak Chinese" is {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}. In everyday talk the two are close.

## Key points

- {们|men} makes pronouns (and people) plural; never after a number, never for things.
- Country + {人|rén} = nationality. {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}？ asks where someone is from.
- {汉语|Hàn yǔ} and {中文|Zhōng wén} both mean Chinese; {中文|Zhōng wén} leans to the written language.
- {会|huì} + verb: can (a learned skill). Answer {会|huì} / {不|bú}{会|huì}.
- {呢|ne} after a noun or pronoun: "and you?", "what about...?"
- {也|yě} and {都|dōu} go after the subject, before the verb (and before {不|bù}); together {也|yě}{都|dōu}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Family: 有, 没有, 的, 几 and 个
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say who you are, where you're from and what you speak. This lesson is about the
people around you: your family, and how many brothers and sisters you have. You'll learn the
verb {有|yǒu} (to have) and its negative, {的|de} for "my" and "the teacher's", the words for
"this" and "that", {和|hé} for "and", and your first **[[measure word]]**, {个|gè}, which Chinese
needs whenever it counts.

## Having: 有 and 没有

{有|yǒu} means "to have":

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}。 — I have an older brother.
{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{中文|Zhōng wén}{名字|míng zi}。 — She has a Chinese name.

The negative of {有|yǒu} is {没有|méi yǒu}, **never** ~~{不|bù}{有|yǒu}~~. This is the one verb that
{不|bù} can't negate:

{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}。 — I don't have an older sister.
{他|tā}{没有|méi yǒu}{中文|Zhōng wén}{名字|míng zi}。 — He doesn't have a Chinese name.

Questions work as before: add {吗|ma}, and answer with the verb.

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}{吗|ma}？ — Do you have an older brother?
{有|yǒu}。 — Yes. / {没有|méi yǒu}。 — No.

{有|yǒu} also means "there is, there are" ({家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}…, "at home there is..."), which
lesson 17 teaches. And {没有|méi yǒu} has a second job, "didn't", in lesson 25.

## Family words

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {爸爸|bà ba} | dad, father |
| {妈妈|mā ma} | mum, mother |
| {哥哥|gē ge} | older brother |
| {姐姐|jiě jie} | older sister |
| {家|jiā} | home; family |
| {家人|jiā rén} | family members, (one's) family |

Chinese has no single everyday word for "brother" or "sister": you always say whether they're
older or younger. Younger brothers and sisters, {弟弟|dì di} and {妹妹|mèi mei}, come in the next
lesson. Each of these words doubles one character, and the second syllable is in the neutral
tone: *bàba, māma, gēge, jiějie*.

{家|jiā} is both the place, "home", and the people, "family": {我|wǒ}{家|jiā} is "my home" or "my
family". {家人|jiā rén} is the members of a family, the people: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{家人|jiā rén}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}
(my family are all well).

## Whose? 的

{的|de} after a person or pronoun shows who something belongs to, like English "'s" or "my,
your":

| | |
|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi} | my name |
| {你|nǐ}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī} | your teacher |
| {老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{名字|míng zi} | the teacher's name |
| {安娜|Ān nà}{的|de}{家人|jiā rén} | Anna's family |

This is **[[possessive 的]]**. {的|de} is in the neutral tone, and the owner always comes first, the
thing owned last. {我|wǒ}{的|de} alone means "mine": {这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de} (this is mine).

### When 的 is dropped

With family members, home, and people or groups you belong to, {的|de} is usually left out after a
pronoun:

{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma} — my mum
{你|nǐ}{哥哥|gē ge} — your older brother
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā} — my home, my family
{我们|wǒ men}{老师|lǎo shī} — our teacher

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{妈妈|mā ma} isn't wrong, but it sounds heavier, as if you were stressing "*my* mother".
With things, keep {的|de}: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}, never ~~{我|wǒ}{名字|míng zi}~~ in careful
speech.

## This and that: 这 and 那

{这|zhè} is "this" and {那|nà} is "that". With {是|shì} they introduce or point out people and things:

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}。 — This is my mum.
{那|nà}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — That's our teacher.
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}？ — What's this?

{这|zhè}{是|shì}… is how you introduce people: there's no separate phrase like "let me introduce".
Mind the tones: {那|nà} (fourth, "that") and {哪|nǎ} (third, "which") from lesson 2. In speech you
may also hear *zhèi* and *nèi* for 这 and 那, especially before a measure word; you'll meet that
in lesson 14.

## Counting people and things: 个

In English you say "three brothers". In Chinese a number can't go straight before a noun: a
**[[measure word]]** must come between them. The general one, used for people and many things, is
{个|gè}:

| Number | Measure word | Noun | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {一|yí} | {个|gè} | {哥哥|gē ge} | one older brother |
| {三|sān} | {个|gè} | {姐姐|jiě jie} | three older sisters |
| {五|wǔ} | {个|gè} | {人|rén} | five people |
| {十|shí} | {个|gè} | {学生|xué sheng} | ten students |

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}。 — I have one older brother.
{我们|wǒ men}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{五|wǔ}{个|gè}{人|rén}。 — There are five of us in my family.

Without {个|gè}, ~~{三|sān}{姐姐|jiě jie}~~ is wrong for "three older sisters" (in a family it would be heard as "third sister", a way of naming siblings by birth order). Other measure words go with particular
kinds of things (books, clothes, animals) and come in later lessons; {个|gè} is always a safe
first choice for people.

Two things about the sound:

- {一|yī} changes to *yí* before {个|gè}, a fourth tone: {一|yí}{个|gè}. You'll often hear {个|gè} itself
  light, almost neutral, in quick speech.
- "Two people" uses a special word for two, {两|liǎng}: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}, never 二个. That's the
  next lesson. Until then, count with one and three to ten.

## How many? 几

{几|jǐ} asks "how many?" when you expect a small number, roughly under ten. Like every number, it
needs a measure word:

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{姐姐|jiě jie}？ — How many older sisters do you have?
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{姐姐|jiě jie}。 — I have one.
{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}？ — How many people are there in your family?

The question word stays where the answer goes: {几|jǐ}{个|gè} becomes {一|yí}{个|gè} or {四|sì}{个|gè}.
No {吗|ma} is added. For large numbers you'll use {多少|duō shao} (lesson 4), and for family size
the next lesson shows a special measure word, {口|kǒu}.

## And: 和

{和|hé} joins nouns and pronouns: "A and B".

{爸爸|bà ba}{和|hé}{妈妈|mā ma} — Dad and Mum
{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge} — my brother and I
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{姐姐|jiě jie}。 — I have an older brother and an older sister.

With three or more, separate them with the enumeration comma 、 and put {和|hé} before the last:
{爸爸|bà ba}、{妈妈|mā ma}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}.

**{和|hé} does not join sentences or verbs.** English "and" can join anything; {和|hé} can't:

- ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。~~ Use a comma:
  {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}，{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — I'm a student and my brother is a
  teacher.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}{和|hé}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。~~ Use {也|yě}:
  {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}，{也|yě}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 (Or join just the nouns:
  {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}{和|hé}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。)

When {和|hé} joins two subjects, {都|dōu} often follows: {爸爸|bà ba}{和|hé}{妈妈|mā ma}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}
(Dad and Mum are both teachers).

## Dialogue: a family photo

Li Ming looks at a photo on Anna's phone.

```dialogue
# A family photo
李明: {安娜|Ān nà}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{家人|jiā rén}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, is this your family?
安娜: {是|shì}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}。
= Yes. This is my dad, and this is my mum.
李明: {那|nà}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{吗|ma}？
= Is that your older sister?
安娜: {是|shì}，{她|tā}{叫|jiào}{莉莉|Lì lì}。{她|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。
= Yes, her name is Lily. She's a teacher.
李明: {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}{吗|ma}？
= Do you have an older brother?
安娜: {有|yǒu}，{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}。{他|tā}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
= Yes, I have one older brother. He's a student.
李明: {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}？
= How many people are there in your family?
安娜: {五|wǔ}{个|gè}：{爸爸|bà ba}、{妈妈|mā ma}、{姐姐|jiě jie}、{哥哥|gē ge}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= Five: Dad, Mum, my sister, my brother and me. And you?
李明: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}，{也|yě}{没有|méi yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{三|sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}：{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}。
= I don't have an older brother or an older sister. There are three of us: my dad, my mum and me.
```

Notice how Anna answers {几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}？ with just {五|wǔ}{个|gè}: the noun can be dropped, but the
measure word stays. And Li Ming says {爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma} as one pair, with no 、 or {和|hé} between them: for
"Mum and Dad" that's normal. {莉莉|Lì lì} is a Chinese name chosen for Lily.

## My family

> {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{四|sì}{个|gè}{人|rén}：{爸爸|bà ba}、{妈妈|mā ma}、{哥哥|gē ge}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{也|yě}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}。

There are four people in my family: Dad, Mum, my older brother and me. My dad is a teacher, and
my mum is a teacher too. My brother is a student. I don't have an older sister. Make your own
version: it uses every pattern in this lesson.

```speak
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}。
= This is my mum.
{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}{吗|ma}？
= Do you have an older sister?
{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}。
= I don't have an older brother.
{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}？
= How many people are there in your family?
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{姐姐|jiě jie}。
= I have an older brother and an older sister.
{那|nà}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}。
= That's the teacher's name.
```

## Pronunciation

- {有|yǒu} and {几|jǐ} are third tones. Before another third tone they rise: {有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè} is
  said *yóu jǐ gè*, and {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu} is said *wó yǒu*.
- {没有|méi yǒu}: *méi* rises, *yǒu* dips. Don't say "may-you"; *ou* is as in "dough".
- {这|zhè}: *zh* is retroflex, like "j" with the tongue curled back; *e* is the "uh" sound.
- {和|hé}: the same "uh" vowel, rising.
- {姐姐|jiě jie}: *ie* is "yeh". The first syllable dips, the second is light.
- {爸爸|bà ba} and {妈妈|mā ma} sound like the first words babies say. The tones still matter:
  {妈|mā} is high and level, {爸|bà} falls.


## Characters
{=

| Character | Traditional | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 有 | same | to have; there is | yǒu | 月 | 6 | {有|yǒu}, {没有|méi yǒu} |
| 没 | 沒 | not (have) | méi | 氵 | 7 | {没有|méi yǒu}, {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 的 | same | (possessive particle) | de | 白 | 8 | {的|de}, {我|wǒ}{的|de} (my, mine) |
| 这 | 這 | this | zhè | 辶 | 7 | {这|zhè}, {这个|zhè ge} (lesson 14) |
| 那 | same | that | nà | 阝 | 6 | {那|nà}, {那个|nà ge} (lesson 14) |
| 和 | same | and | hé | 口 | 8 | {和|hé} |
| 家 | same | home, family | jiā | 宀 | 10 | {家|jiā}, {家人|jiā rén}, {大家|dà jiā} (lesson 23) |
| 爸 | same | dad | bà; ba | 父 | 8 | {爸爸|bà ba} |
| 妈 | 媽 | mum | mā; ma | 女 | 6 | {妈妈|mā ma} |
| 哥 | same | older brother | gē; ge | 口 | 10 | {哥哥|gē ge} |
| 姐 | same | older sister | jiě; jie | 女 | 8 | {姐姐|jiě jie} |
| 几 | 幾 | how many; a few | jǐ | 几 | 2 | {几|jǐ} |
| 个 | 個 | (general measure word) | gè | 丨 | 3 | {个|gè}, {一|yí}{个|gè} |

The second syllable of the family words is neutral, so 爸, 妈, 哥 and 姐 show both readings. Filing
notes: 个 is under 丨 here, but many dictionaries put it under 人; 和 is under 口 here and under 禾 in
some modern dictionaries. 有 looks as if it had 月 "moon" at the bottom, and is filed there, but
that part was once a different element, usually explained as 肉 "meat" (a hand holding meat);
lesson 17 shows how the "meat" form ⺼ differs from 月.

### Radicals: 辶, 日 and 宀

- **辶 "walking"** ({走之|zǒu zhī}): 16 characters, many about movement and roads: 这, and later
  {边|biān} (side), {道|dào} (road, in {知道|zhī dào}) and {还|hái} (still). It's three strokes: a dot,
  a zigzag, then a long flat sweep. **It's written last**, after the part it carries: in 这, write
  文 first, then 辶 underneath it.
- **日 "sun"** ({日|rì}): 12 characters, many about light and time: {是|shì} (lesson 1) has it on
  top, and {明天|míng tiān} (tomorrow), {早|zǎo} (early) and {时间|shí jiān} (time) come in Module 2. Don't
  confuse it with 目 "eye" (one more stroke inside) or the wider, flatter 曰.
- **宀 "roof"** ({宝盖|bǎo gài}, "treasure cover"): 12 characters, often about houses: {家|jiā},
  and {字|zì} from lesson 1. Three strokes: a dot, a short vertical, and a horizontal that turns
  down with a hook.

Other radicals in this lesson: 父 "father" on top of 爸; 白 "white" on the left of 的; 阝 on the
right of 那 (taught in lesson 4); 氵 in 没; and 女 again in 妈 and 姐.

Memory notes (true sound clues, plus our own pictures):

- 妈 is 女 (woman) + 马 ({马|mǎ}, horse), which gives the sound *ma*. 姐 is 女 + 且 (*qiě*, the sound
  part). 爸 is 父 (father) + 巴 (*bā*), the sound. Meaning on one side, sound on the other: you'll
  see this again and again.
- 哥 is 可 stacked on 可: two of the same, like the doubled word {哥哥|gē ge}.
- 家: a roof (宀) over 豕, an old character for "pig". The traditional explanation is a home where
  the pigs are kept under the same roof; take it as a memory aid.
- 这: something "this" close enough to walk (辶) to.
- 个: a person (人) with a stick (丨) to count with.

### Stroke order

- 这: 文 first (dot, horizontal, left-falling, right-falling), then 辶 last: dot, zigzag, sweep.
- 那: the left part first, then 阝: a turning stroke with a curved hook, then the vertical.
- 几: just two strokes: the left-falling stroke, then the horizontal-turn-curve with a hook.
- 个: 人 first (left-falling, then the dot-like right stroke), then the vertical.
- 有: the horizontal first, then the long left-falling stroke, then 月 inside.
- 家: 宀 first, then 豕 from the top down.

```trace
有没的这那和家
```

```trace
爸妈哥姐几个
```

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{有|yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}~~: {有|yǒu} takes {没|méi}: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{姐姐|jiě jie}。
- Counting without a measure word: ~~{三|sān}{姐姐|jiě jie}~~ → {三|sān}{个|gè}{姐姐|jiě jie}.
- {几|jǐ} without a measure word: ~~{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{哥哥|gē ge}？~~ → {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}？
- English order with {的|de}: the owner comes first: {老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}, not {名字|míng zi}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}
  ("the name's teacher").
- {和|hé} between sentences or verbs. Use a comma or {也|yě}.
- 二个 for "two". Two before a measure word is {两|liǎng}: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}.
- "Brother" without older or younger: Chinese always says which.

## Key points

- {有|yǒu}: to have. Negative {没有|méi yǒu}, never 不有. Answer {有|yǒu} / {没有|méi yǒu}.
- {的|de}: owner + {的|de} + thing ({老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}); dropped with family and home
  ({我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}, {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}).
- {这|zhè}{是|shì}… / {那|nà}{是|shì}…: this is / that is; the way to introduce someone.
- Number + measure word + noun: {一|yí}{个|gè}{哥哥|gē ge}. {个|gè} is the general measure word.
- {几|jǐ} + measure word asks "how many?" for small numbers.
- {和|hé} joins nouns only, never sentences or verbs.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, age and 两
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The pinyin course took you from {一|yī} to {九十九|jiǔ shí jiǔ}. This lesson goes up to 9,999,
with zero inside numbers, and shows the special word for "two" that Chinese uses when it counts
things. With numbers in hand you can say how old people are, ask about ages politely, ask "how
many?" for any number, and finish your family: younger brothers and sisters, sons, daughters and
children.

## Numbers to 99: a reminder

Chinese numbers are built the way you'd write them: tens, then ones.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 {十一|shí yī} | 12 {十二|shí èr} | 20 {二十|èr shí} | 21 {二十一|èr shí yī} |
| 35 {三十五|sān shí wǔ} | 68 {六十八|liù shí bā} | 90 {九十|jiǔ shí} | 99 {九十九|jiǔ shí jiǔ} |

{十|shí} is "ten", {二十|èr shí} "two tens". In these numbers each character is its own
**[[numeral]]**, a number word; this course writes them as one word.

## Hundreds and thousands: 百 and 千

{百|bǎi} is "hundred" and {千|qiān} "thousand". Read the number from the biggest place down, just
as you'd say "three thousand four hundred and fifty-six", but without "and":

| Number | Chinese |
|---|---|
| 100 | {一百|yì bǎi} |
| 345 | {三百四十五|sān bǎi sì shí wǔ} |
| 999 | {九百九十九|jiǔ bǎi jiǔ shí jiǔ} |
| 1,000 | {一千|yì qiān} |
| 3,456 | {三千四百五十六|sān qiān sì bǎi wǔ shí liù} |
| 9,999 | {九千九百九十九|jiǔ qiān jiǔ bǎi jiǔ shí jiǔ} |

Three details:

- **Say the "one".** 100 is {一百|yì bǎi}, "one hundred", never just {百|bǎi}. And {一|yī} changes its
  tone before {百|bǎi} and {千|qiān}, as before any third or first tone: *yì bǎi*, *yì qiān*. At the end
  of a number it stays *yī*: {十一|shí yī}, {一百零一|yì bǎi líng yī}.
- **Ten after a hundred is "one ten".** 110 is {一百一十|yì bǎi yī shí}, not 一百十. On its own, ten is
  simply {十|shí}.
- **A round number at the end can be shortened in speech**: {一百五|yì bǎi wǔ} is 150 and
  {两千三|liǎng qiān sān} 2,300, because the place is understood. Write the full form when you aren't
  sure: {一百五十|yì bǎi wǔ shí}.

Big numbers above 9,999 count in ten thousands, a different system from English. That's for
HSK 2.

## Zero inside a number: 零

{零|líng} is zero. Inside a number it fills an empty place, and you say it **once**, however many
zeros there are in a row:

| Number | Chinese | |
|---|---|---|
| 105 | {一百零五|yì bǎi líng wǔ} | one hundred, zero, five |
| 1,005 | {一千零五|yì qiān líng wǔ} | only one 零 for two empty places |
| 1,050 | {一千零五十|yì qiān líng wǔ shí} | |
| 2,026 | {两千零二十六|liǎng qiān líng èr shí liù} | |
| 1,500 | {一千五百|yì qiān wǔ bǎi} | zeros at the end aren't said |

Note that 1,005 and 1,050 both have one {零|líng}; the words after it tell them apart. When a
number is read digit by digit (a year, a phone number, a room), 0 is also {零|líng}, but those come
in Module 2.

## Two: 二 or 两?

Chinese has two words for "two":

- {二|èr} for counting and inside numbers: {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān}…; {十二|shí èr}, {二十|èr shí},
  {一百零二|yì bǎi líng èr}. Also for "second" later on.
- {两|liǎng} before a measure word, when you count things or people: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén} (two
  people), {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{妹妹|mèi mei} (two younger sisters). Never ~~二个~~.

Before {百|bǎi} you'll hear both {二百|èr bǎi} and {两百|liǎng bǎi}; before {千|qiān}, {两千|liǎng qiān} is the
usual one. In 12, 22 or 102 the last digit is always {二|èr}: {十二|shí èr}{个|gè}{人|rén}, twelve people.

## How old? Age with 岁

Age is said with {岁|suì}, "years old", a measure word for years of age:

{我|wǒ}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。 — I'm twenty.
{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{八|bā}{岁|suì}。 — My younger sister is eight.
{我|wǒ}{女儿|nǚ ér}{两|liǎng}{岁|suì}。 — My daughter is two.

Look at what's missing: {是|shì}. A number of years is enough to be the predicate. This is a
noun-predicate sentence, like the ones for dates and prices you'll meet later. In the negative,
{是|shì} comes back: {他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}，{他|tā}{十九|shí jiǔ}{岁|suì}。 (He isn't 20, he's 19.)
And "two years old" uses {两|liǎng}, because {岁|suì} is a measure word; 12 is still {十二|shí èr}{岁|suì}.

### Asking someone's age: 几岁 and 多大

Chinese asks children and adults differently:

| Ask | Who | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {几岁|jǐ suì} | a child (roughly under ten) | {你|nǐ}{几岁|jǐ suì}{了|le}？ — How old are you? |
| {多大|duō dà} | a young adult, a classmate, a colleague | {你|nǐ}{多大|duō dà}？ — How old are you? |

{几|jǐ} expects a small number, so {几岁|jǐ suì} suits a child; asked of an adult it sounds as if you
took them for a child. {多|duō} before an adjective means "how": {多大|duō dà} is "how big", so "how
old". The {了|le} often added for children makes it sound friendly; you'll learn that word in
lesson 20. With older people, asking age is less common; the polite form is
{您|nín}{多大|duō dà}{年纪|nián jì}？ ({年纪|nián jì}, "age", a word for later levels).

## How many? 多少 and 几

You know {几|jǐ} from lesson 3. Its partner is {多少|duō shao}, "how many, how much", literally
"many-few" (the second syllable is neutral):

| | {几|jǐ} | {多少|duō shao} |
|---|---|---|
| Expected number | small, under about ten | any number |
| Measure word | always: {几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén} | optional: {多少|duō shao}{人|rén} or {多少|duō shao}{个|gè}{人|rén} |

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}？ — How many children do you have?
{中国|Zhōng guó}{有|yǒu}{多少|duō shao}{人|rén}？ — How many people does China have?

{多|duō} on its own means "many, much". It usually takes {很|hěn}: {很多|hěn duō}{人|rén}, lots of people.

## Children and the rest of the family

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {弟弟|dì di} | younger brother |
| {妹妹|mèi mei} | younger sister |
| {儿子|ér zi} | son |
| {女儿|nǚ ér} | daughter |
| {孩子|hái zi} | child; one's child (son or daughter) |

With {哥哥|gē ge} and {姐姐|jiě jie} from lesson 3 you have all four siblings. {孩子|hái zi} is both "a
child" in general and "one's own child": {您|nín}{有|yǒu}{孩子|hái zi}{吗|ma}？ (Do you have children?)

### Family size: 口

To say how many people are in a family, Chinese uses {口|kǒu}, "mouth", as the measure word: the
people who eat at one table.

{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}？ — How many people are there in your family?
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{五|wǔ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}。 — There are five of us.

For people, {口|kǒu} is used only for this, the number of people in a household. For anyone else
(students, friends, children) use {个|gè}: {三|sān}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}, never 三口孩子. {几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}, as in lesson 3, is
fine too and more casual.

## Dialogue: Teacher Wang's children

After class, David meets Teacher Wang with her two children.

```dialogue
# After class
大卫: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{您|nín}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}{吗|ma}？
= Teacher Wang, are these your children?
王老师: {是|shì}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{女儿|nǚ ér}，{那|nà}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{儿子|ér zi}。
= Yes. This is my daughter, and that's my son.
大卫: {您|nín}{女儿|nǚ ér}{几岁|jǐ suì}？
= How old is your daughter?
王老师: {她|tā}{六|liù}{岁|suì}，{我|wǒ}{儿子|ér zi}{九|jiǔ}{岁|suì}。{大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{多大|duō dà}？
= She's six, and my son is nine. David, how old are you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。
= I'm twenty.
王老师: {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}？
= How many people are there in your family?
大卫: {六|liù}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}。{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{弟弟|dì di}{和|hé}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{妹妹|mèi mei}。
= Six. I have a younger brother and two younger sisters.
王老师: {他们|tā men}{多大|duō dà}？
= How old are they?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{弟弟|dì di}{十五|shí wǔ}{岁|suì}，{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{一|yí}{个|gè}{十二|shí èr}{岁|suì}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{八|bā}{岁|suì}。
= My brother is fifteen; one of my sisters is twelve and one is eight.
```

Notice that David uses {几岁|jǐ suì} for the teacher's young daughter, and the teacher uses {多大|duō dà} for David.
{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{妹妹|mèi mei} counts with {两|liǎng}, while {十二|shí èr}{岁|suì} ends in {二|èr}. {一|yí}{个|gè}…，{一|yí}{个|gè}…
is "one... the other...".

```speak
{一百零五|yì bǎi líng wǔ}
= 105
{两千零二十六|liǎng qiān líng èr shí liù}
= 2,026
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{妹妹|mèi mei}。
= I have two younger sisters.
{你|nǐ}{多大|duō dà}？
= How old are you?
{我|wǒ}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。
= I'm twenty.
{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}？
= How many people are there in your family?
```

## Pronunciation

- {百|bǎi} and {几|jǐ}, {九|jiǔ}, {五|wǔ} are third tones, so watch for 3+3: {九百|jiǔ bǎi} is said
  *jiú bǎi*, {五百|wǔ bǎi} *wú bǎi*, {几口|jǐ kǒu} *jí kǒu*. Pinyin still writes the third tone.
- {两|liǎng}: *l* + *iang*, a third tone; before {个|gè} it stays low: *liǎng gè*.
- {岁|suì}: *s* + *ui* (short for *uei*), "sway" with a falling tone. Keep it apart from
  {水|shuǐ} (water), which has *sh*.
- {儿子|ér zi} and {女儿|nǚ ér}: *er* is said with the tongue curled back, like American "are". In
  {女儿|nǚ ér} both syllables are full; in {儿子|ér zi} the second is light.
- {女|nǚ}: ü after *n* keeps its dots. Say "ee" with rounded lips.
- {零|líng} ends in *-ng*; {您|nín} from lesson 1 ends in *-n*.


## Characters
{=

| Character | Traditional | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 零 | same | zero | líng | 雨 | 13 | {零|líng}, {一百零五|yì bǎi líng wǔ} |
| 百 | same | hundred | bǎi | 白 | 6 | {百|bǎi}, {一百|yì bǎi} |
| 千 | same | thousand | qiān | 十 | 3 | {千|qiān}, {两千|liǎng qiān} |
| 两 | 兩 | two (with a measure word) | liǎng | 一 | 7 | {两|liǎng}, {两|liǎng}{个|gè} |
| 岁 | 歲 | year of age | suì | 山 | 6 | {岁|suì}, {几岁|jǐ suì} |
| 多 | same | many, much | duō | 夕 | 6 | {多|duō}, {多少|duō shao}, {多大|duō dà} |
| 少 | same | few, little | shǎo; shao in {多少|duō shao} | 小 | 4 | {多少|duō shao}, {少|shǎo} (lesson 25) |
| 儿 | 兒 | son; (the r ending) | ér | 儿 | 2 | {儿子|ér zi}, {女儿|nǚ ér}, {哪儿|nǎr} (lesson 9) |
| 子 | same | child; (noun ending) | zǐ; zi | 子 | 3 | {儿子|ér zi}, {孩子|hái zi} |
| 女 | same | woman, female | nǚ | 女 | 3 | {女儿|nǚ ér}, {女|nǚ} (lesson 5) |
| 孩 | same | child | hái | 子 | 9 | {孩子|hái zi} |
| 弟 | same | younger brother | dì; di | 弓 | 7 | {弟弟|dì di} |
| 妹 | same | younger sister | mèi; mei | 女 | 8 | {妹妹|mèi mei} |

子 is read *zǐ* on its own and in some words, but in most words it's a light ending, *zi*:
{儿子|ér zi}, {孩子|hái zi}, and later {桌子|zhuō zi} (table) and {饺子|jiǎo zi} (dumplings). 儿 is also the
-r ending of {哪儿|nǎr} and {一点儿|yì diǎnr}, and in that use it adds no syllable. 零 is filed under 雨
"rain" (its top); 两 under 一; 岁 under 山 "mountain".

### Radicals: 阝, 人 and 大

- **阝 "ear"**: 10 characters. It looks like one radical but it's two, depending on the side. On
  the right ({右耳旁|yòu ěr páng}, "right ear") it comes from 邑, "town": {那|nà}, {都|dōu} (lesson 2;
  {都|dū} is also read "capital city"). On the left ({左耳旁|zuǒ ěr páng}, "left ear") it comes from
  阜, "mound, hill": you'll see it in {院|yuàn} of {医院|yī yuàn} (hospital) in lesson 21. Both are
  written the same way: a curved turning stroke, then a vertical.
- **人 "person"** at the top: 7 characters, where 人 spreads out as a roof: {会|huì} (lesson 2),
  {今天|jīn tiān} (today) in lesson 6. On the left it's 亻 (lesson 1). 个 has the same roof but is
  filed under 丨.
- **大 "big"**: 7 characters. 大 is a person with arms stretched wide. Add a line on top and you
  have {天|tiān} (sky, day: lesson 6); add a dot underneath and it's {太|tài} (too: lesson 12).

The family characters use radicals you know: 女 in 妹 (and in 女 itself), 子 in 孩 (a child, 子,
next to 亥). 弟 is under 弓 "bow".

Memory notes:

- 妹 is 女 + 未 (*wèi*), the sound part.
- 孩 is 子 (child) + 亥 (*hài*), which gives the sound *hái*.
- 多 is 夕 on top of 夕: "evening" twice, so many evenings. The doubling is real; the story is a
  memory aid.
- 少 is 小 (small) with an extra stroke: small, so few.
- 儿 is two legs: in older forms, a small child (the traditional character 兒 shows a child's head).
- 岁: 山 (mountain) over 夕. The traditional form, 歲, is quite different; this is one of the
  simplifications.

### Stroke order

- 女: three strokes, the bent stroke first (down-left, then down-right), then the left-falling
  stroke, then the horizontal on top of both. Learners often start with the horizontal; don't.
- 九 (from the pinyin course): the left-falling stroke first, then the horizontal that turns,
  curves and hooks.
- 两: the top horizontal, the vertical, the turning stroke with a hook, then the two 人 shapes
  inside, left one first.
- 少: the vertical first, then a short left-falling stroke on the left and a dot on the right, then the
  long left-falling stroke.
- 千: the short left-falling stroke on top, then the horizontal, then the vertical.
- 儿: the left-falling stroke, then the vertical that bends right and hooks up.

```trace
零百千两岁多少
```

```trace
儿子女孩弟妹
```

Write it: 百 两 岁 多 少 儿 子 女. Three times each from memory, then check.

=}

## Common mistakes

- 二个 for "two people". Before a measure word it's {两|liǎng}: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}.
- {两|liǎng} at the end of a number: 12 is {十二|shí èr}, never 十两.
- Forgetting the "one": 100 is {一百|yì bǎi}, 1,000 {一千|yì qiān}.
- Too many zeros: 1,005 is {一千零五|yì qiān líng wǔ}, with one {零|líng}.
- {是|shì} with age in a positive sentence: ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}~~ sounds odd. Say
  {我|wǒ}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。
- {几岁|jǐ suì} to an adult. Use {多大|duō dà}.
- {几|jǐ} without a measure word, or for a big number: for a school or a city use {多少|duō shao}.
- {口|kǒu} for anything but family size.

## Key points

- Numbers go from the biggest place down: {三千四百五十六|sān qiān sì bǎi wǔ shí liù}. Say the {一|yì} in
  {一百|yì bǎi} and {一千|yì qiān}.
- {零|líng} fills empty places inside a number, once per gap; zeros at the end aren't said.
- {二|èr} in counting and numbers; {两|liǎng} before a measure word.
- Age: {我|wǒ}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}, without {是|shì}. Ask children {几岁|jǐ suì}, adults {多大|duō dà}.
- {几|jǐ}: small numbers, measure word required. {多少|duō shao}: any number, measure word optional.
- Family size: {几|jǐ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}？

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Jobs and workplaces: 在 + place
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson finishes Module 1. You can already introduce yourself and your family; now you'll
say what people do and where they are: at home, at school, at a company. The key word is {在|zài},
"to be at" and "at", and the key rule is where Chinese puts the place: **before the verb**. You'll
also learn to say "a male teacher" or "a Chinese teacher" by putting one noun in front of another.

## Where someone is: 在 as a verb

{在|zài} + a place means "to be at, to be in":

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 — I'm at home.
{她|tā}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。 — She's at school.
{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}。 — My dad is at the office (at the company).

Don't use {是|shì} here: {是|shì} links two nouns ("A is B"), {在|zài} says where something is.
~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{家|jiā}~~ would mean "I am a home".

The negative is {不|bú}{在|zài} (*bú* before the fourth tone), and the question takes {吗|ma}:

{你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？ — Is your mum at home?
{在|zài}。 — Yes. / {不|bú}{在|zài}，{她|tā}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}。 — No, she's at work.

To ask where, use {哪儿|nǎr}, "where", a word from lesson 9: {你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ (Where are you?)
As always, the question word stands where the answer goes.

## Where something happens: 在 before the verb

{在|zài} + place can also go before another verb, to say where the action happens. Here it works
like "at" or "in":

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — I work at a company.
{他|tā}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — He works at a university.
{我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — We speak Chinese at school.

**The place comes before the verb**, the opposite of English "I work *at a company*". A Chinese
sentence sets the scene first (who, then where) and ends with what happens:

| Subject | (adverb) | 在 + place | Verb (+ object) |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | | {在|zài}{公司|gōng sī} | {工作|gōng zuò} |
| {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma} | {也|yě} | {在|zài}{公司|gōng sī} | {工作|gōng zuò} |
| {他们|tā men} | {都|dōu} | {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào} | {说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} |
| {我|wǒ} | {不|bú} | {在|zài}{大学|dà xué} | {工作|gōng zuò} |

Adverbs such as {也|yě}, {都|dōu} and {不|bù} come before {在|zài}: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{工作|gōng zuò}
(I don't work at a university). ~~{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}~~ is the English order and
sounds wrong to Chinese ears.

{在|zài} has a third use, "in the middle of doing", which lesson 10 teaches: {他|tā}{在|zài}{工作|gōng zuò}
(he's working).

## Work: 工作

{工作|gōng zuò} is both a verb, "to work", and a noun, "a job, work":

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — I work at a hospital. (verb)
{你|nǐ}{的|de}{工作|gōng zuò}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！ — You have a good job! (noun)
{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{工作|gōng zuò}{吗|ma}？ — Do you have a job? (noun)

{医院|yī yuàn} (hospital) is a lesson 21 word, glossed here because doctors need it.

### What do you do?

The usual question is {你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？, "what work do you do?" ({做|zuò}, "to
do", is a lesson 9 word.) The answer usually uses {是|shì} or {在|zài}:

{你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？ — What do you do?
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 — I'm a doctor.
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — I work for a company.

With an older person or a stranger, use {您|nín}: {您|nín}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？ Students
answer {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng} or {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}.

## Jobs and places

| Person | Place |
|---|---|
| {老师|lǎo shī} teacher | {学校|xué xiào} school |
| {学生|xué sheng} student | {学校|xué xiào} school |
| {大学生|dà xué shēng} university student | {大学|dà xué} university |
| {医生|yī shēng} doctor | {医院|yī yuàn} hospital (lesson 21) |
| (an office worker) | {公司|gōng sī} company, firm |

{学校|xué xiào} is any school; {大学|dà xué}, "big learning", is a university or college. A
{大学生|dà xué shēng} is a university student: notice that {生|shēng} has its full tone in
{大学生|dà xué shēng} and {医生|yī shēng}, but is light in {学生|xué sheng}. {公司|gōng sī} covers any company,
and {在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò} is the everyday way to say "I have an office job".

## A male teacher, a Chinese teacher: nouns before nouns

In Chinese a **[[modifier]]**, the word that describes a noun, always comes before it. Many
modifiers are simply another noun put in front, without {的|de}:

| Modifier + noun | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {男|nán}{老师|lǎo shī} | a male teacher |
| {女|nǚ}{医生|yī shēng} | a female doctor |
| {中国|Zhōng guó}{老师|lǎo shī} | a Chinese teacher (a teacher from China) |
| {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī} | a Chinese teacher (a teacher of Chinese) |
| {大学|dà xué}{老师|lǎo shī} | a university teacher |
| {美国|Měi guó}{公司|gōng sī} | an American company |

English "a Chinese teacher" is ambiguous; Chinese isn't: {中国|Zhōng guó}{老师|lǎo shī} is about where the
teacher is from, {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī} about what they teach.

This works when the modifier names a type or a category: what kind of teacher, what kind of
company. When it says whose, {的|de} is needed (lesson 3): {我|wǒ}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}, {大学|dà xué}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}
(the university's name).

In sentences, {男|nán} (male) and {女|nǚ} (female) go in front of a noun like this: {男|nán}{学生|xué sheng}, {女|nǚ}{老师|lǎo shī},
and later {男朋友|nán péng you} (boyfriend). They can't be the predicate: "he is male" isn't ~~{他|tā}{很|hěn}{男|nán}~~.
(On forms and on toilet doors they stand alone: {男|nán} "male, men", {女|nǚ} "female, women".)

## Dialogue: meeting Li Ming's parents

Anna visits Li Ming's home and meets his parents. The speakers are {爸爸|bà ba} (Li Ming's dad) and
{妈妈|mā ma} (his mum).

```dialogue
# At Li Ming's home
李明: {安娜|Ān nà}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}。
= Anna, this is my dad, and this is my mum.
安娜: {您好|nín hǎo}！{您好|nín hǎo}！
= Hello! Hello!
爸爸: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}{吗|ma}？
= Hello! Are you a university student?
安娜: {是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。{您|nín}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？
= Yes, I study Chinese at university. What do you do?
爸爸: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= I'm a doctor. I work at a hospital.
安娜: {您|nín}{也|yě}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}{吗|ma}？
= Are you a doctor too?
妈妈: {不|bú}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{美国|Měi guó}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= No, I work for an American company.
李明: {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}！
= My mum speaks English!
安娜: {太好了|tài hǎo le}！{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{你|nǐ}{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
= Great! Li Ming, your parents are really nice.
```

{学|xué} (to study) is a lesson 19 word. Anna answers {您|nín} to both parents: they're older, and
she's a guest. In real life she'd probably call them {叔叔|shū shu} (uncle) and {阿姨|ā yí} (auntie),
the friendly titles Chinese children and young people use for their friends' parents; the honors
lesson on names says more.

## What people do

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{刘华|Liú Huá}，{是|shì}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{工作|gōng zuò}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
>
> {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{弟弟|dì di}，{他|tā}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。

My name is Liu Hua. I'm a Chinese teacher, and I work at a university. My dad is a doctor, and
my mum works for a company. I have a younger brother; he's a university student.

```speak
{你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？
= What do you do?
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= I work for a company.
{她|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。
= She's a doctor.
{你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？
= Is your mum at home?
{他|tā}{不|bú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。
= He isn't at school.
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。
= I'm a university student.
```

## Pronunciation

- {在|zài}: *z* like the "ds" in "kids", then *ai*, falling. Keep it apart from {再|zài} in
  {再见|zài jiàn}, which sounds the same but means "again".
- {工作|gōng zuò}: *gōng* is high and level with *-ng*; *zuò* is *z* + *uo*, falling.
- {公司|gōng sī}: two first tones, high and level. *si* is a buzzing "s", not "see".
- {学校|xué xiào}: *x* is soft, like "sh" with a smile; *iao* glides in one syllable.
- {医生|yī shēng}: both first tones; don't drop *sh* to *s*.
- {男|nán} and {女|nǚ}: *n* in both; *-an* in {男|nán}, *ü* in {女|nǚ}.


## Characters
{=

| Character | Traditional | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 在 | same | to be at; at, in | zài | 土 | 6 | {在|zài}, {现在|xiàn zài} (lesson 7) |
| 工 | same | work | gōng | 工 | 3 | {工作|gōng zuò} |
| 作 | same | to do, to make | zuò | 亻 | 7 | {工作|gōng zuò} |
| 医 | 醫 | medicine, to heal | yī | 匸 | 7 | {医生|yī shēng}, {医院|yī yuàn} (lesson 21) |
| 公 | same | public | gōng | 八 | 4 | {公司|gōng sī} |
| 司 | same | to manage | sī | 口 | 5 | {公司|gōng sī} |
| 校 | same | school | xiào | 木 | 10 | {学校|xué xiào} |
| 男 | same | male | nán | 田 | 7 | {男|nán}, {男朋友|nán péng you} (lesson 23) |

Filing notes: 医 is under 匸 here and under the similar 匚 "box" in many dictionaries; the
traditional form, 醫, is far more complex. 在 is filed under 土 at its bottom right.

### Radicals: 木, 土 and 囗

- **木 "tree, wood"** ({木|mù}): 24 characters. 木 is a tree:
  trunk, branches and roots. On the left it squeezes narrower and its last stroke becomes a dot:
  {校|xiào} (school). You'll see it in {机|jī} of {手机|shǒu jī} (mobile phone, lesson 10), {本|běn}
  (lesson 13) and {果|guǒ} of {水果|shuǐ guǒ} (fruit, lesson 14).
- **土 "earth, soil"** ({土|tǔ}): 9 characters. {在|zài} has it at the bottom right; later {块|kuài}
  (lesson 13) and {坐|zuò} (to sit, lesson 18). On the left it becomes narrow, with a rising last
  stroke: 块. Don't confuse 土 (short top line) with 士 (long top line) in {女士|nǚ shì} (lesson 12).
- **囗 "enclosure"**: 6 characters, all a box around something: {四|sì}, {国|guó} (lesson 2), and
  {回|huí} (to return, lesson 9). The box is closed last. A small 口 "mouth" inside a character is a
  different radical; 囗 is the big frame around the whole.

Memory notes:

- 男 is 田 (field) on top of 力 (strength, a plough in the oldest forms): the one who works in the
  fields. This is the usual explanation of the character's origin; it reflects an old division
  of farm work, not a rule about who does what.
- 校 is 木 + 交 (*jiāo*), the sound part.
- 作 is 亻 + 乍 (*zhà*), the sound part: a person doing something.
- 工 looks like a carpenter's square or a tool: work.
- 公: 八 (to divide) over 厶 (private): sharing out what's private makes it public. Old dictionaries
  explain it like this; take it as a memory aid.

### Stroke order

- 在: the horizontal, then the long left-falling stroke, then the short vertical, then 土
  (horizontal, vertical, horizontal).
- 医: the top horizontal of the frame first, then 矢 inside, and the bent stroke that closes the
  frame on the left and bottom last.
- 力 in 男: the horizontal that turns down with a hook first, then the left-falling stroke through
  it. Many learners write the left-falling stroke first; don't.
- 司: the turning stroke with a hook first, then the short horizontal, then 口.
- 公: the two strokes of 八, then 厶 (a bent stroke, then the dot).

```trace
在工作医公司校男
```

Write it: 在 工 作 男. Three times each from memory, then check.

=}

## Common mistakes

- The place after the verb: ~~{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}~~. Place first:
  {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
- {是|shì} for location: ~~{她|tā}{是|shì}{学校|xué xiào}~~. Use {在|zài}: {她|tā}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。
- An adverb after {在|zài}: ~~{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{也|yě}{工作|gōng zuò}~~. Adverbs come first:
  {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
- {男|nán} or {女|nǚ} alone as "man" or "woman". They go before a noun: {男|nán}{老师|lǎo shī}.
- Mixing up {中国|Zhōng guó}{老师|lǎo shī} (from China) and {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī} (teaches Chinese).
- {学生|xué sheng} with a full second tone, or {大学生|dà xué shēng} with a light one. Learn each with its
  word.

## Key points

- {在|zài} + place: "to be at". {他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 Negative {不|bú}{在|zài}.
- {在|zài} + place + verb: where something happens. The place always comes **before** the verb,
  after the subject and any adverbs.
- {你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？ asks what someone does; answer with {是|shì} + job or
  {在|zài} + place + {工作|gōng zuò}.
- {工作|gōng zuò} is a verb (to work) and a noun (a job).
- A noun or {男|nán} / {女|nǚ} in front of a noun says what kind: {男|nán}{老师|lǎo shī}, {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}.
  For whose, use {的|de}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. That's the end of Module 1: the module quiz checks all five lessons.

lessons.title: Chinese names
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've been meeting {李明|Lǐ Míng} and Teacher Wang since lesson 1, and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} since the pinyin course. This lesson
looks at how Chinese names work: which part is the family name, which surnames are most common,
how given names are chosen, how people address each other, and how you can choose a Chinese name
of your own. It's an honors lesson: optional, for extra depth.

## Family name first

A Chinese name puts the **family name** (surname) first and the **given name** after it:

| Name | Family name | Given name |
|---|---|---|
| {王芳|Wáng Fāng} | {王|Wáng} | {芳|Fāng} |
| {李明|Lǐ Míng} | {李|Lǐ} | {明|Míng} |
| {张小红|Zhāng Xiǎo hóng} | {张|Zhāng} | {小红|Xiǎo hóng} |

The order goes from the general to the particular, like Chinese dates (year, month, day) and
addresses (country, city, street). Titles follow the same logic and come **after** the name:
{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī} (Teacher Wang), {李医生|Lǐ yī shēng} (Doctor Li), and in lesson 12
{王先生|Wáng xiān sheng} (Mr Wang) and {李女士|Lǐ nǚ shì} (Ms Li).

In pinyin the family name and the given name are written as two words, each with a capital, and
a two-character given name is joined into one word: *Wáng Fāng*, *Zhāng Xiǎohóng*. (In the
markup of this course every syllable is spaced so that it sits over its character, but the
spelling rule is one word per name part.) When Chinese people write their names in English, some
keep this order (Wang Fang) and some swap it to fit Western forms (Fang Wang), so it's worth
asking which part is the family name.

## The most common family names

Most family names are a single character, and a few are very common. According to the 2020
national name report of China's Ministry of Public Security, based on household registration,
the five most common were {王|Wáng}, {李|Lǐ}, {张|Zhāng}, {刘|Liú} and {陈|Chén}, and together they
covered 30.8 percent of the registered population of the mainland: roughly three people in ten.
Rankings like this come from registration data and change a little from year to year, so treat
the figure as approximate.

| Surname | Pinyin | Also a word meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {王|Wáng} | Wáng | king |
| {李|Lǐ} | Lǐ | plum |
| {张|Zhāng} | Zhāng | (a measure word for flat things, HSK 3) |
| {刘|Liú} | Liú | (no everyday meaning) |
| {陈|Chén} | Chén | old, stale (in a few words) |

A family name doesn't carry that meaning when it's a name: {王芳|Wáng Fāng} has nothing to do
with kings. Because so many people share a few surnames, the full name matters more than in
English, and saying someone's full name, {王芳|Wáng Fāng}, is normal and friendly, not cold.

A small number of family names have two characters, such as {欧阳|Ōu yáng}, {司马|Sī mǎ} and
{诸葛|Zhū gě}. They are rare: the 2020 report counted about 1.1 million people named {欧阳|Ōu yáng}, one
of the most common of them.

## Given names

Given names have one or two characters, and two is the usual choice today. In the name report for
2019, about 84 percent of registered names had three characters (a one-character surname plus a
two-character given name) and 14 percent had two.

There is no stock of ready-made given names like John or Maria in English. Parents combine
characters for their meaning and their sound, so two people rarely share the same given name
unless it's a popular combination. Characters that often appear in names include:

| Character | Meaning | Example name |
|---|---|---|
| {明|míng} | bright | {李明|Lǐ Míng} |
| {芳|fāng} | fragrant | {王芳|Wáng Fāng} |
| {红|hóng} | red | {张小红|Zhāng Xiǎo hóng} |
| {华|huá} | splendid; China | {刘华|Liú Huá} |
| {文|wén} | writing, culture | {陈文|Chén Wén} |
| {静|jìng} | calm, quiet | {王静|Wáng Jìng} |

Some characters are more often chosen for girls (flowers, beauty, grace) and some for boys
(strength, greatness), but many names, such as those with {明|míng} or {文|wén}, are used for anyone.
You can't always tell from the name alone. Tones matter too: parents usually avoid a name that
sounds flat, or like an unlucky or silly phrase, when the tones are said aloud.

### Family names after marriage

In mainland China a person keeps their own name when they marry. The Civil Code gives each
spouse the right to use their own name (Article 1056), so a married couple usually have
different family names. A child normally takes the father's or the mother's family name; the
law allows either (Article 1015), and the father's is the more common choice.

## Asking someone's name politely

You know {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ from lesson 1. It's fine with classmates, children and
people your age. With an older person, or in a formal setting, Chinese politely asks for the
family name first:

{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ — What is your (honourable) family name?
{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}，{叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 — My family name is Wang; I'm Wang Fang.

{姓|xìng} is a verb, "to have the family name", an HSK 2 word. {贵|guì} (lesson 13) means
"expensive, honoured": {贵姓|guì xìng} is "honourable surname". It's only for asking. You never use
it about yourself: the answer is {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}, never ~~{我|wǒ}{贵姓|guì xìng}{王|Wáng}~~. To ask about a
third person, say {他|tā}{姓|xìng}{什么|shén me}？ (What's his family name?).

## Addressing people

How you address someone depends on how well you know them and how old they are:

| Form | Example | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| family name + title | {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}, {李医生|Lǐ yī shēng} | teachers, doctors, anyone in a role; always safe |
| full name | {王芳|Wáng Fāng} | classmates, colleagues, people your age |
| given name | {芳|Fāng} | close friends, partners and family (two-character given names are used alone more often) |
| {小|xiǎo} + family name | {小王|Xiǎo Wáng} | a younger colleague or friend: friendly, informal |
| {老|lǎo} + family name | {老王|Lǎo Wáng} | an older colleague or friend: friendly and respectful, not "old" in a rude sense |
| {叔叔|shū shu} / {阿姨|ā yí} | | "uncle" / "auntie": a friend's parents, or older adults in general |

{小王|Xiǎo Wáng} and {老王|Lǎo Wáng} are for people you know. You wouldn't call a new boss or a stranger
{老王|Lǎo Wáng}. {叔叔|shū shu} and {阿姨|ā yí} are what Chinese children and young adults call their
friends' parents and older neighbours: in lesson 5, Anna could have greeted Li Ming's parents with
{叔叔好|shū shu hǎo}！ and {阿姨好|ā yí hǎo}！ Family members are usually addressed by their relationship
rather than by name: a younger brother says {哥哥|gē ge}, not the brother's name.

## Choosing a Chinese name

Learners usually end up with one of two kinds of Chinese name.

1. **A sound loan of your own name.** The syllables imitate it: Anna becomes {安娜|Ān nà} and David
   {大卫|Dà wèi}. Foreign names in Chinese newspapers are written like this. The result is clearly
   foreign, often three or four syllables, and easy to recognise.
2. **A name built like a Chinese one.** Choose a common family name that sounds like your own
   (Lee or Leigh: {李|Lǐ}; a name starting with W: {王|Wáng}; a name starting with Ch: {陈|Chén}), then
   one or two characters with a meaning you like: {李明|Lǐ Míng}, {王文|Wáng Wén}.

Some advice for the second kind:

- Ask a Chinese speaker to check it. A combination that looks fine character by character can
  sound like an odd or unlucky phrase, or like the name of someone famous.
- Say it aloud with its tones. A good name is easy to say and clear to hear.
- Avoid grand or old-fashioned meanings ("dragon emperor") unless you want people to smile.
- Keep it short: one family name and one or two given-name characters.

Either kind is fine for class. Many people use a sound loan at first and are given a
Chinese-style name later by a teacher or friend.

```speak
{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？
= What is your family name? (polite)
{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}，{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。
= My family name is Li; I'm Li Ming.
{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, Teacher Wang!
{阿姨好|ā yí hǎo}！
= Hello! (to a friend's mother or an older woman)
```

## Dialogue: whose name is that?

```dialogue
# Names at a party
安娜: {您好|nín hǎo}！{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？
= Hello! May I ask your family name?
陈文: {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{陈|Chén}，{叫|jiào}{陈文|Chén Wén}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= My family name is Chen; I'm Chen Wen. And you?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。
= I'm Anna. I'm American.
陈文: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{中文|Zhōng wén}{名字|míng zi}{吗|ma}？
```
