```dialogue
= Anna, do you have a Chinese name?
安娜: {有|yǒu}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{中文|Zhōng wén}{名字|míng zi}{叫|jiào}{安美|Ān Měi}。
= Yes, my Chinese name is An Mei.
陈文: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！{安|Ān}{也|yě}{是|shì}{中国人|Zhōng guó rén}{的|de}{姓|xìng}。
= Very nice! An is a Chinese family name too.
```

Anna's Chinese-style name keeps the sound of the first syllable of {安娜|Ān nà}: {安|Ān} is a real
Chinese family name. {美|měi} means "beautiful", the {美|Měi} of {美国|Měi guó}. Here {姓|xìng} is a
noun, "family name".

## Key points

- Family name first, then the given name; titles come after the name: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}.
- Most family names are one character. {王|Wáng}, {李|Lǐ}, {张|Zhāng}, {刘|Liú} and {陈|Chén} were the top
  five in the 2020 report, about three people in ten together.
- Given names are one or two characters chosen for meaning and sound; there's no fixed list.
- Married people keep their own names; children take the father's or the mother's family name.
- Polite question: {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ Answer: {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}… Never use {贵|guì} about yourself.
- {小|xiǎo} / {老|lǎo} + family name between people who know each other; {叔叔|shū shu} and {阿姨|ā yí}
  for a friend's parents.
- A Chinese name can be a sound loan ({安娜|Ān nà}) or built like a Chinese name ({安美|Ān Měi}).

lessons.title: How characters began
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've now learned more than 80 characters, and the memory notes have kept saying things like
"女 gives the meaning, 马 gives the sound". This honors lesson steps back and asks where
characters came from: what the oldest Chinese writing looks like, how characters were built, and
why knowing that makes new characters easier to learn. It's optional, and nothing in it is needed
for the HSK.

## The oldest Chinese writing

The oldest large body of Chinese writing is carved on bones and shells from the late Shang
dynasty, over 3,000 years ago (historians date the pieces to roughly 1250–1050 BCE). The kings
of the Shang used them to ask their ancestors questions: will the harvest be good, will it rain,
should the army set out? A priest heated an ox shoulder blade or the flat underside of a turtle
shell until it cracked, read the answer from the cracks, and the question, and often the result,
were carved beside them. These are the oracle-bone inscriptions, {甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén}, "shell
and bone writing".

Most of them come from Anyang, in today's Henan province, the site of the last Shang capital.
Scholars recognised the marks as writing only in 1899; the usual story is that a scholar named
Wang Yirong noticed carvings on "dragon bones" bought as medicine. Since then more than 100,000
inscribed pieces have been found, and several thousand different characters identified, of which
only part can be read with confidence.

Writing then appears on bronze: the bronze inscriptions, {金文|jīn wén}, cast into ritual
cauldrons and bells of the late Shang and the Western Zhou dynasty (about 1046–771 BCE). Shang
bronzes carry a few characters, often a clan name; some Zhou bronzes carry texts of hundreds of
characters. Over the following centuries the shapes grew more regular and less like pictures,
until they became the characters written today. In the 1950s and 1960s mainland China simplified
many of them (official lists were published in 1956 and 1964): those are the simplified
characters this course uses, while Taiwan and Hong Kong kept the traditional forms.

## Four ways characters were made

Around 100 CE the scholar Xu Shen finished the first great dictionary of characters, the
{说文解字|Shuō wén jiě zì}, "explaining simple and analysing compound characters". It has 9,353
entries, and it describes six kinds of character, the {六书|liù shū}. Four of them explain how
most characters were made.

### 1. Pictures: pictographs

A **[[pictograph]]** is a character that began as a drawing of a thing. Described in words, here is
what the oldest forms of some characters looked like:

| Character | Was a drawing of |
|---|---|
| {人|rén} person | a person seen from the side, leaning forward |
| {日|rì} sun | a circle with a dot or short line in it; the brush later made it square |
| {月|yuè} moon | a crescent moon |
| {口|kǒu} mouth | an open mouth |
| {山|shān} mountain | three peaks rising from one line |
| {水|shuǐ} water | a winding stream with drops on both sides |
| {木|mù} tree | a tree: branches above, roots below |
| {门|mén} door | the two wings of a swinging door, still clear in the traditional form 門 |
| {马|mǎ} horse | a horse standing on end, with mane, legs and tail (traditional 馬) |
| {鱼|yú} fish | a fish standing on its head: head, scaly body, tail (traditional 魚) |

Animals were often drawn upright like this, probably so they would fit into the vertical columns
of writing. Pictographs are where everyone starts, but there are only a few hundred of them.

### 2. Pointers: indicative characters

Some ideas can't be drawn as things, so a mark points at them:

- {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān}: one, two and three strokes.
- {上|shàng} (up, above) and {下|xià} (down, below): in the oldest forms, a short mark above or below a
  longer line.
- {本|běn} (root, origin): {木|mù} (tree) with a mark at the bottom, pointing at the root.

### 3. Meanings combined: compound characters

Two meaningful parts can join to make a new meaning:

- {休|xiū} (to rest): 亻 (a person) beside {木|mù} (a tree). This is the usual explanation: someone
  resting against a tree.
- {林|lín} (woods) is two trees; {森|sēn} (forest) is three.
- {好|hǎo} (good) is {女|nǚ} (woman) + {子|zǐ} (child). The traditional explanation is "a mother with
  her child", which makes a fine memory aid; scholars debate how the character really arose.
- {明|míng} (bright) is usually explained as {日|rì} (sun) + {月|yuè} (moon). Some old forms have a
  window in place of the sun: moonlight shining through a window. Either way, it's light.

### 4. Meaning plus sound: phonetic-semantic characters

The fourth kind is by far the biggest. A **[[phonetic-semantic character]]** joins a part that hints
at the meaning (usually the radical) with a part that hints at the sound. You've met many:

| Character | Meaning part | Sound part |
|---|---|---|
| {妈|mā} mother | 女 woman | {马|mǎ} |
| {吗|ma} (question particle) | 口 mouth (speech) | {马|mǎ} |
| {们|men} (plural) | 亻 person | {门|mén} |
| {哪|nǎ} which | 口 mouth | {那|nà} |
| {校|xiào} school | 木 wood | 交 *jiāo* |
| {孩|hái} child | 子 child | 亥 *hài* |
| {妹|mèi} younger sister | 女 woman | 未 *wèi* |
| {语|yǔ} language | 讠 speech | 吾 *wú* |

The sound part rarely gives the exact modern reading. Pronunciation has changed a great deal
over 3,000 years, so it gives a clue: often the same final ({妈|mā}, {马|mǎ}, {吗|ma}), sometimes
only a similar syllable ({校|xiào} and 交 *jiāo*). Even so, by common estimates eight or nine
characters out of ten are of this kind. The reason is practical: pictures can't show "which" or
"language", but a meaning part plus a sound part can write any word.

### Borrowed characters

Among the other categories, one is worth knowing: a character could be borrowed for another
word that sounded the same. {来|lái} (to come), from lesson 9, began as a picture of a wheat plant;
the usual explanation is that it was borrowed for the word "come", and wheat was later written
with another character, {麦|mài}. The old picture is gone from the meaning but survives in the
shape.

## What this means for you

- **Radicals give meaning clues.** 氵 suggests water, 讠 speech, 女 women, 木 trees and wood. A
  character you don't know with 讠 probably has something to do with speaking.
- **Sound parts give reading clues.** If you know {马|mǎ}, then {妈|mā} and {吗|ma} are easy, and when
  you meet 码 (*mǎ*, code) in a phone number, you can guess it too. The clue isn't always right,
  but it's right often enough to help.
- **Stories are aids, not history.** This course's memory notes say when a story is the
  traditional explanation and when it's just a picture to help you remember. Both are useful; just
  don't mistake one for the other.

Here are some characters you know, sorted by kind:

| Kind | Characters |
|---|---|
| pictographs | {人|rén} {日|rì} {月|yuè} {口|kǒu} {女|nǚ} {子|zǐ} {儿|ér} {大|dà} |
| indicative | {一|yī} {二|èr} {三|sān} {上|shàng} {下|xià} |
| compound | {好|hǎo} {男|nán} (field + strength) |
| phonetic-semantic | {妈|mā} {吗|ma} {们|men} {哪|nǎ} {校|xiào} {孩|hái} {妹|mèi} {语|yǔ} {姐|jiě} {爸|bà} |

{大|dà} is a person with arms spread wide, and {子|zǐ} a baby with a big head and outstretched arms.
{上|shàng} and {下|xià} are taught in lesson 7, and {山|shān}, {木|mù}, {门|mén}, {马|mǎ} and {鱼|yú} come in later
courses or as parts of other characters; the pinyin above them tells you how to say them.

```speak
{甲骨文|jiǎ gǔ wén}
= oracle-bone inscriptions
{人|rén}、{日|rì}、{月|yuè}、{山|shān}、{水|shuǐ}
= person, sun, moon, mountain, water
{妈|mā}、{马|mǎ}、{吗|ma}
= mother, horse, question particle
```

## Key points

- The oldest large body of Chinese writing is the oracle-bone inscriptions of the late Shang,
  over 3,000 years ago; bronze inscriptions followed.
- Xu Shen's dictionary (about 100 CE) described six kinds of characters.
- Pictographs began as drawings ({人|rén}, {日|rì}, {月|yuè}, {山|shān}, {水|shuǐ}); indicatives point at an idea
  ({上|shàng}, {下|xià}); compounds join meanings ({休|xiū}, {林|lín}).
- Most characters are phonetic-semantic: a meaning part plus a sound part ({妈|mā} = 女 + {马|mǎ}).
- Simplified characters were standardised in mainland China in 1956 and 1964.
- Use radicals as meaning clues and sound parts as reading clues; treat stories as memory aids
  unless they are labelled as the character's history.

lessons.title: Days, dates and weeks
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 taught you how to meet people: names, countries, families, numbers and jobs. This module
is about time: the date, the clock, your day, where you're going and what people are doing right
now. It starts with the calendar.

By the end of this lesson you can say and ask today's date and the day of the week, say
yesterday, today and tomorrow, read a date the way Chinese writes it, and say a year. You'll also
learn eight new characters, including {年|nián} (year) and {天|tiān} (day), which you'll see on every calendar.

The good news first: Chinese dates are built from numbers you already know. There are no month
names to learn and only one pattern for the weekdays. Most of the work is putting the pieces in
the right order.

## Characters

{=
This section describes the simplified shapes, so it stays in simplified characters even when you
switch the course to traditional. Where a character's traditional form differs, it's given in
brackets beside it; the radicals and stroke counts are those of the simplified form. The tracing
pads and the notecards follow the script you've chosen.

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 今 | now, the present | jīn | 人 | 4 | {今天|jīn tiān}, {今年|jīn nián} (this year: lesson 25) |
| 天 | day; sky | tiān | 大 | 4 | {今天|jīn tiān}, {明天|míng tiān}, {星期天|xīng qī tiān} |
| 明 | bright; next (day, year) | míng | 日 | 8 | {明天|míng tiān}, {明年|míng nián} (next year: lesson 25) |
| 昨 | yesterday | zuó | 日 | 9 | {昨天|zuó tiān} |
| 星 | star | xīng | 日 | 9 | {星期|xīng qī}, {星期天|xīng qī tiān}, {星期日|xīng qī rì} |
| 期 | period of time | qī | 月 | 12 | {星期|xīng qī}, {星期日|xīng qī rì} |
| 号 (traditional 號) | number; day of the month | hào | 口 | 5 | {号|hào}, {几号|jǐ hào} |
| 年 | year | nián | 干 | 6 | {年|nián}, {今年|jīn nián} |

The radical column shows the part a dictionary files the character under. 年 is filed under 干
here, as in the old Kangxi dictionary; some modern mainland dictionaries file it under its first
stroke, 丿, instead. Don't let that worry you: radicals are a way of sorting, and dictionaries
sort a few characters differently.

How the shapes work (true history where it's known, and labelled when it's only a memory aid):

- 明: the sun 日 and the moon 月 side by side. "Bright" is how the character is usually explained;
  some of its oldest forms show a window instead of the sun, with moonlight coming in. In
  {明天|míng tiān} it means "the next (day)".
- 昨 and 星 are sound-and-meaning characters, the most common kind: 日 (sun, day) gives the
  meaning area, and the other part hints at the sound. In 昨 the right side is 乍 *zhà*; in 星 the
  bottom is 生 *shēng* (as in {学生|xué sheng}), close to *xīng*. The 日 on top of 星 once stood for
  a shining star.
- 期: 其 *qí* on the left hints at the sound *qī*, and 月, the moon, gives the meaning. People
  measured long stretches of time by the moon.
- 年: the oldest forms show a person carrying ripe grain on their back. One harvest, one year.
- 天: a person 大 with a line over the head. The oldest forms draw the head itself big, and "the
  top" came to mean the sky above, then the day.
- 今 (memory aid only): a roof 人 over one short moment, now.
- 号 (memory aid only): a mouth 口 on top, calling out a number.

### New radicals: 月, 巾, 子

- **月** "moon", called {月字旁|yuè zì páng} when it stands on the left. Six characters of the
  Chinese track are filed under it. So far: 月 itself (from the pinyin course), 期 (this lesson)
  and 有 (lesson 3). In 有 the bottom part was originally a piece of meat in a hand, not the moon;
  lesson 17 has more on this "meat moon", which looks the same in print.
- **巾** "cloth, towel" ({巾字旁|jīn zì páng}): six characters of the track. So far: 师 in
  {老师|lǎo shī}, where 巾 is the right side. 市 (market, lesson 14) and 常 (often, lesson 15) come
  later.
- **子** "child" ({子字旁|zǐ zì páng}): five characters of the track. You've met four: 子 in
  {儿子|ér zi} and {孩子|hái zi}, 孩, 字 (a child under a roof 宀) and 学 (a child at the bottom).
  When 子 is on the left, as in 孩, its last stroke rises to the right.

### Stroke order: 年

年 is one of the characters people often write in the wrong order. It has six strokes:

1. the short left-falling stroke 丿 at the top;
2. the short horizontal beside it;
3. the second, longer horizontal;
4. the **short vertical on the left**, going down from the second horizontal;
5. the long horizontal across the middle;
6. the long vertical down the right, written last because it cuts through everything.

The rule from the pinyin course, "a vertical that crosses everything comes last", is what decides
step 6. In 期, write the left part 其 first (its two verticals before the inner horizontals) and
then 月.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
今天明昨星期号年
```

✎ **Write it**: 今, 天 and 年 are on the list of characters the new HSK expects you to write by
hand by level 2. Write each three times on paper or the pad, from memory, then check them.
=}

## Days: {今天|jīn tiān}, {明天|míng tiān}, {昨天|zuó tiān}

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {昨天|zuó tiān} | yesterday |
| {今天|jīn tiān} | today |
| {明天|míng tiān} | tomorrow |

All three end in {天|tiān}, "day". 今 *jīn* is "now", 明 *míng* "next", 昨 *zuó* "the one before". They are
**[[time words]]**: nouns that name a time. A time word goes **before the verb**, either straight after the
subject or at the very front of the sentence:

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — I'm working tomorrow.

{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — Tomorrow I'm working.

Both are correct; putting the time first gives it a little more weight, like "Tomorrow, …" in
English. What you can't do is put it at the end, English style: *{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{明天|míng tiān}
is wrong.

Notice also that the verb doesn't change. {我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò} is "I work", "I'm working" or "I'll
work"; the time word tells you when. Chinese has no tense endings at all.

{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{今天|jīn tiān}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。 — Teacher Wang is at school today.

{昨天|zuó tiān}{她|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 — Yesterday she was at home.

The second sentence is past, with no change to {在|zài}: {昨天|zuó tiān} does all the work.

## The week: {星期一|xīng qī yī} to {星期天|xīng qī tiān}

{星期|xīng qī} means "week". Add a number and you have the weekdays, starting from Monday:

| Chinese | Day |
|---|---|
| {星期一|xīng qī yī} | Monday |
| {星期二|xīng qī èr} | Tuesday |
| {星期三|xīng qī sān} | Wednesday |
| {星期四|xīng qī sì} | Thursday |
| {星期五|xīng qī wǔ} | Friday |
| {星期六|xīng qī liù} | Saturday |
| {星期天|xīng qī tiān} or {星期日|xīng qī rì} | Sunday |

Sunday is the only day without a number: there's no *{星期七|xīng qī qī}. {星期天|xīng qī tiān} is the
everyday spoken word; {星期日|xīng qī rì} is the written and more formal one, the one you'll see on
calendars, timetables and forms. Both are correct, and you'll hear {星期日|xīng qī rì} too.

The {一|yī} in {星期一|xīng qī yī} keeps its first tone, *yī*. As the pinyin course showed, {一|yī} changes
its tone when it counts something ({一个|yí gè}, {一天|yì tiān}), but not when it's a digit, part of a
bigger number, or the name of a place in a series. So numbers in dates, days and years are always
*yī*: {一月|yī yuè}, {一号|yī hào}, {星期一|xīng qī yī}.

To ask which day it is, put {几|jǐ} (how many, which number; lesson 3) in the number's place:

{今天|jīn tiān}{星期几|xīng qī jǐ}？ — What day is it today?

{今天|jīn tiān}{星期三|xīng qī sān}。 — Today is Wednesday.

## Months and dates: {月|yuè} and {号|hào}

Months are numbers too: number + {月|yuè} (month, moon).

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {一月|yī yuè} January | {四月|sì yuè} April | {七月|qī yuè} July | {十月|shí yuè} October |
| {二月|èr yuè} February | {五月|wǔ yuè} May | {八月|bā yuè} August | {十一月|shí yī yuè} November |
| {三月|sān yuè} March | {六月|liù yuè} June | {九月|jiǔ yuè} September | {十二月|shí èr yuè} December |

The day of the month is number + {号|hào} in speech: {一号|yī hào} (the 1st), {十六号|shí liù hào} (the
16th), {三十一号|sān shí yī hào} (the 31st). The numbers here name a position in a series, "the
first, the sixteenth": they are **[[ordinals]]** in meaning, even though Chinese uses the plain number.
(Chinese also has a word for "-th", {第|dì}, for "the first person", "the second time": that's
lesson 14.)

In writing, the day is {日|rì} (the character you learned in the pinyin course, "sun, day"):
{十六日|shí liù rì}. Speak {号|hào}, write {日|rì}. On a form, a ticket or in a newspaper you'll see {日|rì}; in
conversation and in messages between friends, {号|hào}.

Ask with {几|jǐ} again:

{今天|jīn tiān}{几号|jǐ hào}？ — What's the date today?

{几月几号|jǐ yuè jǐ hào}？ — What month and day? (What's the date?)

{十一月|shí yī yuè}{二十号|èr shí hào}。 — November the 20th.

Careful with one pair. {一月|yī yuè} is January, but "one month", an amount of time, is
{一个月|yí gè yuè}, with the measure word {个|gè} (lesson 3) and *yí* before the fourth tone of {个|gè}. In
the same way {两个月|liǎng gè yuè} is "two months" and {二月|èr yuè} is February. Lesson 7 has more
on amounts of time.

## Big to small: the order of a date

English can say "Monday, 16 November 2026" or "November 16, 2026". Chinese has one order, from the
biggest unit to the smallest: year, month, day, then the weekday.

{二|èr}〇{二|èr}{六|liù}{年|nián}{十一月|shí yī yuè}{十六号|shí liù hào}，{星期一|xīng qī yī} — Monday, 16 November 2026

This big-to-small order runs through the whole language. You'll see it again with times (lesson
7), with time words in a sentence (lesson 8), and in addresses, which start with the country and
end with the house number.

Dates are very often written with Arabic numerals, which Chinese readers use all the time:

> 2026{年|nián}11{月|yuè}16{日|rì}　{星期一|xīng qī yī}

That's the form on a phone, a receipt or a form, and you read it exactly the same way.

## Years: digit by digit

A year is read one digit at a time, then {年|nián}:

| Year | Said |
|---|---|
| 1998{年|nián} | {一|yī}{九|jiǔ}{九|jiǔ}{八|bā}{年|nián} *yī jiǔ jiǔ bā nián* |
| 2000{年|nián} | {二|èr}{零|líng}{零|líng}{零|líng}{年|nián} *èr líng líng líng nián* |
| 2026{年|nián} | {二|èr}{零|líng}{二|èr}{六|liù}{年|nián} *èr líng èr liù nián* |

Not "nineteen ninety-eight" or "two thousand and twenty-six": just the digits. {一|yī} stays *yī*,
because it's a digit, and zero is {零|líng} (lesson 4). When a year is written in characters, the
zero is usually the small circle 〇, also read *líng*: {二|èr}〇{二六|èr liù}{年|nián}. (The app shows no pinyin over 〇,
because it isn't a character with a reading of its own, only a written sign for {零|líng}.)

To ask the year, use {哪|nǎ} (which; lesson 2) with {年|nián}: {哪年|nǎ nián}？ — Which year? People also say
{哪一年|nǎ yì nián}, with *yì* before the second tone of {年|nián}.

## {年|nián} and {天|tiān} count themselves

Most nouns need a measure word between the number and the noun: {三个人|sān gè rén}, three people
(lesson 3). {年|nián} and {天|tiān} don't. They work as their own measure words, so you count them directly:

| Correct | Wrong | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {一天|yì tiān} | *{一个天|yí gè tiān} | one day |
| {两天|liǎng tiān} | *{两个天|liǎng gè tiān} | two days |
| {三年|sān nián} | *{三个年|sān gè nián} | three years |

Use {两|liǎng}, not {二|èr}, before them, exactly as before a measure word (lesson 4): {两年|liǎng nián}.
In {一天|yì tiān} and {一年|yì nián}, {一|yī} counts an amount, so its tone changes (*yì* before a first or
second tone).

{星期|xīng qī} and {月|yuè} are ordinary nouns and do need {个|gè}: {一个星期|yí gè xīng qī} (one week),
{两个月|liǎng gè yuè} (two months).

## Sentences with no verb: {今天|jīn tiān}{星期一|xīng qī yī}

Look again at {今天|jīn tiān}{星期三|xīng qī sān}。 There's no verb: no {是|shì}. A date, a day of the week, an
age or a time can be the whole predicate, the part of the sentence that says something about the
subject. This is called a **[[noun predicate]]**, and it's normal, everyday Chinese:

{今天|jīn tiān}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。 — Today is Monday.

{明天|míng tiān}{十七号|shí qī hào}。 — Tomorrow is the 17th.

{我|wǒ}{二十岁|èr shí suì}。 — I'm twenty. (lesson 4)

You may put {是|shì} in: {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。 is also correct, a little more
emphatic. But in two places {是|shì} is needed:

- **In the negative**: {今天|jīn tiān}{不是|bú shì}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。 — Today isn't Monday. Never
  *{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{星期一|xīng qī yī}: {不|bù} needs a verb (or an adjective) to negate, and {是|shì} is that verb. {不|bù} is *bú* before
  the fourth tone of {是|shì}.
- **In most yes/no questions with {吗|ma}**: {明天|míng tiān}{是|shì}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{吗|ma}？ — Is
  tomorrow Saturday? Questions with {几|jǐ} don't need it: {明天|míng tiān}{星期几|xīng qī jǐ}？

## Pronunciation

- {星期|xīng qī}: two first tones, both high and level. The *q* is like English "ch" with the
  tongue tip down, and *xīng* has the same *x* (a soft "sh").
- {几号|jǐ hào}: third tone then fourth. Keep *jǐ* low.
- {几月|jǐ yuè}: third then fourth. In {几月几号|jǐ yuè jǐ hào} no two third tones touch, so nothing
  changes. But in {几点|jǐ diǎn} (lesson 7) they do, and it's said *jí diǎn*.
- {昨天|zuó tiān}: *zuó* rises. *z* is like the "ds" in "beds".
- {星期日|xīng qī rì}: the Chinese *r* is close to the "s" in "pleasure" with the tongue curled up.
- {九月|jiǔ yuè} and {五月|wǔ yuè}: third tone before fourth, a low dip without the rise at the end
  (the "half third" from the pinyin course).
```speak
{今天|jīn tiān}{几号|jǐ hào}？
= What's the date today?
{今天|jīn tiān}{十一月|shí yī yuè}{十六号|shí liù hào}。
= Today is 16 November.
{明天|míng tiān}{星期几|xīng qī jǐ}？
= What day is it tomorrow?
{明天|míng tiān}{星期二|xīng qī èr}。
= Tomorrow is Tuesday.
{昨天|zuó tiān}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}。
= Yesterday was Sunday.
{我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{不|bù}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= I don't work on Saturdays.
```

## Dialogue: what's the date?

{安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) is a student of Chinese; {李明|Lǐ Míng} is a classmate at her university.

```dialogue
# What day is it?
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}，{今天|jīn tiān}{几号|jǐ hào}？
= Li Ming, what's the date today?
李明: {今天|jīn tiān}{十一月|shí yī yuè}{二十号|èr shí hào}。
= Today is 20 November.
安娜: {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{星期四|xīng qī sì}{吗|ma}？
= Is it Thursday today?
李明: {不是|bú shì}，{今天|jīn tiān}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}。{明天|míng tiān}{星期六|xīng qī liù}。
= No, today is Friday. Tomorrow is Saturday.
安娜: {星期六|xīng qī liù}{你|nǐ}{工作|gōng zuò}{吗|ma}？
= Do you work on Saturday?
李明: {不|bù}{工作|gōng zuò}。{星期六|xīng qī liù}{和|hé}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= No. I'm at home on Saturday and Sunday. And you?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}，{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。
= I'm at school on Saturday, and I'm at home on Sunday.
```

Two details. Anna's yes/no question uses {是|shì}, and so does the "no" answer: {不是|bú shì}. And look
at where the days go: before the verb, and before {都|dōu} (all, both: lesson 2), which sums them up.
{星期六|xīng qī liù}{和|hé}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{家|jiā} is "Saturday and Sunday, I'm at home on both".

## Reading: a desk calendar

> **2026{年|nián}11{月|yuè}**
>
> **21**
>
> {星期六|xīng qī liù}

A page from a desk calendar: the year and the month at the top, the day in big numbers, and the
weekday at the bottom. It's Saturday, 21 November 2026. How would you say it? {二|èr}{零|líng}{二|èr}{六|liù}{年|nián}{十一月|shí yī yuè}{二十一号|èr shí yī hào}，{星期六|xīng qī liù}。
Notice {二十一|èr shí yī}: {一|yī} at the end of a number stays *yī*.

## Common mistakes

- **English order for dates.** *{十六号|shí liù hào}{十一月|shí yī yuè} puts the day first. Chinese
  goes from big to small: {十一月|shí yī yuè}{十六号|shí liù hào}.
- **Time words at the end.** *{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{星期六|xīng qī liù}. Put the time before the
  verb: {我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{工作|gōng zuò}.
- **{不|bù} without {是|shì}.** *{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{星期一|xīng qī yī}. Say {今天|jīn tiān}{不是|bú shì}{星期一|xīng qī yī}.
- **"Seventh day".** There's no {星期七|xīng qī qī}. Sunday is {星期天|xīng qī tiān} or {星期日|xīng qī rì}.
- **A month vs a month name.** {一月|yī yuè} is January; one month is {一个月|yí gè yuè}.
- **{个|gè} with {天|tiān} and {年|nián}.** *{两个天|liǎng gè tiān}: say {两天|liǎng tiān}, {两年|liǎng nián}.
- **Reading years as numbers.** 2026 is *èr líng èr liù*, not *liǎng qiān líng èr shí liù*.

## Key points

- {昨天|zuó tiān}, {今天|jīn tiān}, {明天|míng tiān}: time words go before the verb, after the subject
  or at the front.
- Weekdays: {星期|xīng qī} + {一|yī} to {六|liù}; Sunday {星期天|xīng qī tiān} (spoken) or {星期日|xīng qī rì}
  (written). Ask {星期几|xīng qī jǐ}？
- Months: number + {月|yuè}. Dates: number + {号|hào} (spoken) or {日|rì} (written). Ask {几月几号|jǐ yuè jǐ hào}？
- Big to small: year, month, day, weekday. Years are read digit by digit, {一|yī} stays *yī*.
- {年|nián} and {天|tiān} count without {个|gè}: {两天|liǎng tiān}, {三年|sān nián}; {星期|xīng qī} and {月|yuè} take {个|gè}.
- Noun predicates: {今天|jīn tiān}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。 The negative needs {是|shì}: {不是|bú shì}.
- New characters: 今 天 明 昨 星 期 号 年.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling the time
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 6 gave you the calendar: days, weeks, months and years, always from the biggest unit to the
smallest. Now the clock. By the end of this lesson you can ask and tell the time, say "half
past", give the part of the day (morning, noon, afternoon), say when you do something, and say for
how long: the difference between "two o'clock" and "two hours", which English makes with the same
word and Chinese doesn't.

Ten new characters come with it, five of them in the words {上午|shàng wǔ}, {中午|zhōng wǔ} and
{下午|xià wǔ}, which you'll read on every timetable.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 点 (traditional 點) | dot; o'clock | diǎn | 灬 | 9 | {点|diǎn}, {几点|jǐ diǎn}, {一点儿|yì diǎnr} (a little: lesson 12) |
| 分 | divide; minute | fēn | 刀 | 4 | {分|fēn}, {分钟|fēn zhōng} |
| 钟 (traditional 鐘) | clock, bell | zhōng | 钅 | 9 | {分钟|fēn zhōng} |
| 半 | half | bàn | 十 | 5 | {半|bàn}, {一半|yí bàn} (lesson 15) |
| 时 (traditional 時) | time; hour | shí | 日 | 7 | {小时|xiǎo shí}, {时间|shí jiān}, {时候|shí hou} (lesson 25) |
| 现 (traditional 現) | appear; present | xiàn | 王 | 8 | {现在|xiàn zài} |
| 间 (traditional 間) | between; room | jiān | 门 | 7 | {时间|shí jiān}, {房间|fáng jiān} (room: lesson 17) |
| 上 | up, above; earlier | shàng (and others) | 一 | 3 | {上午|shàng wǔ}, {早上|zǎo shang} (lesson 8) |
| 午 | noon | wǔ | 十 | 4 | {上午|shàng wǔ}, {中午|zhōng wǔ}, {下午|xià wǔ} |
| 下 | down, below; later | xià | 一 | 3 | {下午|xià wǔ}, {下班|xià bān} (lesson 8) |

上 is *shàng* on its own and in {上午|shàng wǔ}, but neutral, *shang*, in {早上|zǎo shang} and
{晚上|wǎn shang} (lesson 8). The pinyin over each word always shows the right one.

How the shapes work:

- 上 and 下: a short mark above or below a line. They are among the few characters that are
  simply signs for an idea ("indicatives"), like 一, 二, 三. In {上午|shàng wǔ} and
  {下午|xià wǔ} they mean "before" and "after": the part of the day before noon and the part after.
- 分: 八 on top (which once meant "split apart") and 刀, a knife, below: cutting something into
  parts. A minute is a part of an hour.
- 半: in its old form, 八 (split) over 牛 (an ox): an ox cut down the middle, in half.
- 钟 and 时 are sound-and-meaning characters. 钟 is metal 钅 + 中 *zhōng* for the sound: a bell,
  then a clock. 时 is the sun 日 + 寸; in the traditional form 時 the right side is 寺 *sì*, a
  sound hint.
- 现: 王 here is really "jade" (see below) and 见 is "see". It's usually explained as the gleam of
  jade catching the eye: "to appear", and from there "present, now".
- 间: the sun 日 shining through a gap in a door 门. That's the traditional explanation, and the
  older form 閒 showed the moon in the door. A gap is something "between", and the word
  {时间|shí jiān} is "time", the stretch between moments.
- 点: in the traditional form 點, the four dots at the bottom belong to 黑 "black": a small black
  spot, a dot. The hours on a clock face are dots.
- 午 (memory aid only): a pole at midday. Don't confuse it with 牛 (ox, lesson 14): in 牛 the
  vertical stroke pokes up through the top; in 午 it starts below the first stroke.

### New radicals: 钅, 王, 灬

- **钅** "metal" ({金字旁|jīn zì páng}): the side form of 金 (gold, metal). Seven characters of the
  track have it. So far: 钟. Next comes 钱 (money, lesson 13). It has five strokes, the last
  one a vertical that turns up to the right; 金 on its own has eight.
- **王** "jade" ({王字旁|wáng zì páng}, also called {斜玉旁|xié yù páng}, "slanting jade side"): it
  looks like 王 *wáng* (king; the common surname 王 of {王芳|Wáng Fāng}), but on the left of a
  character it stands for 玉 "jade". Six characters of the track have it. So far: 现. Next:
  班 (shift, class: lesson 8) and 玩 (play: lesson 22). On the left, its last stroke rises to the
  right instead of lying flat.
- **灬** "fire" ({四点底|sì diǎn dǐ}, "four-dot bottom"): the form 火 (fire) takes at the bottom of
  a character. Five characters of the track have it. So far: 点. Next: 热 (hot, lesson 20). (In
  点 itself, as you saw, the dots come from 黑 "black"; dictionaries still file it here.)

### Stroke order

- 上: the vertical first, then the short horizontal, then the long base.
- 下: the top horizontal first, then the vertical, then the dot.
- 半 and 分: the two short strokes at the top come first (left, then right).
- 间 and other characters with 门: the dot, then the left vertical, then the right side that turns
  down into a hook, and only then what's inside.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
点分钟半时
```

```trace
现间上午下
```

✎ **Write it**: nine of these ten are characters the new HSK expects you to write by hand by
level 2: 点 分 半 时 现 间 上 午 下 (all but 钟). Write each three times on paper or the pad,
from memory, then check them.
=}

## What time is it? {现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？

{现在|xiàn zài} is "now", a time word like {今天|jīn tiān}. {点|diǎn} is "o'clock", and {几点|jǐ diǎn} asks
"what o'clock?":

{现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？ — What time is it (now)?

{现在|xiàn zài}{八点|bā diǎn}。 — It's eight o'clock.

The answer is a noun predicate again (lesson 6): no verb, no {是|shì} needed. {几点|jǐ diǎn} is two third
tones, said *jí diǎn*.

The hours are number + {点|diǎn}:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {一点|yī diǎn} 1:00 | {四点|sì diǎn} 4:00 | {七点|qī diǎn} 7:00 | {十点|shí diǎn} 10:00 |
| {两点|liǎng diǎn} 2:00 | {五点|wǔ diǎn} 5:00 | {八点|bā diǎn} 8:00 | {十一点|shí yī diǎn} 11:00 |
| {三点|sān diǎn} 3:00 | {六点|liù diǎn} 6:00 | {九点|jiǔ diǎn} 9:00 | {十二点|shí èr diǎn} 12:00 |

One hour is different: two o'clock is {两点|liǎng diǎn}, never *{二点|èr diǎn}. {点|diǎn} counts like
a measure word, and before a measure word "two" is {两|liǎng} (lesson 4). But twelve o'clock is
{十二点|shí èr diǎn}: inside a bigger number it's always {二|èr}. And one o'clock is *yī diǎn*: in a
clock time, {一|yī} is a number on the dial and keeps its tone.

## Minutes and half past: {分|fēn} and {半|bàn}

Minutes are number + {分|fēn}, after the hour. Biggest unit first, as with dates:

{九点十分|jiǔ diǎn shí fēn} — 9:10

{三点四十五分|sān diǎn sì shí wǔ fēn} — 3:45

{八点零五分|bā diǎn líng wǔ fēn} — 8:05

With a single-figure minute, people usually say {零|líng} before it, as in a written time with "05":
{八点零五分|bā diǎn líng wǔ fēn}. (You'll also hear {八点五分|bā diǎn wǔ fēn}; both are fine.) With
ten minutes or more, {分|fēn} is often dropped in speech: {九点二十|jiǔ diǎn èr shí} is 9:20.

{半|bàn} is "half". After the hour it's half past:

{七点半|qī diǎn bàn} — 7:30 (half past seven)

{七点三十分|qī diǎn sān shí fēn} says the same thing; {半|bàn} is what people normally say.

You'll also hear two other ways to give the time, which belong to later levels: {一刻|yí kè}, a
quarter of an hour ({八点一刻|bā diǎn yí kè}, 8:15), and {差|chà}, "short of"
({差五分九点|chà wǔ fēn jiǔ diǎn}, five to nine). It's enough to recognise them for now.

## Parts of the day: {上午|shàng wǔ}, {中午|zhōng wǔ}, {下午|xià wǔ}

| Word | Meaning | Roughly |
|---|---|---|
| {上午|shàng wǔ} | morning (before noon) | until about 11 or 12 |
| {中午|zhōng wǔ} | noon, midday | about 11 to 1 |
| {下午|xià wǔ} | afternoon | from noon or 1 to about 6 |

{午|wǔ} is noon: {上午|shàng wǔ} is the part above, before it; {中午|zhōng wǔ} the middle of it;
{下午|xià wǔ} the part below, after it. These words go **before** the clock time, never after it as
"a.m." and "p.m." do in English. Big to small again:

{上午|shàng wǔ}{十点|shí diǎn} — 10 a.m.

{下午|xià wǔ}{三点半|sān diǎn bàn} — 3:30 p.m.

{中午|zhōng wǔ}{十二点|shí èr diǎn} — 12 noon

Lesson 8 adds the early morning and the evening ({早上|zǎo shang}, {晚上|wǎn shang}). Timetables,
tickets and phones often use the 24-hour clock instead, written in figures: 14:30 is said
{十四点三十|shí sì diǎn sān shí} or, in everyday speech, {下午|xià wǔ}{两点半|liǎng diǎn bàn}.

## When: before the verb

A time when something happens is a time word (lesson 6), and it goes before the verb, after
the subject or at the front:

{我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。 — I have class at eight. ({上课|shàng kè}, to have class: lesson 19)

{下午|xià wǔ}{两点|liǎng diǎn}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 — At two in the afternoon I'm at home.

{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{上午|shàng wǔ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}，{下午|xià wǔ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}。 —
Teacher Wang is at school in the morning and at the office in the afternoon.

With a day and a clock time together, the day comes first: {明天|míng tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{三点|sān diǎn}
(tomorrow at 3 p.m.). Lesson 8 practises long time phrases like this one.

You don't need a word for "at": {八点|bā diǎn} alone means "at eight".

## How long: {小时|xiǎo shí} and {分钟|fēn zhōng}

English uses "hour" and "minute" for both the clock and an amount of time: "at two" but "for two
hours", "ten past" but "ten minutes". Chinese keeps them apart:

| A point on the clock | An amount of time |
|---|---|
| {两点|liǎng diǎn} two o'clock | {两个小时|liǎng gè xiǎo shí} two hours |
| {十分|shí fēn} ten minutes past (the hour) | {十分钟|shí fēn zhōng} ten minutes |
| {半|bàn} half past | {半个小时|bàn gè xiǎo shí} half an hour |

An amount of time is a **[[duration]]**. {小时|xiǎo shí} (hour) is a noun and normally takes the measure
word {个|gè}: {一个小时|yí gè xiǎo shí} (one hour; *yí* before the fourth tone of {个|gè}), {三个小时|sān gè xiǎo shí}
(three hours), {几个小时|jǐ gè xiǎo shí} (how many hours). In writing you'll also see
{一小时|yì xiǎo shí} without {个|gè}. {分钟|fēn zhōng} (minute) is a measure word itself, so no {个|gè}:
{十分钟|shí fēn zhōng}, {五分钟|wǔ fēn zhōng}.

One and a half hours puts {半|bàn} after the measure word: {一个半小时|yí gè bàn xiǎo shí}, not
*{一个小时半|yí gè xiǎo shí bàn}.

Where does a duration go? **After the verb**, the opposite of a time when:

{我|wǒ}{一天|yì tiān}{工作|gōng zuò}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}。 — I work eight hours a day.

{你|nǐ}{一天|yì tiān}{工作|gōng zuò}{几个小时|jǐ gè xiǎo shí}？ — How many hours a day do you work?

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{半个小时|bàn gè xiǎo shí}。 — I have half an hour.

Compare: {我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{工作|gōng zuò} — I work at eight (when: before the verb).
{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí} — I work for eight hours (how long: after the verb).
A handy way to remember it: the time when sets the scene before the action starts; the duration
measures the action once it's said.

## Time: {时间|shí jiān}

{时间|shí jiān} is "time" as an amount you have, use or don't have:

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{吗|ma}？ — Do you have time?

{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。 — I don't have time now.

It's not used to ask the clock time: "What time is it?" is {现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？, not
{时间|shí jiān}. And "when" is another word again, {什么时候|shén me shí hou}, literally "what time":
you'll hear it all the time, and lesson 25 teaches {时候|shí hou} properly.

## Pronunciation

- Third tones meet often in times: {几点|jǐ diǎn}, {两点|liǎng diǎn}, {九点|jiǔ diǎn}, {五点|wǔ diǎn}
  are all said with a rising first syllable: *jí diǎn, liáng diǎn, jiú diǎn, wú diǎn*. The pinyin
  keeps the dictionary tones; your voice makes the change.
- {分钟|fēn zhōng}: two first tones, high and level. *zh* is like the "j" in "jam" with the tongue
  curled back.
- {小时|xiǎo shí}: third, then second. *sh* is curled back too; *shí* rises.
- {现在|xiàn zài}: two falling tones. *x* is a soft "sh" with the tongue tip down; *z* is "ds".
- {上午|shàng wǔ} and {下午|xià wǔ}: fourth, then third. Let the *wǔ* stay low.
- {半|bàn} falls sharply. Don't confuse it with 班 *bān* (in {上班|shàng bān}, lesson 8), which is high
  and level.

```speak
{现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？
= What time is it now?
{现在|xiàn zài}{两点|liǎng diǎn}。
= It's two o'clock.
{现在|xiàn zài}{九点半|jiǔ diǎn bàn}。
= It's half past nine.
{下午|xià wǔ}{三点十分|sān diǎn shí fēn}。
= 3:10 p.m.
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{十分钟|shí fēn zhōng}。
= I have ten minutes.
{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{吗|ma}？
= Do you have time?
```

## Dialogue: do you have time?

{孙丽|Sūn Lì} works at a company; {大卫|Dà wèi} (David) is a student she knows.

```dialogue
# Before class
大卫: {孙丽|Sūn Lì}，{现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？
= Sun Li, what time is it?
孙丽: {现在|xiàn zài}{十点半|shí diǎn bàn}。
= It's half past ten.
大卫: {十点半|shí diǎn bàn}？{我|wǒ}{十一点|shí yī diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。
= Half past ten? I have class at eleven.
孙丽: {你|nǐ}{现在|xiàn zài}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{吗|ma}？
= Do you have time now?
大卫: {有|yǒu}，{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{半个小时|bàn gè xiǎo shí}。
= Yes, I have half an hour.
孙丽: {中午|zhōng wǔ}{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{吗|ma}？
= Are you at school at noon?
大卫: {在|zài}。{下午|xià wǔ}{两点|liǎng diǎn}{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。
= Yes. I'm at school at two in the afternoon too.
孙丽: {我|wǒ}{下午|xià wǔ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}，{我|wǒ}{一天|yì tiān}{工作|gōng zuò}{九个小时|jiǔ gè xiǎo shí}。
= I'm at the office in the afternoon. I work nine hours a day.
```

Look at the answers: {有|yǒu} and {在|zài} on their own mean "yes". Chinese answers a yes/no
question by repeating the verb, and lesson 26 has more on this. And notice both kinds of time:
{十一点|shí yī diǎn} before {上课|shàng kè}, {九个小时|jiǔ gè xiǎo shí} after {工作|gōng zuò}.

## Reading: opening times

> **{上课|shàng kè}{时间|shí jiān}**
>
> {星期一|xīng qī yī} — {星期五|xīng qī wǔ}
>
> {上午|shàng wǔ} 8:00 — 12:00
>
> {下午|xià wǔ} 1:30 — 5:30
>
> {星期六|xīng qī liù}、{星期日|xīng qī rì}：{没有|méi yǒu}{课|kè}

A school's class times ({上课|shàng kè}{时间|shí jiān}): Monday to Friday, 8 to 12 in the morning and
1:30 to 5:30 in the afternoon. On Saturday and Sunday there are no classes ({没有|méi yǒu}{课|kè}: {课|kè}, class or lesson, is a
lesson-19 word). Signs like this use figures for times and {星期日|xīng qī rì}, the written word
for Sunday. How long is the morning session? Four hours: {四个小时|sì gè xiǎo shí}.

## Common mistakes

- ***{二点|èr diǎn}.** Two o'clock is {两点|liǎng diǎn}. But 12:00 is {十二点|shí èr diǎn}.
- **{下午|xià wǔ} after the time.** *{三点|sān diǎn}{下午|xià wǔ} is English order. Say
  {下午|xià wǔ}{三点|sān diǎn}.
- **A clock time for a duration.** "Two hours" is {两个小时|liǎng gè xiǎo shí}, not {两点|liǎng diǎn}
  (two o'clock). "Ten minutes" is {十分钟|shí fēn zhōng}, not {十分|shí fēn} (ten past).
- **Duration before the verb.** *{我|wǒ}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}{工作|gōng zuò}: a duration follows
  the verb, {我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}.
- **Time when after the verb.** *{我|wǒ}{上课|shàng kè}{八点|bā diǎn}: say
  {我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}.
- **{个|gè} with {分钟|fēn zhōng}, or {半|bàn} in the wrong place.** {十分钟|shí fēn zhōng} (no {个|gè});
  {一个半小时|yí gè bàn xiǎo shí} (not {一个小时半|yí gè xiǎo shí bàn}).
- **{时间|shí jiān} for the clock time.** Ask {几点|jǐ diǎn}？

## Key points

- {现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？ — {现在|xiàn zài}{八点|bā diǎn}。 Hours: number + {点|diǎn}; two
  o'clock is {两点|liǎng diǎn}.
- Minutes: number + {分|fēn} ({零|líng} before a single figure); half past: {半|bàn}.
- {上午|shàng wǔ}, {中午|zhōng wǔ}, {下午|xià wǔ} go before the clock time.
- Time when: before the verb ({我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}). Duration: after it
  ({工作|gōng zuò}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}).
- {点|diǎn} vs {小时|xiǎo shí}, {分|fēn} vs {分钟|fēn zhōng}: a point on the clock vs an amount of time.
- {时间|shí jiān}: time you have ({有时间|yǒu shí jiān}); "when" is {什么时候|shén me shí hou} (lesson 25).
- New characters: 点 分 钟 半 时 现 间 上 午 下.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: My day
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now give a date (lesson 6) and a clock time (lesson 7). This lesson puts them to work in
the most useful kind of conversation at this level: your day. When do you get up, start work,
have lunch, finish, eat dinner, go to bed?

By the end you can describe a daily routine from morning to night, put several time words in the
right order ({明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}, tomorrow at seven in the morning), say
"early" and "late", greet someone in the morning, and you'll meet a kind of verb that behaves
unlike any English verb: the separable verb.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 早 | early; morning | zǎo | 日 | 6 | {早上|zǎo shang}, {早饭|zǎo fàn}, {早|zǎo} |
| 晚 | late; evening | wǎn | 日 | 11 | {晚上|wǎn shang}, {晚饭|wǎn fàn}, {晚|wǎn} |
| 起 | rise, get up | qǐ | 走 | 10 | {起床|qǐ chuáng}, {对不起|duì bu qǐ} |
| 床 | bed | chuáng | 广 | 7 | {起床|qǐ chuáng} |
| 睡 | sleep | shuì | 目 | 13 | {睡觉|shuì jiào}, {睡|shuì} (lesson 21) |
| 觉 (traditional 覺) | sleep (noun); feel | jiào (and others) | 见 | 9 | {睡觉|shuì jiào}, {觉得|jué de} (to feel, think: lesson 20) |
| 班 | shift; class | bān | 王 | 10 | {上班|shàng bān}, {下班|xià bān} |
| 饭 (traditional 飯) | cooked rice; meal | fàn | 饣 | 7 | {早饭|zǎo fàn}, {午饭|wǔ fàn}, {晚饭|wǎn fàn} |

觉 has two readings: *jiào* "a sleep" in {睡觉|shuì jiào}, and *jué* "to feel" in {觉得|jué de}
(lesson 20). Learn each one inside its word.

How the shapes work:

- 晚, 饭 and 起 are sound-and-meaning characters. 晚: the sun 日 (time of day) + 免 *miǎn*. 饭:
  food 饣 + 反 *fǎn*. 起: walk 走 + 己 *jǐ*. The sound hints are rough, as they often are: Chinese
  pronunciation has changed a lot since these characters were made.
- 睡: an eye 目 + 垂 *chuí* "to droop": eyelids drooping, sleep.
- 班: two pieces of jade 王 王 with a knife between them (the middle strokes). Cutting jade into
  parts led to "dividing", then to "a group, a shift, a class".
- 床: in today's form, a shelter 广 with wood 木 inside: the wooden bed in the house. The older
  form 牀 has 爿, a drawing of a bed stood on its end, where 床 has 广.
- 觉: in the traditional form 覺, the top is the top of 學 (study), a sound hint, and 见 (see) is
  at the bottom: waking up and seeing clearly.
- 早 (memory aid only): the sun 日 just above a cross 十, the horizon. Early.

Watch the right side of 起: it's 己 *jǐ*, whose left side is open at the top. Two look-alikes
come later, 已 (already) and 巳 (a zodiac sign), which close it more.

### New radicals: 目, 饣, 走

- **目** "eye" ({目字旁|mù zì páng}): nine characters of the track. So far: 睡. Next: 看 (look,
  lesson 9), where the eye is under a hand, and 真 (really, lesson 15). Don't confuse 目 (two
  inner strokes) with 日 (one).
- **饣** "food" ({食字旁|shí zì páng}): the side form of 食 (food). Six characters of the track have
  it. So far: 饭. You'll also see it in 饺 of {饺子|jiǎo zi} (dumplings, lesson 11). Three
  strokes: a left-falling stroke, a short horizontal that hooks down, and a vertical that turns up.
- **走** "walk" ({走字旁|zǒu zì páng}): 走 is "to walk" itself. Five characters of the track have
  it. So far: 起. Next: 超 in {超市|chāo shì} (supermarket, lesson 14). On the left, 走 stretches its
  last stroke along the bottom, under the other part.

### Stroke order

- 起: write all seven strokes of 走 first, including the long sweep along the bottom, then 己.
- 班: the left 王 (its last stroke rising), then the dot and the left-falling stroke in the
  middle, then the right 王 (its last stroke flat and long).
- 饭: the three strokes of 饣 first, then 反.
- 觉: the three short strokes on top (left, middle, right), then the cover 冖, then 见.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
早晚起床睡觉班饭
```

✎ **Write it**: none of this lesson's characters is on the handwriting list, but 早 and 晚 are
short and common. Write each three times from memory if you'd like the practice.
=}

## From morning to night

| Word | Meaning | Roughly |
|---|---|---|
| {早上|zǎo shang} | (early) morning | from getting up to about 9 |
| {上午|shàng wǔ} | morning (before noon) | until about 11 or 12 (lesson 7) |
| {中午|zhōng wǔ} | noon, midday | about 11 to 1 |
| {下午|xià wǔ} | afternoon | until about 6 |
| {晚上|wǎn shang} | evening; night | from about 6 until bedtime |

{早上|zǎo shang} and {上午|shàng wǔ} overlap. {早上|zǎo shang} is the early part, when you get up
and have breakfast; {上午|shàng wǔ} is the whole morning up to noon, the time of morning classes and
meetings. {早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn} (7 a.m.) sounds right; {上午|shàng wǔ}{十点|shí diǎn} (10 a.m.)
too. {晚上|wǎn shang} covers both the evening and the night until people go to sleep: {晚上|wǎn shang}{十一点|shí yī diǎn}
is 11 p.m.

In {早上|zǎo shang} and {晚上|wǎn shang}, {上|shàng} is neutral: *zǎo shang*, *wǎn shang*. In {上午|shàng wǔ}
it keeps its tone.

## Big to small: long time phrases

When you give a day and a time together, they line up from the biggest unit to the smallest, as
dates do (lesson 6):

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn} | tomorrow at 7 a.m. |
| {星期六|xīng qī liù}{晚上|wǎn shang}{八点半|bā diǎn bàn} | on Saturday at 8:30 p.m. |
| {昨天|zuó tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{三点|sān diǎn} | yesterday at 3 p.m. |
| {十一月|shí yī yuè}{二十号|èr shí hào}{上午|shàng wǔ}{十点|shí diǎn} | on 20 November at 10 a.m. |

English goes the other way ("at 7 a.m. tomorrow"), so this is worth practising aloud. The whole
phrase is one time word and sits **before the verb**, after the subject or at the front:

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 — I'm getting up at seven
tomorrow morning.

{明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}{我|wǒ}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 — Same meaning.

A useful pattern: the day can go in front and the clock time after the subject, but not the other
way round: {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{七点|qī diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng} is fine, *{七点|qī diǎn}{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{起床|qǐ chuáng}
is not. Bigger before smaller, always.

## Routine verbs: {起床|qǐ chuáng}, {睡觉|shuì jiào}, {上班|shàng bān}, {下班|xià bān}

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {起床|qǐ chuáng} | to get up (out of bed) |
| {睡觉|shuì jiào} | to sleep; to go to bed |
| {上班|shàng bān} | to go to work, start work |
| {下班|xià bān} | to finish work, leave work |

{上|shàng} and {下|xià} here mean "go on" and "come off" a shift ({班|bān}). You'll see the same
pair in {上课|shàng kè} and {下课|xià kè} (start and finish class, lesson 19).

{我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 — I get up at half past six.

{他|tā}{晚上|wǎn shang}{十一点|shí yī diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。 — He goes to bed at eleven at night.

{你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{上班|shàng bān}？ — What time do you start work?

{我|wǒ}{下午|xià wǔ}{五点|wǔ diǎn}{下班|xià bān}。 — I finish work at five.

These sentences describe a habit, but Chinese doesn't need a word for "usually" or "every day" to
say so: {我|wǒ}{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{起床|qǐ chuáng} can mean "I (always) get up at 6:30" or "I'm
getting up at 6:30 (today)", and the situation makes it clear. When you want "every day", the
word is {每天|měi tiān}, which comes in HSK 2.

## Meals: {早饭|zǎo fàn}, {午饭|wǔ fàn}, {晚饭|wǎn fàn}

{饭|fàn} is cooked rice and, by extension, a meal. Put a time of day in front and you have the three
meals:

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {早饭|zǎo fàn} | breakfast |
| {午饭|wǔ fàn} | lunch |
| {晚饭|wǎn fàn} | dinner, supper |

The verb is {吃|chī}, to eat (lesson 11 teaches it properly):

{我|wǒ}{七点|qī diǎn}{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn}。 — I have breakfast at seven.

{你|nǐ}{中午|zhōng wǔ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{吃|chī}{午饭|wǔ fàn}{吗|ma}？ — Do you have lunch at the
office?

Look at the word order there: subject, time ({中午|zhōng wǔ}), place ({在|zài}{公司|gōng sī},
lesson 5), verb, object. **Time before place**, both before the verb: that's the normal order in
Chinese.

## Early and late: {早|zǎo} and {晚|wǎn}

{早|zǎo} and {晚|wǎn} are adjectives, "early" and "late". Like other adjectives (lesson 1) they
usually take {很|hěn} when they're the predicate, and they need no {是|shì}:

{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo}！ — You're early!

{晚上|wǎn shang}{十二点|shí èr diǎn}{很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}。 — Midnight is late.

{八点|bā diǎn}{上班|shàng bān}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo}{吗|ma}？ — Is starting at eight early?

{很早|hěn zǎo} and {很晚|hěn wǎn} are two third tones: said *hén zǎo*, *hén wǎn*.

{早|zǎo} is also a greeting. In the morning, people who know each other say {早|zǎo}！ or
{你早|nǐ zǎo}！ (said *ní zǎo*), "Morning!". {早上好|zǎo shang hǎo} (good morning) is a little more
formal; you'll hear it in shops, schools and offices. {下午好|xià wǔ hǎo} (good afternoon) and
{晚上好|wǎn shang hǎo} (good evening) exist too, but they belong to presenters, meetings and other
formal moments; in everyday life, after the morning, {你好|nǐ hǎo} does the job.

## Separable verbs

Look inside {睡觉|shuì jiào}: {睡|shuì} is "to sleep" and {觉|jiào} is "a sleep", a noun. The word is
built like "to sleep a sleep": a verb with its own object already inside. {起床|qǐ chuáng} is "rise
(from) bed", {上班|shàng bān} "go on (a) shift". Words like these are **[[separable verbs]]**: in some
sentences the two parts come apart and other words go between them.

You don't need to split them yet. What matters now is a consequence: because the object is
already inside, **nothing else can come straight after the word as an object**. English says "I
slept eight hours", but *{睡觉|shuì jiào}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí} is wrong. Chinese either uses the
verb alone ({睡|shuì}, lesson 21), or puts the duration inside the word, between the verb and its
noun: {睡|shuì}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}{的|de}{觉|jiào}, "sleep an eight-hour sleep". Just recognise
that for now; lessons 19 and 21 come back to it.

Asking and answering work on the whole word, as with any verb:

{你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}？ — What time do you go to bed?

{我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{不|bú}{上班|shàng bān}。 — I don't work on Saturdays. (*bú* before the
fourth tone of {上|shàng})

## Pronunciation

- {早|zǎo}: *z* (like "ds") and a low dip. {早饭|zǎo fàn} is third then fourth: the *zǎo* stays low,
  then *fàn* falls.
- {起床|qǐ chuáng}: *q* (like "ch" with the tongue tip down) then *ch* (like "ch" in "church" with
  the tongue curled back). The two sound different: practise *qǐ … chuáng* slowly.
- {睡觉|shuì jiào}: two falling tones. *sh* curled back, *j* tongue tip down.
- {上班|shàng bān}, {下班|xià bān}: fourth then first. {班|bān} is high and level, not falling like
  {半|bàn} (half).
- {晚上|wǎn shang}, {早上|zǎo shang}: third tone, then neutral. After a third tone, the neutral
  syllable is a little higher than you might expect.

```speak
{早|zǎo}！
= Morning!
{你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}？
= What time do you get up?
{我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。
= I get up at half past six.
{我|wǒ}{七点|qī diǎn}{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn}，{八点|bā diǎn}{上班|shàng bān}。
= I have breakfast at seven and start work at eight.
{我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{十一点|shí yī diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= I go to bed at eleven at night.
{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo}！
= You're early!
```

## Dialogue: early bird

{孙丽|Sūn Lì} works at a company; {安娜|Ān nà} is a student. They meet outside their building one morning.

```dialogue
# Good morning
孙丽: {安娜|Ān nà}，{早|zǎo}！
= Morning, Anna!
安娜: {早|zǎo}！{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo}！
= Morning! You're early!
孙丽: {我|wǒ}{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{上班|shàng bān}。{你|nǐ}{早上|zǎo shang}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}？
= I start work at half past six. What time do you get up in the morning?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{六点|liù diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}，{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I get up at six and have breakfast at half past six. And you?
孙丽: {我|wǒ}{五点半|wǔ diǎn bàn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn}。
= I get up at half past five. I have breakfast at the office.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{下班|xià bān}？
= What time do you finish work?
孙丽: {下午|xià wǔ}{四点|sì diǎn}。{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn}，{十点|shí diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= At four in the afternoon. In the evening I have dinner at home and go to bed at ten.
安娜: {十点|shí diǎn}？{我|wǒ}{十二点|shí èr diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= Ten? I go to bed at twelve.
孙丽: {十二点|shí èr diǎn}？{很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}！
= Twelve? That's late!
```

Notice {早|zǎo} as the greeting and as the adjective in {你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo},
and the order in {晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn}: time, subject,
place, verb, object.

## Reading: a day in figures

Here is {孙丽|Sūn Lì}'s weekday as she wrote it on a note:

| Time | |
|---|---|
| 5:30 | {起床|qǐ chuáng} |
| 6:30 | {上班|shàng bān}，{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn} |
| 12:00 | {吃|chī}{午饭|wǔ fàn} |
| 4:00 | {下班|xià bān} |
| 7:00 | {吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn} |
| 10:00 | {睡觉|shuì jiào} |

And as sentences:

> {我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{五点半|wǔ diǎn bàn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}，{六点半|liù diǎn bàn}{上班|shàng bān}。{中午|zhōng wǔ}{十二点|shí èr diǎn}{吃|chī}{午饭|wǔ fàn}。{下午|xià wǔ}{四点|sì diǎn}{下班|xià bān}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{七点|qī diǎn}{吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn}，{十点|shí diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

I get up at half past five in the morning and start work at half past six. I have lunch at twelve
noon. I finish work at four in the afternoon, have dinner at seven in the evening and go to bed at
ten.

</details>

How many hours is her working day? From 6:30 to 4:00: {九个半小时|jiǔ gè bàn xiǎo shí}, nine and a
half hours.

## Common mistakes

- **Small before big.** *{七点|qī diǎn}{明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}: say {明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}.
- **Time words after the verb.** *{我|wǒ}{起床|qǐ chuáng}{六点|liù diǎn}: say {我|wǒ}{六点|liù diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}.
- **Place before time.** {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{晚上|wǎn shang}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn} sounds wrong; the
  normal order is time, then place: {我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}.
- **An object after a separable verb.** *{睡觉|shuì jiào}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}. Recognise
  {睡|shuì}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}{的|de}{觉|jiào}; lesson 21 has the simple way.
- **{是|shì} with {早|zǎo} and {晚|wǎn}.** *{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{早|zǎo}: adjectives take {很|hěn}, not {是|shì}:
  {你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo}.
- **{早上|zǎo shang} for 10 a.m.** By ten it's {上午|shàng wǔ}.

## Key points

- The day: {早上|zǎo shang}, {上午|shàng wǔ}, {中午|zhōng wǔ}, {下午|xià wǔ}, {晚上|wǎn shang}.
- Long time phrases go big to small ({明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}) and sit before
  the verb. Time comes before place.
- {起床|qǐ chuáng}, {睡觉|shuì jiào}, {上班|shàng bān}, {下班|xià bān}; meals {早饭|zǎo fàn},
  {午饭|wǔ fàn}, {晚饭|wǎn fàn} with {吃|chī}.
- {早|zǎo}, {晚|wǎn}: adjectives with {很|hěn}. {早|zǎo}！ / {你早|nǐ zǎo}！ is "Morning!".
- Separable verbs ({睡觉|shuì jiào}, {起床|qǐ chuáng}, {上班|shàng bān}) have an object inside, so no
  other object follows them.
- New characters: 早 晚 起 床 睡 觉 班 饭.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Going and coming: 去, 来, 想, 要
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far your sentences have mostly been about being somewhere: {在|zài}{家|jiā}, {在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}.
Now people move. This lesson teaches going, coming and going back, saying where to and what for,
and saying what you'd like to do or are going to do. With the time words of lessons 6 to 8 you
can then make plans: "On Saturday I'd like to go to the shops and buy some things."

The grammar is pleasantly simple: no word for "to" before a place, and no word for "to" or "in
order to" before a purpose. Chinese just puts the verbs in a row, in the order things happen.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 去 | go | qù | 厶 | 5 | {去|qù}, {去年|qù nián} (last year: lesson 25) |
| 来 (traditional 來) | come | lái | 木 | 7 | {来|lái} |
| 回 | return | huí | 囗 | 6 | {回|huí}, {回家|huí jiā} |
| 想 | think; want to; miss | xiǎng | 心 | 13 | {想|xiǎng} |
| 要 | want; will | yào (and others) | 覀 | 9 | {要|yào}, {不要|bú yào} (don't: lesson 21) |
| 做 | do, make | zuò | 亻 | 11 | {做|zuò}, {做饭|zuò fàn} (to cook: lesson 12) |
| 事 | matter, business | shì | 亅 | 8 | {事|shì}, {没事|méi shì} (lesson 21) |
| 东 (traditional 東) | east | dōng | 一 | 5 | {东西|dōng xi} |
| 西 | west | xī (and others) | 西 | 6 | {东西|dōng xi} |
| 买 (traditional 買) | buy | mǎi | 大 | 6 | {买|mǎi}, {买东西|mǎi dōng xi} |
| 看 | look, watch, read | kàn | 目 | 9 | {看|kàn}, {好看|hǎo kàn} (good-looking: lesson 15) |

Dictionaries disagree about a few of these radicals: 来 is filed under 木 here (and under 一 in
many modern dictionaries), and 买 under 大 (others put it under its first stroke). 要 and 西 show
the same top, 覀, the form 西 takes when something sits below it.

How the shapes work:

- 来: the oldest form is a drawing of a wheat plant. The word for "come" sounded the same, so it
  borrowed the picture. Many characters were "borrowed" like this.
- 要: also borrowed. It first drew a person with hands on their waist (the word for "waist" is
  *yāo*, now written 腰).
- 看: a hand 手 (flattened on top) held over an eye 目, shading it to look into the distance.
- 回: a swirl, one square turning inside another: going round and coming back.
- 买: in the traditional form 買, a net 罒 over a shell 貝. Shells were money in early China: you
  "net" goods with money.
- 想: 相 *xiāng* gives the sound and 心 (heart) the meaning. Thinking was done with the heart.
- 做: a person 亻 and 故 *gù*. It's a later form of 作 (in {工作|gōng zuò}), with the same meaning.
- 东: people often explain the traditional form 東 as the sun 日 rising behind a tree 木, in the
  east. Historians think the oldest form showed a sack tied at both ends, borrowed for its sound.
- 西: the oldest form is usually read as a bird's nest: birds settle on their nests when the sun
  goes down in the west.
- 去 and 事 (memory aids): 去 is earth 土 over 厶, someone leaving the ground they stood on; 事 is a
  hand holding a stick upright, the long vertical through the middle: getting on with business.

### New radicals: 广, 戈, 雨

None of this lesson's characters uses them, but three characters you know do, and so do some
coming soon:

- **广** "shelter" ({广字旁|guǎng zì páng}): a roof with one wall, a building against a cliff. Five
  characters of the track. So far: 床 (bed, lesson 8). On its own, 广 *guǎng* means "wide", as
  in the city name Guangzhou ({广州|Guǎng zhōu}).
- **戈** "dagger-axe" ({戈字旁|gē zì páng}), an ancient weapon on a long shaft. Four characters of
  the track. So far: 我 (I, from the pinyin course). It's the right side of 我, with the long
  hooked diagonal and the dot at the top right, which is the last stroke of 我.
- **雨** "rain" ({雨字头|yǔ zì tóu}, "rain head"): it sits on top of weather words. Four characters
  of the track. So far: 零 (zero, lesson 4: rain on top, 令 *lìng* below for the sound; it first
  meant falling drops). Next: 雨 (rain) and 雪 (snow) in lesson 20. On top, 雨 is flatter, and its
  four dots are short.

### Stroke order

- 东: the horizontal, then a stroke that falls left and turns right (one stroke), then the vertical
  hook, then the two short strokes left and right.
- 事: the long vertical hook through the middle is the **last** stroke, as in 年 (lesson 6).
- 买: it's 乛 on top of 头 (head, an HSK 2 character). Write 乛 first, then 头 in its own order:
  the two dots, the horizontal, the left-falling stroke, then the last dot.
- 回: the outer box's left side and top-right, then the whole inner 口, then the outer bottom,
  which closes the box last.
- 来: the horizontal, the two short strokes (left, right), the long horizontal, the vertical, then
  left-falling and right-falling.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
去来回想要做
```

```trace
事东西买看
```

✎ **Write it**: 去, 来 and 要 are on the handwriting list. Write each three times on paper or the
pad, from memory, then check them.

## Going, coming and going back: {去|qù}, {来|lái}, {回|huí}

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {去|qù} | to go (away from here) |
| {来|lái} | to come (to here) |
| {回|huí} | to go back, return (home, to where you belong) |

The place comes straight after the verb, with no word for "to":

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}。 — I'm going to school.

{他|tā}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}。 — He's coming to China.

{我|wǒ}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — I'm going home.

{来|lái} and {去|qù} depend on where the speaker is, more strictly than English "come" and "go". If
you're at home on the phone, you say {你|nǐ}{来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？ (Are you coming to my
place?), but if you're at the office talking about home, {我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{回|huí}{家|jiā}
(I go back home in the evening). In English you might say "I'm coming to your party" when you mean
"going": in Chinese, unless you're at the party, it's {去|qù}.

{回|huí} is going back to where you belong: {回家|huí jiā} (go home), {回国|huí guó} (go back to your
country), {回公司|huí gōng sī} (go back to the office).

The time goes before the verb, as always:

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}。 — I'm going to the office tomorrow.

{我|wǒ}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 — I'm not going on Sunday. (*bú* before the fourth
tone of {去|qù}; but {不来|bù lái}, {不回|bù huí}.)

## Where to? {哪儿|nǎr}

{哪儿|nǎr} is "where" in everyday speech: {哪|nǎ} (which, lesson 2) + the erhua ending -r, one syllable.
It goes in the sentence where the answer will go:

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where are you going?

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}。 — I'm going to school.

{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where are you?

{她|tā}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}{工作|gōng zuò}？ — Where does she work?

In the last one, {在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr} comes before the verb, like {在|zài} + place in lesson 5. The
erhua form is typical of Beijing and the north; elsewhere, and in writing, people more often say
{哪里|nǎ lǐ}, which lesson 16 teaches. Both are standard.

Careful with tones: {哪儿|nǎr} (third tone, "where?") is not {那儿|nàr} (fourth tone, "there",
lesson 16).

## Going to do something: verbs in a row

To say why you're going somewhere, add the second action straight after the first:

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — I'm going to the shop to buy some things.
({商店|shāng diàn}, shop: lesson 13)

{你|nǐ}{来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — Come to my place for a meal. ({吃|chī}{饭|fàn},
to eat, have a meal: lesson 11; {吧|ba} makes a suggestion: lesson 12)

{他|tā}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{午饭|wǔ fàn}。 — He goes home for lunch.

{妈妈|mā ma}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{看|kàn}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。 — Mum is going to school to see
Teacher Wang.

There's no word for "to", "for" or "and" between the verbs. A sentence like this, with two or more
verbs (often each with its own object) one after another and the same subject, is a **serial verb
construction**. The order is the order of events: first you go, then you buy. That's why the
purpose comes second, and why the English order "buy things at the shop" doesn't work:
*{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn} sounds like "I buy things, then go to the shop".

Time words and negation go before the first verb, because they cover the whole chain:

{我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — On Saturday I'm going
shopping.

{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bú}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — I'm not going
shopping today.

Questions ask about the part you don't know: {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}？
(What are you going to the shop to buy?)

## Would like to, want to, will: {想|xiǎng} and {要|yào}

Both go before a verb, and both translate as "want to", but they feel different.

**{想|xiǎng}** + verb: would like to, feel like, want to (a wish, gentle):

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}。 — I'd like to go to China.

{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？ — What would you like to do?

**{要|yào}** + verb: want to (firmly), be going to, will (a decision or plan):

{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}。 — I'm going to China. / I want to go to China (and I will).

{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{上班|shàng bān}。 — Tomorrow I have to work / I'm working.

{想|xiǎng} is a wish; {要|yào} sounds decided. When you're unsure, {想|xiǎng} is the polite choice:
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}… is how you start a request in a shop or at a counter. {要|yào} can also take a
noun directly, "want, would like to have": in a café, {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{茶|chá} (I'd like tea;
{茶|chá}, tea: lesson 11) is normal and not rude.

{想|xiǎng} has two more meanings of its own: "to think" ({我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}… "I think…") and "to
miss" someone: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{妈妈|mā ma} — I miss Mum. Said *wó xiǎng* (two third tones).

**The negative** of both is usually {不想|bù xiǎng}: "don't want to".

{我|wǒ}{不想|bù xiǎng}{去|qù}。 — I don't want to go.

{不要|bú yào} + verb usually means "don't!", telling someone not to do something (lesson 21), so
{我|wǒ}{不要|bú yào}{去|qù} sounds like a child refusing. For "I don't want to", say {不想|bù xiǎng}.

## What are you doing? {做|zuò}, {事|shì}, {东西|dōng xi}

{做|zuò} is "to do, to make". {做什么|zuò shén me} asks about plans and activities:

{你|nǐ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you doing on Saturday?

{你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？ — What work do you do? (lesson 5)

{事|shì} is a matter, a thing to do, business. {有事|yǒu shì} is "to have something on, be busy
with something":

{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？ — Are you busy tomorrow? (Have you got anything
on?)

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}，{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 — I've got something on, I'm not going.

{东西|dōng xi} is a thing, things, stuff: physical objects. {买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi} (buy things) is
the everyday way to say "go shopping". So {事|shì} is a thing to do; {东西|dōng xi} is a thing you
can hold.

Literally, {东西|dōng xi} is "east-west". Said with both full tones, {东西|dōng xī}, it really means
"east and west"; as "thing" the second syllable is neutral, *dōngxi*. You only need the "thing"
word now.

## Buying and looking: {买|mǎi} and {看|kàn}

{买|mǎi} is "to buy". Its partner {卖|mài} "to sell" (lesson 13) has the same syllable with the fourth
tone, so say {买|mǎi} low: *mǎi*.

{看|kàn} is "to look at, watch, read", and also "to go and see, visit" someone:

{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。 — I'm reading. ({书|shū}, book: lesson 13)

{我|wǒ}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}。 — On Sunday I'm going to
see my parents.

## Pronunciation

- {去|qù}: *q* (tongue tip down, a puff of air) + *ü* written u: round your lips for *ü*, as in
  {女|nǚ}. Not "koo".
- {来|lái} rises; {买|mǎi} dips; {卖|mài} falls. Practise *lái, mǎi, mài*.
- {想|xiǎng}: *x* (soft "sh", tongue down) + *iang*. {想去|xiǎng qù}: third then fourth.
- {要|yào} falls sharply; {做|zuò} falls too. *z* in {做|zuò} is "ds", and *uo* sounds like "wo".
- {哪儿|nǎr}: one syllable, third tone, curl the tongue at the end. In {去哪儿|qù nǎr}, keep it low.
- {东西|dōng xi}: high level, then a light neutral *xi*.

```speak
{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where are you going?
{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。
= I'm going to the shop to buy some things.
{你|nǐ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{想|xiǎng}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= What would you like to do on Saturday?
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{看|kàn}{妈妈|mā ma}。
= I'd like to go home and see my mum.
{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？
= Are you busy tomorrow?
{我|wǒ}{不想|bù xiǎng}{去|qù}。
= I don't want to go.
```

## Dialogue: weekend plans

{大卫|Dà wèi} and {宋佳|Sòng Jiā}, a student whose family lives in another city, talk on Friday afternoon. {上海|Shàng hǎi} is Shanghai.

```dialogue
# Weekend plans
大卫: {宋佳|Sòng Jiā}，{星期六|xīng qī liù}{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= Song Jia, what would you like to do on Saturday?
宋佳: {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{看|kàn}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm going home to see my mum. And you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= I'd like to go to the shops. Where's your family's home?
宋佳: {在|zài}{上海|Shàng hǎi}。{我|wǒ}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{回|huí}{来|lái}。
= In Shanghai. I'll be back on Sunday morning.
大卫: {星期天|xīng qī tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？
= Have you got anything on on Sunday afternoon?
宋佳: {没有|méi yǒu}。
= No.
大卫: {你|nǐ}{来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}，{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？
= Come to my place for a meal, OK?
宋佳: {好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{来|lái}？
= Great! What time shall I come?
大卫: {五点|wǔ diǎn}。
= Five.
```

Notes on the dialogue:

- {回|huí}{来|lái}: "come back". When Song Jia talks about returning to the city where she's
  speaking, it's {回|huí} + {来|lái}, back towards here. As one word, {回来|huí lái} is HSK 2's.
- {好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？ after a suggestion is "OK?", "all right?". {好|hǎo}！ answers it.
- {没有|méi yǒu} on its own answers {有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？: the verb again, negated, with {事|shì}
  left out because it's obvious.

## Reading: a note on the table

> {妈妈|mā ma}：{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{哥哥|gē ge}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。{我们|wǒ men}{六点|liù diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn}。
>
> {小明|Xiǎo míng}

A note from a child, {小明|Xiǎo míng} (Xiaoming), to Mum. Where have they gone, and when are they
coming back? To the shops, with an older brother, home at six for dinner. Notes like this start
with the name of the person they're for and a colon, and end with the writer's name.

## Common mistakes

- **A word for "to".** There's none before a place: {去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}, not *{去|qù}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}
  ({到|dào} is "arrive", lesson 18).
- **Purpose first.** *{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}: go first, then do,
  {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}.
- **{不要|bú yào} for "don't want".** Say {我|wǒ}{不想|bù xiǎng}{去|qù}; {不要|bú yào} + verb is "don't!".
- **{来|lái} for going to someone else's place.** If you're not there, it's {去|qù}:
  {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}.
- **{哪儿|nǎr} and {那儿|nàr}.** *nǎr* (third tone) asks "where?"; *nàr* (fourth) means "there".
- **{东西|dōng xi} for a task.** "I have things to do" is {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}, not
  {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{东西|dōng xi} (I have stuff, objects).

## Key points

- {去|qù}, {来|lái}, {回|huí} + place, with no word for "to". {来|lái} is towards the speaker.
- {哪儿|nǎr}: where (spoken). {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ {你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}{工作|gōng zuò}？
- Serial verbs: go, then do: {去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}. Time and {不|bù} go before
  the first verb.
- {想|xiǎng} + verb: would like to (a wish); {要|yào} + verb: want to, will (decided). Negative:
  {不想|bù xiǎng}.
- {做什么|zuò shén me}: what (are you) doing; {有事|yǒu shì}: be busy; {东西|dōng xi}: things, objects.
- New characters: 去 来 回 想 要 做 事 东 西 买 看.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
