lessons.title: On the phone: 在, 正在 and 呢
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last lesson of this module takes everything onto the phone. You'll learn to answer and make a
call, ask for someone, say who you are, give a phone number the way Chinese speakers read it
(with a surprise for the number 1), and ask "who?". The main grammar point is how to say that
something is going on right now: "He's sleeping", "I'm on the phone", "What are you doing?".

You already know {在|zài} as "to be at" ({他|tā}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}) and as "at" before a verb
({他|tā}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}, lesson 5). Here it gets a third job.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 喂 | hello (on the phone); hey | wèi | 口 | 12 | {喂|wèi} |
| 打 | hit, strike; make (a call) | dǎ | 扌 | 5 | {打电话|dǎ diàn huà} |
| 电 (traditional 電) | electricity | diàn | 曰 | 5 | {电话|diàn huà}, {电脑|diàn nǎo} (computer: lesson 17) |
| 话 (traditional 話) | speech, words | huà | 讠 | 8 | {电话|diàn huà}, {说话|shuō huà} |
| 手 | hand | shǒu | 手 | 4 | {手机|shǒu jī} |
| 机 (traditional 機) | machine | jī | 木 | 6 | {手机|shǒu jī}, {飞机|fēi jī} (plane: lesson 18) |
| 正 | straight, upright; just | zhèng | 止 | 5 | {正在|zhèng zài} |
| 找 | look for | zhǎo | 扌 | 7 | {找|zhǎo} |
| 知 | know | zhī | 矢 | 8 | {知道|zhī dào} |
| 道 | road, way | dào | 辶 | 12 | {知道|zhī dào} |
| 谁 (traditional 誰) | who | shéi | 讠 | 10 | {谁|shéi} |
| 听 (traditional 聽) | listen | tīng | 口 | 7 | {听|tīng}, {好听|hǎo tīng} (nice to hear: lesson 22) |

电 is filed under 曰 here; other dictionaries put it under 田 or 日, which it resembles.

How the shapes work:

- 电: the traditional form 電 has rain 雨 on top and 申 below, and 申 began as a drawing of
  lightning. Lightning from the rain clouds: electricity. The simplified form keeps the lightning.
- 手: a drawing of a hand, the fingers spread. As a side part it becomes 扌 (see below).
- 话: speech 讠 + 舌 (tongue). Words come off the tongue.
- 道: walking 辶 + a head 首: the way you head along, a road. In {知道|zhī dào} the second syllable
  is often light in speech: *zhīdao*.
- 正: a line 一 over 止 (a foot): walking straight to a goal. "Straight, upright", then "just
  (now)".
- 喂, 机 and 谁 are sound-and-meaning characters: 喂 = mouth 口 + 畏 *wèi*; 机 = wood 木 + 几 *jī*
  (machines were once made of wood); 谁 = speech 讠 + 隹 *zhuī*.
- 打: hand 扌 + 丁 *dīng* (also a nail): hitting.
- 听: an old character that was chosen as the simplified form of 聽, which has an ear 耳 on the
  left. In 听 the mouth 口 is on the left: think of it as listening to what a mouth says.
- 知: an arrow 矢 and a mouth 口. One old explanation: someone who knows speaks as fast and straight
  as an arrow flies.
- 找 (memory aid only): a hand 扌 reaching for 戈, the dagger-axe of lesson 9. Where did I put it?

### New radicals: 扌, 田, 门

- **扌** "hand" ({提手旁|tí shǒu páng}, "lifting-hand side"): the side form of 手. It's the most
  common radical of this module: seventeen characters of the track have it. So far: 打 and 找.
  Three strokes: a horizontal, a vertical with a hook to the left, then a stroke rising to the
  right.
- **田** "field" ({田字旁|tián zì páng}): a field divided into plots. Four characters of the track.
  So far: 男 (man, lesson 5): a field 田 above 力 (strength), the one who works the fields, as the
  character is traditionally explained.
- **门** "door, gate" ({门字框|mén zì kuàng}, "door frame"): 门 *mén* is the word "door" itself.
  Four characters of the track. So far: 间 (lesson 7). Next: 问 (to ask, lesson 16), a mouth 口 at
  the door. Characters with 门 are written frame first: the dot, the left vertical, the right side
  with its hook, then what's inside.

### Stroke order

- 道: write 首 first, then 辶 last. 辶 always comes last (lesson 3), even though it's on the left.
- 正: the top horizontal, the middle vertical, the short horizontal to the right, the short
  vertical on the left, and the long bottom stroke last.
- 电: 日 first, then the vertical that runs down through it and turns right with a hook, last.
- 机: 木 on the left changes its last stroke, the sweep to the right, into a short dot, so that
  几 has room.
- 讠 in 话 and 谁: two strokes, a dot and then one stroke that turns and rises.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
喂打电话手机
```

```trace
正找知道谁听
```

✎ **Write it**: 打 is on the handwriting list. Write it three times on paper or the pad, from
memory, then check it.
=}

## Something going on: {在|zài}, {正在|zhèng zài} and {呢|ne}

To say an action is in progress, put {在|zài} before the verb:

{他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。 — He's sleeping.

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。 — I'm on the phone.

{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you doing?

There are three ways to mark it, and they can be combined:

| Pattern | Example | Feel |
|---|---|---|
| {在|zài} + verb | {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。 | the usual way |
| {正在|zhèng zài} + verb | {他|tā}{正在|zhèng zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。 | "right now, just at this moment" |
| verb … {呢|ne} | {他|tā}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。 | spoken, a little informal |
| {在|zài} / {正在|zhèng zài} … {呢|ne} | {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。 | very common in speech |

{正|zhèng} means "just, exactly", so {正在|zhèng zài} stresses that the action is happening at
exactly the moment you mean. {呢|ne} at the end of a statement adds "that's how things are right
now". You've met {呢|ne} as the follow-up question "and you?" ({你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？, lesson 2); at the
end of a statement it's a different use of the same word.

Grammar calls this kind of marking **[[aspect]]**: it tells you how an action unfolds (going on,
finished, just started), not when it happens. An action seen as going on at a certain moment is in
the **[[progressive aspect]]**, like English "is doing". Chinese verbs have no tenses, and the
progressive doesn't mean "now" by itself: add a time word and it can be any time.

{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{八点|bā diǎn}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。 — At eight
yesterday evening I was on the phone.

{明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{十点|shí diǎn}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上班|shàng bān}。 — At ten
tomorrow morning, I'll be at work.

Asking and answering:

{他|tā}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{吗|ma}？ — Is he on the phone?

{他|tā}{在|zài}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{呢|ne}？ — What's he doing?

To say someone isn't doing something, the negative is {没在|méi zài} + verb: {他|tā}{没在|méi zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
(He isn't sleeping.) Not {不|bù}: {不在|bú zài} means "isn't here". In practice people often just say
what is going on instead: {他|tā}{没在|méi zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{他|tā}{在|zài}{工作|gōng zuò}。

**Three jobs for {在|zài}**, side by side:

| Use | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb "be at" (lesson 5) | {他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 | He's at home. |
| "at" + place, before the verb (lesson 5) | {他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{工作|gōng zuò}。 | He works at home. |
| progressive, straight before the verb | {他|tā}{在|zài}{工作|gōng zuò}。 | He's working. |

If {在|zài} is followed by a place, it's "at"; if it's followed by a verb, it's the progressive.
With both, add {呢|ne} for "right now": {他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{工作|gōng zuò}{呢|ne}。 — He's
working at home (at the moment).

## Hello? {喂|wèi}

{喂|wèi} answers the phone: {喂|wéi}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！ or, more politely, {喂|wéi}，{您好|nín hǎo}！
Look at the tone. The dictionary gives {喂|wèi}, fourth tone, and that's how it sounds when you
call out to someone, "Hey!". On the phone almost everyone says it with a rising tone, *wéi*,
softer and questioning: "Hello?". The pinyin in this course shows *wéi* in phone calls; the word
list keeps the dictionary form, *wèi*.

A sharp falling {喂|wèi}！ to a stranger in the street sounds rude. To get someone's attention
politely, say {你好|nǐ hǎo} first.

## Making a call: {打电话|dǎ diàn huà}, {电话|diàn huà}, {手机|shǒu jī}

| Chinese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {电话|diàn huà} | telephone; phone call |
| {手机|shǒu jī} | mobile phone (literally "hand machine") |
| {打电话|dǎ diàn huà} | to make a phone call, to phone |

{打|dǎ} is "to hit, strike": you "strike" a call. To call someone's mobile, use {打|dǎ} with it:
{我|wǒ}{打|dǎ}{他|tā}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}。 (I'll call his mobile.) "To phone a person", with the
person named, needs {给|gěi} (for, to): that's lesson 23's pattern. Until then, say who you're
calling separately, or use {找|zhǎo} (below).

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。 — I'm on the phone.

{你|nǐ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{吧|ba}。 — Call in the evening. ({吧|ba}, suggestion:
lesson 12)

## Phone numbers: 1 is *yāo*

A phone number is read one digit at a time, like a year (lesson 6). But **1 is read *yāo***, not
*yī*, because *yī* is easy to mishear as *qī* (7) on a phone line.

| Digit | Said in a phone number |
|---|---|
| 0 | {零|líng} |
| 1 | {一|yāo} *yāo* |
| 2 | {二|èr} (never {两|liǎng}) |
| 7 | {七|qī} |

So 123 4567 8910 is said *yāo èr sān, sì wǔ liù qī, bā jiǔ yāo líng*. (The phone numbers in this
course are made up: real mainland mobile numbers start with 13 to 19, never 12.) People group the digits,
usually 3 + 4 + 4 for a mobile number, with a little pause between the groups.

The same goes for other numbers read digit by digit: room numbers ({房间|fáng jiān}, room: lesson 17)
such as 105, said *yāo líng wǔ*, and often bus numbers. Prices, ages, dates and amounts use the normal
*yī*: only digit-by-digit numbers switch to *yāo*.

The number itself is {号|hào} (number, lesson 6) in {手机号|shǒu jī hào}, "mobile number", the
everyday word. You'll also see {电话号码|diàn huà hào mǎ} (telephone number) and {号码|hào mǎ}
(number), which are HSK 3 words.

{你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机号|shǒu jī hào}{是|shì}{多少|duō shao}？ — What's your mobile number?

Notice {多少|duō shao} (how many, how much: lesson 4), not {几|jǐ}: a phone number is a long
number, and {几|jǐ} only asks about small ones.

## Who? {谁|shéi}

{谁|shéi} is "who", and like every question word it stays where the answer goes:

{谁|shéi}{在|zài}{说话|shuō huà}？ — Who's talking?

{他|tā}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}？ — Who is he?

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}？ — Whose mobile is this? ({谁|shéi}{的|de}, whose)

You'll also hear *shuí*, the older reading still used in songs and careful speech; *shéi* is what
most people say.

## Looking for someone: {找|zhǎo}

{找|zhǎo} is "to look for": {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{找|zhǎo}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}。 (I'm looking for my
phone.) On the phone and at a door, {找|zhǎo} + person is how you ask for someone:

{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。 — I'd like to speak to Teacher Wang. (Literally "I'm
looking for".)

{你|nǐ}{找|zhǎo}{谁|shéi}？ — Who would you like to speak to?

{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo} is said *wó zhǎo* (two third tones).

## Knowing, talking, listening: {知道|zhī dào}, {说话|shuō huà}, {听|tīng}

**{知道|zhī dào}** is "to know" a fact, a piece of information:

{我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}。 — I know.

{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。 — I don't know.

{你|nǐ}{知道|zhī dào}{他|tā}{的|de}{手机号|shǒu jī hào}{吗|ma}？ — Do you know his mobile number?

Knowing a person, being acquainted, is a different verb, {认识|rèn shi}, in lesson 23. You can't
say {我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng} for "I know Wang Fang" (it would mean "I've heard of
her").

**{说话|shuō huà}** is "to talk, to speak": {说|shuō} (to say, speak; lesson 2) + {话|huà} (words).
It's another verb with its own object inside, like the separable verbs of lesson 8, so it stands
alone: {谁|shéi}{在|zài}{说话|shuō huà}？ For a language, use {说|shuō}: {他|tā}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}.

**{听|tīng}** is "to listen (to)":

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{听|tīng}。 — I'm listening.

{你|nǐ}{听|tīng}！ — Listen!

{听|tīng}{老师|lǎo shī}{说|shuō}。 — Listen to the teacher.

{听|tīng} is listening, paying attention. Hearing something without trying, "to hear", is
{听见|tīng jiàn} (lesson 24).

## Pronunciation

- {电话|diàn huà}: two fourth tones, both falling. {说话|shuō huà}: first then fourth.
- {手机|shǒu jī}: third then first. Keep *shǒu* low, then jump up to a high level *jī*.
- {知道|zhī dào}: *zh* curled back, *zhī* high and level; *dào* falls and is often light.
- {谁|shéi}: *sh* curled back + *ei* like "ay" in "say", rising.
- {找|zhǎo} vs {早|zǎo} (early): *zh* is curled back, *z* is not. Same tone, different sound.
- {听|tīng}: *t* with a puff of air, high and level, ending in *-ng*.
- {正在|zhèng zài}: two fourth tones. *zh* curled back in the first, *z* flat in the second.

```speak
{喂|wéi}，{您好|nín hǎo}！
= Hello? (answering the phone)
{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。
= I'd like to speak to Teacher Wang.
{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{呢|ne}？
= What are you doing?
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。
= I'm on the phone.
{他|tā}{正在|zhèng zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= He's sleeping right now.
{谁|shéi}{在|zài}{说话|shuō huà}？
= Who's talking?
{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。
= I don't know.
```

## Dialogue: a phone call

{安娜|Ān nà} calls her classmate {李明|Lǐ Míng} at home. His mother, {妈妈|mā ma} in the dialogue,
answers. ({同学|tóng xué}, classmate: lesson 19; {医院|yī yuàn}, hospital: lesson 21.)

```dialogue
# A phone call
妈妈: {喂|wéi}？
= Hello?
安娜: {喂|wéi}，{您好|nín hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。
= Hello! May I speak to Li Ming?
妈妈: {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{他|tā}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{吗|ma}？
= He's asleep. Are you his classmate?
安娜: {是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。{他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}？{现在|xiàn zài}{下午|xià wǔ}{三点|sān diǎn}！
= Yes, my name's Anna. He's sleeping? It's three in the afternoon!
妈妈: {他|tā}{晚上|wǎn shang}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}，{早上|zǎo shang}{八点|bā diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= He works at the hospital at night and comes home to sleep at eight in the morning.
安娜: {他|tā}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}？
= What time does he get up?
妈妈: {五点|wǔ diǎn}。{你|nǐ}{知道|zhī dào}{他|tā}{的|de}{手机号|shǒu jī hào}{吗|ma}？
= At five. Do you know his mobile number?
安娜: {知道|zhī dào}。{我|wǒ}{六点|liù diǎn}{打|dǎ}{他|tā}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}。
= Yes. I'll call his mobile at six.
妈妈: {好|hǎo}。
= All right.
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！{再见|zài jiàn}！
= Thank you! Goodbye!
```

Look at three things. The mother answers with a rising {喂|wéi}？. Anna uses {您|nín} to an older
person she doesn't know well, and the mother uses {你|nǐ} to a young person. And {知道|zhī dào}。
alone answers "Do you know…?": the verb again means "yes".

## Reading: a name card

> **{张丽|Zhāng Lì}**
>
> {大学|dà xué}{医院|yī yuàn}　{医生|yī shēng}
>
> {手机|shǒu jī}：126 0101 2468
>
> {电话|diàn huà}：010 0123 4567

An invented name card: {张丽|Zhāng Lì} (Zhang Li) is a doctor at a university hospital. How do you
read her mobile number aloud? *yāo èr liù, líng yāo líng yāo, èr sì liù bā*. {电话|diàn huà} on a card is
the office landline; 010 is the area code for Beijing.

## Common mistakes

- **{不|bù} for the negative progressive.** *{他|tā}{不在|bú zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}: the progressive is
  negated with {没|méi}, {他|tā}{没在|méi zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}.
- **The progressive after the verb.** *{他|tā}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{在|zài}: {在|zài} goes before the
  verb; only {呢|ne} goes at the end.
- **{一|yī} in phone numbers.** Say *yāo*: 139 is *yāo sān jiǔ*.
- **{两|liǎng} in phone numbers.** It's always {二|èr} digit by digit.
- **{知道|zhī dào} for people.** For "I know her" use {认识|rèn shi} (lesson 23).
- **{几|jǐ} for a phone number.** Ask {多少|duō shao}: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机号|shǒu jī hào}{是|shì}{多少|duō shao}？
- **A sharp {喂|wèi}！ to a stranger.** It's for phone calls and people you know.

## Key points

- Progressive: {在|zài} + verb, {正在|zhèng zài} + verb (right now), verb … {呢|ne}, or both.
  Negative: {没在|méi zài} + verb. With a time word it can be past or future.
- {在|zài} + place = at; {在|zài} + verb = in the middle of doing.
- {喂|wéi}？ on the phone (dictionary tone *wèi*). {我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}… — May I speak to…?
- {打电话|dǎ diàn huà}, {电话|diàn huà}, {手机|shǒu jī}; numbers digit by digit, with 1 said *yāo*.
- {谁|shéi} (who), {知道|zhī dào} (know a fact), {说话|shuō huà} (talk), {听|tīng} (listen).
- New characters: 喂 打 电 话 手 机 正 找 知 道 谁 听.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. That's the end of module 2: its module quiz is next.

lessons.title: The Chinese calendar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is an honors lesson: optional, for curiosity. Lesson 6 taught the dates of everyday life,
{十一月|shí yī yuè}{十六号|shí liù hào}, {星期一|xīng qī yī}. But hang a calendar on a wall in China and
you'll see a second set of small characters under the big numbers: the traditional calendar, which
still sets the dates of the biggest festivals. This lesson explains the two calendars, the twelve
animals of the zodiac, the other words you'll hear for "week", and how to write a date on a form.

None of the new words here are course vocabulary; they're glossed, so you can read without
learning them.

## Two calendars

| Chinese | Literally | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| {公历|gōng lì} | "public calendar" | the Gregorian calendar, the one used worldwide |
| {农历|nóng lì} | "farming calendar" | the traditional Chinese calendar |

Work, school, trains and phones run on {公历|gōng lì}: every date in lesson 6 is a {公历|gōng lì} date.
In everyday speech people also call the two {阳历|yáng lì} ("sun calendar") and {阴历|yīn lì} ("moon
calendar").

The traditional calendar is often called "lunar", but it's really **lunisolar**: it follows both
the moon and the sun.

- **The moon** sets the months. Each month follows one cycle of the moon, so it has 29 or 30 days,
  and twelve of them make about 354 days.
- **The sun** sets the year. That's eleven days short of a solar year, so about every two or three
  years a whole extra month, a leap month ({闰月|rùn yuè}), is added: seven times in nineteen years.
  That keeps the festivals in the same season.
- The sun's year is also divided into twenty-four "solar terms" ({二十四节气|èr shí sì jié qì}),
  about fifteen days each, with names such as {立春|lì chūn} ("start of spring", around 4 February).
  They were made for farming, which is where the name {农历|nóng lì} comes from.

### Writing lunar dates

Traditional dates are written in Chinese numerals, with their own words for the months and days:

| Lunar date | Chinese | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1st month | {正月|zhēng yuè} | 正 is read *zhēng* here, not *zhèng* |
| 12th month | {腊月|là yuè} | the last month, before the new year |
| 1st to 10th day | {初一|chū yī} … {初十|chū shí} | {初|chū} means "beginning" |
| 15th day | {十五|shí wǔ} | full moon |

So the first day of the year is {正月初一|zhēng yuè chū yī}, and the fifteenth day of the eighth month
is {八月十五|bā yuè shí wǔ}. China's standard for numbers in print says the same: Gregorian dates in
figures, traditional dates in Chinese characters.

### Side by side

A wall calendar for the week of the 2026 Spring Festival looked like this:

| {星期一|xīng qī yī} | {星期二|xīng qī èr} | {星期三|xīng qī sān} | {星期四|xīng qī sì} |
|---|---|---|---|
| **16** | **17** | **18** | **19** |
| {除夕|chú xī} | {春节|Chūn jié} | {初二|chū èr} | {初三|chū sān} |

The big figures are February 2026 ({公历|gōng lì}). Under them: {除夕|chú xī}, New Year's Eve, then
{春节|Chūn jié}, the Spring Festival, which is {正月初一|zhēng yuè chū yī}, then the second and third
days of the first month.

## The festivals move

Because the traditional months follow the moon, the festivals land on a different {公历|gōng lì}
date every year.

| Festival | Traditional date | In the Gregorian calendar |
|---|---|---|
| {春节|Chūn jié} Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) | {正月初一|zhēng yuè chū yī} | a new moon between 21 January and 20 February |
| {元宵节|Yuán xiāo jié} Lantern Festival | {正月十五|zhēng yuè shí wǔ} | the first full moon of the year, two weeks later |
| {端午节|Duān wǔ jié} Dragon Boat Festival | {五月初五|wǔ yuè chū wǔ} | late May or June |
| {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié} Mid-Autumn Festival | {八月十五|bā yuè shí wǔ} | September or early October |

The Spring Festival fell on 17 February in 2026, and falls on 6 February in 2027. The Lantern
Festival closes the new-year celebrations. The Mid-Autumn Festival is for family reunions under
the full moon.

## The twelve animals

Each traditional year belongs to one of twelve animals, the {生肖|shēng xiào}, always in this
order:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 {鼠|shǔ} rat | 4 {兔|tù} rabbit | 7 {马|mǎ} horse | 10 {鸡|jī} rooster |
| 2 {牛|niú} ox | 5 {龙|lóng} dragon | 8 {羊|yáng} goat, sheep | 11 {狗|gǒu} dog |
| 3 {虎|hǔ} tiger | 6 {蛇|shé} snake | 9 {猴|hóu} monkey | 12 {猪|zhū} pig |

{羊|yáng} covers both sheep and goats, so you'll see "Year of the Goat" and "Year of the Sheep" for
the same year. The cycle repeats every twelve years: 2026 is the year of the horse ({马年|mǎ nián})
from the Spring Festival on 17 February, and 2027 the year of the goat ({羊年|yáng nián}) from
6 February.

The animal year changes at the Spring Festival, not on 1 January, so someone born in January
belongs to the year before. (Some astrologers count from {立春|lì chūn} instead; for ordinary
conversation, the Spring Festival is what people use.)

The verb is {属|shǔ}, "to belong to (a sign)":

{你|nǐ}{属|shǔ}{什么|shén me}？ — What's your (zodiac) animal?

{我|wǒ}{属|shǔ}{马|mǎ}。 — I was born in the year of the horse.

Asking someone's animal is a friendly, indirect way to talk about age, and people enjoy it. Many
also link the animals with personality or luck. That's popular belief, like horoscopes elsewhere,
and this course doesn't take sides on it.

```dialogue
# What's your animal?
安娜: {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你|nǐ}{属|shǔ}{什么|shén me}？
= Wang Fang, what's your zodiac animal?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{属|shǔ}{马|mǎ}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm a horse. And you?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}1998{年|nián}5{月|yuè}……
= I don't know. I'm from May 1998…
王芳: 1998{年|nián}5{月|yuè}？{你|nǐ}{属|shǔ}{虎|hǔ}。
= May 1998? You're a tiger.
安娜: {虎|hǔ}？{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！
= A tiger? Great!
王芳: {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{也|yě}{属|shǔ}{虎|hǔ}。
= My mum is a tiger too.
```

Wang Fang checks the month because of the Spring Festival rule: the 1998 Spring Festival was on
28 January, so May 1998 is safely in the tiger year. (Read the years aloud digit by digit:
*yī jiǔ jiǔ bā nián*.)

## Three words for "week"

| Word | Days | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| {星期|xīng qī} | {星期一|xīng qī yī} … {星期天|xīng qī tiān} | the standard word, in speech and writing (lesson 6) |
| {周|zhōu} | {周一|zhōu yī} … {周日|zhōu rì} | writing, signs, timetables, apps; also {周末|zhōu mò} (weekend) |
| {礼拜|lǐ bài} | {礼拜一|lǐ bài yī} … {礼拜天|lǐ bài tiān} | informal speech, especially in the south |

All three number the days in the same way. {周|zhōu} ("cycle") is short, so it's popular on signs and
screens: {周一|zhōu yī}{至|zhì}{周五|zhōu wǔ} is "Monday to Friday" ({至|zhì}, to). {礼拜|lǐ bài}
originally meant "worship"; it came to mean "week" because the weekly day of worship marked the
seven-day cycle. The seven-day week as it's used today came to China from the West in modern
times; the traditional calendar doesn't count in weeks.

## Writing a date on a form

On forms, tickets and documents, a {公历|gōng lì} date is written in figures from big to small, the
order of speech:

> {姓名|xìng míng}：{安娜|Ān nà}
>
> {出生日期|chū shēng rì qī}：1998{年|nián}5{月|yuè}20{日|rì}

({姓名|xìng míng}, full name; {出生日期|chū shēng rì qī}, date of birth; {日期|rì qī} alone is
"date".) Notice {日|rì}, not {号|hào}, in writing (lesson 6). The short form with hyphens is also
standard: 1998-05-20. It's allowed only for a complete date, and it always runs year, month, day.

Don't write the English or European order: 05/20/1998 or 20/05/1998 would confuse a Chinese
reader, who expects the year first. If a form gives you boxes labelled {年|nián}, {月|yuè} and
{日|rì}, just fill in the figures.

## Key points

- {公历|gōng lì} (Gregorian) for daily life; {农历|nóng lì} (traditional, lunisolar) for festivals.
  Lunar months have 29 or 30 days; a leap month keeps the seasons in place.
- Lunar dates are written in characters: {正月初一|zhēng yuè chū yī}, {八月十五|bā yuè shí wǔ}.
- {春节|Chūn jié} falls between 21 January and 20 February; {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié} is {八月十五|bā yuè shí wǔ}.
- Twelve animals, from {鼠|shǔ} (rat) to {猪|zhū} (pig); the year changes at the Spring Festival.
  {你|nǐ}{属|shǔ}{什么|shén me}？ — {我|wǒ}{属|shǔ}{马|mǎ}。
- "Week": {星期|xīng qī} (standard), {周|zhōu} (written, signs), {礼拜|lǐ bài} (informal speech).
- On forms: 1998{年|nián}5{月|yuè}20{日|rì} or 1998-05-20, year first.

lessons.title: Numbers in daily life
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is an honors lesson: optional, for curiosity. You can now count, give dates and times and
read a phone number with *yāo*. This lesson is about how numbers live in everyday China: counting
on one hand, numbers some people like and avoid, phone numbers, prices, and house numbers and
floors. The new words are glossed; none of them is course vocabulary.

## Counting on one hand

Chinese speakers can show every number from one to ten on one hand. One to five are what you'd
expect: that many fingers held up. Six to ten have their own shapes:

| Number | The usual mainland gesture |
|---|---|
| 6 {六|liù} | the thumb and the little finger stretched out, the other three fingers folded |
| 7 {七|qī} | the tips of the thumb, index and middle fingers pinched together |
| 8 {八|bā} | the thumb and index finger stretched out in an L, the others folded |
| 9 {九|jiǔ} | the index finger bent into a hook, the others in a fist |
| 10 {十|shí} | a closed fist, or two index fingers crossed (one from each hand) like the character {十|shí} |

Crossed fingers copy the character {十|shí} itself. The gestures vary, especially for seven to ten. In parts
of the south, and among Chinese speakers elsewhere in Asia, the L-shape can mean seven rather than
eight, so if a price matters, say the number too.

You'll see these gestures at market stalls, across a noisy room, and when someone repeats a
number to make sure you understood. A shopkeeper who holds up the L-shape and says
{八块|bā kuài} means eight kuai (lesson 13: {块|kuài} is the spoken word for the yuan).

## Numbers that sound like other words

Chinese has many words that sound alike, so some numbers sound like other words. These are
customs that some people keep, more or less seriously, not rules:

| Number | Sounds like | So |
|---|---|---|
| 8 {八|bā} | the *fā* of {发财|fā cái}, to become rich | the most popular number |
| 6 {六|liù} | {流|liú}, to flow | {六六大顺|liù liù dà shùn}, "everything goes smoothly" |
| 9 {九|jiǔ} | {久|jiǔ}, long-lasting | a wish for lasting love: 99 or 999 roses |
| 4 {四|sì} | {死|sǐ}, death | avoided by some |

**Eight** is the favourite. Phone numbers full of eights are sought after and can cost extra,
and the opening ceremony of the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing began at 8 p.m.
on 8 August 2008, a date chosen for its eights.

**Four** is the one some people avoid. *sì* and *sǐ* differ only in their tones. Some buildings
skip the 4th floor, and sometimes the 14th and 24th as well; some people avoid fours in phone
numbers and addresses. Plenty of people don't mind at all.

Number puns also live online. 520, read *wǔ èr líng*, sounds a little like {我爱你|wǒ ài nǐ}, "I love
you". People text 520 for it, and 20 May (5/20) has become an unofficial day for couples.

## Phone numbers: yāo, and groups of digits

Mobile numbers in mainland China have eleven digits and start with 1, so almost every mobile
number begins with *yāo*. They're usually written and said in three groups, 3 + 4 + 4:

> 126 0101 2468 — *yāo èr liù, líng yāo líng yāo, èr sì liù bā* (a made-up number)

When someone gives you a number, it's polite and normal to read it back, group by group. The digit
2 is always {二|èr} in a phone number, never {两|liǎng}.

Three short numbers are worth knowing. Like all phone numbers, they're read with *yāo*:

| Number | Said | For |
|---|---|---|
| 110 | *yāo yāo líng* | police |
| 119 | *yāo yāo jiǔ* | fire |
| 120 | *yāo èr líng* | ambulance |

Landlines have an area code in front: Beijing's is 010, *líng yāo líng*.

## Prices: {块|kuài} and {元|yuán}

Lesson 13 teaches money properly; here is the shape of it. On price tags and receipts the yuan is
written {元|yuán}, or as the sign ¥ before the figure: 15{元|yuán}, ¥15. In speech, people say
{块|kuài}: {十五块|shí wǔ kuài}. A price is read like any amount, not digit by digit: 120{元|yuán} is
{一百二十块|yì bǎi èr shí kuài}, with *yì* (counting), not *yāo*.

So the same figures can be read two ways. 120 on a price tag is *yì bǎi èr shí*; 120 on an
ambulance is *yāo èr líng*.

## Addresses and floors

Chinese addresses run from big to small, like dates: city, district, street, then the number with
{号|hào} (number, lesson 6):

> {花园路|Huā yuán Lù} 8{号|hào}，3{号楼|hào lóu}，501

(An invented address: Garden Road, No. 8, Building 3, flat 501.) {号楼|hào lóu} after a figure is
"building number …", since big housing estates have many buildings. The flat number often starts
with the floor: 501 is on the fifth floor, read *wǔ líng yāo*, digit by digit like a room number.

Floors are counted the American way: the floor at street level is the first, {一楼|yī lóu} (1st
floor), and the one above is {二楼|èr lóu} (2nd floor). In British English those are the ground floor
and the first floor. {楼|lóu} (floor, building) and {层|céng} (storey) are HSK 2 and HSK 3 words:
{五楼|wǔ lóu} or 5{层|céng} is the fifth floor. A lift may jump from 3 to 5, for the reason above.

```speak
{八块|bā kuài}
= eight kuai
{五楼|wǔ lóu}
= the fifth floor
```

## Key points

- Six to ten on one hand: thumb and little finger (6), pinched fingertips (7), L-shape (8), hook
  (9), fist or crossed fingers (10). Gestures vary; say the number too.
- Some people like {八|bā} (sounds like the *fā* of {发财|fā cái}, get rich), {六|liù} and {九|jiǔ}, and avoid {四|sì}
  (sounds like {死|sǐ}). Customs, not rules.
- Mobile numbers: eleven digits starting with 1, said in groups 3 + 4 + 4 with *yāo*. 110 police,
  119 fire, 120 ambulance.
- Prices are amounts ({一百二十块|yì bǎi èr shí kuài}); phone and room numbers are digit strings
  (*yāo èr líng*).
- Addresses go big to small; {一楼|yī lóu} is the floor at street level.

lessons.title: Eating and drinking: 吃, 喝, 喜欢
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 gave you the day: {早饭|zǎo fàn}, {午饭|wǔ fàn} and {晚饭|wǎn fàn}, and {想|xiǎng} and
{要|yào} for what you'd like to do. This module is about food and shopping, and it starts with the
two verbs you'll use at every meal, {吃|chī} (to eat) and {喝|hē} (to drink). You'll learn to say
what you like with {喜欢|xǐ huan}, what you'd like to eat now with {想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}, and the names
of the everyday staples: rice, noodles, dumplings and buns. At the end there's your first
reading text of the course: a short note in which someone describes what they eat in a day.

## Eating and drinking: {吃|chī} and {喝|hē} + what

Chinese puts the thing eaten or drunk after the verb, as English does:

{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi}。 — I eat steamed buns. / I'm having steamed buns.
{他|tā}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — He drinks tea. / He's having tea.
{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you eating? / What will you have?

As in every sentence so far, the verb doesn't change: {吃|chī} is "eat", "eats", "am eating" and
"will eat". Time words such as {早上|zǎo shang} or {中午|zhōng wǔ} go before the verb, never at the
end (lesson 08):

{我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — I drink tea in the morning.
{中午|zhōng wǔ}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — At noon I eat at school.

The second sentence also puts the place with {在|zài} before the verb, as you learned in lesson 05.

Which verb? Food is eaten with {吃|chī}; anything you drink takes {喝|hē}: {喝|hē}{水|shuǐ} (drink
water), {喝|hē}{茶|chá} (drink tea). Saying ~~{吃|chī}{水|shuǐ}~~ for "drink water" is a typical
beginner's slip.

## {饭|fàn}: a meal, and rice

{饭|fàn} is cooked rice, and because rice is the centre of a traditional meal in much of China, it
also means "a meal" in general. {吃|chī}{饭|fàn} is simply "to eat, to have a meal", whatever is on the
table, and it's the phrase you'll hear most:

{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — We're going to eat.
{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吗|ma}？ — Do you eat at home?

You know the three meals already: {早饭|zǎo fàn}, {午饭|wǔ fàn}, {晚饭|wǎn fàn}. When you mean the
rice itself, on a plate or in a bowl, say {米饭|mǐ fàn}: {米|mǐ} is the grain, so {米饭|mǐ fàn} is
"rice meal", cooked rice.

{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{米饭|mǐ fàn}。 — I'd like (some) rice.

Among friends you may hear {你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ ("Have you eaten?") used as a
friendly greeting, more "how are you?" than a real question about food. The {了|le} in it is
lesson 25's; for now just recognise it.

## {菜|cài}: dishes and vegetables

{菜|cài} is a dish, the food that goes with the rice or noodles: meat, fish, tofu or vegetables,
cooked. It also means "vegetable", and context tells you which:

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{菜|cài}？ — What dish is this?
{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài}。 — I really like Chinese food.
{妈妈|mā ma}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{菜|cài}。 — Mum's going to buy food (for meals: vegetables, meat…).

{中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài} is Chinese food, Chinese cooking, built like {中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}.
{买|mǎi}{菜|cài} is the everyday way to say "do the food shopping".

## Staple foods

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {米饭|mǐ fàn} | (cooked) rice | eaten everywhere; the main staple in much of the south |
| {面条儿|miàn tiáor} | noodles | made from wheat flour; also said {面条|miàn tiáo} |
| {饺子|jiǎo zi} | dumplings (jiaozi) | crescent-shaped, boiled; filled with meat and vegetables |
| {包子|bāo zi} | steamed stuffed buns (baozi) | a soft bread-like bun with a filling, a common breakfast |
| {菜|cài} | dish; vegetable | what you eat with the staple |
| {茶|chá} | tea | |
| {水|shuǐ} | water | |

{面条儿|miàn tiáor} ends in the *-r* sound (erhua) that's typical of Beijing and the north; many
speakers, especially in the south, say {面条|miàn tiáo}. Both are right. The honors lesson
"Rice, noodles and dumplings" says more about where each staple is eaten.

The character 饺 in {饺子|jiǎo zi} belongs to HSK 3, so this course always shows it with pinyin.
You only need to recognise the word now.

## Liking: {喜欢|xǐ huan} + a thing, or + an action

{喜欢|xǐ huan} (to like) takes a noun, just like English:

{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{茶|chá}。 — I like tea.
{她|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 — She likes dumplings.

It also takes a whole verb phrase, where English says "like doing" or "like to do". This is more
common in Chinese than a bare noun:

{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 — I like eating dumplings. / I like dumplings.
{他|tā}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — He doesn't like (drinking) tea.

Make it negative with {不|bù} in front: {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}. Never ~~{没|méi}{喜欢|xǐ huan}~~:
liking is a state, and states take {不|bù}. Add {很|hěn} for "really like": {很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}.
Here {很|hěn} keeps its full meaning, "very much", unlike the weak {很|hěn} before an adjective
(lesson 01).

Ask with {吗|ma}, and answer with the verb, the usual short answer in Chinese (there's no single
word for "yes"):

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}{吗|ma}？ — Do you like rice?
— {喜欢|xǐ huan}。/ {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。 — Yes (I do). / No (I don't).

{也|yě} and {都|dōu} go before {喜欢|xǐ huan}, as before any verb: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}
(I like it too), {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi} (we all like buns).

## Wanting to eat now: {想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}, {想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}

{喜欢|xǐ huan} is what you like in general. For what you feel like having now, use {想|xiǎng}
(would like to) from lesson 09, with the verb after it:

{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？ — What would you like to eat?
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}。 — I'd like some noodles.
{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}，{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}。 — I don't want tea; I'd like water.

Keep the verb. {想|xiǎng} with a noun and no verb usually means "to miss": {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{妈妈|mā ma}
is "I miss my mum". So "I'd like some tea" is {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}, not ~~{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{茶|chá}~~.

{要|yào} works too and sounds firmer, the way you order: {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{饺子|jiǎo zi} ("I'll have
dumplings"). Lesson 12 makes ordering polite.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 吃 | eat | chī | 口 | 6 | {吃|chī}, {吃|chī}{饭|fàn}, {好吃|hǎo chī} (tasty, lesson 12) |
| 喝 | drink | hē | 口 | 12 | {喝|hē}, {喝|hē}{茶|chá} |
| 米 | rice (grain) | mǐ | 米 | 6 | {米饭|mǐ fàn} |
| 面 (traditional 麵 for noodles) | noodles, flour; face, side | miàn | 面 | 9 | {面条儿|miàn tiáor}, {面包|miàn bāo} (bread, lesson 12) |
| 条 (traditional 條) | strip, long thin thing | tiáo | 木 | 7 | {面条儿|miàn tiáor} |
| 包 | wrap; bun; bag | bāo | 勹 | 5 | {包子|bāo zi}, {面包|miàn bāo} (bread) |
| 茶 ✎ | tea | chá | 艹 | 9 | {茶|chá}, {喝|hē}{茶|chá} |
| 水 | water | shuǐ | 水 | 4 | {水|shuǐ}, {水果|shuǐ guǒ} (fruit, lesson 14) |
| 菜 | dish; vegetable | cài | 艹 | 11 | {菜|cài}, {中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài} |
| 喜 | joy; to like | xǐ | 口 | 12 | {喜欢|xǐ huan} |
| 欢 (traditional 歡) | glad, merry | huan (huān) | 欠 | 6 | {喜欢|xǐ huan} |

The other eight are written the same in traditional script. Tables, radicals and stroke counts in
this section describe the simplified forms; in Traditional the tracing pads show 麵, 條 and 歡.

- 吃 and 喝 both have 口 (mouth) on the left: things you do with your mouth, like 叫 and 吗,
  which you know. Most characters with 口 on the left have to do with the mouth or with sound.
- 米 looks like grains scattered around a stalk. It's also the radical of the character: the
  radical can be the whole character.
- 面 stands for two old words. In simplified Chinese one character writes both "face, side" and
  "noodles, flour"; traditional Chinese writes noodles and flour as 麵 (with 麥 "wheat" on the
  left) and keeps 面 for "face, side". So {面条儿|miàn tiáor} and {面包|miàn bāo} switch to 麵 in
  traditional script. That's why this course never uses 面 on its own for "noodles".
- 欢 is read with a neutral tone in {喜欢|xǐ huan}, its full reading is huān (as in a word you'll
  meet in HSK 3, {欢迎|huān yíng}, welcome).

Dictionaries sometimes file a character under a different radical from the one in the table
(the table follows one common list, Make Me a Hanzi's). When you look up a character, try the
other component too.

### New radicals

艹, "grass on top" ({草字头|cǎo zì tóu}). Three short strokes across the top of a character: a
horizontal and two short verticals. It comes from a picture of plants, and characters with it
are often plants or things made from them. You have two already: 茶 (tea, the leaves of a plant)
and 菜 (vegetables). 苹 in {苹果|píng guǒ} (apple, lesson 14) is the next.

彳, "double person" ({双人旁|shuāng rén páng}). It looks like 亻 (the person radical) with an
extra stroke on top, which is how it got its name, but it isn't a person: it comes from a
drawing of a road or crossroads, and characters with it often have to do with walking or going.
You met it in 很 (lesson 01), where it only tells you which character it is, not the meaning.
得 in {觉得|jué de} (to feel, to think; lesson 20) has it too.

白, "white" ({白|bái}). A small 日 with a short stroke on top. As a character it means
"white" (you'll learn it in lesson 21). It's the left side of 的 (lesson 03), and it's the lower part of
百 (a hundred, lesson 04: 一 over 白). In both of those it's just a building block of the form.

### Stroke order

- 水: the middle hook first (a vertical stroke that hooks left at the bottom), then the left
  side, then the two strokes on the right. Four strokes in all; resist drawing the left and
  right sides first.
- 米: the two short dots on top first (left, then right), then the horizontal, the vertical,
  and last the two falling strokes at the bottom (left, then right).
- 吃, 喝: the 口 on the left comes first and is written small: left vertical, then the top and
  right side in one stroke, then the bottom.
- 茶, 菜: 艹 first: the horizontal, then the left and right short verticals.

```trace trad=吃喝米麵條包
吃喝米面条包
```

```trace
茶水菜喜欢
```

Write it: 茶 is one of the characters to know by hand. Write it three times on paper or on the
pad, from memory, then check its strokes against the pad.

=}

## Dialogue: lunch time

The speakers are {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) and her classmate {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫), a student from
abroad.

```dialogue
# Lunch time
王芳: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài}{吗|ma}？
= David, do you like Chinese food?
大卫: {很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}！{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{和|hé}{包子|bāo zi}。
= Very much! I like dumplings and steamed buns.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}{吗|ma}？
= Do you like rice?
大卫: {喜欢|xǐ huan}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= Yes. And you?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}，{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}。
= I like noodles; I don't like rice.
大卫: {现在|xiàn zài}{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}，{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吗|ma}？
= It's twelve o'clock. Do you want to go and eat?
王芳: {想|xiǎng}！{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？
= Yes! What would you like to eat?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。
= I'd like dumplings.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{什么|shén me}？
= What would you like to drink?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}。{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？
= I'll have water. Are you having tea?
```

Notice how both of them answer with the verb alone: {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {想|xiǎng}. The last line,
{我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}, is a present-tense sentence used for a decision: "I'll have water."

## Reading: what Li Ming eats

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài}。{早上|zǎo shang}{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}，{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。{中午|zhōng wǔ}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}{和|hé}{菜|cài}。{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{会|huì}{做|zuò}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{会|huì}{做|zuò}。{今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}，{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}。

Read it twice: once for the gist, once slowly with the pinyin. Then answer:

1. What does Li Ming have in the morning?
2. Who can make dumplings?
3. What does he want to eat today, and what doesn't he want?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Two steamed buns and some tea ({两|liǎng}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}，{喝|hē}{茶|chá}).
2. His mother, and Li Ming too ({我|wǒ}{也|yě}{会|huì}{做|zuò}).
3. Dumplings; he doesn't want noodles.

"My name is Li Ming and I'm a university student. I really like Chinese food. In the morning I
have two steamed buns and drink tea. At noon I eat rice and a dish at school. In the evening I
go home to eat. My mum can make dumplings, and so can I. Today is Saturday; I want to eat
dumplings, not noodles."
</details>

Notice the order inside each sentence: time ({早上|zǎo shang}, {中午|zhōng wǔ}), then the person,
then the place ({在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}), then the verb and what is eaten.

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài}。
= I like Chinese food.
{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？
= What would you like to eat?
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
= I'd like some tea.
{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}。
= I don't like drinking water.
{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。
= We're going to eat.
```

## Pronunciation

- {吃|chī}: *ch* is made with the tongue tip curled back (like *zh* and *sh*), with a puff of air;
  the *-i* after it is the buzzing vowel you learned in the pinyin course, not "ee". High and level.
- {喝|hē}: the *e* is a back vowel, like the "u" in English "duh" said with unrounded lips. It isn't
  the English word "he".
- {茶|chá} rises; {菜|cài} falls. Say {喝|hē}{茶|chá} and {吃|chī}{菜|cài} in pairs to feel the
  difference between a 2nd and a 4th tone after a 1st.
- {水|shuǐ} is spelled *ui* but said *uei*: "shway" with a dip.
- {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {饺子|jiǎo zi}, {包子|bāo zi}: the second syllable is short and light (neutral
  tone).
- {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī} and {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan} start with two third tones in a row: the first
  one rises (said *wó xiǎng*, *wó xǐhuan*), as in {你好|nǐ hǎo}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{吃|chī}{水|shuǐ}~~, ~~{吃|chī}{茶|chá}~~: drinks take {喝|hē}.
- Time at the end, English-style: ~~{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi}{早上|zǎo shang}~~. Say
  {我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi} or {早上|zǎo shang}{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{喜欢|xǐ huan}~~: "don't like" is {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{茶|chá}~~ for "I'd like tea": keep the verb, {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}.
- Adding {是|shì} before the verb: ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{茶|chá}~~. {是|shì} links two nouns;
  {喜欢|xǐ huan} is already the verb.
- Writing the bottom of 茶 as a plain 木: under 艹 and 人, its vertical stroke ends in a hook and
  the last two strokes are short dots.

## Key points

- {吃|chī} + food, {喝|hē} + drink; the object follows the verb, and time and place come before it.
- {饭|fàn} is a meal and cooked rice; {吃|chī}{饭|fàn} is "to eat"; {米饭|mǐ fàn} is the rice itself.
- {菜|cài} is a dish and a vegetable; {中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài} is Chinese food.
- {喜欢|xǐ huan} + noun or + verb phrase; negative {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}; answer with the verb.
- {想|xiǎng}{吃|chī} / {想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}: what you'd like now. Keep the verb after {想|xiǎng}.
- New radicals: 艹 (grass), 彳 (double person), 白 (white).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: At a restaurant: 请, 吧, 一下, 一点儿
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11 you said what you like and what you'd like to eat. This lesson takes you to a
{饭店|fàn diàn} (restaurant) and makes your Chinese polite and friendly. You'll ask people to do
things with {请|qǐng} (please), make suggestions with {吧|ba} (let's…), soften a request with
{一下|yí xià}, ask for a little of something with {一点儿|yì diǎnr}, react with {太|tài}…{了|le}
("so good!", "too much!") and address people as {先生|xiān sheng} and {女士|nǚ shì}. You'll also
learn the characters of three phrases you've been saying since the pinyin course:
{谢谢|xiè xie}, {不客气|bú kè qi} and {没关系|méi guān xi}.

## Please: {请|qǐng} + verb

Put {请|qǐng} in front of a verb to ask someone, politely, to do it. It's what hosts, waiters and
teachers say all the time:

{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — Please have some tea.
{请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}。 — Please sit down. ({坐|zuò}, to sit, is lesson 18's word.)
{请|qǐng}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Please speak Chinese.
{请|qǐng}{您|nín}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — Please have some tea. (to someone you address with {您|nín})

{请|qǐng} always comes before the verb, never after it, and it isn't added to the end like
English "please". It also means "to invite" and "to treat (someone to something)":

{我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — Let me treat you to a meal. / It's my treat.

When the bill comes and a friend says {我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}！, they mean they're paying.

## Let's: {吧|ba} for suggestions

{吧|ba} at the end of a sentence turns it into a suggestion. With {我们|wǒ men} it's "let's";
with {你|nǐ} it's a gentle "why don't you…":

{我们|wǒ men}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — Let's eat.
{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{饭店|fàn diàn}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go to a restaurant.
{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}{吧|ba}。 — Have a little water.

The usual answer is {好|hǎo} (OK) or {好|hǎo}{的|de} (all right). Compare {吧|ba} with {吗|ma}:

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {我们|wǒ men}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}。 | Let's have dumplings. (a suggestion) |
| {我们|wǒ men}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吗|ma}？ | Are we having dumplings? (a real question) |

Both particles are neutral in tone and come last; only the meaning differs. ({吧|ba} has another
use, checking what you think is true, which lesson 26 covers.)

## A little softer: verb + {一下|yí xià}

{一下|yí xià} after a verb means "(do it) once, briefly, for a moment". It makes the action sound
small and easy, so a request sounds lighter and more polite. A word or phrase that does this job
is called a **[[softener]]**:

{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}。 — Let me have a look.
{请|qǐng}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。 — Just a moment, please. ({等|děng}, to wait, is an HSK 2 word.)
{你|nǐ}{听|tīng}{一下|yí xià}。 — Have a listen.
{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{一下|yí xià}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — Could I see Teacher Wang, please? (at an office door or on the phone)

{一下|yí xià} goes right after the verb, and an object follows it ({找|zhǎo}{一下|yí xià}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}).
Note the tone: {一|yī} becomes *yí* because {下|xià} is a fourth tone.

## A little: {一点儿|yì diǎnr}

{一点儿|yì diǎnr} is "a little, a bit, some". It goes after the verb and before the noun, if there
is one:

{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — I'll eat a little.
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}。 — I'd like a little water.
{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{米饭|mǐ fàn}。 — I'd like a bit of rice.
{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — I can speak a little Chinese.

The last one is worth learning by heart. Like {一下|yí xià}, {一点儿|yì diǎnr} softens: {喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}
sounds friendlier than just {喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}. In the south and in writing you'll often see
{一点|yì diǎn}, without the *-r*.

Lesson 21 brings a similar-looking word, {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}, which goes *before* an adjective and
complains ("a bit too…"). Keep {一点儿|yì diǎnr} after the verb for now.

## So…! Too…! {太|tài}…{了|le}

{太|tài} + adjective + {了|le} is an exclamation. It can praise ("so good!") or complain ("too
much!"); the situation tells you which:

{太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！ — Great! / That's wonderful!
{饺子|jiǎo zi}{太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}{了|le}！ — The dumplings are so good!
{太|tài}{多|duō}{了|le}！ — That's too much!

In this pattern {了|le} belongs to {太|tài}: learn {太|tài}…{了|le} as a frame. (The other uses of
{了|le} come in lessons 20 and 25.) In the negative, {不|bú}{太|tài} means "not very" and drops the
{了|le}:

{不|bú}{太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}。 — Not very tasty.
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{太|tài}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — I don't really like tea.

## {好吃|hǎo chī}: good to eat

{好|hǎo} + a verb makes an adjective: "good to (do)". {好吃|hǎo chī} is "good to eat", tasty.

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{菜|cài}？{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}！ — What is this dish? It's delicious!
{妈妈|mā ma}{的|de}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。 — Mum's dumplings are very good.

For drinks, people say {好喝|hǎo hē}: {这|zhè}{茶|chá}{很|hěn}{好喝|hǎo hē} (this tea is good). You'll
meet {好看|hǎo kàn} (good-looking) in lesson 15 and {好听|hǎo tīng} (nice to listen to) in lesson 22.

## Cooking: {做饭|zuò fàn}

{做饭|zuò fàn} is "to cook (a meal)": {做|zuò} (to do, to make) + {饭|fàn} (a meal).

{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{做饭|zuò fàn}{吗|ma}？ — Can you cook?
{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{买|mǎi}{菜|cài}。 — My dad cooks and my mum does the food shopping.

You can also {做|zuò} a particular dish: {做|zuò}{饺子|jiǎo zi}, {做|zuò}{菜|cài}.

## At the table: {杯子|bēi zi}, {面包|miàn bāo}, {饭店|fàn diàn}

- {杯子|bēi zi} is a cup or a glass. The character {杯|bēi} on its own counts cupfuls, like a
  measure word: {一|yì}{杯|bēi}{茶|chá} (a cup of tea), {两|liǎng}{杯|bēi}{水|shuǐ} (two glasses of
  water). Lesson 13 explains measure words with nouns; see also the reference sheet.
- {面包|miàn bāo} is bread, literally "flour bun" ({包|bāo}, bun). Like {面条儿|miàn tiáor}, it's written
  麵包 in traditional characters.
- {饭店|fàn diàn} is a restaurant; in names it's often a hotel ({北京饭店|Běi jīng Fàn diàn}, the
  Beijing Hotel). {店|diàn} (shop) is an HSK 2 character, so it keeps its pinyin in this course.

## Mr and Ms: {先生|xiān sheng} and {女士|nǚ shì}

Put the title *after* the surname, the opposite of English:

{王|Wáng}{先生|xiān sheng} — Mr Wang
{李|Lǐ}{女士|nǚ shì} — Ms Li

On their own they're polite ways to address a man or a woman you don't know, such as a
customer: {先生|xiān sheng}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！ (Hello, sir!) {女士|nǚ shì}，{请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}。 (Please
take a seat, madam.) {先生|xiān sheng} also means "husband": {我|wǒ}{先生|xiān sheng} is "my husband".
{女士|nǚ shì} is formal and polite, the word on signs and in announcements.

To call a waiter, people say {服务员|fú wù yuán} (waiter, server: a word outside this course).

## The characters of thanks and apologies

You've been saying these since the pinyin course; now you can read them:

| Phrase | Meaning | New characters |
|---|---|---|
| {谢谢|xiè xie} | thank you | {=谢=} |
| {不客气|bú kè qi} | you're welcome | {=客=} ({=气=} is lesson 20's) |
| {没关系|méi guān xi} | it doesn't matter, that's all right | {=关=}, {=系=} |

{谢谢|xiè xie} answers {请|qǐng}…; {不客气|bú kè qi} (literally "no need to be so polite")
answers {谢谢|xiè xie}; {没关系|méi guān xi} answers {对不起|duì bu qǐ} (sorry).

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 谢 (traditional 謝) | thank | xiè | 讠 | 12 | {谢谢|xiè xie} |
| 客 | guest | kè | 宀 | 9 | {不客气|bú kè qi} |
| 关 (traditional 關) | close; concern | guān | 丷 | 6 | {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 系 (traditional 係 in 没关系) | link, relation | xi (xì on its own) | 糸 | 7 | {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 请 (traditional 請) | please; invite | qǐng | 讠 | 10 | {请|qǐng}, {请问|qǐng wèn} (excuse me, may I ask; lesson 16) |
| 吧 | (suggestion particle) | ba | 口 | 7 | {吧|ba} |
| 杯 | cup | bēi | 木 | 8 | {杯子|bēi zi} |
| 太 | too; extremely | tài | 大 | 4 | {太|tài} |
| 先 | first, before | xiān | 儿 | 6 | {先生|xiān sheng} |
| 士 | scholar; person (in titles) | shì | 士 | 3 | {女士|nǚ shì} |

The other six are written the same in traditional script; in Traditional the tracing pads show
謝, 關, 係 and 請.

- 谢 and 请 have 讠, "speech", from lesson 02: thanking and asking are things you say. The right
  side of 请 is 青 (*qīng*), which gives the sound: 请 is *qǐng*. This is the commonest kind of
  character, one part for meaning and one for sound.
- 吧 is 口 + 巴 (*bā*): a spoken particle with a sound part, like 吗 (口 + 马 *mǎ*).
- 杯 has 木 (wood): early cups were often wooden. (A memory aid; the right side, 不, is usually
  explained as giving the sound.)
- 太 is 大 with a dot: "big, and then some", too much.
- 客 has the roof 宀 (from lesson 03) on top: a guest is someone under your roof (a memory aid;
  the lower part, 各, is usually explained as the sound part).
- 系 in {没关系|méi guān xi} is 係 in traditional characters; 系 is also a separate word, "university
  department" (*xì*), which stays 系. The app picks the right form from the word.
- 士 and 土 (earth, the radical of 在) are easy to confuse: in 士 the *top* horizontal is longer,
  in 土 the *bottom* one is.

### New radicals

儿, "legs" ({儿|ér}). The character 儿 (child, son; lesson 04) is also a radical at the bottom
of characters, where it looks like two legs. You've seen it in 先 (this lesson), and you'll meet
元 (yuan) in lesson 13.

工, "work" ({工|gōng}). The character 工 from {工作|gōng zuò} (lesson 05), usually explained as a picture of a tool.
As a radical it shows up in a few characters of later courses, such as 左 (left) and 差 (poor,
lacking).

见, "see" ({见|jiàn}). Its traditional form 見 is an eye (目) on legs (儿): 见 is "to see" ({再见|zài jiàn} is "see you again"). As a
radical it sits at the bottom of 觉 in {睡觉|shuì jiào} (lesson 08) and on the right of 视 in
{电视|diàn shì} (television, lesson 17). The character itself is taught in lesson 23.

### Stroke order

- 讠 (in 谢 and 请): two strokes, the dot, then one stroke that goes across, turns down and ends
  with a small upward flick.
- 关: the two short strokes on top first (left, then right), then the two horizontals, then the
  left-falling and the right-falling strokes.
- 太: write 大 first; the dot inside is the last stroke.
- 先: the short left-falling stroke, the horizontal, the vertical, the long horizontal, then
  the two strokes of 儿 (left-falling, then the bent stroke with a hook).
- 谢: three parts from left to right: 讠, then 身, then 寸 (horizontal, vertical hook, dot).

## Dialogue: dinner out

The speakers are {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明), his friend {安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and a waiter, {服务员|fú wù yuán}
(服务员).

```dialogue
# At the restaurant
服务员: {先生|xiān sheng}，{女士|nǚ shì}，{你们|nǐ men}{好|hǎo}！{请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}，{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
= Hello, sir, madam! Please take a seat, and have some tea.
李明: {谢谢|xiè xie}。{安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？
= Thank you. Anna, what would you like to eat?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'd like dumplings. And you?
李明: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{我们|wǒ men}{要|yào}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{菜|cài}{吧|ba}。
= I'd like dumplings too. Let's have dumplings and one dish.
服务员: {好|hǎo}。{你们|nǐ men}{要|yào}{米饭|mǐ fàn}{吗|ma}？
= Fine. Would you like rice?
安娜: {不|bú}{要|yào}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}。
= No, thank you. I'd like a little water.
服务员: {好|hǎo}{的|de}，{请|qǐng}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。
= Certainly, just a moment, please.
安娜: {饺子|jiǎo zi}{太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}{了|le}！
= The dumplings are so good!
李明: {菜|cài}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。
= The dish is very good too.
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}，{今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}！
= Li Ming, today it's my treat!
李明: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！
= Great! Thank you!
安娜: {不客气|bú kè qi}。
= You're welcome.
```

The waiter uses {请|qǐng} twice and {一下|yí xià} once: service language is full of softeners. Li
Ming's {我们|wǒ men}…{吧|ba} is a suggestion, and Anna's {我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ} means she's paying.

## Reading: a note on the table

> {安娜|Ān nà}：{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{今天|jīn tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{做饭|zuò fàn}。{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{做|zuò}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{也|yě}{会|huì}{做|zuò}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}。{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{什么|shén me}？{我|wǒ}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{下班|xià bān}，{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{面包|miàn bāo}{和|hé}{茶|chá}{吧|ba}。{我们|wǒ men}{晚上|wǎn shang}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}！{谢谢|xiè xie}！——{孙丽|Sūn Lì}

1. Who is cooking tonight, and where?
2. When will the writer get home?
3. What does she ask Anna to buy?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Sun Li, at home ({在|zài}{家|jiā}{做饭|zuò fàn}).
2. At eight ({八|bā}{点|diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}); she finishes work at seven.
3. A little bread and some tea.

"Anna, hi! Tonight I'd like to cook at home. I can make dumplings and noodles too. What would
you like to eat? I finish work at seven and get home at eight. Why don't you go and buy a little
bread and some tea? Let's eat at home tonight! Thanks! — Sun Li"
</details>

The two {吧|ba} sentences are suggestions: the first a request to Anna, the second "let's".

## Say it

```speak
{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
= Please have some tea.
{我们|wǒ men}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。
= Let's eat.
{请|qǐng}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。
= Just a moment, please.
{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。
= I can speak a little Chinese.
{太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}{了|le}！
= It's so good!
{今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}。
= Today it's my treat.
```

## Pronunciation

- {请|qǐng}: *q* is like English "ch" in "cheese" with the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth,
  and *-ing* is a full *ing*. Third tone, low.
- {先生|xiān sheng}: *x* is a soft "sh" with the tongue tip down. The second syllable is neutral:
  *xiānsheng*, not *xiān shēng*.
- {女士|nǚ shì}: *ü* (rounded lips, tongue as for "ee"), then *shì* with the tongue curled back.
- {一下|yí xià}, {一点儿|yì diǎnr}: {一|yī} changes before the next tone, rising before a 4th tone
  (*yí xià*) and falling before the others (*yì diǎnr*). In {一点儿|yì diǎnr} the *-n* disappears:
  it sounds like *diǎr*.
- {吧|ba} is short and light, like {吗|ma}.
- {好吃|hǎo chī}: the third tone before a first tone stays low (a "half third").

## Common mistakes

- ~~{坐|zuò}{请|qǐng}~~ or "{坐|zuò}, {请|qǐng}" for "sit, please": {请|qǐng} comes first, {请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}~~: {一点儿|yì diǎnr} goes after the verb,
  {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}.
- Leaving out {了|le}: textbook Chinese keeps it, {太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}{了|le}！ You'll also hear
  {太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī}！ without it in casual speech, but learn the full frame first. (The negative
  {不|bú}{太|tài}{好吃|hǎo chī} has no {了|le}.)
- {吧|ba} and {吗|ma} mixed up: {我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba} suggests, {我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{吗|ma}？ asks.
  ({走|zǒu}, to leave, is an HSK 2 word.)
- ~~{先生|xiān sheng}{王|Wáng}~~: the surname comes first, {王|Wáng}{先生|xiān sheng}.
- {好吃|hǎo chī} for drinks: a drink is {好喝|hǎo hē}.

## Key points

- {请|qǐng} + verb: please (do); {我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ} = my treat.
- Sentence + {吧|ba}: let's… / why don't you…; answer {好|hǎo}.
- Verb + {一下|yí xià}: briefly, a softener ({看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}, {等|děng}{一下|yí xià}).
- Verb + {一点儿|yì diǎnr} (+ noun): a little ({喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}).
- {太|tài} + adjective + {了|le}: so…! / too…!; {不|bú}{太|tài} + adjective: not very.
- Surname + {先生|xiān sheng} / {女士|nǚ shì}: Mr / Ms.
- New characters for old friends: {=谢=} ({谢谢|xiè xie}), {=客=} ({不客气|bú kè qi}), {=关=} and {=系=}
  ({没关系|méi guān xi}).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: How much is it? Money and measure words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can order food and drink now; this lesson lets you pay for it. You'll ask
{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ (how much?), understand and say prices in {块|kuài} and {元|yuán}, say
whether something is {贵|guì} (expensive) or {便宜|pián yi} (cheap), and tell {买|mǎi} (buy) from
{卖|mài} (sell), which differ only in tone. You'll also put numbers in front of things the
Chinese way, with a measure word between: {一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū} (a book), {两|liǎng}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}
(two pieces of clothing). The numbers to 9,999 from lesson 04 are all you need.

## How much? {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？

{钱|qián} is money, and {多少|duō shao} is "how much, how many" (lesson 04). Put the thing first:

{面包|miàn bāo}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much is the bread?
{茶|chá}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much is the tea?
{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much is one book?

The answer puts the price where {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián} was. Like dates and ages, prices make a
sentence without {是|shì} (a noun predicate):

{面包|miàn bāo}{五|wǔ}{块|kuài}。 — The bread is five kuai.
{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{四十|sì shí}{块|kuài}。 — One book is forty kuai.

For a small sum you'll also hear {几|jǐ}{块|kuài}{钱|qián}？ ("how many kuai?"), with {几|jǐ} for
small numbers, as in lesson 03.

## Money: {块|kuài} in speech, {元|yuán} in writing

China's money is the renminbi ({人民币|rén mín bì}, "people's currency", RMB), counted in yuan. In
speech, people almost always say {块|kuài}; prices written on tags, menus and receipts use
{元|yuán} (or the sign ¥). Both are measure words that follow the number:

| Written | Said | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 5元 | {五|wǔ}{块|kuài} | 5 yuan |
| 2元 | {两|liǎng}{块|kuài} | 2 yuan (two: {两|liǎng}, not {二|èr}) |
| 12元 | {十二|shí èr}{块|kuài} | 12 yuan |
| 38元 | {三十八|sān shí bā}{块|kuài} | 38 yuan |
| 100元 | {一百|yì bǎi}{块|kuài} | 100 yuan |
| 105元 | {一百零五|yì bǎi líng wǔ}{块|kuài} | 105 yuan |
| 20.50元 | {二十|èr shí}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ} | 20.50 yuan |

The last line needs a word of explanation. A yuan is divided into ten smaller units, the *jiao*,
spoken {毛|máo} and written {角|jiǎo}; you'll learn those two words in HSK 3. In speech the last unit
is usually left off, so a number after {块|kuài} is tenths: {二十|èr shí}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ} is
twenty yuan fifty, {三|sān}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ} is 3.50. For 200 you'll hear both {两百|liǎng bǎi} and
{二百|èr bǎi}.

{钱|qián} often follows the measure word in a full answer: {五|wǔ}{块|kuài}{钱|qián} ("five kuai
of money"). Leaving it out, {五|wǔ}{块|kuài}, is just as common.

## Number + measure word + noun

English says "a book", "two shirts", "three apples". Chinese puts a **[[measure word]]** between the
number and the noun, always; you met the general one, {个|gè}, in lesson 03. The three parts
together are a **[[quantity phrase]]**:

| Number | Measure word | Noun | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {一|yì} | {本|běn} | {书|shū} | a book |
| {两|liǎng} | {本|běn} | {书|shū} | two books |
| {一|yí} | {件|jiàn} | {衣服|yī fu} | a piece of clothing (a top, a coat) |
| {三|sān} | {个|gè} | {包子|bāo zi} | three steamed buns |
| {一|yí} | {块|kuài} | {面包|miàn bāo} | a piece of bread |
| {一|yí} | {件|jiàn} | {事|shì} | a matter, a thing to do |

- {本|běn} counts books and other bound things (notebooks, magazines).
- {件|jiàn} counts clothes, especially for the upper body (shirts, jackets), and matters or
  pieces of business: {一|yí}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}.
- {块|kuài} is a lump or piece of something (bread, cake, soap) as well as the money word.
- {个|gè} is the general measure word, for people and for things that have no special one; it
  is usually said with a light tone after a number, but this course writes it *gè*.

The noun can drop out when everyone knows what you're counting: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}
(I'll buy two [books]). The measure word can't: ~~{两|liǎng}{书|shū}~~ is wrong. The reference
sheet "Measure words" lists every measure word of HSK 1 with its nouns.

Watch the tone of {一|yī} before a measure word: *yì* before tones 1–3 ({一|yì}{本|běn}), *yí*
before a 4th tone ({一|yí}{件|jiàn}, {一|yí}{块|kuài}, {一|yí}{个|gè}).

## Dear or cheap: {贵|guì} and {便宜|pián yi}

{贵|guì} (expensive) and {便宜|pián yi} (cheap) are adjectives. Like {好|hǎo} in {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo},
they follow the subject directly, usually with {很|hěn}, and with no {是|shì}:

{书|shū}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}。 — Books are expensive.
{面包|miàn bāo}{很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi}。 — The bread is cheap.
{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}！ — That's too expensive!
{不|bú}{贵|guì}。 — It's not expensive.

At markets and small stalls people sometimes ask for a lower price with {便宜|pián yi}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{吧|ba}！
("make it a little cheaper!"); in shops and supermarkets prices are usually fixed. {一点儿|yì diǎnr} after an
adjective means "a bit more so" (lesson 21 says more).

{便宜|pián yi} has a surprise in it: 便 is read *pián* here, and *biàn* in other words such as
{方便|fāng biàn} (convenient, HSK 3). Its second syllable is neutral: *piányi*.

## Buy and sell: {买|mǎi} and {卖|mài}

These two differ only in tone, so say them carefully:

- {买|mǎi}, third tone (low, dipping): to buy. {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{书|shū}。 — I'm buying books.
- {卖|mài}, fourth tone (falling): to sell. {他|tā}{卖|mài}{书|shū}。 — He sells books.

{你们|nǐ men}{卖|mài}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？ (Do you sell tea?) is how you ask a shop if they have
something. {=The characters differ by one part: 卖 has 十 on top of 买. A memory aid: to *sell*,
you put more (十, ten) on the counter.=} In traditional script the pair is {+卖+} and {+买+}: there
the top of {+卖+} is 士.

## Shops: {店|diàn}, {商店|shāng diàn}, {书店|shū diàn}

{店|diàn} is a shop or store; it forms the names of kinds of shops:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {商店|shāng diàn} | shop, store (general) |
| {书店|shū diàn} | bookshop |
| {饭店|fàn diàn} | restaurant (and hotel, in names) |
| {店|diàn} | shop, store (on its own and at the end of names) |

The character 店 belongs to HSK 2, so it always has its pinyin in this course; you only need to
recognise the words.

## A price list

Signs like this one are a task of the HSK 1 reading paper: read the prices aloud in {块|kuài}.

| | |
|---|---|
| {包子|bāo zi} | 2元 |
| {面包|miàn bāo} | 4.50元 |
| {米饭|mǐ fàn} | 3元 |
| {面条儿|miàn tiáor} | 15元 |
| {饺子|jiǎo zi} | 22元 |
| {茶|chá} | 8元 |

<details>
<summary>The prices said aloud</summary>

{两|liǎng}{块|kuài}, {四|sì}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}, {三|sān}{块|kuài}, {十五|shí wǔ}{块|kuài},
{二十二|èr shí èr}{块|kuài}, {八|bā}{块|kuài}.
</details>

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 钱 (traditional 錢) | money | qián | 钅 | 10 | {钱|qián}, {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián} |
| 块 (traditional 塊) | lump, piece; kuai | kuài | 土 | 7 | {块|kuài}, {一块儿|yí kuàir} (together, HSK 3) |
| 元 | yuan; first | yuán | 儿 | 4 | {元|yuán} |
| 卖 (traditional 賣) | sell | mài | 十 | 8 | {卖|mài} |
| 贵 (traditional 貴) | expensive; precious | guì | 贝 | 9 | {贵|guì} |
| 便 | cheap (in 便宜); convenient | pián, and others | 亻 | 9 | {便宜|pián yi}, {方便|fāng biàn} (HSK 3) |
| 宜 | suitable | yi (yí) | 宀 | 8 | {便宜|pián yi} |
| 商 | trade, business | shāng | 口 | 11 | {商店|shāng diàn} |
| 本 | root; (measure for books) | běn | 木 | 5 | {本|běn}, {本子|běn zi} (notebook, HSK 2) |
| 书 ✎ (traditional 書) | book; writing | shū | 丨 | 4 | {书|shū}, {书店|shū diàn} |
| 件 | item; (measure for clothes, matters) | jiàn | 亻 | 6 | {件|jiàn} |

The other six are written the same in traditional script; in Traditional the tracing pads show
錢, 塊, 賣, 貴 and 書.

- 钱 has 钅, "metal" (lesson 07, in {分钟|fēn zhōng}): coins were metal. 贵 has 贝, "shell": cowrie shells were
  used as money in ancient China, and many characters about value contain 贝 (the traditional
  forms of {买|mǎi} 買 and {卖|mài} 賣 do too).
- 本 is 木 (tree) with a short line across the bottom marking the root: "root, origin". Its use
  as the measure word for books came much later.
- 件 is 亻 (person) + 牛 (ox). Old dictionaries explain it as dividing up property, an ox being a
  big item; take it as a memory aid.
- 元 has 儿 at the bottom, the "legs" radical from lesson 12.
- 书 is short (4 strokes) but its order is unusual (below). Its traditional form is 書.

### New radicals

曰, "to say" ({曰|yuē}). It looks like 日 (sun) but is wider and flatter; it was a mouth with
something coming out of it. Make Me a Hanzi files 电 (electricity, lesson 10) under it; some
dictionaries put 电 under 田 instead. You'll see it in 最 (most, HSK 2) and 更 (even more, HSK 3).

矢, "arrow" ({矢|shǐ}). On the left of 知 in {知道|zhī dào} (lesson 10). Later: 短 (short) and
矮 (low) in HSK 3.

米, "rice" ({米|mǐ}). The character from {米饭|mǐ fàn} (lesson 11). As a radical, on the left,
it's narrower and its last stroke becomes a dot: you'll see it in 糖 (sugar) and 糕 (cake) in
HSK 3, foods made from grains.

### Stroke order

- 书: four strokes: the horizontal that turns down (横折), then a second horizontal that turns
  down and ends with a hook (横折钩), then the long vertical through the middle, and last the dot at
  the top right.
- 卖: 十 first, then the top of 买 (a horizontal ending in a small hook), the two dots, and
  大 at the bottom.
- 钱: 钅 first (five strokes from the top down; the vertical that rises at the end comes last),
  then the right side: the two horizontals, the long slanting hook, the left-falling stroke and
  the dot, last.
- 本: write 木, then the short horizontal at the bottom.

```trace
钱块元卖贵便
```

```trace
宜商本书件
```

Write it: 书 is one of the characters to know by hand. Write it three times from memory, then
check the order on the pad.

=}

## Dialogue: at a small shop

{李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) buys something for breakfast. The other speaker is a shop assistant,
{店员|diàn yuán} (店员).

```dialogue
# At a small shop
李明: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你们|nǐ men}{卖|mài}{面包|miàn bāo}{吗|ma}？
= Hello! Do you sell bread?
店员: {卖|mài}。{一|yí}{个|gè}{面包|miàn bāo}{五|wǔ}{块|kuài}。
= Yes. One roll is five kuai.
李明: {茶|chá}{呢|ne}？{茶|chá}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
= And the tea? How much is the tea?
店员: {茶|chá}{三十八|sān shí bā}{块|kuài}。
= The tea is thirty-eight kuai.
李明: {三十八|sān shí bā}{块|kuài}？{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}！
= Thirty-eight? That's too expensive!
店员: {不|bú}{贵|guì}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{的|de}{中国|Zhōng guó}{茶|chá}。
= It isn't expensive. This is very good Chinese tea.
李明: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{买|mǎi}{茶|chá}，{买|mǎi}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{面包|miàn bāo}{吧|ba}。
= I won't buy tea; I'll take two rolls.
店员: {好|hǎo}{的|de}。{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{面包|miàn bāo}{十|shí}{块|kuài}。
= All right. Two rolls are ten kuai.
李明: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{一百|yì bǎi}{块|kuài}。
= Here's a hundred.
店员: {找|zhǎo}{你|nǐ}{九十|jiǔ shí}{块|kuài}。{谢谢|xiè xie}！
= Here's ninety change. Thank you!
李明: {谢谢|xiè xie}，{再见|zài jiàn}！
= Thanks, goodbye!
```

{店员|diàn yuán} (shop assistant) is a word outside this course. {找|zhǎo} (to look for, lesson 10)
also means "to give change": {找|zhǎo}{你|nǐ}{九十|jiǔ shí}{块|kuài} is "(I) give you ninety back".
Many people in China pay by phone, scanning a code; cash and the phrase are still part of
daily life.

## Reading: Saturday shopping

> {星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}{上午|shàng wǔ}，{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}。{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{面包|miàn bāo}{和|hé}{茶|chá}，{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。{面包|miàn bāo}{很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{三|sān}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}。{茶|chá}{不|bù}{便宜|pián yi}，{一百二十|yì bǎi èr shí}{块|kuài}。{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{说|shuō}：“{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}！”{书店|shū diàn}{的|de}{书|shū}{也|yě}{不|bù}{便宜|pián yi}，{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{六十八|liù shí bā}{块|kuài}。{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}，{她|tā}{说|shuō}：“{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{大学|dà xué}{的|de}{书店|shū diàn}{吧|ba}。”

1. How much is one bread roll?
2. What does Wang Fang say about the tea?
3. Where does she suggest going, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. 3.50 yuan ({三|sān}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}).
2. That it's too expensive ({太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}): it costs 120 yuan.
3. The university bookshop ({大学|dà xué}{的|de}{书店|shū diàn}), because the book in this
   bookshop (68 yuan) isn't cheap either.

"On Saturday morning Wang Fang and I go to the shops. I want to buy bread and tea; Wang Fang
wants to buy a book. The bread is cheap, three fifty a roll. The tea isn't cheap: a hundred and
twenty. Wang Fang says, 'That's too expensive!' The books at the bookshop aren't cheap either:
sixty-eight for one book. Wang Fang doesn't want to buy it. She says, 'Let's go to the
university bookshop.'"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
= How much is one book?
{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}！
= That's too expensive!
{便宜|pián yi}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{吧|ba}！
= Make it a bit cheaper!
{你们|nǐ men}{卖|mài}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？
= Do you sell tea?
{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}。
= I'll take two (books).
```

## Pronunciation

- {买|mǎi} / {卖|mài}: the most important tone pair of the lesson. Low and dipping for buying,
  falling for selling. Say {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi} (said *wó mǎi*: two third tones) and {他|tā}{卖|mài}.
- {钱|qián} rises and {千|qiān} (thousand) is level: {一千|yì qiān}{块|kuài}{钱|qián} has both.
- {块|kuài}: *k* with a puff of air, then *uai* as one glide, "kwai".
- {元|yuán}: after *y*, *u* is *ü*: lips rounded as for "oo", tongue as for "ee".
- {便宜|pián yi}: *pián* with a puff on the *p*; *yi* light and short.
- {书|shū}: *sh* with the tongue curled back, then *u*, level and high.

## Common mistakes

- No measure word: ~~{两|liǎng}{书|shū}~~, ~~{三|sān}{衣服|yī fu}~~. Say {两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū},
  {三|sān}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}.
- {二|èr} before a measure word: ~~{二|èr}{块|kuài}~~. Two of anything is {两|liǎng}: {两|liǎng}{块|kuài}.
- {是|shì} before an adjective: ~~{书|shū}{是|shì}{贵|guì}~~. Say {书|shū}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}.
- Price at the start, English-style: ~~{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}{面包|miàn bāo}？~~ The thing comes
  first: {面包|miàn bāo}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
- {买|mǎi} and {卖|mài} said with the same tone: {我|wǒ}{卖|mài}{书|shū} means "I sell books".
- Reading 便 in {便宜|pián yi} as *biàn*.

## Key points

- X {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ asks a price; the answer replaces {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}, with no {是|shì}.
- {块|kuài} in speech, {元|yuán} in writing; {二十|èr shí}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ} = 20.50; two yuan is
  {两|liǎng}{块|kuài}.
- Quantity phrase: number + measure word + noun: {一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}, {一|yí}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu},
  {三|sān}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}.
- {很|hěn}{贵|guì} / {很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi} / {太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le} / {不|bú}{贵|guì}: adjectives with no {是|shì}.
- {买|mǎi} (3rd tone) buys, {卖|mài} (4th tone) sells.
- {商店|shāng diàn}, {书店|shū diàn}, {饭店|fàn diàn}, {店|diàn}.
- New radicals: 曰 (say), 矢 (arrow), 米 (rice).
