lessons.title: Tea: 茶
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can say {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{茶|chá} and {请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}. This optional lesson is about the
drink itself: the kinds of Chinese tea and their names, a few famous teas and where they grow,
and how tea fits into everyday life and hospitality. It's culture first, with Chinese as a
bonus: the tea words here are glossed and aren't part of your vocabulary reviews.

## Where tea comes from

The tea plant is a kind of camellia. Botanists think it probably comes from the borderlands of
south-west China and northern Myanmar, and China is still the world's largest tea producer. Tea
grows mostly in the south of the country, on hillsides with warm, wet weather; among the biggest
producing provinces are Fujian, Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou.

People in China have drunk tea for well over a thousand years. In the 8th century, under the
Tang dynasty, a writer named {陆羽|Lù Yǔ} (Lu Yu) wrote {茶经|Chá jīng}, *The Classic of Tea*, the
oldest known book about tea: how to grow it, make it, brew it and drink it.

## Six kinds of tea

Chinese tea is usually sorted into six kinds. All of them come from the same plant; what
differs is how the leaves are treated after picking, above all how much they're allowed to
oxidise (darken in the air, as a cut apple does; Chinese speaks of "fermenting").

| Chinese | Pinyin | English | How it's made | A famous example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| {绿茶|lǜ chá} | lǜchá | green tea | heated soon after picking, so it stays green | {龙井|Lóng jǐng} (Longjing, "Dragon Well") |
| {白茶|bái chá} | báichá | white tea | very little processing, only lightly oxidised | |
| {黄茶|huáng chá} | huángchá | yellow tea | like green tea, but the leaves are left to yellow before drying | |
| {乌龙茶|wū lóng chá} | wūlóngchá | oolong | partly oxidised | {铁观音|Tiě guān yīn} (Tieguanyin) |
| {红茶|hóng chá} | hóngchá | black tea | oxidised all the way | {祁门|Qí mén}{红茶|hóng chá} (Keemun) |
| {黑茶|hēi chá} | hēichá | dark tea | fermented in heaps or stored to mature; some improve with age | {普洱茶|Pǔ ěr chá} (Pu'er) |

Note the colours. What English calls "black tea" is {红茶|hóng chá}, "red tea", in Chinese: the
name describes the reddish colour of the tea in the cup. {黑茶|hēi chá}, literally "black tea", is
a different kind, the aged "dark tea". So if you want an English breakfast-style tea in China,
ask for {红茶|hóng chá}.

Green tea is the everyday tea in much of China: in recent years more than half of the tea China
produces has been green.

## Famous teas and where they grow

| Tea | Kind | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| {龙井|Lóng jǐng} (Longjing) | green | around West Lake in Hangzhou, Zhejiang |
| {碧螺春|Bì luó chūn} (Biluochun) | green | around Lake Tai near Suzhou, Jiangsu |
| {铁观音|Tiě guān yīn} (Tieguanyin) | oolong | Anxi County, Fujian |
| {祁门|Qí mén}{红茶|hóng chá} (Keemun) | black ("red") | Qimen County, Anhui |
| {普洱茶|Pǔ ěr chá} (Pu'er) | dark | Pu'er and other parts of Yunnan |

Many teas are named after their place, like wines: {祁门|Qí mén} is a county, and {普洱|Pǔ ěr} a
city.

## Tea in daily life

- With guests: offering tea is the first thing many hosts do when a visitor arrives:
  {请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 A good host keeps the cup topped up. Younger family members show respect
  by serving tea to older ones, and at many weddings the couple serve tea to their elders.
- Teahouses: a {茶馆|chá guǎn} (teahouse) is a place to sit, talk and drink tea for hours.
  In Guangdong and other Cantonese-speaking areas, "drinking tea" (*yum cha*) means a morning or
  lunchtime meal of small dishes (dim sum) with tea.

## Tapping the table

In many places in southern China, and in Cantonese-speaking communities around the world, you
may see someone tap the table with two bent fingers while their cup is being filled. It's a
silent "thank you", handy when you're in the middle of talking.

A popular story explains where it comes from: the Qianlong emperor (18th century) was
travelling in disguise and poured tea for a servant. The servant couldn't kneel to thank him
without giving the emperor away, so he "bowed" with his fingers on the table instead. It's a
story, not history, and the custom isn't universal: if in doubt, a smile and {谢谢|xiè xie} always
work.

## Ordering and talking about tea

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{什么|shén me}{茶|chá}？ — What kind of tea do you like?
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{绿茶|lǜ chá}。 — I like green tea.
{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{红茶|hóng chá}。 — I'd like a cup of black tea.
{这个|zhè ge}{茶|chá}{很|hěn}{好喝|hǎo hē}！ — This tea is delicious!
{你|nǐ}{再|zài}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{吧|ba}。 — Have a little more. ({再|zài}, again, more: lesson 23)

{好喝|hǎo hē} is the drinking partner of {好吃|hǎo chī}. In a modern café you'll also find
{奶茶|nǎi chá}, milk tea.

The speakers are {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) and her teacher, {李老师|Lǐ lǎo shī} (李老师).

```dialogue
# A visit
王芳: {李|Lǐ}{老师|lǎo shī}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！{请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}，{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
= Hello, Teacher Li! Please sit down and have some tea.
李老师: {谢谢|xiè xie}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{茶|chá}？
= Thank you. What tea is this?
王芳: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{绿茶|lǜ chá}，{龙井|Lóng jǐng}。{您|nín}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{绿茶|lǜ chá}{吗|ma}？
= It's green tea, Longjing. Do you like green tea?
李老师: {很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}！{真|zhēn}{好喝|hǎo hē}。
= Very much! It's really good.
王芳: {您|nín}{再|zài}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{吧|ba}。
= Have a little more.
李老师: {好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}。
= Yes, thank you.
```

Wang Fang uses {您|nín} with her teacher and offers tea twice; refilling the cup is part of being a
good host.

## Reading: tea at home

> {我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。{早上|zǎo shang}{他|tā}{喝|hē}{绿茶|lǜ chá}，{下午|xià wǔ}{喝|hē}{红茶|hóng chá}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}，{她|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}。{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{来|lái}{客人|kè rén}，{爸爸|bà ba}{说|shuō}：“{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}！”

{家|jiā}{里|lǐ} is "at home" ({里|lǐ}, inside, is lesson 16's), and {客人|kè rén} is a guest: 客 from
{不客气|bú kè qi} + 人.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"My dad really likes tea. In the morning he drinks green tea, in the afternoon black tea. My mum
doesn't drink tea; she likes water. When guests come to our home, Dad says, 'Please have some
tea!'"
</details>

## Words in this lesson

These are for recognition only; several of them ({绿茶|lǜ chá}, {红茶|hóng chá}, {奶茶|nǎi chá}) are
HSK 2 words you'll learn properly later.

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {绿茶|lǜ chá} | green tea |
| {红茶|hóng chá} | black tea (literally "red tea") |
| {乌龙茶|wū lóng chá} | oolong tea |
| {黑茶|hēi chá} | dark tea (aged) |
| {奶茶|nǎi chá} | milk tea |
| {好喝|hǎo hē} | nice to drink, tasty (of drinks) |
| {茶馆|chá guǎn} | teahouse |
| {客人|kè rén} | guest |
| {杯|bēi} | cup (as a measure word: {一|yì}{杯|bēi}{茶|chá}) |

## Key points

- Six kinds of Chinese tea, by how the leaves are processed: green, white, yellow, oolong,
  "red" (black) and dark.
- English "black tea" is {红茶|hóng chá}; {黑茶|hēi chá} is aged dark tea such as Pu'er.
- Famous teas are named after places: Longjing (Zhejiang), Tieguanyin (Fujian), Keemun (Anhui),
  Pu'er (Yunnan).
- Offering tea ({请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}) and refilling cups is basic hospitality; tapping two fingers
  is a silent thank-you in some places.

lessons.title: Rice, noodles and dumplings
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11 you learned {米饭|mǐ fàn}, {面条儿|miàn tiáor}, {饺子|jiǎo zi} and {包子|bāo zi}. This optional
lesson looks at where these staples are eaten, what they mean at festivals and birthdays, and
how to behave with chopsticks. The extra words are glossed; they aren't part of your vocabulary
reviews.

## North and south: wheat and rice

China is often described as two food regions. As a broad tendency:

| | North | South |
|---|---|---|
| Main grain | wheat | rice |
| Everyday staples | {面条儿|miàn tiáor}, {饺子|jiǎo zi}, {包子|bāo zi}, {馒头|mán tou} | {米饭|mǐ fàn} |

The rough dividing line is usually drawn along the Qinling mountains and the Huai River, in the
middle of the country: north of it, more wheat is grown and eaten; south of it, rice. It's only a
tendency: both grains are eaten all over the country, and city menus mix every region's food.
But if someone says {南方人|nán fāng rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}，{北方人|běi fāng rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}{和|hé}{饺子|jiǎo zi}
("southerners like rice, northerners like noodles and dumplings"), this is the picture they have
in mind. ({南方|nán fāng} is the south and {北方|běi fāng} the north; both are HSK 3 words.)

## Steamed buns: {包子|bāo zi} and {馒头|mán tou}

Two kinds of steamed bun look alike but aren't the same:

- {包子|bāo zi} has a filling: meat, vegetables, or something sweet. The name comes from {包|bāo},
  "to wrap": the dough is wrapped round the filling.
- {馒头|mán tou} (mantou) is plain, with no filling. In the north it's an everyday staple, eaten
  with dishes the way rice is eaten in the south.

Both are common for breakfast: {早上|zǎo shang}{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}。

## Dumplings at New Year

{饺子|jiǎo zi} are crescent-shaped dumplings, usually boiled. In northern China, eating them at
the Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) is one of the most important customs of the year:

- On New Year's Eve, families make the dumplings together and eat them around midnight, as the
  old year turns into the new one.
- Their shape is said to look like a {元宝|yuán bǎo}, a boat-shaped gold or silver ingot once used
  as money, so eating them is a wish for a prosperous year.
- Some families hide a coin in one dumpling; whoever finds it is said to have good luck in the
  coming year.

Making dumplings is {包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}, "wrapping dumplings": {我们|wǒ men}{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}！
In the south, where rice is the staple, families traditionally ate rice foods at New Year
instead, such as sweet {汤圆|tāng yuán} (glutinous rice balls) or {年糕|nián gāo} (rice cake), though
dumplings are now eaten there too.

## Noodles for a long life

On birthdays, many families eat {长寿面|cháng shòu miàn}, "long-life noodles". The idea is simple:
long noodles stand for a long life, so you try not to cut or break them while cooking or eating.
(HSK 2 has a lesson on birthday customs.)

## Chopsticks: a few manners

{筷子|kuài zi} (chopsticks) is an HSK 3 word. A few things to avoid:

- Don't stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. Upright sticks in rice look like the
  incense sticks offered to the dead, so it's a reminder of funerals and is felt to be unlucky.
  Lay them across the bowl or on the rest instead.
- Don't point at people with your chopsticks, or wave them while you talk.
- Don't drum on bowls or the table with them.

## Dialogue: New Year's Eve

The speakers are {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) and her friend {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫).

```dialogue
# New Year's Eve
王芳: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{今天|jīn tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{我们|wǒ men}{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}！
= David, let's make dumplings tonight!
大卫: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{会|huì}{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。
= Great! I can't make dumplings.
王芳: {没关系|méi guān xi}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{会|huì}。{她|tā}{包|bāo}{的|de}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{非常|fēi cháng}{好吃|hǎo chī}。
= Never mind, my mum can. Her dumplings are delicious.
大卫: {我们|wǒ men}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}？
= What time do we eat them?
王芳: {十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}。{一|yí}{个|gè}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{钱|qián}！
= At twelve. There's a coin in one of the dumplings!
大卫: {真|zhēn}{的|de}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{吃|chī}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{饺子|jiǎo zi}！
= Really? I'm going to eat lots of dumplings!
```

{包|bāo} is "to wrap", the verb inside {包子|bāo zi}; {她|tā}{包|bāo}{的|de}{饺子|jiǎo zi} is "the dumplings
she wraps". {饺子|jiǎo zi}{里|lǐ} is "in the dumpling" ({里|lǐ}, inside: lesson 16), and {真|zhēn}{的|de}{吗|ma}？
is "Really?"

## Reading: north and south

> {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{北京|Běi jīng}{人|rén}，{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}{和|hé}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{是|shì}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{人|rén}，{她|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{米饭|mǐ fàn}。{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{包子|bāo zi}。

{同学|tóng xué} (classmate) is a lesson 19 word; {上海|Shàng hǎi} is Shanghai.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"I'm from Beijing; I like noodles and dumplings. My classmate is from Shanghai; she likes rice.
We both like steamed buns."
</details>

## Words in this lesson

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {馒头|mán tou} | plain steamed bun (mantou) |
| {包|bāo} | to wrap; {包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}, to make dumplings |
| {南方|nán fāng} / {北方|běi fāng} | the south / the north |
| {元宝|yuán bǎo} | old gold or silver ingot |
| {汤圆|tāng yuán} | sweet glutinous rice balls |
| {年糕|nián gāo} | New Year rice cake |
| {长寿面|cháng shòu miàn} | long-life (birthday) noodles |
| {筷子|kuài zi} | chopsticks |

## Key points

- Broadly, wheat foods (noodles, dumplings, buns) in the north and rice in the south, with the
  Qinling–Huai River line as the rough divide; today both are eaten everywhere.
- {包子|bāo zi} are filled; {馒头|mán tou} are plain.
- Northern families make and eat {饺子|jiǎo zi} on New Year's Eve; their shape recalls old ingots.
- Long noodles on birthdays wish for a long life.
- Never stand chopsticks upright in rice.

lessons.title: Where is it? 在 and position words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 05 you met {在|zài} as a verb ({他|tā}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}, "he's at the company") and
before a verb ({他|tā}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}, "he works at a company"). This module is about places: where
things are, what's in a room, how you get somewhere and what you do at school. This first lesson
gives you the words to say exactly *where*: "in the cup", "on the book", "here", "over there",
"where?", and the polite way to ask a stranger, {请问|qǐng wèn}.

You'll learn:

- X {在|zài} + place: "X is (at, in) the place";
- **[[place words]]**, and how to turn an ordinary noun into one with a position word ({杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ},
  {书|shū}{上|shàng});
- {这儿|zhèr} / {这里|zhè lǐ}, {那儿|nàr} / {那里|nà lǐ}, {哪儿|nǎr} / {哪里|nǎ lǐ};
- person + {这儿|zhèr} / {那儿|nàr}: "with me", "at the teacher's";
- {请问|qǐng wèn}…{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ for asking the way.

## X {在|zài} + place: where something is

To say where a person or thing is, put the thing first, then {在|zài}, then the place. {在|zài} is
the verb: it does the work of English "is" in "is at home", so no {是|shì} is needed.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 — My phone is at home.

{老师|lǎo shī}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}。 — The teacher is at school.

{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where are you?

The negative is {不|bú}{在|zài} (*bú*, because {在|zài} is a fourth tone), and the questions are the
ones you know: {吗|ma}, or the A-not-A form {在|zài}{不|bu}{在|zài} with a light *bu*.

{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{不|bú}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。 — Teacher Wang isn't here. ({王|Wáng} is a surname.)

{你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？ — Is your mum at home?

{他|tā}{在|zài}{不|bu}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}？ — Is he at the company (or not)?

A short answer repeats the verb: {在|zài}。 (Yes, he is.) / {不|bú}{在|zài}。 (No, he isn't.)

Time words still come before the verb, either before or after the subject, as in lesson 07:

{我|wǒ}{上午|shàng wǔ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}，{下午|xià wǔ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 — I'm at school in the
morning and at home in the afternoon.

## Place words and position words

After {在|zài}, Chinese needs a place word: a word that names a place. Some nouns are places
already. Others are just things, and a thing isn't a place: English says "in the cup", with a
preposition in front, but Chinese turns the cup into a place by adding a position word after it,
"cup-inside". These position words are called **[[locatives]]**.

| Locative | Meaning | Example | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| {上|shàng} | on, on top of, above | {书|shū}{上|shàng} | on the book |
| {下|xià} | under, below | {衣服|yī fu}{下|xià} | under the clothes |
| {里|lǐ} | in, inside | {杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ} | in the cup |
| {外|wài} | outside | {学校|xué xiào}{外|wài} | outside the school |
| {前|qián} | in front of; before | {饭|fàn}{前|qián} | before meals |
| {后|hòu} | behind; after | {饭|fàn}{后|hòu} | after meals |

{水|shuǐ}{在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}。 — The water is in the cup.

{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{书|shū}{上|shàng}。 — The phone is on the book.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{衣服|yī fu}{下|xià}。 — My phone is under the clothes.

Always the thing first, then the locative: {杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}, never ~~{里|lǐ}{杯子|bēi zi}~~. Think
of it as "the cup's inside", "the book's top".

**How natural is each one alone?** {上|shàng} and {里|lǐ} go straight after nouns all the time in
everyday speech: {书|shū}{上|shàng}, {家|jiā}{里|lǐ}, {手机|shǒu jī}{里|lǐ} (in the phone). {下|xià},
{外|wài}, {前|qián} and {后|hòu} alone after a noun sound compact, the way signs, labels and set
phrases put it: {饭|fàn}{前|qián} and {饭|fàn}{后|hòu} are what a medicine label says ("before / after
meals"), and {八|bā}{点|diǎn}{前|qián} is "before eight o'clock". In ordinary speech people usually
make them two syllables with {边|biān} ("side"), as in {外边|wài bian} (outside): that's lesson 17.

{前|qián} and {后|hòu} work for time as well as space, just like English "before" and "after":

{饭|fàn}{后|hòu}{我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — After meals I drink tea.

{请|qǐng}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{前|qián}{来|lái}。 — Please come before eight.

### Which nouns need a locative?

| Kind of noun | After {在|zài} | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Countries and cities | never add {里|lǐ} | {在|zài}{中国|Zhōng guó}, {在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng} (Beijing), not ~~{在|zài}{中国|Zhōng guó}{里|lǐ}~~ |
| Buildings and institutions | fine alone; add {里|lǐ} for "inside" | {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào} (at school), {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ} (inside the school, on its grounds) |
| Things | need a locative | {在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}, {在|zài}{书|shū}{上|shàng}; not ~~{在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}~~ |

The middle group ({家|jiā}, {学校|xué xiào}, {公司|gōng sī}, {商店|shāng diàn}, {超市|chāo shì},
{饭店|fàn diàn}, {书店|shū diàn}, {大学|dà xué}) is the easy one: both are right, and {里|lǐ} only adds
"inside". {在|zài}{家|jiā} and {在|zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ} both mean "at home".

{他|tā}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{里|lǐ}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — He's in the supermarket buying things.

**Pronunciation.** After a noun, and in {这里|zhè lǐ} / {那里|nà lǐ}, {里|lǐ} is often said lightly,
almost *li* with no tone. This course writes *lǐ* everywhere; say it lightly when you hear others do.

## Here, there and where

You learned {哪儿|nǎr} (where) in lesson 09. It has a family:

| | with {儿|ér} (northern speech) | with {里|lǐ} (used everywhere) |
|---|---|---|
| here | {这儿|zhèr} | {这里|zhè lǐ} |
| there | {那儿|nàr} | {那里|nà lǐ} |
| where? | {哪儿|nǎr} | {哪里|nǎ lǐ} |

The {儿|ér} forms belong to Beijing and the north, where *-r* endings are everywhere. The {里|lǐ}
forms are heard all over China and are the usual ones in writing. They mean the same, so use the
pair that matches the people around you. Both kinds are place words already, so they never take
another locative:

{书|shū}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。 — The book is here.

{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪里|nǎ lǐ}？ — Where are you?

{请|qǐng}{来|lái}{这儿|zhèr}。 — Please come here.

**Watch the tones.** {哪|nǎ} (which, where) and {那|nà} (that, there) differ only in tone: third
against fourth. {哪儿|nǎr}？ is "where?", {那儿|nàr} is "there". In {哪里|nǎ lǐ} two third tones meet,
so it's said *ná lǐ* (the 3 + 3 rule), though the pinyin stays nǎ lǐ.

(You'll also hear {哪里|nǎ lǐ} as a modest reply to a compliment, "oh, not at all". That's a later
lesson's business; here it simply asks "where?")

## Person + {这儿|zhèr} / {那儿|nàr}: "with me", "at the teacher's"

A person isn't a place, so ~~{书|shū}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}~~ is wrong. To say "the book is with me" (I've
got it), add {这儿|zhèr} to the person: "my here". For someone else, {那儿|nàr}: "their there".

{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}。 — Your book is with me. (I've got your book.)

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{你|nǐ}{那儿|nàr}{吗|ma}？ — Is my phone with you? (Have you got my
phone?)

{他|tā}{在|zài}{老师|lǎo shī}{那儿|nàr}。 — He's at the teacher's (with the teacher).

{这儿|zhèr} goes with the speaker ({我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}, {我们|wǒ men}{这儿|zhèr}: "where I am, where we
are") and {那儿|nàr} with anyone else. {这里|zhè lǐ} and {那里|nà lǐ} work the same way.

## Asking the way: {请问|qǐng wèn}

{请问|qǐng wèn} is {请|qǐng} (please, lesson 12) + {问|wèn} (to ask): "may I ask". Say it first when you
ask a stranger a question, the way English says "excuse me" before a question. It's polite, never
cold, and fine with anyone.

{请问|qǐng wèn}，{超市|chāo shì}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Excuse me, where's the supermarket?

{请问|qǐng wèn}，{您|nín}{是|shì}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？ — Excuse me, are you Teacher Wang?

Don't use {请问|qǐng wèn} for "excuse me, sorry" when you bump into someone: that's
{对不起|duì bu qǐ}. {请问|qǐng wèn} is only for asking.

Typical answers point: {在|zài}{那儿|nàr}。 (Over there.) {在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。 (Right here.)
{在|zài}{书店|shū diàn}{里|lǐ}。 (Inside the bookshop.) {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。 (I don't know.)

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 里 (traditional 裡) | inside, in | lǐ (often light: li) | 里 | 7 | {里|lǐ}, {这里|zhè lǐ}, {那里|nà lǐ}, {哪里|nǎ lǐ} |
| 前 | front; before | qián | 刂 | 9 | {前|qián}, {饭|fàn}{前|qián} |
| 后 (traditional 後) ✎ | back, behind; after | hòu | 口 | 6 | {后|hòu}, {饭|fàn}{后|hòu} |
| 外 | outside | wài | 夕 | 5 | {外|wài}, {外边|wài bian} (lesson 17) |
| 问 (traditional 問) | to ask | wèn | 门 | 6 | {请问|qǐng wèn}, {问|wèn} (lesson 23) |

### New radical: 刂, the standing knife

刂 is the side form of {刀|dāo} (knife). Its Chinese name is {立刀旁|lì dāo páng}, "standing-knife
side": the knife stood up on the right of a character. It has two strokes, a short vertical and
then a long vertical with a hook. Seven characters in this track contain it. So far you've met
it in {前|qián}; {到|dào} (to arrive) in lesson 18 has it too. Many 刂 characters have to do with
cutting, but in {前|qián} the knife adds no meaning you can see today; treat it as part of the shape.

Make Me a Hanzi, the stroke data this course uses, files {前|qián} under 刂. Some dictionaries file it
under 丷, the two short strokes on top, so look there too if a dictionary's 刂 section doesn't have it.

### Notes on the others

- {里|lǐ} is its own radical. In traditional script, "inside" is {裡|lǐ}: {里|lǐ} with the clothing
  radical 衤 added (the old meaning was the lining of a garment). On its own, traditional {里|lǐ} is a
  village or a distance (the {里|lǐ} in {公里|gōng lǐ}, kilometre, later). The traditional switch shows {裡|lǐ} in
  this lesson's words.
- {后|hòu} has {口|kǒu} (mouth) as its radical in Make Me a Hanzi's analysis. Traditional script
  writes "behind, after" as {後|hòu}, a completely different character; traditional {后|hòu} means
  "empress, queen" (and is a surname). The switch shows {後|hòu}.
- {外|wài} is {夕|xī} (evening, a moon-like shape) + {卜|bǔ}. Memory aid: a moon on the left,
  and a stick on the right pointing *out* of the character.
- {问|wèn} is a mouth {口|kǒu} inside a door {门|mén} (the door radical from lesson 10). That's close
  to its real history: {口|kǒu} gives the meaning (asking is done with the mouth) and {门|mén} once
  gave the sound. Traditional: {問|wèn}.

### Stroke order

- **里**: write the box first, including its bottom line (strokes 1–4: left side, top and right
  side, the middle line, the bottom line). Then the long vertical (5) goes from the top of the box
  straight down through it, and the two horizontals of the base come last, the bottom one longest.
- **后**: the two left-falling strokes come first: the short one on top (from right to left), then
  the long one down the left side. Then the horizontal, then {口|kǒu}.
- **问**: {门|mén} first: the dot, the left vertical, then the top and right side with its hook.
  {口|kǒu} goes inside last. {门|mén} is open at the bottom, so it's finished before what's inside.
- **前**: the two short strokes on top (left one, then right one), the long horizontal, then the
  left part (vertical, the top and right side with a hook, two short lines), then the knife.

Trace the new characters stroke by stroke:

```trace
里前后外问
```

✎ **Write it**: {后|hòu} is one of the 100 characters the HSK expects you to write by hand by level 2.
Write it three times from memory, on paper or on the pad, then check the stroke order above.
=}

## Dialogue: looking for Teacher Li

{汤姆|Tāng mǔ} (Tom), a new student, asks {王芳|Wáng Fāng}, a student at the university, for help.

```dialogue
# At the university
汤姆: {请问|qǐng wèn}，{这里|zhè lǐ}{是|shì}{大学|dà xué}{吗|ma}？
= Excuse me, is this the university?
王芳: {是|shì}。{你|nǐ}{找|zhǎo}{谁|shéi}？
= Yes. Who are you looking for?
汤姆: {我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{李|Lǐ}{老师|lǎo shī}。{他|tā}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= I'm looking for Teacher Li. Where is he?
王芳: {李|Lǐ}{老师|lǎo shī}{现在|xiàn zài}{不|bú}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}，{在|zài}{书店|shū diàn}{里|lǐ}。
= Teacher Li isn't here right now. He's in the bookshop.
汤姆: {书店|shū diàn}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where's the bookshop?
王芳: {在|zài}{那儿|nàr}。{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{那|nà}{是|shì}{书店|shū diàn}。
= Over there. Look, that's the bookshop.
汤姆: {谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！
= Thank you!
王芳: {不客气|bú kè qi}。
= You're welcome.
```

{李|Lǐ} is a surname. {这里|zhè lǐ}{是|shì}{大学|dà xué}{吗|ma}？ uses {是|shì}, not {在|zài}: it says
what this place *is*, not where something is. {你|nǐ}{看|kàn} ("you look") is how Chinese says
"look!" when pointing something out.

## Reading: a note on the table

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} leaves a note for her mother.

> {妈妈|mā ma}：
>
> {我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{不|bú}{在|zài}{家|jiā}，{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}，{下午|xià wǔ}{五|wǔ}{点|diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{不|bú}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}，{在|zài}{爸爸|bà ba}{那儿|nàr}。{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{茶|chá}{在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}，{饭|fàn}{后|hòu}{请|qǐng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？{在|zài}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{上|shàng}！
>
> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}

1. Where is Wang Fang now, and when will she be home?
2. Who has her mother's phone?
3. Where is the mother's book?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

Mum, I'm not at home now, I'm at school; I'll be home at five in the afternoon. Your phone isn't
with me, Dad has it. Dad is at the company; he'll be home at seven this evening. The tea is in the cup; please drink it after your meal.
Where's your book? On your clothes! Wang Fang

1. At school; at five in the afternoon. 2. Her father. 3. On her clothes (on top of the pile).

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{请问|qǐng wèn}，{超市|chāo shì}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Excuse me, where's the supermarket?
{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}。
= Over there.
{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{你|nǐ}{那儿|nàr}{吗|ma}？
= Have you got my phone?
{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}。
= I've got your book.
{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪里|nǎ lǐ}？
= Where are you?
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}。
= I'm at home.
```

## Common mistakes

- Adding {是|shì}: "He is at school" is {他|tā}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}, not ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{学校|xué xiào}~~
  (that says he *is* a school). {在|zài} already means "be at".
- English order: ~~{在|zài}{书|shū}{上|shàng}{手机|shǒu jī}~~ or ~~{上|shàng}{书|shū}~~. The thing that's
  somewhere comes first, then {在|zài}, then the place; the locative follows its noun.
- Leaving out the locative after a thing: ~~{水|shuǐ}{在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}~~. A cup isn't a place until
  it has {里|lǐ}.
- Adding {里|lǐ} to a country or city: ~~{在|zài}{中国|Zhōng guó}{里|lǐ}~~. Just {在|zài}{中国|Zhōng guó}.
- ~~{书|shū}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}~~ for "I've got the book": a person needs {这儿|zhèr} or {那儿|nàr}.
- Mixing up {哪儿|nǎr} and {那儿|nàr}: the third tone asks, the fourth tone points.
- {请问|qǐng wèn} for an apology. To say sorry, use {对不起|duì bu qǐ}.

## Key points

- X {在|zài} place: {手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{家|jiā}. Negative {不|bú}{在|zài}; questions with {吗|ma},
  {在|zài}{不|bu}{在|zài} or {哪儿|nǎr}.
- A thing becomes a place with a locative after it: {杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}, {书|shū}{上|shàng},
  {衣服|yī fu}{下|xià}. {上|shàng} and {里|lǐ} are everyday; bare {下|xià} {外|wài} {前|qián} {后|hòu}
  are compact ({饭|fàn}{后|hòu}); speech adds {边|biān} (lesson 17).
- Countries and cities never take {里|lǐ}; buildings may; things must.
- {这儿|zhèr} / {这里|zhè lǐ}, {那儿|nàr} / {那里|nà lǐ}, {哪儿|nǎr} / {哪里|nǎ lǐ}: same meaning: the {儿|ér}
  forms are northern, the {里|lǐ} forms general.
- Person + {这儿|zhèr} / {那儿|nàr} makes a place: {书|shū}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}.
- {请问|qǐng wèn} opens a question to a stranger.


The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: There is a…: 有 for existence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 answered "where is it?": {我|wǒ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}, "my book is on
the table". This lesson turns the sentence round to say what there *is* somewhere: "there's a
book on the table", "there's no TV in my room". You already know the verb: {有|yǒu}, "to have",
from lesson 03. You'll also learn:

- the **[[existential sentence]]**: place + {有|yǒu} + thing, and when to use it instead of {在|zài};
- position words with {边|biān} ("side"): {外边|wài bian}, {这边|zhè biān}, {那边|nà biān} and more;
- {住|zhù} (to live, to stay) and {住|zhù}{在|zài} + place;
- words for a room: {房间|fáng jiān}, {桌子|zhuō zi}, {椅子|yǐ zi}, {电脑|diàn nǎo}, {电视|diàn shì}.

## Place + {有|yǒu} + thing: "there is"

Start with the place (a place word, often a noun + locative), then {有|yǒu}, then what's there:

| Place | {有|yǒu} | Thing |
|---|---|---|
| {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} | {有|yǒu} | {一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 |
| {房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ} | {有|yǒu} | {电脑|diàn nǎo}。 |
| {学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian} | {有|yǒu} | {一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 |

{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 — There's a book on the table.

{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}。 — There's a computer in the room.

{学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 — There's a supermarket outside the school.

A sentence like this, which says that something exists somewhere, is an existential
sentence. It's the same {有|yǒu} as "have": {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo} is "I have a computer", and
{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo} is "the room has a computer", which is how Chinese says
"there's a computer in the room".

**Usually no {在|zài} before the place.** English starts "In the room there is…", so learners often write
{在|zài}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}. You'll hear that in speech, but it's less natural:
the place itself is the subject of {有|yǒu}, so just say {房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}.

The negative is {没有|méi yǒu}, as always with {有|yǒu} (never ~~{不|bù}{有|yǒu}~~). After {没有|méi yǒu}
leave out the number:

{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{没有|méi yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}。 — There's no TV in the room.

Questions use {吗|ma}, {有|yǒu}{没有|méi yǒu}, or a question word:

{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}？ — What's on the table?

{你|nǐ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}{吗|ma}？ — Is there a TV in your room?

{那儿|nàr}{有|yǒu}{没有|méi yǒu}{超市|chāo shì}？ — Is there a supermarket there?

{商店|shāng diàn}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}？ — How many people are there in the shop?

Short answers: {有|yǒu}。 (There is.) / {没有|méi yǒu}。 (There isn't.)

A person + {这儿|zhèr} is a place too, so {我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{茶|chá} means "I've got tea here",
and {你|nǐ}{那儿|nàr}{有|yǒu}{书|shū}{吗|ma}？ "have you got any books there?"

### Counting furniture

Furniture has its own measure words ({张|zhāng} for tables, {把|bǎ} for chairs; HSK 3 teaches
them), so for now leave the number out and say {房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{桌子|zhuō zi}{和|hé}{椅子|yǐ zi}:
"there are a table and chairs in the room". Rooms themselves take {个|gè}:
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{三|sān}{个|gè}{房间|fáng jiān}, "our flat has three rooms".

## {在|zài} or {有|yǒu}?

Both sentences can describe the same table. The difference is what the listener already knows.

| | Pattern | Example | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| {在|zài} | thing + {在|zài} + place | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。 My book is on the table. | the thing is known; the news is *where* it is |
| {有|yǒu} | place + {有|yǒu} + thing | {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 There's a book on the table. | the place is known; the news is *what* is there |

Chinese likes to put what both speakers know first and the news last. A known thing ({我|wǒ}{的|de}{书|shū},
{那|nà}{本|běn}{书|shū}, {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}) goes before {在|zài}. A new thing ("a book", "some
people") goes after {有|yǒu}, often with {一|yī} + measure word for "a".

So ask {我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ when you're looking for your phone, and
{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{超市|chāo shì}{吗|ma}？ when you want to know whether there's a supermarket nearby.
{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} sounds odd for the same reason "A book is on
the table" sounds odd in English: a new thing usually doesn't open the sentence.

## Position words with {边|biān}

{边|biān} means "side". Added to a locative it makes a two-syllable position word, the form people
use most in speech:

| | Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {上|shàng} + {边|biān} | {上边|shàng bian} | on top, above | {桌子|zhuō zi}{上边|shàng bian} |
| {下|xià} + {边|biān} | {下边|xià bian} | below, under | {椅子|yǐ zi}{下边|xià bian} |
| {里|lǐ} + {边|biān} | {里边|lǐ bian} | inside | {房间|fáng jiān}{里边|lǐ bian} |
| {外|wài} + {边|biān} | {外边|wài bian} | outside | {学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian} |
| {前|qián} + {边|biān} | {前边|qián bian} | in front | {电视|diàn shì}{前边|qián bian} |
| {后|hòu} + {边|biān} | {后边|hòu bian} | behind, at the back | {商店|shāng diàn}{后边|hòu bian} |

In these words {边|biān} is usually light: *wài bian*, *qián bian*. Three things make them
different from the one-syllable locatives of lesson 16:

- They're the everyday spoken forms. Bare {前|qián}, {后|hòu}, {外|wài} and {下|xià} after a noun sound
  like a label; {学校|xué xiào}{前边|qián bian}, {商店|shāng diàn}{外边|wài bian} sound like talk.
  (With {上|shàng} and {里|lǐ}, both are fine: {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} and {桌子|zhuō zi}{上边|shàng bian}.)
- They can stand alone, without a noun in front: {外边|wài bian}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng} (it's cold outside; {冷|lěng}, cold, is a lesson 20 word),
  {里边|lǐ bian}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{吗|ma}？ (is anyone inside?). One syllable can't: ~~{外|wài}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}~~.
- {的|de} may come between a noun and the {边|biān} word: {学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{外边|wài bian}. It's
  optional; most people leave it out.

You'll also hear the same words with {面|miàn} instead of {边|biān}: {外面|wài miàn}, {里面|lǐ miàn}. They
mean the same; HSK 2 teaches them.

### {这边|zhè biān}, {那边|nà biān}: over here, over there

{这边|zhè biān} ("this side") and {那边|nà biān} ("that side") point to an area rather than a spot, a
bit like "over here" and "over there". Here {边|biān} keeps its first tone. They're place words, like
{这儿|zhèr} and {那儿|nàr}:

{请|qǐng}{来|lái}{这边|zhè biān}。 — Please come over here (this way).

{超市|chāo shì}{在|zài}{那边|nà biān}。 — The supermarket is over there.

{那边|nà biān}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}。 — There are lots of people over there.

## Living and staying: {住|zhù}, {住|zhù}{在|zài}

{住|zhù} is "to live (somewhere)" and also "to stay" in a hotel. It usually takes {在|zài} + place
*after* it:

{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — I live in Beijing.

{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where do you live?

{他|tā}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。 — He lives on campus.

{我们|wǒ men}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{这个|zhè ge}{饭店|fàn diàn}。 — We're staying at this hotel.

This is unusual. In lesson 05 the place came before the verb: {他|tā}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}.
With {住|zhù} you can say {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{住|zhù} too, but {住|zhù}{在|zài} is far more
common: think of it as "live-at" in one go. In speech people also drop {在|zài}:
{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{这个|zhè ge}{饭店|fàn diàn}.

Hotel rooms are numbers. Say each digit, and read 1 as *yāo*, as in phone numbers:
{我|wǒ}{住|zhù} 301 (*sān líng yāo*)。

## Words for a room

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {房间|fáng jiān} | room | a room in a home or a hotel |
| {桌子|zhuō zi} | table, desk | {子|zi} is a light noun ending, as in {杯子|bēi zi} |
| {椅子|yǐ zi} | chair | |
| {电脑|diàn nǎo} | computer | "electric brain" |
| {电视|diàn shì} | television | "electric seeing"; {看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}, watch TV |

{电|diàn} (electric) builds many modern words: {电话|diàn huà} ("electric speech", telephone), {电脑|diàn nǎo},
{电视|diàn shì}. Notice the tones: all four are *diàn*, fourth tone.

Things are often *on* a screen: {在|zài}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{上|shàng} (on the computer), {在|zài}{手机|shǒu jī}{上|shàng}
(on the phone).

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 边 (traditional 邊) ✎ | side, edge | biān (light: bian) | 辶 | 5 | {边|biān}, {外边|wài bian}, {这边|zhè biān}, {那边|nà biān} |
| 房 | house, room | fáng | 户 | 8 | {房间|fáng jiān} |
| 桌 | table | zhuō | 木 | 10 | {桌子|zhuō zi} |
| 椅 | chair | yǐ | 木 | 12 | {椅子|yǐ zi} |
| 脑 (traditional 腦) | brain | nǎo | ⺼ | 10 | {电脑|diàn nǎo} |
| 视 (traditional 視) | look at | shì | 见 | 8 | {电视|diàn shì} |
| 住 | live, stay | zhù | 亻 | 7 | {住|zhù} |

### New radicals: ⺼ "meat moon" and 户 "door"

- **⺼**, the "meat moon" ({肉月旁|ròu yuè páng}): the side form of {肉|ròu} (meat, flesh). In modern
  print it looks exactly like {月|yuè} (moon), but it comes from a different old shape, and it
  marks characters about the body. {脑|nǎo} (brain) has it; so does {能|néng} (can), lesson 19.
  Eight characters in this track have it. Compare the real moon in {明|míng} and {期|qī}. Most
  dictionaries file ⺼ and 月 together under 月, so look there.
- **户** ({户|hù}): a one-leaf door, and by extension a household. In {房|fáng} it sits on top and
  gives the meaning (a building with a door); {方|fāng} underneath gives the sound. Three characters
  in this track have it.

### Notes on the others

- {边|biān} is {力|lì} (strength) inside the "walk" radical 辶 you met in {这|zhè} (lesson 03).
  Traditional: {邊|biān}, a much longer character.
- {桌|zhuō} and {椅|yǐ} both have {木|mù} (wood) at the bottom or on the left. Memory aid: tables and
  chairs are made of wood.
- {脑|nǎo}: ⺼ (body) + a lid over a box with a cross inside. Memory aid: the skull. Traditional: {腦|nǎo}.
- {视|shì}: {见|jiàn} (see, lesson 12's radical) gives the meaning, and the left side is 礻, the
  short form of {示|shì}, which matches the sound. Don't write 衤 there (the clothing radical of
  {衣|yī}, one stroke more): both start with a dot, but 礻 ends with one short stroke at the bottom right and 衤 with two.
  Traditional: {視|shì}.
- {住|zhù}: 亻 (person) + {主|zhǔ} (master, a later character), which gives the sound: a person
  who stays.

### Stroke order

- **边**: like {这|zhè}, the inside first and 辶 last: {力|lì} (the top-and-side stroke with a hook, then
  the left-falling stroke), then the dot, the zigzag and the long sweep along the bottom of 辶.
- **房**: 户 (dot, the top and side, the horizontal, the long left-falling stroke), then {方|fāng}:
  dot, horizontal, the stroke that goes across and down with a hook, and *then* the left-falling
  stroke. In {方|fāng} the hook comes before the left-falling stroke.
- **脑**: ⺼ (4 strokes), then the dot and horizontal of the lid, the cross (left-falling, then
  dot), and the box last: its left side and bottom in one stroke, then its right side.
- **视**: 礻 is dot, horizontal-and-falling, vertical, dot; then {见|jiàn}.

Trace the new characters:

```trace
边房桌椅脑视住
```

✎ **Write it**: {边|biān} is one of the 100 handwriting characters. Write it three times from
memory, inside first, 辶 last.
=}

## Dialogue: Anna's new room

{安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) has moved into a room at her university. {王芳|Wáng Fāng} asks about it.

```dialogue
# A new room
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Anna, where do you live?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。
= I live on campus.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= What's your room like?
安娜: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{桌子|zhuō zi}、{椅子|yǐ zi}{和|hé}{电脑|diàn nǎo}。
= Very nice! There's a desk, a chair and a computer in it.
王芳: {有|yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}{吗|ma}？
= Is there a TV?
安娜: {没有|méi yǒu}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{手机|shǒu jī}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}。
= No. I watch on my phone.
王芳: {那边|nà biān}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}？
= What's that over there?
安娜: {那边|nà biān}？{那|nà}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}！
= Over there? Those are my clothes!
```

The pause mark 、 separates items in a list ({桌子|zhuō zi}、{椅子|yǐ zi}{和|hé}{电脑|diàn nǎo}); {和|hé} joins
the last two. {有|yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}{吗|ma}？ leaves out the place: it's clear from the talk.

## Reading: my home

> {我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{有|yǒu}{三|sān}{个|gè}{房间|fáng jiān}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{桌子|zhuō zi}、{椅子|yǐ zi}{和|hé}{电脑|diàn nǎo}，{没有|méi yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}。{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{书|shū}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{杯子|bēi zi}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？{在|zài}{椅子|yǐ zi}{下边|xià bian}！{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}，{他们|tā men}{晚上|wǎn shang}{在|zài}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}。

1. How many rooms does the home have?
2. What is on the writer's table?
3. Where do the parents watch TV, and when?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

I live in Beijing. Our home isn't big; it has three rooms. In my room there's a table, a chair
and a computer, but no TV. On the table there are lots of books and a cup. Where are my clothes?
Under the chair! My parents' room has a TV; they watch TV in their room in the evening.

1. Three. 2. Lots of books and a cup. 3. In their room, in the evening.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}？
= What's on the table?
{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。
= There's a book on the table.
{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{没有|méi yǒu}{电视|diàn shì}。
= There's no TV in the room.
{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{超市|chāo shì}{吗|ma}？
= Is there a supermarket around here?
{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where do you live?
{请|qǐng}{来|lái}{这边|zhè biān}。
= This way, please.
```

## Common mistakes

- {在|zài} in front of the place in a {有|yǒu} sentence: {在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{书|shū} is
  heard, but it's less natural. The place is the subject: {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{书|shū}.
- English order: {有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} copies "there is a book
  on the table". It's possible, but the usual order puts the place first.
- {不|bù}{有|yǒu}: the negative of {有|yǒu} is always {没有|méi yǒu}.
- A known thing after {有|yǒu}: {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī} works when you're
  listing what's on the table, but to say where your phone is, use {我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}.
  Known things take {在|zài}.
- One-syllable locatives standing alone: ~~{外|wài}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}~~. Use {外边|wài bian}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{北京|Běi jīng}{在|zài}~~ or ~~{在|zài}{住|zhù}{北京|Běi jīng}~~: it's {住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}.
- Writing 衤 instead of 礻 in {视|shì}.

## Key points

- Place + {有|yǒu} + thing: what there is somewhere (an existential sentence); no {在|zài} before
  the place; negative {没有|méi yǒu}.
- Thing + {在|zài} + place: where a known thing is. Known first, news last.
- {边|biān} words ({上边|shàng bian}, {外边|wài bian}, {前边|qián bian}…) are the spoken locatives, with a
  light *bian*; they can stand alone. {这边|zhè biān}, {那边|nà biān}: over here, over there.
- {住|zhù}{在|zài} + place: live, stay. {在|zài} + place comes after {住|zhù}.
- {房间|fáng jiān}, {桌子|zhuō zi}, {椅子|yǐ zi}, {电脑|diàn nǎo}, {电视|diàn shì}.


The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Getting there: 坐, 开车, 怎么
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can say where places are and what's in them. Now you need to get there. This lesson teaches
the words for vehicles and the sentence pattern for "by train", "by taxi", "by plane"; how to ask
"how?" with {怎么|zěn me}; and {到|dào}, "to arrive, to get to". It builds on the serial verbs of
lesson 09 ({去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}: go to the shop to buy things), which now get
another verb in front.

You'll learn:

- {坐|zuò} + vehicle + {去|qù} / {来|lái} / {回|huí} + place: travelling by something;
- {开|kāi} and {开车|kāi chē}: to open, to switch on, to drive;
- {怎么|zěn me} + verb: how to do something; {怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}？ how do you get there?;
- {到|dào}: to arrive, to get to;
- {车|chē}, {出租车|chū zū chē}, {火车|huǒ chē}, {飞机|fēi jī}.

## Vehicles

| Word | Meaning | Made of |
|---|---|---|
| {车|chē} | vehicle; car | |
| {出租车|chū zū chē} | taxi | {出租|chū zū} (to rent out) + {车|chē} |
| {火车|huǒ chē} | train | {火|huǒ} (fire) + {车|chē}: from the days of steam |
| {飞机|fēi jī} | plane | {飞|fēi} (to fly) + {机|jī} (machine, as in {手机|shǒu jī}) |

{车|chē} on its own is any vehicle with wheels, most often a car; {我|wǒ}{的|de}{车|chē} is "my car".
In cities you'll also need two HSK 2 words: {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} (city bus) and {地铁|dì tiě}
(underground, metro).

## {坐|zuò} + vehicle: travelling by

{坐|zuò} means "to sit", as in {请|qǐng}{坐|zuò} (please sit down) from lesson 12. You sit in a train or
a taxi, so {坐|zuò} + vehicle is "to go by", "to take":

{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē} — take the train

{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē} — take a taxi

{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī} — fly (take a plane)

To say where you're going, add {去|qù}, {来|lái} or {回|huí} + place *after* the vehicle. The means
of travel comes first, then the going:

| Who | When | How ({坐|zuò} + vehicle) | Going + place | (Why) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | {明天|míng tiān} | {坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē} | {去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}。 | |
| {妈妈|mā ma} | | {坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē} | {回|huí}{家|jiā}。 | |
| {我们|wǒ men} | {下午|xià wǔ} | {坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē} | {去|qù}{超市|chāo shì} | {买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 |

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — Tomorrow I'm going to Beijing by train.

{妈妈|mā ma}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — Mum is taking a taxi home.

{我们|wǒ men}{下午|xià wǔ}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{去|qù}{超市|chāo shì}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — This
afternoon we're taking a taxi to the supermarket to do some shopping.

The verbs line up in the order things happen: you get on the train, you go to Beijing, you do
your shopping. That's the logic of Chinese serial verbs, so English "to Beijing by train" is
reversed: "by train" comes first. If you put the vehicle last, {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}
means "I'm going to Beijing to take a train", which is a different plan.

**Negatives and questions.** {不|bù} goes before the first verb, the one that's being denied:

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{去|qù}，{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}。 — I'm not flying there; I'm
going by train.

{你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？ — Are you going by train?

**Three zuò.** {坐|zuò} (sit, go by), {做|zuò} (do, make; lesson 09) and the {作|zuò} of {工作|gōng zuò}
(lesson 05) sound exactly the same. {坐|zuò} has two people on the ground {土|tǔ}; {做|zuò} and {作|zuò}
have the person radical 亻. Listen to the context: {坐|zuò}{车|chē}, {做|zuò}{饭|fàn}, {工作|gōng zuò}.

## {开|kāi} and {开车|kāi chē}: to drive

{开|kāi} is a busy verb. Its basic idea is "open", and it covers starting machines and driving:

| | Meaning | |
|---|---|---|
| {开|kāi}{车|chē} | to drive (a car) | {他|tā}{开车|kāi chē}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}。 He drives to work (the company). |
| {开|kāi} + machine | to switch on | {开|kāi}{电视|diàn shì} (turn on the TV), {开|kāi}{电脑|diàn nǎo} |
| {开|kāi} + door, shop | to open | {开|kāi}{门|mén} (open the door; {门|mén} is an HSK 2 word) |

{开车|kāi chē} already has its object, {车|chē}, so don't add another: "to drive a car" is just
{开车|kāi chē}. Other vehicles go after {开|kāi} instead of {车|chē}: {他|tā}{开|kāi}{出租车|chū zū chē}, "he
drives a taxi" (he's a taxi driver). {开|kāi}{飞机|fēi jī} is "to fly a plane", what a pilot does;
a passenger {坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}.

Driving is a learned skill, so it takes {会|huì} (lesson 02):

{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}{吗|ma}？ — Can you drive?

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}。 — I can't drive.

Lesson 19 sorts out {会|huì} from the other "can" words.

## {怎么|zěn me} + verb: how?

{怎么|zěn me} goes right before a verb and asks how it's done:

{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}？ — How are you getting there?

{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}？ — How do you get to school?

— {我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{去|qù}。 — I take a taxi.

"Taxi" {中文|Zhōng wén}{怎么|zěn me}{说|shuō}？ — How do you say "taxi" in Chinese?

The answer repeats the pattern with the means of travel in the {怎么|zěn me} slot.

Don't confuse {怎么|zěn me} with {怎么样|zěn me yàng} from lesson 15. {怎么样|zěn me yàng} stands at the end
and asks "what is it like?": {你|nǐ}{的|de}{车|chē}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ (How's your car? What's your
car like?). {怎么|zěn me} needs a verb after it: {怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}, {怎么|zěn me}{说|shuō}.

You'll also hear {怎么|zěn me} as "how come?", showing surprise: {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{不|bú}{去|qù}？ "How
come you're not going?" For now, use it for "how".

## {到|dào}: to arrive, to get to

{到|dào} + place is "to arrive at, to get to":

{我|wǒ}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}。 — I get to school at eight.

{火车|huǒ chē}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}？ — What time does the train get in?

{飞机|fēi jī}{下午|xià wǔ}{三|sān}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — The plane arrives in Beijing at three in
the afternoon.

Compare {去|qù}: {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng} is about going, {我|wǒ}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng} about arriving. The
time words still come before the verb.

**How long it takes.** {要|yào} (lesson 09) + a length of time is "it takes":

{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{要|yào}{五|wǔ}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — It takes five hours to
Beijing by train.

{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{要|yào}{二十|èr shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 — It's twenty minutes by taxi.

Here {到|dào} + place is "to (a place)" inside a longer sentence. You'll meet {从|cóng}…{到|dào}
("from… to…") in HSK 2.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 坐 | sit; travel by | zuò | 土 | 7 | {坐|zuò}, {请|qǐng}{坐|zuò} |
| 开 (traditional 開) | open; drive; switch on | kāi | 廾 | 4 | {开|kāi}, {开车|kāi chē} |
| 车 (traditional 車) | vehicle, car | chē | 车 | 4 | {车|chē}, {开车|kāi chē}, {火车|huǒ chē}, {出租车|chū zū chē} |
| 出 | go out | chū | 凵 | 5 | {出租车|chū zū chē} |
| 租 | rent | zū | 禾 | 10 | {出租车|chū zū chē} |
| 火 | fire | huǒ | 火 | 4 | {火车|huǒ chē} |
| 飞 (traditional 飛) | fly | fēi | 飞 | 3 | {飞机|fēi jī} |
| 到 | arrive; to | dào | 刂 | 8 | {到|dào} |

### New radicals: 车, 火, 禾

- **车** ({车|chē}, vehicle): its old form drew a cart from above, an axle with a wheel at each end.
  Traditional {車|chē} still looks like that. On the left of a character (later: {辆|liàng}, the
  measure word for vehicles) its second horizontal becomes a stroke rising to the right, written last, after the vertical. Four
  characters in this track have it.
- **火** ({火|huǒ}, fire): a picture of flames. At the bottom of a character it becomes four dots,
  灬, which you met in lesson 07 in {点|diǎn}. Four characters in this track have 火 itself.
- **禾** ({禾|hé}, standing grain): a plant with a drooping head of grain. In {租|zū} it gives the
  meaning (rent and land tax were once paid in grain) and {且|qiě} on the right gave the sound. {和|hé} (and,
  lesson 03) has 禾 on its left too, though Make Me a Hanzi files it under 口. Three characters in
  this track have 禾.

### Notes on the others

- {坐|zuò}: two people {人|rén} sitting on the ground {土|tǔ}: the usual explanation of the shape, and
  an easy one to remember.
- {开|kāi}: the traditional form {開|kāi} is a door {門|mén} with two hands lifting the bar inside.
  Simplification kept the hands and the bar and dropped the door.
- {出|chū}: memory aid: two mountains stacked up, and the way out goes over them.
- {飞|fēi}: simplified from {飛|fēi}, a drawing of wings; the simplified form keeps only part of it.
- {到|dào}: {至|zhì} (to reach) gives the meaning, and the knife 刂 from lesson 16 is {刀|dāo}, which gave
  the sound *dào*.

### Stroke order

- **车**: horizontal, then the stroke that falls left and turns right (one stroke), the second
  horizontal, and the vertical last, through the middle.
- **开**: two horizontals, then the left-falling stroke, then the vertical on the right.
- **火**: the two short strokes first (left dot, then the right one), then the long left-falling
  stroke and the long right-falling one.
- **坐**: the left {人|rén} (two strokes), the right {人|rén}, then {土|tǔ}: horizontal, the long vertical
  through the middle, the bottom horizontal.
- **出**: as the tracing pad draws it (Make Me a Hanzi): the upper part's left-and-bottom stroke, its
  short right side, then the long middle stroke from the top down through both parts, then the
  lower part's left-and-bottom stroke and its right side.
- **到**: in {至|zhì} the last stroke rises to the right (it would be flat in {至|zhì} alone), then 刂.
- **飞**: the big hooked stroke first, then the left-falling stroke and the dot.

Trace the new characters:

```trace
坐开车出租火飞到
```
=}

## Dialogue: going home

{陈静|Chén Jìng} is going home tomorrow. {李明|Lǐ Míng} asks how she's getting there.

```dialogue
# Going home
李明: {陈静|Chén Jìng}，{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？
= Chen Jing, are you going home tomorrow?
陈静: {对|duì}。
= That's right.
李明: {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{回|huí}{家|jiā}？{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{吗|ma}？
= How are you getting home? Are you flying?
陈静: {不|bú}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}，{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。
= No, I'm going home by train.
李明: {坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{要|yào}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}？
= How many hours does the train take?
陈静: {五|wǔ}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{下午|xià wǔ}{三|sān}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}。
= Five hours. It gets in at three in the afternoon.
李明: {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}{火车站|huǒ chē zhàn}？
= How are you getting to the station?
陈静: {坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{去|qù}。
= By taxi.
李明: {我|wǒ}{开车|kāi chē}{去|qù}{那儿|nàr}，{你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{车|chē}{吧|ba}！
= I'm driving there. Come in my car!
陈静: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！
= Great! Thank you!
```

{火车站|huǒ chē zhàn} is the railway station ({站|zhàn}, station, is an HSK 2 word). {你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{车|chē}{吧|ba}
uses {吧|ba} for a suggestion (lesson 12): "how about riding in my car?". {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！ is the
{太|tài}…{了|le} pattern from lesson 12: "that's great!"

## Reading: how we travel

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{陈静|Chén Jìng}，{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{大学|dà xué}{不|bú}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}，{要|yào}{五|wǔ}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}，{他|tā}{开车|kāi chē}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{不|bú}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}，{她|tā}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{去|qù}{上班|shàng bān}。{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{回|huí}{家|jiā}，{他|tā}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}，{上午|shàng wǔ}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}。

1. How does Chen Jing get home from university, and how long does it take?
2. How does her mother get to work?
3. When does her brother arrive?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

My name is Chen Jing and I'm a university student. My home is in Beijing; my university isn't.
I go home by train; it takes five hours. My dad can drive: he drives to work. My mum can't
drive; she takes a taxi to work. Tomorrow my older brother is coming home. He's flying, and he
arrives at ten in the morning.

1. By train; five hours. 2. By taxi. 3. At ten in the morning.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}？
= How are you getting there?
{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}。
= I'm going by train.
{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。
= I'm taking a taxi home.
{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}{吗|ma}？
= Can you drive?
{飞机|fēi jī}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}？
= What time does the plane arrive?
"Taxi" {中文|Zhōng wén}{怎么|zěn me}{说|shuō}？
= How do you say "taxi" in Chinese?
```

## Common mistakes

- English order: ~~{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}~~ for "I'm going to Beijing by train". The
  vehicle comes before the going: {我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}.
- {开|kāi} for passengers: you {坐|zuò} a taxi, a train or a plane; the driver or pilot {开|kāi} it.
- ~~{开车|kāi chē}{出租车|chū zū chē}~~: {开车|kāi chē} already has its object. Say {开|kāi}{出租车|chū zū chē}.
- {怎么|zěn me} without a verb: ~~{你|nǐ}{的|de}{车|chē}{怎么|zěn me}？~~ To ask what something is like, use
  {怎么样|zěn me yàng}.
- Writing {做|zuò} or {作|zuò} for {坐|zuò} (or the other way round): all three are *zuò*.
- {到|dào} for "go": {我|wǒ}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng} is "I arrive in Beijing", not "I'm going to Beijing"
  ({我|wǒ}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}).

## Key points

- {坐|zuò} + vehicle + {去|qù} / {来|lái} / {回|huí} + place (+ purpose): the means first, then the going.
- {开|kāi}: open, switch on, drive; {开车|kāi chē}, drive; {会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}, can drive.
- {怎么|zěn me} + verb: how? {怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}？ {怎么|zěn me}{说|shuō}？ ({怎么样|zěn me yàng}: what's it like?)
- {到|dào} + place: arrive, get to; {要|yào} + time: it takes.
- {车|chē}, {出租车|chū zū chē}, {火车|huǒ chē}, {飞机|fēi jī}.


The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Studying Chinese: 会, 能, 可以
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English has one word, "can", for three different ideas: "I can swim" (I know how), "I can come
tomorrow" (nothing stops me) and "can I sit here?" (am I allowed?). Chinese has a word for each:
{会|huì}, {能|néng} and {可以|kě yǐ}. They're **[[modal verbs]]**, like {想|xiǎng} and {要|yào} from lesson 09.
This lesson sorts them out, and gives you the words for studying: classes, classmates, learning
and writing characters.

You'll learn:

- {会|huì}, {能|néng}, {可以|kě yǐ}: three kinds of "can";
- {学|xué} and {学习|xué xí}: to learn, to study;
- {课|kè}, {上课|shàng kè}, {下课|xià kè}, {上学|shàng xué}: classes and school;
- {写|xiě}, {字|zì}, {汉字|hàn zì}: writing characters;
- {同学|tóng xué}: classmate, and a way to address students.

## Modal verbs

A modal verb goes before another verb and adds an idea such as ability, permission or wish:

| Subject | (Time) | Modal verb | Verb + object |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | | {会|huì} | {说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 |
| {我|wǒ} | {明天|míng tiān} | {能|néng} | {来|lái}。 |
| {我|wǒ} | | {可以|kě yǐ} | {坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？ |
| {我|wǒ} | | {想|xiǎng} | {学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 |

Like other verbs, they never change for person or time. Negatives put {不|bù} before the modal
verb; A-not-A questions double it; short answers are the modal verb alone:

{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{不|bu}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}？ — {会|huì}。 / {不|bú}{会|huì}。 — Can you write
Chinese characters? — Yes. / No.

{可以|kě yǐ} has two syllables, so its A-not-A question usually doubles only the first:
{可|kě}{不|bu}{可以|kě yǐ}？

## {会|huì}: knowing how

{会|huì} is for skills you've learned: languages, driving, cooking, writing characters.

{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — I can speak a little Chinese.

{他|tā}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}。 — He can drive.

{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{不|bú}{会|huì}{做饭|zuò fàn}。 — My mum can't cook.

{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{吗|ma}？ — Can you write this character?

Once you've learned something you {会|huì} it, even when you can't do it right now.

## {能|néng}: being able

{能|néng} says that you're able to do something: you have the strength or the time, or the
situation allows it.

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{能|néng}{来|lái}。 — I can come tomorrow. (I'm free.)

{你|nǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{能|néng}{来|lái}{上课|shàng kè}{吗|ma}？ — Can you come to class today?

{他|tā}{能|néng}{写|xiě}{五|wǔ}{百|bǎi}{个|gè}{汉字|hàn zì}。 — He can write five hundred characters. (That's
how far his ability goes.)

{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{不|bù}{能|néng}{说话|shuō huà}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上课|shàng kè}。 — I can't talk now,
I'm in class.

The last example shows the difference from {会|huì}: you {会|huì}{说话|shuō huà} (you know how to talk),
but you {不|bù}{能|néng}{说话|shuō huà} now, because you're in class. {能|néng} is also the word for "how
much, how far" you can do: five hundred characters, three hours.

## {可以|kě yǐ}: being allowed

{可以|kě yǐ} is "may": it asks for and gives permission.

{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？ — May I sit here?

— {可以|kě yǐ}，{请|qǐng}{坐|zuò}。 — Yes, please do.

{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{吗|ma}？ — May I have a look at your book?

It also suggests a possible choice, like "you could":

{你|nǐ}{可以|kě yǐ}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}。 — You could go by train.

**Saying no.** {不|bù}{可以|kě yǐ} sounds firm, like "you're not allowed to". In everyday talk the
usual refusal is {不|bù}{能|néng} or {不行|bù xíng} ("that won't do"; {行|xíng} is an HSK 3 word):
{这儿|zhèr}{不|bù}{能|néng}{坐|zuò}, "you can't sit here".

**{能|néng} or {可以|kě yǐ}?** In requests the two overlap: {我|wǒ}{能|néng}{坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？ and
{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？ are both natural. {会|huì} never asks permission.

### The three "can"s side by side

| English "can" | Chinese | Ask yourself | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| know how to | {会|huì} | Have I learned it? | {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}。 |
| be able to | {能|néng} | Can I manage it, does the situation let me? | {我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{能|néng}{来|lái}。 |
| may, be allowed to | {可以|kě yǐ} | Is it allowed, is it OK? | {我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}{吗|ma}？ |

You already know two more modal verbs: {想|xiǎng} (would like to) and {要|yào} (want to, will).
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{学|xué}{开车|kāi chē}, "I'd like to learn to drive". The reference sheet "Modal verbs"
has all five.

## Learning: {学|xué} and {学习|xué xí}

Both mean "to learn, to study", and both can take an object.

- {学|xué} is the everyday word for learning a subject or a skill. It can take a verb:
  {学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} (learn Chinese), {学|xué}{开车|kāi chē} (learn to drive), {学|xué}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}
  (learn to write characters).
- {学习|xué xí} is "to study", a little more formal and general. It's happy on its own:
  {他|tā}{在|zài}{学习|xué xí} (he's studying), {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{学习|xué xí} (I'm a student in
  Beijing), and with a subject: {学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}.

When you learn *to do* something, {学|xué} is the usual word: {学|xué}{开车|kāi chē}. You may hear
{学习|xué xí}{开车|kāi chē} too, but it sounds more formal; {学|xué} is the safe choice.
You've seen {学|xué} in many words already: {学生|xué sheng}, {学校|xué xiào}, {大学|dà xué}.

## Classes and school

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {课|kè} | class, lesson | {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè}, Chinese class |
| {上课|shàng kè} | go to class; class starts | {我们|wǒ men}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。 Our class starts at eight. |
| {下课|xià kè} | class ends; get out of class | {你|nǐ}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{下课|xià kè}？ What time do you finish class? |
| {上学|shàng xué} | go to school (as a pupil) | {我|wǒ}{儿子|ér zi}{早上|zǎo shang}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{去|qù}{上学|shàng xué}。 |

{上|shàng} and {下|xià} work here as in {上班|shàng bān} and {下班|xià bān} (lesson 08): {上|shàng} is to go to
or start, {下|xià} to finish and leave.

{上课|shàng kè} is a verb with its object built in ({上|shàng} + {课|kè}, "attend class"), like {睡觉|shuì jiào}
and {开车|kāi chē}. So it can't take another object. To say which class, put the subject before
{课|kè}:

{我|wǒ}{下午|xià wǔ}{上|shàng}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè}。 — I have Chinese class this afternoon.

not ~~{我|wǒ}{下午|xià wǔ}{上课|shàng kè}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}~~.

## Writing: {写|xiě}, {字|zì}, {汉字|hàn zì}

{写|xiě} is "to write". What you write is often {字|zì}: a written character, or handwriting.

{这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？ — How do you write this character?

{他|tā}{的|de}{字|zì}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — His handwriting is beautiful.

{汉字|hàn zì} is a Chinese character in particular: {汉|hàn} as in {汉语|Hàn yǔ}. A *word* is
{词|cí} (HSK 2), and a word can have one character or several: {学生|xué sheng} is one {词|cí} written
with two {字|zì}. Chinese speakers count what they can read in {字|zì}: "I know two hundred
characters" is {我|wǒ}{认识|rèn shi}{两|liǎng}{百|bǎi}{个|gè}{汉字|hàn zì} ({认识|rèn shi}, to know, is lesson 23's).

### How characters are learned

Every lesson's Characters section follows the same steps, much as Chinese children learn
too:

1. **Meet the character in words.** {字|zì} on its own is hard to remember; {汉字|hàn zì},
   {写字|xiě zì}, {名字|míng zi} give it meaning.
2. **Look at its parts.** Most characters have a radical that hints at the meaning (讠 speech,
   ⺼ body, 木 wood) and often a part that hints at the sound ({方|fāng} in {房|fáng}, {果|guǒ} in
   {课|kè}).
3. **Learn the stroke order** and trace it. The order is part of the character: it makes your
   handwriting readable and matches handwriting input on phones.
4. **Write it from memory.** For the ✎ characters, write each one three times without looking,
   then check.
5. **Review** with the notecards and the questions until you recognise each character at a glance.

## {同学|tóng xué}: classmates

{同|tóng} is "same", so {同学|tóng xué} is someone who studies with you: a classmate, a fellow
student.

{安娜|Ān nà}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}。 — Anna is my classmate.

Teachers call a class {同学们|tóng xué men} ("students, everyone"), and in China students and teachers
often call a student they don't know {同学|tóng xué}: {同学|tóng xué}，{请问|qǐng wèn}{书店|shū diàn}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
"Excuse me (fellow student), where's the bookshop?"

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 习 (traditional 習) ✎ | practise | xí | 冫 | 3 | {学习|xué xí} |
| 课 (traditional 課) | class, lesson | kè | 讠 | 10 | {课|kè}, {上课|shàng kè}, {下课|xià kè} |
| 写 (traditional 寫) ✎ | write | xiě | 冖 | 5 | {写|xiě} |
| 同 ✎ | same | tóng | 口 | 6 | {同学|tóng xué} |
| 能 | can, be able | néng | ⺼ | 10 | {能|néng} |
| 可 ✎ | may; can | kě | 口 | 5 | {可以|kě yǐ} |
| 以 ✎ | use; by | yǐ | 人 | 4 | {可以|kě yǐ} |

### New radical: 冫, two-dot water

冫 is called {两点水|liǎng diǎn shuǐ}, "two-dot water". Three-dot water 氵 (lesson 02) is liquid
water; two-dot water is water frozen still: ice and cold. You'll meet it in {冷|lěng} (cold) in the
next lesson. Its two strokes are a dot and a short stroke rising to the right. Eight characters in
this track have it.

Make Me a Hanzi files {习|xí} under 冫 because its last two strokes look like it, but {习|xí} has
nothing to do with ice: many dictionaries file it under 乙 (written 乛 here). Its traditional
form {習|xí} has {羽|yǔ} (feathers) on top: the old explanation is a young bird practising flying.

### Notes on the others

- {课|kè}: 讠 (speech, lesson 02) + {果|guǒ} (fruit, from {苹果|píng guǒ}), which once gave the sound.
  Traditional: {課|kè}.
- {写|xiě}: 冖 (a cover) on top. Traditional {寫|xiě} has 宀 (roof) and many more strokes.
- {同|tóng}: a frame open at the bottom with 一 and 口 inside. Make Me a Hanzi files it under 口;
  many dictionaries use the frame 冂.
- {能|néng}: its oldest form drew a bear; the meaning "able" was borrowed, and "bear" got a new
  character later. It has ⺼ (lesson 17) on the left.
- {可|kě} and {以|yǐ} only appear together in this course, in {可以|kě yǐ}; both are very common
  in later words.

### Stroke order

- **习**: three strokes: the top-and-side stroke with a hook, the dot, and then a stroke that
  *rises* from bottom left to top right. It isn't a dot.
- **写**: the dot and the hooked cover 冖, then a short horizontal, the zigzag stroke ending in a
  hook, and the long horizontal last.
- **同**: the left side, then the top-and-right side with its hook (the frame is open at the
  bottom), then the short horizontal and 口 inside.
- **能**: the whole left side first, top to bottom (厶, then ⺼), then the right side: the upper
  匕, then the lower one.
- **可**: the long top horizontal, 口, and the hooked vertical last.
- **以**: the left stroke goes down and flicks up to the right; then the dot; then the long
  left-falling stroke and the final dot.

Trace the new characters:

```trace
习课写同能可以
```

✎ **Write it**: five of today's characters are handwriting characters: {习|xí}, {写|xiě}, {同|tóng},
{可|kě}, {以|yǐ}. Write each three times from memory, then check the stroke order above.
=}

## Dialogue: in Chinese class

The teacher, {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}, and two students, {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) and {大卫|Dà wèi} (David).
In the labels, {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī} is the teacher and {同学们|tóng xué men} the whole class.

```dialogue
# Chinese class
王老师: {同学们|tóng xué men}{好|hǎo}！{现在|xiàn zài}{上课|shàng kè}。
= Hello, everyone! Let's begin.
同学们: {老师|lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, teacher!
王老师: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, can you write this character?
安娜: {会|huì}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}“{学|xué}”，{学习|xué xí}{的|de}{学|xué}。
= Yes. It's xué, the xué in xuéxí.
王老师: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！{大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= Very good! David, how about you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}，{不|bú}{会|huì}{写|xiě}。{老师|lǎo shī}，{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}{书|shū}{吗|ma}？
= I can say it, but I can't write it. Teacher, may I look at the book?
王老师: {可以|kě yǐ}。
= You may.
安娜: {老师|lǎo shī}，{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{能|néng}{来|lái}{上课|shàng kè}。
= Teacher, I can't come to class tomorrow.
王老师: {没关系|méi guān xi}。{你|nǐ}{可以|kě yǐ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{学习|xué xí}。
= That's all right. You can study at home.
```

{学习|xué xí}{的|de}{学|xué}, "the xué of xuéxí", is how Chinese speakers tell you which character
they mean: they name a word it's in. Many characters share a sound, so this is the quickest way to
say which one.

## Reading: my Chinese class

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。{我们|wǒ men}{早上|zǎo shang}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}，{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}{下课|xià kè}。{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{也|yě}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{一些|yì xiē}{汉字|hàn zì}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{安娜|Ān nà}{能|néng}{写|xiě}{三|sān}{百|bǎi}{个|gè}{字|zì}！{下午|xià wǔ}{我们|wǒ men}{不|bú}{上课|shàng kè}，{可以|kě yǐ}{去|qù}{书店|shū diàn}{买|mǎi}{书|shū}。

1. What time does David's class start and end?
2. How many characters can Anna write?
3. What can the students do in the afternoon?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

My name is David, and I'm studying Chinese in Beijing. Our class starts at eight in the morning
and finishes at twelve. I can speak a little Chinese, and I can write some characters too. My
classmate Anna can write three hundred characters! We don't have class in the afternoon, so we
can go to the bookshop and buy books.

1. At eight; at twelve. 2. Three hundred. 3. Go to the bookshop and buy books.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？
= Can you speak Chinese?
{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。
= I can speak a little.
{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{不|bù}{能|néng}{来|lái}。
= I can't come tomorrow.
{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？
= May I sit here?
{这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？
= How do you write this character?
{我们|wǒ men}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{下课|xià kè}？
= What time does our class finish?
```

## Common mistakes

- {能|néng} for a learned skill: "I can speak Chinese" is {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}.
  {我|wǒ}{能|néng}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} suggests that you're able to right now, or allowed to.
- {会|huì} for permission: ~~{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr}{吗|ma}？~~ asks whether you know how to sit
  here (or whether you will). Ask with {可以|kě yǐ} or {能|néng}.
- The modal verb after the main verb: ~~{我|wǒ}{说|shuō}{会|huì}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}~~. It goes first:
  {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}.
- An object after {上课|shàng kè}: ~~{上课|shàng kè}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}~~. Say {上|shàng}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè}.
- {学习|xué xí} + verb for learning a skill: {学|xué}{开车|kāi chē} is the everyday way to say "learn to drive".
- {=Writing the last stroke of {习|xí} as a dot. It rises to the right.=}

## Key points

- Modal verbs go before the main verb; {不|bù} before the modal; short answers are the modal alone.
- {会|huì}: learned skill. {能|néng}: able; the situation allows; how much. {可以|kě yǐ}: allowed;
  a possible choice. In requests {能|néng} and {可以|kě yǐ} both work.
- {学|xué} + subject or skill (also + verb); {学习|xué xí}: study (also alone).
- {上课|shàng kè} / {下课|xià kè}: class starts / ends; {上学|shàng xué}: go to school. {上|shàng}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè},
  not ~~{上课|shàng kè}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}~~.
- {写|xiě}{字|zì}, {写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}; {字|zì} is a character, {词|cí} (HSK 2) a word.
- {同学|tóng xué}: classmate; {同学们|tóng xué men}, everyone in the class.
