lessons.title: The weather and change: 了
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Talking about the weather is how many conversations start, in Chinese as in English. This lesson
gives you the words for it ({天气|tiān qì}, {冷|lěng}, {热|rè}, {下雨|xià yǔ}, {雪|xuě}) and, with them, one of
the most useful little words in Chinese: {了|le} at the end of a sentence, which says that
something has changed: "it's raining now", "it's got cold", "I'm not going after all". You'll
also learn {觉得|jué de}, for saying how you feel and what you think.

You'll learn:

- {天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ and adjectives for the weather;
- {下雨|xià yǔ} and {下雪|xià xuě}: rain and snow;
- **[[change-of-state 了]]**: {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}, {天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}, {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le};
- {觉得|jué de} + a clause: "I feel…", "I think…".

## How's the weather?

{天气|tiān qì} is "weather" ({天|tiān}, sky, day + {气|qì}, air). Ask about it with
{怎么样|zěn me yàng} from lesson 15, and answer with an adjective. Remember that an adjective is the
predicate by itself, with {很|hěn} (often unstressed) or another degree word, and no {是|shì}:

{今天|jīn tiān}{天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ — What's the weather like today?

{今天|jīn tiān}{天气|tiān qì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — The weather's nice today.

{北京|Běi jīng}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。 — It's cold in Beijing.

{这儿|zhèr}{非常|fēi cháng}{热|rè}。 — It's extremely hot here.

{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}{也|yě}{不|bú}{热|rè}。 — Today it's neither cold nor hot.

Chinese often uses {天|tiān} for "the weather" in short sentences: {天|tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}, "it's cold
(the day is cold)". There's no "it" in Chinese weather talk; the place or the day is the subject.

**{太|tài}…{了|le} again.** {太|tài} + adjective + {了|le} (lesson 12) is "too…" or, as an exclamation,
"so…!":

{太|tài}{冷|lěng}{了|le}！ — It's so cold! / It's too cold!

{今天|jīn tiān}{太|tài}{热|rè}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}。 — It's too hot today; I don't feel like
going.

The {了|le} in {太|tài}…{了|le} belongs to that pattern. The new {了|le} below is a different job.

## Rain and snow: {下雨|xià yǔ}, {下雪|xià xuě}

{雨|yǔ} is rain and {雪|xuě} snow. Rain and snow "come down", so the verb is {下|xià}, the same
{下|xià} as "below":

{下雨|xià yǔ} — to rain ("come-down rain")

{下雪|xià xuě} — to snow

{今天|jīn tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — It's raining today. / It rains today.

{明天|míng tiān}{会|huì}{下雪|xià xuě}{吗|ma}？ — Will it snow tomorrow? ({会|huì}: will, likely)

{外边|wài bian}{在|zài}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — It's raining outside. ({在|zài}: in progress, lesson 10)

These are verb + object, like {上课|shàng kè} and {开车|kāi chē}. Words can go between the two parts:
{下|xià}{大|dà}{雨|yǔ}, "rain heavily" (come down big rain). And {雨|yǔ} can be a subject on its own:
{雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{大|dà}, "the rain is heavy".

## {了|le} for a new situation

Put {了|le} at the very end of a sentence and it says that the situation is new: something has
started, stopped or changed, or the speaker has just noticed it.

| Without {了|le} | With {了|le} |
|---|---|
| {天|tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。 It's cold. | {天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}。 It's got cold. (It wasn't before.) |
| {今天|jīn tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 It's a rainy day. | {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}！ It's started raining! |
| {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 I'm not going. | {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}。 I'm not going any more (I've changed my mind). |
| {他|tā}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。 He's a university student. | {他|tā}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}{了|le}。 He's a university student now. |
| {现在|xiàn zài}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}。 It's eight. | {现在|xiàn zài}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{了|le}。 It's eight already. |

More examples:

{我|wǒ}{女儿|nǚ ér}{五|wǔ}{岁|suì}{了|le}。 — My daughter is five now.

{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{了|le}！ — I can write characters now!

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{了|le}。 — I've got a computer now.

{下课|xià kè}{了|le}。 — Class is over. (It's the end of class.)

The {了|le} goes at the end of the whole sentence, after any object. Its English often has "now",
"already", "not… any more", "has got", or the "-s started" of "it's started raining". This
{了|le} is called change-of-state {了|le}.

**{不|bù}…{了|le}: no longer.** With {不|bù} or {没有|méi yǒu} the change is that something stops:

{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{了|le}。 — He's not a student any more.

{不|bú}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 — It's stopped raining.

{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{钱|qián}{了|le}。 — I've run out of money.

**Questions.** Add {吗|ma} after {了|le}: {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ "Is it raining (now)?"

**It isn't a past tense.** {了|le} doesn't mean "past". {昨天|zuó tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}, "yesterday was
cold", needs no {了|le}: the time word shows it's past, and nothing has changed. Lesson 25 teaches a
second {了|le}, after a verb, for completed actions ({我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}). For now,
use {了|le} at the end of a sentence for something new.

**Pronunciation.** This {了|le} is always light, with no tone: *le*. It never takes stress.

## {觉得|jué de}: to feel, to think

{觉得|jué de} + a whole sentence says how something seems to you: what you feel, or your
opinion.

{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。 — I feel cold.

{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}。 — I don't think it's cold today.

{你|nǐ}{觉得|jué de}{这个|zhè ge}{房间|fáng jiān}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ — What do you think of this room?

— {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — I think it's very nice.

{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{汉字|hàn zì}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — I think Chinese characters are beautiful.

Everything after {觉得|jué de} is a normal sentence: subject (if needed) + adjective with {很|hěn}, no
{是|shì}. To disagree, the {不|bù} usually goes after {觉得|jué de}, into the opinion:
{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}, "I don't feel cold" (I feel not-cold). {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{觉得|jué de}{冷|lěng} also
exists and is a bit stronger: "I don't find it cold at all".

For "I think" as an opinion, usually use {觉得|jué de} rather than {想|xiǎng}: {想|xiǎng} is mostly
"would like to" or "to miss" (lesson 09). ({我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng} + a sentence also exists, closer to "I
suppose…", but {觉得|jué de} is the everyday word for your opinion.) {得|de} in {觉得|jué de} is light.

## Characters

{=
| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 气 (traditional 氣) | air, gas | qì (light: qi) | 气 | 4 | {天气|tiān qì}, {不客气|bú kè qi} |
| 冷 | cold | lěng | 冫 | 7 | {冷|lěng} |
| 热 (traditional 熱) | hot | rè | 灬 | 10 | {热|rè} |
| 雨 | rain | yǔ | 雨 | 8 | {雨|yǔ}, {下雨|xià yǔ} |
| 雪 | snow | xuě | 雨 | 11 | {雪|xuě}, {下雪|xià xuě} |
| 了 ✎ | (change; completion) | le (and others) | 亅 | 2 | {了|le}, {太|tài}…{了|le} |
| 得 | (in {觉得|jué de}) | de (and others) | 彳 | 11 | {觉得|jué de} |

No new radicals this time; every radical here is one you know:

- {气|qì} is its own radical: wisps of vapour rising. You've written it already, light, in
  {不客气|bú kè qi}. Traditional: {氣|qì}, with {米|mǐ} (rice) inside (memory aid: steam
  rising from cooking rice).
- {冷|lěng}: two-dot water 冫 (ice, lesson 19) + {令|lìng}, which gives the sound. Ice means cold.
- {热|rè}: the four fire dots 灬 (lessons 07 and 18) at the bottom. Fire means heat. Traditional:
  {熱|rè}.
- {雨|yǔ}: a picture of drops falling from the sky, under a line for the sky and a frame for the
  clouds. As a radical on top of a character it's squeezed flat: compare {雨|yǔ} with the top of
  {雪|xuě}.
- {雪|xuě}: 雨 on top and 彐 below. In its older form the lower part was a broom: memory aid, snow
  is the rain you can sweep up.
- {了|le}: just two strokes, and one of the most frequent characters in Chinese. It's also *liǎo*
  in some later words ({了解|liǎo jiě}, to understand, HSK 3).
- {得|de}: 彳 ("step", lesson 11) + {日|rì} + 一 + {寸|cùn}. It's *de* in {觉得|jué de} and has two other
  readings, *dé* and *děi*, that later levels teach.

### Stroke order

- **气**: the short left-falling stroke first, then the two horizontals, then the long stroke that
  goes across, bends down and ends in a hook to the right.
- **雨**: the top horizontal; the left side; the top-and-right side with its hook; the middle
  vertical; then the four dots, left pair first, then the right pair.
- **雪**: the squeezed 雨 on top changes shape: its left side shrinks to a dot, and the frame becomes
  a cover with a hook. Then 彐: the top-and-side stroke and two horizontals.
- **了**: the top stroke goes across and down to the left in one movement; then the hooked vertical.
- **冷**: 冫 (dot, rising stroke), then {令|lìng}: the roof 人, the dot, the bent stroke, the last dot.
- **热**: the hand 扌 on the left (horizontal, hooked vertical, rising stroke), then {丸|wán}
  (left-falling, the bent hook, the dot), and the four dots last, from left to right.

Trace the new characters:

```trace
气冷热雨雪了得
```

✎ **Write it**: {了|le} is a handwriting character. Write it three times from memory: two strokes,
the top one in a single movement.
=}

## Dialogue: a phone call

{安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) is in Beijing; her friend {陈静|Chén Jìng} is at her university, in the south. Anna calls her.

```dialogue
# On the phone
陈静: {喂|wèi}，{安娜|Ān nà}！{北京|Běi jīng}{天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= Hello, Anna! What's the weather like in Beijing?
安娜: {北京|Běi jīng}{下雪|xià xuě}{了|le}！{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。{你|nǐ}{那儿|nàr}{呢|ne}？
= It's snowing in Beijing! It's very cold. What about where you are?
陈静: {我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}，{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
= It's not cold here. It's started raining.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{来|lái}{北京|Běi jīng}{吗|ma}？
= Are you coming to Beijing tomorrow?
陈静: {不|bù}{来|lái}{了|le}。{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{北京|Běi jīng}{太|tài}{冷|lěng}{了|le}！
= Not any more. I think Beijing is too cold!
安娜: {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。{雪|xuě}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}！
= I think it's lovely. The snow is beautiful!
陈静: {好|hǎo}，{好|hǎo}。{我|wǒ}{下|xià}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{去|qù}。
= All right, all right. I'll come next week.
```

{喂|wèi} is said with a rising tone on the phone, *wéi* (lesson 10). {你|nǐ}{那儿|nàr} and {我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}
are "where you are" and "where I am" (lesson 16). {下|xià}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} is "next week": {下|xià}
before a time word means "next". {不|bù}{来|lái}{了|le} is the change-of-state {了|le}: Chen Jing has
changed her plan.

## Reading: a weather diary

> {今天|jīn tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{天气|tiān qì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{不|bù}{冷|lěng}{也|yě}{不|bú}{热|rè}。{我|wǒ}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{上课|shàng kè}。{中午|zhōng wǔ}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。{下午|xià wǔ}{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{在|zài}{家|jiā}{学习|xué xí}。{晚上|wǎn shang}{不|bú}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{下雪|xià xuě}{了|le}！{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{雪|xuě}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。{明天|míng tiān}{会|huì}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。

1. What was the weather like in the morning?
2. What changed at noon, and what changed in the evening?
3. Where did the writer spend the afternoon?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

The weather was nice this morning, neither cold nor hot. I went to school at eight for class. At
noon it started raining, and it rained hard. In the afternoon I felt cold and studied at home. In the evening the rain stopped, and it started snowing! I think snow
is beautiful. It'll be cold tomorrow.

1. Nice: neither cold nor hot. 2. At noon it started raining; in the evening the rain stopped and
it began to snow. 3. At home, studying.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{今天|jīn tiān}{天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= What's the weather like today?
{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}！
= It's started raining!
{天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}。
= It's got cold.
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}。
= I'm not going after all.
{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{热|rè}。
= I feel hot.
{你|nǐ}{觉得|jué de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= What do you think?
```

## Common mistakes

- {是|shì} before an adjective: ~~{天气|tiān qì}{是|shì}{冷|lěng}~~. Say {天气|tiān qì}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}.
- {了|le} as a past tense: ~~{昨天|zuó tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}{了|le}~~ for "yesterday was cold". A time word
  is enough. Use {了|le} for a change: {今天|jīn tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}.
- {了|le} in the middle of the sentence for a change: ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}{学校|xué xiào}~~. It goes
  at the very end: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{了|le}.
- English order for rain: ~~{雨|yǔ}{下|xià}~~ for "it rains". The verb comes first: {下雨|xià yǔ}.
- {觉得|jué de} + {是|shì} + adjective: ~~{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{是|shì}{冷|lěng}~~. After {觉得|jué de} comes a normal
  sentence: {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}.
- {想|xiǎng} for an opinion: "I think it's nice" is usually {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.

## Key points

- {天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ Adjectives as predicates: {很|hěn}{冷|lěng}, {非常|fēi cháng}{热|rè},
  {太|tài}{冷|lěng}{了|le}！, {不|bù}{冷|lěng}{也|yě}{不|bú}{热|rè}.
- {下雨|xià yǔ}, {下雪|xià xuě}: verb + object; {下|xià}{大|dà}{雨|yǔ}.
- Change-of-state {了|le} at the end of the sentence: something new has started, stopped or changed.
  {不|bù}…{了|le}: not any more. It isn't a past tense.
- {觉得|jué de} + clause: I feel, I think. {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}.

lessons.title: Rivers and mountains
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

China is a big country with very different landscapes: high mountains in the west, wide plains
in the east, deserts in the north, two great rivers flowing towards the sea. This honors lesson
is a short tour of them, with the Chinese names you'll see on maps and hear in conversation.
None of the new words here are vocabulary items: they're glossed where they appear, and the
sentences use the grammar of this module ({在|zài}, {有|yǒu}, adjectives with {很|hěn}, change-of-state
{了|le}).

Figures are rounded. Lengths of rivers and heights of mountains depend on how they're measured,
so sources differ a little.

## Two great rivers

Chinese has two common words for "river": {江|jiāng} and {河|hé}. Both appear in the names of China's
two longest rivers.

| Name | Pinyin | Literally | English name |
|---|---|---|---|
| {长江|Cháng Jiāng} | Cháng Jiāng | "long river" | the Yangtze |
| {黄河|Huáng Hé} | Huáng Hé | "yellow river" | the Yellow River |

**The Yangtze, {长江|Cháng Jiāng}.** At about 6,300 kilometres it's the longest river in Asia and the
third longest in the world. It rises on the high plateau in the west of China and flows east across
the whole country to the East China Sea, which it reaches near Shanghai. {长|cháng} means "long"
(an HSK 2 word), so the Chinese name says exactly what the river is.

**The Yellow River, {黄河|Huáng Hé}.** About 5,460 kilometres long, it's China's second longest
river. It flows through the north, and its name comes from its colour: the water carries huge
amounts of fine yellow-brown soil (loess). {黄|huáng} is "yellow".

In Chinese, river names put the name before the word for river, the way {北京|Běi jīng}{大学|dà xué}
puts the name before "university":

{长江|Cháng Jiāng}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}。 — The Yangtze is very long.

{黄河|Huáng Hé}{在|zài}{中国|Zhōng guó}{北方|běi fāng}。 — The Yellow River is in the north of China.
({北方|běi fāng}: the north)

## The highest mountain in the world

The Himalayas ({喜马拉雅山|Xǐ mǎ lā yǎ Shān}) run along the south-western edge of China. Their highest
peak, Mount Everest, is the highest mountain on Earth. It stands on the border of China and Nepal.
In 2020 China and Nepal announced a new joint measurement of its height: **8,848.86 metres**.

Its Chinese name is {珠穆朗玛峰|Zhū mù lǎng mǎ Fēng}, from its local name, Qomolangma; {峰|fēng} means
"peak". People often shorten it to {珠峰|Zhū Fēng}.

{山|shān} is "mountain" and {高|gāo} "high, tall" (both later words):

{珠峰|Zhū Fēng}{非常|fēi cháng}{高|gāo}。 — Everest is extremely high.

{山|shān}{上|shàng}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{有|yǒu}{雪|xuě}。 — It's cold up on the mountain, and there's snow.

Notice {山|shān}{上|shàng}: a mountain is a thing, so "on the mountain" needs the locative {上|shàng}
(lesson 16).

## Plains and deserts

- **The North China Plain** ({华北平原|Huá běi Píng yuán}): a huge, flat plain in the north and east of China, built
  up over a very long time from the soil that rivers, above all the Yellow River, carried down and
  left behind. It's one of the most densely populated areas in the world, and a great
  wheat-growing region. Beijing lies on its north-western edge.
- **The Gobi** ({戈壁|Gē bì}): a desert stretching across the north of China and Mongolia. Much of it
  isn't sand at all but bare rock and gravel. Its climate is very dry, and its winters are bitterly
  cold.

## North and south

People in China often talk about {北方|běi fāng} (the north) and {南方|nán fāng} (the south) as if they
were two different worlds, and in some ways they are. Geographers draw the line between them
along the Qinling Mountains ({秦岭|Qín lǐng}) and the Huai River ({淮河|Huái Hé}), roughly halfway between
Beijing and the far south.

| | North of the line | South of the line |
|---|---|---|
| January | average below 0 °C: cold, often snow | average above 0 °C |
| Rain | less: under about 800 mm a year | more: over about 800 mm a year |
| Farming | wheat | rice |

This is the broad tendency behind the "northern wheat, southern rice" of the HSK 1 lesson on
staple foods. It even shows in daily life: when city heating systems were built in the 1950s,
public heating was installed only north of the line, so some cities just south of it still have
cold, unheated winters.

{北方|běi fāng}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{会|huì}{下雪|xià xuě}。 — In the north, winters are cold and it can snow.
({冬天|dōng tiān}: winter)

{南方|nán fāng}{很|hěn}{热|rè}，{雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — The south is hot, and there's a lot of rain.

## Reading: a map of China

> {中国|Zhōng guó}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。{中国|Zhōng guó}{有|yǒu}{长江|Cháng Jiāng}{和|hé}{黄河|Huáng Hé}。{长江|Cháng Jiāng}{在|zài}{南方|nán fāng}，{黄河|Huáng Hé}{在|zài}{北方|běi fāng}。{北京|Běi jīng}{也|yě}{在|zài}{北方|běi fāng}，{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。{中国|Zhōng guó}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{山|shān}。{珠峰|Zhū Fēng}{非常|fēi cháng}{高|gāo}，{山|shān}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{雪|xuě}。{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}！

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

China is very big. China has the Yangtze and the Yellow River. The Yangtze is in the south, the
Yellow River in the north. Beijing is in the north too, and winters there are cold. China has
many mountains. Everest is extremely high, and there's snow on it. I'd like to go and have a
look!

</details>

## Words in this lesson

These are for recognition only; they aren't added to your vocabulary reviews.

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {江|jiāng} | jiāng | river (in names, often in the south) |
| {河|hé} | hé | river |
| {长江|Cháng Jiāng} | Cháng Jiāng | the Yangtze |
| {黄河|Huáng Hé} | Huáng Hé | the Yellow River |
| {长|cháng} | cháng | long (HSK 2) |
| {黄|huáng} | huáng | yellow |
| {山|shān} | shān | mountain (HSK 3) |
| {高|gāo} | gāo | high, tall (HSK 2) |
| {珠峰|Zhū Fēng} | Zhū Fēng | Everest (short for {珠穆朗玛峰|Zhū mù lǎng mǎ Fēng}) |
| {北方|běi fāng} / {南方|nán fāng} | běi fāng / nán fāng | the north / the south |
| {冬天|dōng tiān} | dōng tiān | winter (HSK 3) |
| {公里|gōng lǐ} | gōng lǐ | kilometre |

lessons.title: Beijing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

{北京|Běi jīng} has turned up in many of this course's sentences. This honors lesson visits the city
itself: its name, two of its most famous old buildings, its alleys, how people get around, and its
four very different seasons. It's about buildings and daily life, so the history stays short.
New words are glossed; none join your vocabulary reviews.

## The name

{北京|Běi jīng} is {北|běi} (north) + {京|jīng} (capital): "the northern capital". There's also a
{南京|Nán jīng}, "the southern capital", a city on the Yangtze that was the capital at other times
in history. Beijing is the capital of China today. It lies at the north-western edge of the North
China Plain (lesson 20h1), with mountains to the north and west.

English used to spell the name "Peking", from older ways of writing Chinese in the Latin alphabet;
you still see it in "Peking duck" and "Peking University". Pinyin spells it Běijīng, and that's the
name used today.

{北京|Běi jīng}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}{首都|shǒu dū}。 — Beijing is the capital of China. ({首都|shǒu dū}:
capital city)

## The Forbidden City: {故宫|Gù gōng}

In the middle of the old city stands the palace where the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties
lived and ruled. In English it's the Forbidden City; most Chinese speakers call it {故宫|Gù gōng},
"the former palace".

- It was built from 1406 to 1420, and 24 emperors lived in it.
- It covers about 72 hectares, with about 980 buildings set around courtyards, one behind another,
  from south to north.
- Almost all its roofs have yellow glazed tiles: yellow was the emperor's colour.
- Since 1925 it has been a museum, the Palace Museum, and in 1987 it became a UNESCO World Heritage
  site.

{故宫|Gù gōng}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。{故宫|Gù gōng}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}。 — The Forbidden City is
in Beijing. There are lots of people inside.

## The Temple of Heaven: {天坛|Tiān tán}

South-east of the palace is {天坛|Tiān tán}, the Temple of Heaven ({天|tiān}, sky, heaven + {坛|tán}, altar). It
was built at the same time as the palace, finished in 1420. Here the emperors came every year to
pray to Heaven for good harvests. Its best-known building is the round Hall of Prayer for Good
Harvests, with a three-layered roof of blue tiles. It became a World Heritage site in 1998.

Today the grounds are a big public park. In the early morning and late afternoon many local
people come to dance, sing and exercise there.

{早上|zǎo shang}{天坛|Tiān tán}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}。 — In the morning there are lots of people at
the Temple of Heaven.

## Hutongs: {胡同|hú tòng}

Between Beijing's big roads, the old city is laced with {胡同|hú tòng}: narrow alleys formed by rows
of traditional courtyard houses, {四合院|sì hé yuàn} ("four-sided courtyard": rooms on four sides
of a yard). The first hutongs date from the Yuan dynasty, about 700 years ago; the word itself
probably comes from Mongolian. Many hutongs were pulled down from the mid-20th century to make way
for roads and new buildings, and many others are now protected.

In a hutong you might hear: {请问|qǐng wèn}，{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{哪个|nǎ ge}{胡同|hú tòng}？ — Excuse me,
which hutong is your home in?

## Getting around

- **The subway** ({地铁|dì tiě}, HSK 2): Beijing's first line opened in 1969, the first subway in
  China. Today there are many lines, and it's a quick way across the city.
- **Buses** ({公交车|gōng jiāo chē}, HSK 2) and **taxis** ({出租车|chū zū chē}, lesson 18).
- **Bicycles** ({自行车|zì xíng chē}, HSK 3): handy for short trips.

{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{去|qù}{故宫|Gù gōng}。 — I'm taking the subway to the Forbidden City.

## Four seasons

| Season | Weather |
|---|---|
| Winter ({冬天|dōng tiān}) | cold, windy and dry; January averages a few degrees below 0 °C |
| Spring ({春天|chūn tiān}) | warms up quickly, dry; sometimes sandstorms blow in from the north |
| Summer ({夏天|xià tiān}) | hot and humid; most of the year's rain falls now |
| Autumn ({秋天|qiū tiān}) | short and crisp, with little rain |

{北京|Běi jīng}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{夏天|xià tiān}{很|hěn}{热|rè}。 — Beijing is cold in winter and
hot in summer.

{七|qī}{月|yuè}{北京|Běi jīng}{常|cháng}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — In July it often rains in Beijing. ({常|cháng}: often)

## Reading: a postcard from Beijing

> {陈静|Chén Jìng}：
>
> {你|nǐ}{好|hǎo}！{北京|Běi jīng}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{今天|jīn tiān}{下雪|xià xuě}{了|le}！{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{胡同|hú tòng}{里|lǐ}。{明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{去|qù}{故宫|Gù gōng}，{下午|xià wǔ}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{天坛|Tiān tán}。{北京|Běi jīng}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}！
>
> {安娜|Ān nà}

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Chen Jing, hello! Beijing is cold in winter, and today it's started snowing!
I'm in a hutong right now. Tomorrow morning I'm taking the subway to the Forbidden City, and in
the afternoon I'd like to go to the Temple of Heaven. Beijing is beautiful! Anna

</details>

## Words in this lesson

For recognition only; they aren't added to your vocabulary reviews.

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {首都|shǒu dū} | shǒu dū | capital city |
| {故宫|Gù gōng} | Gù gōng | the Forbidden City ("former palace") |
| {天坛|Tiān tán} | Tiān tán | the Temple of Heaven |
| {胡同|hú tòng} | hú tòng | hutong, alley |
| {四合院|sì hé yuàn} | sì hé yuàn | courtyard house |
| {地铁|dì tiě} | dì tiě | subway, metro (HSK 2) |
| {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} | gōng jiāo chē | bus (HSK 2) |
| {自行车|zì xíng chē} | zì xíng chē | bicycle (HSK 3) |
| {春天|chūn tiān}, {夏天|xià tiān}, {秋天|qiū tiān}, {冬天|dōng tiān} | chūn tiān, xià tiān, qiū tiān, dōng tiān | spring, summer, autumn, winter (HSK 3) |
| {常|cháng} | cháng | often |

lessons.title: Feeling ill: 有点儿 and 不要
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about the things people talk about once the first introductions are over: how you
feel, what you like doing, your friends, your pets and what happened. It starts with being ill,
one of the topics of HSK 1, and with three small words that make your Chinese sound much more
natural:

- {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} before an adjective, for "a bit (too)": {我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}。 — I'm a bit cold.
- {不要|bú yào} before a verb, for "don't": {不要|bú yào}{说话|shuō huà}！ — Don't talk!
- {没事|méi shì}: "it's nothing, I'm fine", and also "I'm free".

You also learn to say you're ill, go to the doctor, rest and sleep, and that you're busy. The
change-of-state {了|le} from lesson 20 comes back straight away: {我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le} is "I've
fallen ill", a new situation.

## Being ill: {病|bìng}, {生病|shēng bìng}, {看病|kàn bìng}

{病|bìng} is both a noun (an illness) and a verb (to be ill). The most common way to say you're
ill uses it as a verb with the change-of-state {了|le}:

{我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le}。 — I'm ill. (I wasn't before; now I am.)

{生病|shēng bìng} means the same thing, "to fall ill". It's a verb-object word: {生|shēng} (to get,
to produce) + {病|bìng} (an illness).

{他|tā}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{来|lái}{上班|shàng bān}。 — He's ill, so he isn't coming to work today.

The first question anyone asks is {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？ — "What's wrong?" (literally "you how
became?"). It's a kind question, not a rude one.

To see a doctor is {看病|kàn bìng}, "to look at the illness". The patient says it ("I'm going to
see a doctor"), and so does the doctor ("the doctor sees patients"):

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}。 — I'm going to the hospital to see a doctor.

{王|Wáng}{医生|yī shēng}{上午|shàng wǔ}{看病|kàn bìng}，{下午|xià wǔ}{休息|xiū xi}。 — Dr Wang sees patients in the morning and has the afternoon off.

The first sentence is a serial verb sentence, as in lesson 9: you go ({去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}), and the
purpose comes second ({看病|kàn bìng}). {看病|kàn bìng} is also a separable verb like {睡觉|shuì jiào}:
other words can go between its two parts: {看|kàn}{了|le}{病|bìng} (saw a doctor) puts lesson 25's {了|le} inside it.

In China people often go to a {医院|yī yuàn} (hospital) even for something small like a cold:
hospitals have outpatient departments where you can register and see a doctor. So
{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn} often just means "go to the doctor's".

## A bit (too): {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} before adjectives

{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} goes *before* an adjective. It means "a bit, rather", and it nearly always
describes something you'd rather were different: a complaint, a worry, an excuse.

{今天|jīn tiān}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{热|rè}。 — It's a bit hot today.

{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{贵|guì}。 — This top is a bit expensive.

{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}，{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{出|chū}{去|qù}。 — I'm a bit cold. I don't feel like going out.

(In the last one, {出|chū}{去|qù} is "to go out": {出|chū} from {出租车|chū zū chē}, lesson 18, plus {去|qù}.)

{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} takes the place of {很|hěn}: an adjective predicate needs one or the other, never
both (×{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}).

### Not the same as {一点儿|yì diǎnr}

Lesson 12 taught {一点儿|yì diǎnr} (a little) after a verb: {吃|chī}{一点儿|yì diǎnr} (eat a little).
It can also come *after* an adjective, and then it means "a bit more so", usually in a
request or a comparison. Compare the two in a shop:

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} + adjective | {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{贵|guì}。 | This one is a bit expensive. (a complaint about how it is) |
| adjective + {一点儿|yì diǎnr} | {能|néng}{便宜|pián yi}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{吗|ma}？ | Could it be a bit cheaper? (asking for a change) |
| verb + {一点儿|yì diǎnr} (+ noun) | {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}。 | I'd like to drink a little water. (a small amount) |

A memory hook: {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} starts with {有|yǒu}, "there is": there *is* a bit of a problem.
{一点儿|yì diǎnr} is an amount, "one bit", so it goes where amounts go, after the verb.

## Busy, free and fine: {忙|máng} and {没事|méi shì}

{忙|máng} (busy) works like any adjective: no {是|shì}, and usually {很|hěn} in a plain statement.

{你|nǐ}{忙|máng}{吗|ma}？ — Are you busy?

{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}，{明天|míng tiān}{不|bù}{忙|máng}。 — I'm busy today; tomorrow I'm not.

{你|nǐ}{忙|máng}{什么|shén me}{呢|ne}？ — What are you busy with? (a friendly question, here using {忙|máng} as a verb)

{没事|méi shì} is short for {没有|méi yǒu}{事|shì}, "there's no matter". It has two everyday uses:

1. *"It's nothing, I'm fine."* After an apology, or when someone is worried about you:
   "{对不起|duì bu qǐ}！" "{没事|méi shì}。" — "Sorry!" "No worries." It's a little more casual than
   {没关系|méi guān xi}.
2. *"I'm free, I've nothing on."* {我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{没事|méi shì}。 — I'm free today. This is the
   opposite of {忙|máng}.

## Sleeping and resting: {睡|shuì}, {睡觉|shuì jiào}, {休息|xiū xi}, {白天|bái tiān}

{睡觉|shuì jiào} (lesson 8) is "to sleep, to go to bed" as a whole idea: {我|wǒ}{十一|shí yī}{点|diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}
(I go to bed at eleven). {睡|shuì} is the verb on its own, and it's the one you use when other
words follow it, such as how long:

{我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{睡|shuì}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I sleep eight hours a night.

{你|nǐ}{睡|shuì}{一下|yí xià}{吧|ba}。 — Have a little sleep. (Have a nap.)

Remember that {睡觉|shuì jiào} is separable: the length goes inside it (×{睡觉|shuì jiào}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}), so
with a length of time, just use {睡|shuì}.

{白天|bái tiān} is the daytime, the opposite of {晚上|wǎn shang}: {他|tā}{白天|bái tiān}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{工作|gōng zuò}。
(He sleeps in the day and works at night.) Like other time words, it goes before the verb.

{休息|xiū xi} is "to rest, to take a break", and also "to be off work":

{我们|wǒ men}{休息|xiū xi}{一下|yí xià}{吧|ba}。 — Let's take a short break.

{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{休息|xiū xi}。 — I'm off on Sundays.

{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。 — You need to rest more.

The last one is what friends and doctors say to someone who's ill. {要|yào} here is "need to,
should", and {多|duō} before a verb means "more": {多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}, {多|duō}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ} (drink more water).

## Don't: {不要|bú yào} + verb

To tell someone not to do something, put {不要|bú yào} before the verb. {不|bù} becomes {不|bú}
because {要|yào} is fourth tone.

{不要|bú yào}{说话|shuō huà}！ — Don't talk!

{你|nǐ}{病|bìng}{了|le}，{不要|bú yào}{去|qù}{上班|shàng bān}。 — You're ill. Don't go to work.

{请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。 — Please don't make phone calls here.

The last kind, with {请|qǐng}, is what you'll read on signs. Plain {不|bù} before a verb only
describes: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{茶|chá} is "I don't drink tea", not an order.

{不要|bú yào} can also be the negative of {要|yào} (want): {我|wǒ}{不要|bú yào}{茶|chá}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。 — I don't want tea,
thanks. The two meanings are easy to tell apart: "don't" comes before a verb and is said to
someone else; "don't want" comes before a thing. In speech you'll also hear
{别|bié}, a shorter "don't" (HSK 2).

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 病 | illness; ill | bìng | 疒 | 10 | {病|bìng}, {生病|shēng bìng}, {看病|kàn bìng} |
| 院 | courtyard; institution | yuàn | 阝 | 9 | {医院|yī yuàn}, {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn} (cinema, lesson 22) |
| 休 | to rest | xiū | 亻 | 6 | {休息|xiū xi} |
| 息 | breath; to rest | xī (neutral in {休息|xiū xi}) | 心 | 10 | {休息|xiū xi} |
| 白 | white | bái | 白 | 5 | {白天|bái tiān} |
| 忙 | busy | máng | 忄 | 6 | {忙|máng} |

All six are written the same way in traditional characters.

### New radicals: 忄 and 疒

**忄, the "upright heart"** ({竖心旁|shù xīn páng}). {心|xīn} (heart, mind) changes shape when it stands on
the left of a character: it becomes a tall vertical stroke with a dot on each side. Characters
with it are often about feelings and states of mind. So far you know {忙|máng} (busy: a mind that's
occupied); later come {快|kuài} (fast, happy), {慢|màn} (slow) and others: eight characters of this track
are filed under it. Write the two dots first (left, then right) and the vertical last. At the bottom of a
character, {心|xīn} keeps its full shape, as in {您|nín}, {想|xiǎng} and this lesson's {息|xī}.

**疒, the "sickness" radical** ({病字旁|bìng zì páng}): a roof with a long sweep down the left side and
two small strokes in front of it, often explained as a sick person lying on a bed. Characters with it
are about illness: {病|bìng} now, {疼|téng} (to hurt) in HSK 2. Three characters of this track are filed under it.
Order: the dot on top, the horizontal, the long left-falling stroke, then the dot and the short
rising stroke on the left.

### How the characters are built

- {病|bìng} = 疒 (illness) + {丙|bǐng}, which gives the sound. Most characters are built this way:
  a meaning part and a sound part.
- {院|yuàn} = 阝 (on the left: a mound or wall, lesson 4) + {完|wán} (sound). A {院|yuàn} was first a
  walled courtyard; now it's also an institution, such as a hospital or a cinema.
- {休|xiū} = 亻 (person) + {木|mù} (tree): a person leaning against a tree, resting. This is the
  character's real history, not just a memory aid.
- {息|xī} = {自|zì} + {心|xīn}. {自|zì} was once a drawing of a nose, and {息|xī} first meant "breath": the breath
  going from the heart out through the nose, as old dictionaries explain it.
- {白|bái}: a memory aid only (its history is debated): a sun {日|rì} with a ray of light on top, so
  "white, bright". Write the short top stroke first, then the box.
- {忙|máng} = 忄 (mind) + {亡|wáng}, the sound part.

Stroke traps: in {息|xī} write {自|zì} completely before {心|xīn}; and {心|xīn} goes left dot, the long curved
hook, then the middle and right dots.

```trace
病院休息白忙
```

=}

## Dialogue: on the phone

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} calls her classmate {大卫|Dà wèi} (David), who hasn't come to class.

```dialogue
# {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？
王芳: {喂|wèi}，{大卫|Dà wèi}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Hello, David! Where are you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bú}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}。
= I'm at home. I'm not coming to class today.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？
= What's wrong?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le}，{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}。
= I'm ill. I feel a bit cold.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}{吧|ba}。
= You should go to the hospital and see a doctor.
大卫: {没事|méi shì}。{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{睡|shuì}{一下|yí xià}。
= It's nothing. I want to have a sleep at home.
王芳: {好|hǎo}{吧|ba}。{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}，{不要|bú yào}{看|kàn}{手机|shǒu jī}！
= All right. Get lots of rest, and don't look at your phone!
大卫: {好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！
= OK. Thank you!
王芳: {不客气|bú kè qi}。{再见|zài jiàn}！
= You're welcome. Bye!
```

Notes: {喂|wèi} is said *wéi* on the phone (lesson 10). {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le} has the change-of-state
{了|le}: David had planned to go, and now he isn't. {好|hǎo}{吧|ba} is a slightly reluctant "all right then".

## Reading: a note to the teacher

{李明|Lǐ Míng} sends his teacher a message.

> {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}：
>
> {您好|nín hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}，{不|bù}{能|néng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}。{医生|yī shēng}{说|shuō}{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}。{星期三|xīng qī sān}{我|wǒ}{能|néng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。{对不起|duì bu qǐ}！
>
> {李明|Lǐ Míng}
>
> {星期一|xīng qī yī}

Questions (answers below):

1. Why isn't {李明|Lǐ Míng} going to class?
2. Where is he now?
3. On which day can he come back to class?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

Dear Teacher Wang, hello! This is Li Ming. I've fallen ill today: I feel a bit cold, and I can't come
to class. I'm at the hospital now. The doctor says I need to rest at home for two days. I can come
to class on Wednesday. Sorry! Li Ming, Monday.

1. He's ill ({生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}). 2. At the hospital ({在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}). 3. Wednesday ({星期三|xīng qī sān}): two days' rest
after Monday.
</details>

{两|liǎng}{天|tiān} (two days) comes after {休息|xiū xi} because it says how long: lengths of time follow the
verb (lesson 7), times when something happens go before it ({星期三|xīng qī sān}{我|wǒ}{能|néng}{去|qù}).

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le}。
= I'm ill.
{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？
= What's wrong?
{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}。
= I'm a bit cold.
{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}。
= I'm going to the hospital to see a doctor.
{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。
= You need to rest more.
{不要|bú yào}{说话|shuō huà}！
= Don't talk!
{没事|méi shì}。
= It's nothing.
{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。
= I'm busy today.
```


## Common mistakes

- ×{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{病|bìng} or ×{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{病|bìng}. Being ill is a change: {我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le} or {我|wǒ}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{冷|lěng}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}, ×{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}. {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} goes before the adjective and replaces {很|hěn}.
- Using {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} for a request: ×{能|néng}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{便宜|pián yi}{吗|ma}？ Asking for "a bit more X" is
  adjective + {一点儿|yì diǎnr}: {便宜|pián yi}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}.
- Using {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} for good things: {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{漂亮|piào liang} sounds as if being pretty were a problem. Say
  {很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang} or {非常|fēi cháng}{漂亮|piào liang}.
- ×{不|bù}{说话|shuō huà}！ as an order. Plain {不|bù} only describes ("not talking"); tell someone not to
  with {不要|bú yào}.
- ×{睡觉|shuì jiào}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}. With a length of time use {睡|shuì}: {睡|shuì}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}.

## Key points

- {我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le} / {我|wǒ}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}: I'm ill. {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？: What's wrong? {去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}: go and see a doctor.
- {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} + adjective: a bit (too), for unwelcome things, instead of {很|hěn}. Adjective +
  {一点儿|yì diǎnr}: a bit more so. Verb + {一点儿|yì diǎnr}: a little of something.
- {忙|máng}: busy. {没事|méi shì}: it's nothing; I'm free.
- {睡|shuì} takes a length of time ({睡|shuì}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}); {睡觉|shuì jiào} is the whole idea. {白天|bái tiān}: daytime.
  {休息|xiū xi}: rest, be off; {多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}: rest more.
- {不要|bú yào} + verb: don't. {请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}…: please don't (signs).
- New radicals: 忄 (upright heart) and 疒 (sickness).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: What I like doing: 爱, 唱歌, 看电影
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Free time is one of the first things people ask a new friend about: {你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
(What do you like doing?) This lesson gives you the words to answer: singing, films, reading and
going out to have fun. Along the way it shows three patterns you'll use all the time:

- {爱|ài} + an activity: {我|wǒ}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。 — I love watching films.
- Activities that come with an object in Chinese: {唱|chàng}{歌|gē} (sing songs), {读书|dú shū} (read books).
- {好|hǎo} + verb as an adjective: {好听|hǎo tīng} (nice to listen to), {好玩儿|hǎo wánr} (fun).

## Loving and liking: {爱|ài} and {喜欢|xǐ huan}

{喜欢|xǐ huan} (lesson 11) is "to like". {爱|ài} is "to love", and like {喜欢|xǐ huan} it can take a noun or
a whole activity:

{我|wǒ}{爱|ài}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{家|jiā}。 — I love my family.

{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。 — My dad loves reading.

{你|nǐ}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{什么|shén me}{电影|diàn yǐng}？ — What films do you love watching?

With people, {爱|ài} is strong: family love or romantic love. {我|wǒ}{爱|ài}{你|nǐ} isn't said lightly, and to a
new friend you'd say {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{你|nǐ} at most. With activities it's everyday and warm, and it
often means "tends to, does a lot": {他|tā}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{说话|shuō huà} is "he loves to talk, he talks a lot".

The negatives: {不|bú}{爱|ài} (fourth tone after {不|bù}, so *bú*) and {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}.

{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{不|bú}{爱|ài}{吃|chī}{菜|cài}。 — My younger sister doesn't like eating vegetables.

## Activities with an object: {唱|chàng}{歌|gē}, {读书|dú shū}, {看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}

In English you can just "sing", "eat" or "read". Chinese verbs for everyday activities usually
take a general object when nothing more specific is said:

| Activity | Chinese | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| to sing | {唱|chàng}{歌|gē} | sing songs |
| to read (books); to study | {读书|dú shū} | read books |
| to eat (a meal) | {吃|chī}{饭|fàn} | eat rice |
| to talk | {说话|shuō huà} | speak words |
| to sleep | {睡觉|shuì jiào} | sleep a sleep |
| to cook | {做饭|zuò fàn} | make rice |

So "I like singing" is {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}, not ×{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}. When there is a specific object, it
replaces the general one: {唱|chàng}{中文|Zhōng wén}{歌|gē} (sing Chinese songs), {看|kàn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{电影|diàn yǐng} (watch Chinese
films), {读|dú}{汉字|hàn zì} (read characters aloud).

Two of these have more than one meaning:

- {读书|dú shū} is "to read (books)" and also "to study, to be a student": {我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{读书|dú shū} —
  my older brother is at university.
- {看|kàn} + a thing you look at is "to watch, to read": {看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng} (watch a film), {看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}
  (watch TV), {看|kàn}{书|shū} (read a book), {看|kàn}{手机|shǒu jī} (look at your phone).

### Reading: {读|dú} or {看|kàn}?

Both can be "to read", but they're not the same:

- {读|dú} is reading *aloud*, or reading as study: {请|qǐng}{读|dú}{一下|yí xià}{这些|zhè xiē}{字|zì} (please read these
  characters aloud). A teacher says {读|dú}; a child learning to read {读|dú}.
- {看|kàn} is reading with your eyes, silently, for information or fun: {我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{看|kàn}{书|shū} (I read in the
  evening).

## Going out and having fun: {玩|wán}

{玩|wán} is "to play" for children, and for adults "to have fun, to go out, to visit for fun":

{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{在|zài}{外边|wài bian}{玩|wán}。 — The children are playing outside.

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{玩|wán}。 — I'd like to go to Beijing for a holiday. ({北京|Běi jīng}: Beijing)

{你|nǐ}{来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{玩|wán}{吧|ba}！ — Come over to my place!

{不要|bú yào}{玩|wán}{手机|shǒu jī}{了|le}！ — Stop playing on your phone! (The {了|le} at the end makes it "any more".)

In northern speech you'll often hear it with erhua, {玩儿|wánr}. Ball games have their own verbs,
which come in HSK 2.

## Good to …: {好|hǎo} + verb

Put {好|hǎo} before a verb and you get an adjective: "good to do".

| Word | Literally | Meaning | Said of |
|---|---|---|---|
| {好吃|hǎo chī} | good to eat | tasty, delicious | food |
| {好看|hǎo kàn} | good to look at | good-looking; good (to watch or read) | people, clothes, films, books |
| {好听|hǎo tīng} | good to listen to | nice-sounding, lovely | songs, voices, names, music |
| {好玩儿|hǎo wánr} | good to play | fun | games, places, activities, people |

They behave like any adjective: {很|hěn} before them in a statement, no {是|shì}.

{这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}{很|hěn}{好看|hǎo kàn}。 — This film is really good.

{你|nǐ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。 — Your name sounds lovely.

{北京|Běi jīng}{好玩儿|hǎo wánr}{吗|ma}？ — Is Beijing fun?

Choose by the sense: a film is {好看|hǎo kàn} (you watch it), a song is {好听|hǎo tīng} (you hear it). The
negative is {不|bù} + the whole word: {不|bù}{好看|hǎo kàn}, {不|bù}{好听|hǎo tīng}. For an A-not-A question people say
{好听|hǎo tīng}{不|bu}{好听|hǎo tīng}？ or, often in speech, just {好|hǎo}{不|bu}{好听|hǎo tīng}？ with the first syllable only.

## Films: {电影|diàn yǐng} and {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}

{电影|diàn yǐng} is "electric shadows": {电|diàn} from {电话|diàn huà} and {电视|diàn shì}, and {影|yǐng}, a shadow or image. The
{院|yuàn} from lesson 21's {医院|yī yuàn} makes it a place: {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}, the cinema.

{我们|wǒ men}{晚上|wǎn shang}{去|qù}{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go to the cinema this evening.

That's a serial verb sentence again: go to the place, then do the thing.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 爱 ✎ (traditional 愛) | love | ài | 爫 | 10 | {爱|ài} |
| 唱 | to sing | chàng | 口 | 11 | {唱|chàng}, {唱|chàng}{歌|gē} |
| 歌 | song | gē | 欠 | 14 | {歌|gē}, {唱|chàng}{歌|gē} |
| 影 | shadow; image | yǐng | 彡 | 15 | {电影|diàn yǐng}, {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn} |
| 读 (traditional 讀) | to read (aloud) | dú | 讠 | 10 | {读|dú}, {读书|dú shū} |
| 玩 | to play | wán | 王 | 8 | {玩|wán}, {好玩儿|hǎo wánr} |

The radicals are those the app's stroke data uses. Dictionaries file {玩|wán} under 王 or under {玉|yù}
(jade), whose side form looks like 王; and {爱|ài} under 爫 (a hand reaching down) or under {心|xīn},
the radical of its traditional form {愛|ài}.

### How the characters are built

- {唱|chàng} = 口 (mouth) + {昌|chāng}, which gives the sound: singing is done with the mouth.
- {歌|gē} = {哥|gē} (older brother, lesson 3), which gives the sound exactly, + 欠, a person with an open
  mouth (the radical of {欢|huān} in {喜欢|xǐ huan}). A song is sung with an open mouth.
- {玩|wán} = 王 (here jade) + {元|yuán} (lesson 13), the sound part. It first meant "to handle jade, to toy
  with something precious".
- {影|yǐng}: three slanting strokes 彡 on the right, often explained as rays of light, beside a
  character that's about light and scenery. Take the rays as a memory aid.
- {读|dú} = 讠 (speech, lesson 2) + a right side that looks like {卖|mài} (to sell, lesson 13): a market seller
  reading out the prices, as a memory aid. In the traditional form {讀|dú} the right side was a
  different sound part that only looks like "sell".
- {爱|ài}: a hand (爫) on top, a cover (冖), and {友|yǒu} (friend, lesson 23) underneath. The traditional
  form {愛|ài} has {心|xīn} (heart) and 夂 (a foot) under the cover instead of 友; the simplified form keeps the
  hand and the cover and puts a shape like 友 below. "A hand covering a friend" is a memory aid, not history.

### Stroke order

- {爱|ài}: the four strokes of 爫 (the left-falling stroke on top, two dots, another left-falling
  stroke), then 冖 (dot, then the horizontal with its hook), then 友: *horizontal first*, then the
  long left-falling stroke, the horizontal-and-fall, and the right-falling stroke last.
- {歌|gē}: the two 可 shapes of {哥|gē} one above the other, top first, then 欠 on the right (four strokes:
  left-falling, horizontal hook, left-falling, right-falling).
- {影|yǐng}: everything on the left first (日 at the top, then the rest of it down to the bottom),
  then the three strokes of 彡 from top to bottom.

```trace
爱唱歌影读玩
```

Write it: 爱. It's one of the characters the HSK expects learners to write by hand by level 2.
Write it three times from memory, on paper or the pad, then check.

=}

## Dialogue: Saturday plans

{李明|Lǐ Míng} asks {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) what she's doing at the weekend.

```dialogue
# {星期六|xīng qī liù}
李明: {安娜|Ān nà}，{星期六|xīng qī liù}{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, do you have time on Saturday?
安娜: {有|yǒu}。{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= Yes. What would you like to do?
李明: {我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}{吧|ba}！{你|nǐ}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}{吗|ma}？
= Let's go and see a film! Do you like watching films?
安娜: {爱|ài}{看|kàn}！{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看|kàn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{电影|diàn yǐng}。
= I love it! I really like Chinese films.
李明: {晚上|wǎn shang}{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}，{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？
= And in the evening let's go and sing, OK?
安娜: {唱|chàng}{歌|gē}？{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{会|huì}{唱|chàng}{中文|Zhōng wén}{歌|gē}。
= Sing? I can't sing Chinese songs.
李明: {没事|méi shì}，{很|hěn}{好玩儿|hǎo wánr}！{中文|Zhōng wén}{歌|gē}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。
= It doesn't matter, it's fun! Chinese songs are lovely.
安娜: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{去|qù}！
= OK, I'll come!
```

Notes: {爱|ài}{看|kàn}！ answers with the verb, the usual way to say yes in Chinese (no word for "yes" is
needed). Going out to sing usually means a karaoke place, where friends rent a room with a screen,
which is a popular evening out in China.

## Reading: my family's free time

> {我|wǒ}{家人|jiā rén}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{玩|wán}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{书|shū}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}，{她|tā}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}，{星期六|xīng qī liù}{他|tā}{去|qù}{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}。{我|wǒ}{呢|ne}？{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{读|dú}{中文|Zhōng wén}{书|shū}，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看|kàn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{电影|diàn yǐng}。

{她|tā}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng} is "her singing is lovely": first the topic (she sings songs), then the
comment ({很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}).

Questions:

1. Who goes to the cinema on Saturdays?
2. What does the writer's mother like doing?
3. What does the writer like doing?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

Everyone in my family loves having fun. My dad loves reading: in the evening he reads at home. My
mum likes singing, and she sings beautifully. My older brother loves films: on Saturdays he goes
to the cinema. And me? I like reading Chinese books, and I like Chinese films too.

1. The older brother ({哥哥|gē ge}). 2. Singing ({唱|chàng}{歌|gē}). 3. Reading Chinese books and watching Chinese films.
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= What do you like doing?
{我|wǒ}{爱|ài}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。
= I love watching films.
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。
= I like singing.
{这个|zhè ge}{歌|gē}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。
= This song is lovely.
{北京|Běi jīng}{很|hěn}{好玩儿|hǎo wánr}。
= Beijing is fun.
{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{吧|ba}。
= Let's go to the cinema.
```


## Common mistakes

- ×{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}。 "I like singing" needs the object: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{读|dú}{手机|shǒu jī}。 Reading with your eyes is {看|kàn}: {看|kàn}{手机|shǒu jī}, {看|kàn}{书|shū}. {读|dú} is aloud, or study.
- ×{这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。 You watch a film: {好看|hǎo kàn}. {好听|hǎo tīng} is for songs, voices and names.
- ×{这个|zhè ge}{歌|gē}{是|shì}{好听|hǎo tīng}。 {好听|hǎo tīng} is an adjective: {很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}, no {是|shì}.
- Saying {不|bù}{爱|ài} with a fourth-tone {不|bù}: before {爱|ài} (fourth tone) it's {不|bú}{爱|ài}.
- {我|wǒ}{爱|ài}{你|nǐ} to a new friend. Keep {爱|ài} for family and partners; for friends, {喜欢|xǐ huan}.

## Key points

- {爱|ài} + noun or activity: to love (doing); stronger than {喜欢|xǐ huan}. {不|bú}{爱|ài}: doesn't like.
- Everyday activities take a general object: {唱|chàng}{歌|gē}, {读书|dú shū}, {吃|chī}{饭|fàn}, {说话|shuō huà}, {睡觉|shuì jiào}; a specific
  object replaces it ({唱|chàng}{中文|Zhōng wén}{歌|gē}).
- {读|dú}: read aloud, study. {看|kàn}: read silently, watch. {读书|dú shū}: read; be at school.
- {玩|wán}: play, have fun, go out; {来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{玩|wán}{吧|ba}: come over.
- {好|hǎo} + verb: {好吃|hǎo chī}, {好看|hǎo kàn}, {好听|hǎo tīng}, {好玩儿|hǎo wánr}: adjectives, with {很|hěn}.
- {电影|diàn yǐng}, {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}: film, cinema.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Friends: 给, 问 and two objects
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about meeting people and making friends: introducing someone, saying "nice to
meet you", arranging to see each other again. The grammar is a sentence with two objects:

{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 — I'll give you a book.

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{问|wèn}{你|nǐ}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí}。 — I'd like to ask you a question.

You also learn {给|gěi} before a verb ({给|gěi}{妈妈|mā ma}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}, call Mum), {认识|rèn shi} (to know a person)
and how it differs from {知道|zhī dào} (lesson 10), and you finally get the characters of {再见|zài jiàn}.

## Friends: {朋友|péng you} and its family

{朋友|péng you} (neutral tone on {友|you}) is a friend, a man or a woman. Add {男|nán} or {女|nǚ} and the meaning
changes:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {朋友|péng you} | friend |
| {男朋友|nán péng you} | boyfriend |
| {女朋友|nǚ péng you} | girlfriend |
| {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} | child, kid (a friendly word, and how adults address children) |

So {她|tā}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{女朋友|nǚ péng you} is "she's my girlfriend": for a friend who happens to be a woman, just say
{朋友|péng you}. {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} isn't "a small friend" but a child: a shop assistant or a teacher says
{小朋友|xiǎo péng you}，{你|nǐ}{好|hǎo}！ to a child, and parents talk about {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} the way English speakers say
"kids". A good friend is {好|hǎo}{朋友|péng you}.

{大家|dà jiā} is "everyone, all of you". It opens a talk to a group: {大家|dà jiā}{好|hǎo}！ (Hello, everyone!), and
it often goes with {都|dōu}: {大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng} (everyone is happy).

## Knowing people: {认识|rèn shi} and {知道|zhī dào}

English "know" is two verbs in Chinese:

| | {认识|rèn shi} | {知道|zhī dào} |
|---|---|---|
| Object | a person, a place, a character (things you recognise) | a fact, a piece of information |
| Example | {我|wǒ}{认识|rèn shi}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 — I know Wang Fang. | {我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{她|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — I know she's a teacher. |
| Example | {你|nǐ}{认识|rèn shi}{这|zhè}{个|gè}{字|zì}{吗|ma}？ — Do you know (recognise) this character? | {你|nǐ}{知道|zhī dào}{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{吗|ma}？ — Do you know what his name is? |

You can {知道|zhī dào} about someone you've never met (you know of them); you {认识|rèn shi} people you've met.
{认识|rèn shi} is also "to meet, to get to know": the polite phrase on meeting someone is

{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。 — Nice to meet you. (Knowing you, I'm glad.)

or, the other way round, {很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}. The answer can be the same phrase, or
{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。 (I'm glad to meet you too). To introduce people, say
{这|zhè}{是|shì}… (this is…): {这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{朋友|péng you}{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}。 ({张伟|Zhāng Wěi}: a common full name.)

{高兴|gāo xìng} (glad, happy) is an adjective: {我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}, {他|tā}{不|bù}{高兴|gāo xìng} (he's not happy, he's
upset).

## Two objects: {给|gěi} and {问|wèn}

Some verbs take two objects: a **[[double object]]** sentence. In HSK 1 they're {给|gěi} (to give) and {问|wèn}
(to ask). The person comes first, then the thing:

| Subject | Verb | Person | Thing |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | {给|gěi} | {你|nǐ} | {一个|yí gè}{苹果|píng guǒ}。 |
| {妈妈|mā ma} | {给|gěi} | {孩子|hái zi} | {一点儿|yì diǎnr}{钱|qián}。 |
| {我|wǒ} | {问|wèn} | {老师|lǎo shī} | {一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí}。 |

I'll give you an apple. · Mum gives the child a little money. · I'll ask the teacher a question.
({问题|wèn tí}, "question", is lesson 25's word.)

This is like English "give you an apple", but with {给|gěi} there's no second order: English can also say
"give an apple to you", Chinese can't put the thing first (×{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{一个|yí gè}{苹果|píng guǒ}{你|nǐ}).

{问|wèn} can also take the person and then a whole question:

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{问|wèn}{他|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}。 — Go and ask him what his name is.

Either object can be left out when it's clear: {你|nǐ}{问|wèn}{老师|lǎo shī}{吧|ba} (ask the teacher), {给|gěi}{你|nǐ}！ (Here
you are! — handing something over).

## {给|gěi} before a verb: for, to

{给|gěi} + person can also go *before* another verb, to say who the action is for or who it's
aimed at. English puts this after the verb ("call Mum", "buy something for a friend"); Chinese puts
it before:

{我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。 — I'll call you this evening.

{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{妈妈|mā ma}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yí}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}。 — I bought Mum a top. (For {了|le} after the verb, see lesson 25.)

{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}。 — Let me show you. (Literally "I give you a look".)

The order is the same as with {在|zài} + place: the extra information comes before the main verb.
You'll also hear {我|wǒ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}, but {给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} is the most common order: use it.

## Again and see you: {再|zài} and {见|jiàn}

{再|zài} means "again", for something that hasn't happened yet: you'll do it once more, or later.

{请|qǐng}{再|zài}{说|shuō}{一下|yí xià}。 — Could you say that again, please?

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{再|zài}{来|lái}。 — I'll come again tomorrow.

It sounds exactly like {在|zài} (at, in; lesson 5), so the character tells them apart: {在|zài} is a
place, {再|zài} is another time.

{见|jiàn} is "to see, to meet (someone)": {见|jiàn}{朋友|péng you} (meet a friend), {我们|wǒ men}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{见|jiàn}？ (What time shall we
meet?). Now you can read the goodbye you learned first: {再见|zài jiàn} is "again see", see you again.
The same pattern works with any time:

| | |
|---|---|
| {明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！ | See you tomorrow! |
| {星期六|xīng qī liù}{见|jiàn}！ | See you on Saturday! |
| {晚上|wǎn shang}{见|jiàn}！ | See you this evening! |

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 朋 | friend | péng | 月 | 8 | {朋友|péng you}, {男朋友|nán péng you}, {女朋友|nǚ péng you}, {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} |
| 友 | friend | yǒu (neutral in {朋友|péng you}) | 又 | 4 | {朋友|péng you} |
| 给 (traditional 給) | to give; for | gěi | 纟 | 9 | {给|gěi} |
| 再 | again | zài | 冂 | 6 | {再|zài}, {再见|zài jiàn} |
| 见 (traditional 見) | to see; to meet | jiàn | 见 | 4 | {见|jiàn}, {再见|zài jiàn}, {看见|kàn jiàn} (lesson 24) |
| 认 (traditional 認) | to recognise | rèn | 讠 | 4 | {认识|rèn shi} |
| 识 (traditional 識) | to know | shí (neutral in {认识|rèn shi}) | 讠 | 7 | {认识|rèn shi} |
| 高 | high, tall | gāo | 高 | 10 | {高兴|gāo xìng} |
| 兴 (traditional 興) | mood, interest | xìng (and others) | 八 | 6 | {高兴|gāo xìng} |

{兴|xìng} is read {兴|xīng} (to rise, to flourish) in other words you'll meet later.

### New radicals: 纟 and 又

**纟, "silk"** ({绞丝旁|jiǎo sī páng}, "twisted silk side"): the form that the character for silk thread
takes on the left. Characters with it are often about thread, cloth, tying and linking, and many
colour words have it (HSK 2). Eleven characters of this track are filed under it; {给|gěi} is the first. Three
strokes: two bent strokes like a zigzag, then a rising stroke at the bottom.

**又, "right hand"** ({又|yòu}): a hand drawn with two strokes, the horizontal-and-fall and then the
long right-falling stroke. On its own it's a word meaning "again (it happened again)", which
comes in HSK 3. You've seen it as a part of {欢|huān} in {喜欢|xǐ huan} and of {对|duì} (right, lesson 15), and now it's
the radical of {友|yǒu}: eight characters of this track are filed under it.

### How the characters are built

- {友|yǒu}: in the oldest writing, two right hands side by side, people helping each other. The top
  part is a second hand, flattened. This is the real history of the character.
- {朋|péng}: two 月 side by side. In the oldest writing it showed two strings of shells (once used as
  money) hanging together; the strings later looked like 月. Side by side, like friends.
- {给|gěi} = 纟 (thread) + {合|hé} (to join), the sound part in old Chinese.
- {认|rèn} = 讠 (speech) + {人|rén} (person), which gives the sound in the simplified form. {识|shí} = 讠 +
  {只|zhī} (lesson 24). Both simplified forms are much shorter than the traditional {認識|rèn shi}.
- {见|jiàn}: an eye on top of a person (clearer in the traditional form {見|jiàn}, which has {目|mù}, eye, on
  top of 儿 legs). Seeing is what eyes do.
- {高|gāo}: a picture of a tall building with a roof, a storey and a gate.

### Stroke order

- {再|zài}: the top horizontal first, then the frame (the left vertical, then the right side
  with its hook), then the strokes inside, and the long horizontal across the bottom last: it
  holds the character up.
- {见|jiàn}: the vertical, the horizontal that turns down, the left-falling stroke, and last the
  vertical that bends right and hooks up.
- {兴|xìng}: the three short strokes on top from left to right, the horizontal, then the two
  strokes underneath.
- {友|yǒu}: horizontal first, then the long left-falling stroke, then 又.

```trace
朋友给再见
```

```trace
认识高兴
```

=}

## Dialogue: at a friend's party

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} introduces {安娜|Ān nà} to her friend {张伟|Zhāng Wěi}.

```dialogue
# {认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{朋友|péng you}{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}。{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{安娜|Ān nà}。
= Anna, this is my friend Zhang Wei. Zhang Wei, this is my classmate Anna.
张伟: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= Hello! Nice to meet you.
安娜: {认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= Nice to meet you too.
张伟: {我|wǒ}{能|néng}{问|wèn}{你|nǐ}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí}{吗|ma}？
= Can I ask you a question?
安娜: {可以|kě yǐ}，{你|nǐ}{问|wèn}{吧|ba}。
= Sure, go ahead.
张伟: {你|nǐ}{认识|rèn shi}{这|zhè}{个|gè}{字|zì}{吗|ma}？
= Do you know this character?
安娜: {认识|rèn shi}！{这|zhè}{是|shì}“{爱|ài}”。
= Yes! It's "love".
张伟: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{真|zhēn}{好|hǎo}！
= Your Chinese is really good!
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}！{我|wǒ}{能|néng}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{问|wèn}{你|nǐ}{一些|yì xiē}{汉字|hàn zì}。
= Thanks! Can I call you? I'd like to ask you about some characters.
张伟: {可以|kě yǐ}！{星期六|xīng qī liù}{见|jiàn}！
= Sure! See you on Saturday!
```

Notes: {张伟|Zhāng Wěi} points at a character on his phone. {认识|rèn shi}！ answers with the verb, as Chinese
does. Compliments like {你|nǐ}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{真|zhēn}{好|hǎo} are common, and the easiest reply is {谢谢|xiè xie}.

## Reading: my friends in Beijing

> {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{有|yǒu}{三|sān}{个|gè}{好|hǎo}{朋友|péng you}：{王芳|Wáng Fāng}、{李明|Lǐ Míng}{和|hé}{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}。{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}，{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{李明|Lǐ Míng}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{的|de}{男朋友|nán péng you}，{他|tā}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}{在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}，{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。{星期六|xīng qī liù}{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{家|jiā}{玩|wán}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
>
> — {安娜|Ān nà}

Questions:

1. Who is {李明|Lǐ Míng}?
2. Where does {张伟|Zhāng Wěi} work?
3. What do the friends do on Saturdays?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

I have three good friends in Beijing: Wang Fang, Li Ming and Zhang Wei. Wang Fang is my
classmate: we're both university students. Li Ming is Wang Fang's boyfriend, and he loves
singing. Zhang Wei works at a company and is very busy. On Saturdays we all go to Wang Fang's
place to hang out, and everyone has a great time. — Anna

1. Wang Fang's boyfriend ({王芳|Wáng Fāng}{的|de}{男朋友|nán péng you}). 2. At a company ({在|zài}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}), and he's very busy. 3. They go to
Wang Fang's home and have fun ({去|qù}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{家|jiā}{玩|wán}).
</details>

The mark 、 between the names is the Chinese "list comma", used between items in a list.

## Say it

```speak
{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= Nice to meet you.
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{朋友|péng you}。
= This is my friend.
{我|wǒ}{能|néng}{问|wèn}{你|nǐ}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí}{吗|ma}？
= Can I ask you a question?
{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}。
= I'll call you.
{请|qǐng}{再|zài}{说|shuō}{一下|yí xià}。
= Could you say that again, please?
{大家|dà jiā}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, everyone!
{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！
= See you tomorrow!
```


## Common mistakes

- ×{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{你|nǐ}。 The person comes first: {我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{你|nǐ}。 "Call someone" needs {给|gěi} before the verb: {我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 for "I know Wang Fang" (I've met her). People you've met: {认识|rèn shi}. Facts:
  {知道|zhī dào}.
- Calling a female friend {女朋友|nǚ péng you}. That's "girlfriend": a friend is {朋友|péng you}.
- Writing {在|zài} for "again": ×{明天|míng tiān}{在|zài}{来|lái}. "Again" is {再|zài}: {明天|míng tiān}{再|zài}{来|lái}.
- ×{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{高兴|gāo xìng}。 {高兴|gāo xìng} is an adjective: {很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}.

## Key points

- {朋友|péng you} friend, {男朋友|nán péng you} / {女朋友|nǚ péng you} boyfriend / girlfriend, {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} child, {大家|dà jiā} everyone.
- {认识|rèn shi}: know (people, characters), meet. {知道|zhī dào}: know (facts). {认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}: nice to meet you.
- Double objects: {给|gěi} / {问|wèn} + person + thing, in that order.
- {给|gěi} + person before a verb: {给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} (call you), {给|gěi}{妈妈|mā ma}{买|mǎi}… (buy for Mum).
- {再|zài}: again (not yet happened); {见|jiàn}: see, meet; {明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}, {再见|zài jiàn}.
- New radicals: 纟 (silk) and 又 (hand).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Pets and things: 它, 只, 有的
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Cats and dogs are easy things to talk about with anyone, and they bring a lot of grammar with
them:

- the measure word {只|zhī} for animals: {一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo} (a cat), {两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu} (two dogs);
- {它|tā} and {它们|tā men}, "it" and "they" for animals and things;
- {有的|yǒu de} and {有些|yǒu xiē}, "some": {有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{猫|māo}，{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{狗|gǒu} (some people like cats, others dogs);
- {看见|kàn jiàn} and {听见|tīng jiàn}, "see" and "hear": a verb with its result;
- {还|hái}, "still" and "also", and how it joins two facts together with {也|yě}.

## Dogs and cats: {狗|gǒu}, {猫|māo} and the measure word {只|zhī}

{狗|gǒu} is a dog and {猫|māo} a cat (it's said like the animal sounds, *māo*). Like every noun with a
number, they need a measure word, and for most animals it's {只|zhī}:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 — We have a dog.

{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}。 — She has two cats.

{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}？ — How many cats do you have at home?

{这|zhè}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — This cat is beautiful.

{只|zhī} works for cats, dogs, birds and most small and medium animals, and also for one of a pair:
{一|yì}{只|zhī}{手|shǒu} (one hand). With {一|yī} (one) it's {一|yì}{只|zhī}, *yì zhī*, because {只|zhī} is first tone. For dogs you'll
also hear another measure word, {条|tiáo} (as in {面条儿|miàn tiáor}, for long things): {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{狗|gǒu} is also
common. ×{一个|yí gè}{猫|māo} is a beginner's mistake people will understand, but it sounds wrong.

{=
{只|zhī} has a second reading: {只|zhǐ} (third tone) means "only", a word for HSK 3. In traditional
characters the two are written differently: the measure word is {隻|zhī}, "only" is {只|zhǐ}. The app's
traditional switch shows {隻|zhī} in this lesson.
=}

## It and they: {它|tā} and {它们|tā men}

{它|tā} is "it", for animals and things. It sounds exactly like {他|tā} (he) and {她|tā} (she); only the
character is different. The plural is {它们|tā men}.

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}，{它|tā}{叫|jiào}{大白|Dà bái}。 — I have a cat. It's called Dabai ("Big White").

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}，{它们|tā men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}。 — I have two dogs. They're both small.

Two things to know:

- For *things*, Chinese often leaves "it" out where English needs it: {这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}{很|hěn}{好看|hǎo kàn}，{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}{吧|ba}。 —
  This book is good; read it. No {它|tā} is needed after {看|kàn}.
- For *pets*, many owners say {他|tā} or {她|tā}, as English speakers say "he" or "she" for their
  dog. In speech you can't hear the difference; in writing, {它|tā} is the usual choice for an
  animal.

## Some: {有的|yǒu de} and {有些|yǒu xiē}

{有的|yǒu de} (literally "there are ones that") means "some (of them)". It goes before a noun at the start of
the sentence, and it's often used twice to contrast two groups:

{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{猫|māo}，{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{狗|gǒu}。 — Some people like cats; others like dogs.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}，{有的|yǒu de}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{有的|yǒu de}{不|bú}{会|huì}。 — Of my classmates, some can speak Chinese and some can't.

The noun can be left out when it's clear: {这些|zhè xiē}{苹果|píng guǒ}，{有的|yǒu de}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}。 — Of these apples, some are
expensive.

{有些|yǒu xiē} is "some, a number of", much like {有的|yǒu de} but used more on its own:

{有些|yǒu xiē}{同学|tóng xué}{不|bú}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{这|zhè}{个|gè}{字|zì}。 — Some classmates can't write this character.

{有的|yǒu de} and {有些|yǒu xiē} describe the subject, so they come *before* the verb. For "some" after the verb, as
an object, use {一些|yì xiē} (lesson 14): {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{一些|yì xiē}{水果|shuǐ guǒ} (I'll buy some fruit), not ×{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{有的|yǒu de}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}.

## Seeing and hearing: {看见|kàn jiàn} and {听见|tīng jiàn}

{看|kàn} is "to look, to watch", the action. {看见|kàn jiàn} is "to see": the action plus its result, your eyes
actually taking something in. {见|jiàn} (lesson 23) is the result. In the same way, {听|tīng} is "to
listen" and {听见|tīng jiàn} is "to hear".

A verb with a second verb or adjective that says how it turned out is a **[[result verb]]** (also
called a verb with a result complement). You'll meet many more in HSK 2; {看见|kàn jiàn} and {听见|tīng jiàn} are
the first.

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| {你|nǐ}{看|kàn}！ — Look! | {我|wǒ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}。 — I can see a cat. |
| {你|nǐ}{听|tīng}！ — Listen! | {我|wǒ}{听见|tīng jiàn}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{在|zài}{说话|shuō huà}。 — I can hear someone talking. |

English "I can see" and "I can hear" are just {看见|kàn jiàn} and {听见|tīng jiàn}: no {能|néng} is needed.

Because seeing and hearing usually happen at a moment, these verbs often come with {了|le} (it
happened) or with {没|méi} (it didn't). Lesson 25 explains both; for now, learn these two as phrases:

{你|nǐ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{猫|māo}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you seen my cat?

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{看见|kàn jiàn}。 — I haven't seen it. (I didn't see it.)

## Still and also: {还|hái}

{还|hái} goes before the verb and has two main meanings.

*Still*: something hasn't changed yet.

{他|tā}{还|hái}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。 — He's still asleep.

{现在|xiàn zài}{还|hái}{早|zǎo}。 — It's still early.

*Also, as well, in addition*: one more thing on top of what's been said.

{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 — I have a cat, and a dog as well.

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{苹果|píng guǒ}，{还|hái}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{牛奶|niú nǎi}。 — I want to buy apples, and milk too.

{还有|hái yǒu} on its own starts an extra item: "and also, and there's…". In a shop you'll hear
{还|hái}{要|yào}{什么|shén me}？ (Anything else? — What else do you want?).

### Joining two facts: {也|yě} or {还|hái}?

Both {也|yě} and {还|hái} can mean "also", and both go before the verb. The difference is who or what
is being added:

| | {也|yě} | {还|hái} |
|---|---|---|
| Another person or thing does the same | {他|tā}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}。 — He has a cat; I have one too. | — (not possible) |
| The same person, one more thing | {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{狗|gǒu}。 — I have a cat, and also a dog. | {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{狗|gǒu}。 — I have a cat, and a dog on top of that. |

So with a new subject, only {也|yě} works. With the same subject both work: {也|yě} simply adds, {还|hái}
stresses "and in addition, what's more". This "also" sentence with two clauses is the kind of
joined sentence HSK 1 expects you to read and make.

{还|hái} has another reading, {还|huán} "to give back", which comes in HSK 3.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 狗 | dog | gǒu | 犭 | 8 | {狗|gǒu} |
| 猫 (traditional 貓) | cat | māo | 犭 | 11 | {猫|māo} |
| 它 | it | tā | 宀 | 5 | {它|tā}, {它们|tā men} |
| 只 (traditional 隻 as the measure word; 只 for "only") | (measure word for animals) | zhī (and others) | 口 | 5 | {只|zhī}, {一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo} |
| 还 ✎ (traditional 還) | still; also | hái (and others) | 辶 | 7 | {还|hái}, {还有|hái yǒu} |

{狗|gǒu} and {猫|māo} share the radical 犭, the "dog side" ({反犬旁|fǎn quǎn páng}): the form of {犬|quǎn} (dog) on the left of a
character, found in many animal names. It has three strokes: a left-falling stroke, a long curved
stroke with a hook, and another left-falling stroke across it.

### How the characters are built

- {狗|gǒu} = 犭 (animal) + {句|jù} (sentence: HSK 3), the sound part in old Chinese.
- {猫|māo} = 犭 + {苗|miáo} (a seedling), the sound part: *miáo* is close to *māo*, and to a cat's
  "miaow".
- {它|tā} was first a drawing of a snake (old dictionaries say "a creature with a curling tail"),
  and later became the word "it"; the snake moved to a new character, {蛇|shé} (snake).
- {只|zhī}: the traditional {隻|zhī} is a bird ({隹|zhuī}) held in a hand (又): one bird, a single one. The
  simplified form borrowed the shorter character {只|zhǐ} (only).
- {还|hái} = 辶 (walking, lesson 3) + {不|bù} (not). As a memory aid: not walked away yet, so still here.
  The traditional form {還|hái} has a different sound part.

### Stroke order

- {还|hái}: write {不|bù} first, then 辶 *last*, as in {这|zhè} and {边|biān}: the dot, the bent stroke, then the long
  sweep along the bottom.
- {只|zhī}: 口 first, then the two strokes below it, left then right.
- {它|tā}: the roof 宀 (dot, dot, horizontal hook), then the left-falling stroke, and last the
  vertical that bends right and hooks up.

```trace
狗猫它只还
```

Write it: 还. It's one of the characters the HSK expects learners to write by hand by level 2.
Write it three times from memory, on paper or the pad, then check.

=}

## Dialogue: at Wang Fang's home

{安娜|Ān nà} visits {王芳|Wáng Fāng}.

```dialogue
# {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}{吗|ma}？
安娜: {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{听见|tīng jiàn}{猫|māo}{在|zài}{叫|jiào}。
= Wang Fang, do you have a cat? I can hear a cat miaowing.
王芳: {有|yǒu}！{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。
= Yes! We have two cats, and a dog too.
安娜: {两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}？{它们|tā men}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Two cats? Where are they?
王芳: {一|yì}{只|zhī}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{下边|xià bian}，{一|yì}{只|zhī}{在|zài}{外边|wài bian}。
= One's under the table, and one's outside.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}！{它|tā}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。{它|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= I can see it! It's small and really pretty. What's it called?
王芳: {它|tā}{叫|jiào}{大白|Dà bái}。
= It's called Dabai.
安娜: {狗|gǒu}{呢|ne}？
= What about the dog?
王芳: {狗|gǒu}{还|hái}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。
= The dog's still asleep.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{狗|gǒu}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}！
= Your dog really loves sleeping!
王芳: {对|duì}，{它|tā}{白天|bái tiān}{睡|shuì}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{玩|wán}。
= Yes, it sleeps in the day and plays at night.
```

Notes: {叫|jiào}, which you know as "to be called", is also what animals do: {猫|māo}{在|zài}{叫|jiào}, the cat is
miaowing; {狗|gǒu}{在|zài}{叫|jiào}, the dog is barking. In {一|yì}{只|zhī}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{下边|xià bian} the noun is left out after the measure
word: "one is under the table". {狗|gǒu}{呢|ne}？ is the follow-up {呢|ne} of lesson 2: "and the dog?"

## Reading: Blackie and Dabai

> {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}{和|hé}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}。{狗|gǒu}{叫|jiào}{小黑|Xiǎo hēi}，{猫|māo}{叫|jiào}{大白|Dà bái}。{它们|tā men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好玩儿|hǎo wánr}。{小黑|Xiǎo hēi}{爱|ài}{玩|wán}，{白天|bái tiān}{它|tā}{在|zài}{外边|wài bian}{玩|wán}；{大白|Dà bái}{爱|ài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{白天|bái tiān}{它|tā}{在|zài}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{睡|shuì}。{晚上|wǎn shang}，{小黑|Xiǎo hēi}{和|hé}{大白|Dà bái}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{有的|yǒu de}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{狗|gǒu}，{有的|yǒu de}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{猫|māo}。{我|wǒ}{呢|ne}？{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}！

{小黑|Xiǎo hēi} is "Little Black", a common name for a black dog ({黑|hēi}: black, HSK 2). {我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}: I like
them both ({都|dōu}, "all, both", points back to the cats and dogs).

Questions:

1. Which animal sleeps in the day, and where?
2. Where are the two animals in the evening?
3. Which do the writer's classmates like?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

We have a dog and a cat at home. The dog is called Blackie and the cat is called Dabai. They're
both great fun. Blackie loves playing: in the daytime it plays outside. Dabai loves sleeping: in
the daytime it sleeps in a room. In the evening, Blackie and Dabai are both in my room. Some of
my classmates like dogs, and some like cats. And me? I like them both!

1. The cat, {大白|Dà bái}, in a room ({在|zài}{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}). 2. In the writer's room. 3. Some like dogs and some like
cats ({有的|yǒu de}…，{有的|yǒu de}…).
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}？
= How many cats do you have at home?
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。
= We have a dog.
{它|tā}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= What's it called?
{你|nǐ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{猫|māo}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Have you seen my cat?
{我|wǒ}{听见|tīng jiàn}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{在|zài}{说话|shuō huà}。
= I can hear someone talking.
{他|tā}{还|hái}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。
= He's still asleep.
{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{猫|māo}，{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{狗|gǒu}。
= Some people like cats; others like dogs.
```


## Common mistakes

- ×{一个|yí gè}{猫|māo}, ×{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{狗|gǒu}. Animals take {只|zhī}: {一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}, {两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{有的|yǒu de}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}。 {有的|yǒu de} and {有些|yǒu xiē} belong before the verb ({有的|yǒu de}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}); after the verb use
  {一些|yì xiē}.
- Using {看|kàn} for "see": {你|nǐ}{看|kàn}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{猫|māo}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ asks whether you looked at it, not whether
  you saw it. Say {看见|kàn jiàn}.
- ×{他|tā}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}，{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}。 for "I have one too". A new subject takes {也|yě}: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{猫|māo}.
- Adding {能|néng} for an ordinary "I can see…". {看见|kàn jiàn} already includes it: {我|wǒ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}.
  ({能|néng}{看见|kàn jiàn} is for being *able* to see, for example from far away.)

## Key points

- Animals: {一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}, {两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}, {几|jǐ}{只|zhī}？ (traditional {隻|zhī}).
- {它|tā} / {它们|tā men}: it / they, for animals and things; for things often left out.
- {有的|yǒu de}…，{有的|yǒu de}…: some…, others…; {有些|yǒu xiē}: some. Both before the verb.
- Result verbs: {看|kàn} look → {看见|kàn jiàn} see; {听|tīng} listen → {听见|tīng jiàn} hear.
- {还|hái}: still ({还|hái}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}); also, in addition ({还|hái}{有|yǒu}…). A new subject doing the same takes {也|yě}.
