lessons.title: What happened: 了 and 没有
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Until now, almost every sentence in this course has been about now, habits or plans. This lesson
lets you say what *happened*: what you bought, where you went, what you did when you were at
school.

{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 — I bought a book.

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}。 — I didn't go.

{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you eaten?

Chinese verbs never change their form for time. Instead, a time word says *when*
({昨天|zuó tiān}, {去年|qù nián}), and the little word {了|le} after a verb says the action is *done*. Its negative is
{没|méi} or {没有|méi yǒu}, with no {了|le}. You also learn {的|de}{时候|shí hou} ("when…"), the years ({今年|jīn nián}, {明年|míng nián},
{去年|qù nián}) and the school stages, so that you can tell a short life story at the end.

## Years: {今年|jīn nián}, {明年|míng nián}, {去年|qù nián}

| | Year | Day (lesson 6) |
|---|---|---|
| last | {去年|qù nián} (last year: "the gone year") | {昨天|zuó tiān} (yesterday) |
| this | {今年|jīn nián} (this year) | {今天|jīn tiān} (today) |
| next | {明年|míng nián} (next year) | {明天|míng tiān} (tomorrow) |

The pattern is easy to remember: {今|jīn} is "now, this", {明|míng} "next", and {年|nián} or {天|tiān} decides whether it's a
year or a day. Only "last" differs: {去年|qù nián} but {昨天|zuó tiān}. Like all time words, they go before the verb,
before or after the subject:

{我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。 — I'm twenty this year.

{明年|míng nián}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}{学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Next year I'd like to go to China to study Chinese.

## Done: verb + {了|le}

The **[[completed-action 了]]** goes straight after the verb. It says that the action happened and is
complete:

{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 — I bought a book.

{他|tā}{吃|chī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}。 — He ate two steamed buns.

{昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{了|le}{一个|yí gè}{电影|diàn yǐng}。 — Yesterday I watched a film.

{我|wǒ}{睡|shuì}{了|le}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I slept for eight hours.

Notice that the object in these sentences has a number and a measure word. That's typical: verb +
{了|le} + "how much". A bare object sounds unfinished, as if you were about to add something:
×{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{书|shū}。 ("I bought books, and then…?") When there's no amount to give, put {了|le} at the end of the
sentence instead, after the object:

{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}。 — I've eaten.

{他|tā}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{了|le}。 — He's gone to the hospital. / He went to the hospital.

{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{书|shū}{了|le}。 — I've bought the books.

A {了|le} at the end like this does both jobs at once: the action is done, and that's the new
situation (lesson 20's change-of-state {了|le}).

### {了|le} is not a past tense

{了|le} marks a completed action, not "the past" in general. Two consequences:

- *No {了|le} for past states and habits.* Being something, liking something, doing something
  regularly: the time word is enough.
  {去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{中学生|zhōng xué shēng}。 — Last year I was a secondary-school student. (×{是|shì}{了|le})
  {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{小学生|xiǎo xué shēng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。 — When I was at primary school, I loved singing.
- *Verbs of state rarely take it:* {是|shì}, {在|zài} (to be at), {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {觉得|jué de}, {想|xiǎng} (would like). (You will hear
  {我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{了|le}, "I see, got it": that's lesson 20's change-of-state {了|le}, "now I know".)

## Didn't: {没|méi} / {没有|méi yǒu} + verb

The negative of a completed action is {没|méi} or {没有|méi yǒu} before the verb, and *the {了|le} goes*:

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}。 / {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{买|mǎi}。 — I didn't buy it. / I haven't bought it.

{昨天|zuó tiān}{他|tā}{没|méi}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。 — He didn't go to class yesterday.

×{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}{了|le}: {了|le} says it happened and {没|méi} says it didn't, so they can't go together. {没|méi} and
{没有|méi yǒu} mean the same here; {没|méi} is shorter and more common in speech.

{还|hái} (lesson 24) + {没|méi} is "not yet", often with {呢|ne} at the end:

{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{呢|ne}。 — I haven't eaten yet.

### {不|bù} or {没|méi}?

| {不|bù} + verb | {没|méi} + verb |
|---|---|
| now, habits, the future, wishes: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 — I'm not going. / I won't go. | it didn't happen: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}。 — I didn't go. / I haven't been. |
| {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — I don't drink tea. | {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — I didn't drink the tea. |
| states, also about the past: {去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi}{他|tā}。 — Last year I didn't know him. | {有|yǒu} always: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。 — I don't have time. |

So "I didn't go yesterday" is {昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}, never ×{昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}.

## Asking what happened

Add {吗|ma} to a sentence with {了|le}, or end it with {没有|méi yǒu} ("or not?"):

{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you eaten?

{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{没有|méi yǒu}？ — Have you eaten (or not)?

Answer with the verb, as always:

| Answer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {吃|chī}{了|le}。 | Yes (I've eaten). |
| {没|méi}{吃|chī}。 | No (I haven't eaten). |
| {还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}。 | Not yet. |

{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ is often used as a friendly greeting around mealtimes among people who know each
other, much like "How's it going?". You don't need to explain what you ate.

## The two {了|le} side by side

| | Change of state (lesson 20) | Completed action (this lesson) |
|---|---|---|
| Where | end of the sentence | right after the verb |
| Meaning | now it's so (and wasn't before) | the action is done |
| Example | {天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}。 — It's got cold. | {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yí}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}。 — I bought a top. |
| Example | {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}。 — I'm not going any more. | {他|tā}{喝|hē}{了|le}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}。 — He drank a little water. |
| Negative | {不|bù}…{了|le} (no longer) | {没|méi} + verb, no {了|le} |

The reference sheet "The two {了|le} and {没有|méi yǒu}" sums both up.

## When: …{的|de}{时候|shí hou}

{的|de}{时候|shí hou} after a phrase means "when…, at the time that…". The whole "when" part comes *first*,
like a time word:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{小学生|xiǎo xué shēng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。 — When I was at primary school, I loved singing.

{我|wǒ}{七|qī}{岁|suì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 — When I was seven, we had a dog.

{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{不要|bú yào}{看|kàn}{手机|shǒu jī}！ — Don't look at your phone while you're eating!

English can put "when…" at the end ("I loved singing when I was little"); Chinese can't. {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou} is the
question "when?": {你|nǐ}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}？ (When are you going to Beijing?)

Don't mix up three similar words:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {时候|shí hou} | a point in time: "when" | {我|wǒ}{小|xiǎo}{的|de}{时候|shí hou} — when I was little |
| {时间|shí jiān} | time as an amount (lesson 7) | {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。 — I don't have time. |
| {小时|xiǎo shí} | an hour | {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} — two hours |

People also say {小时候|xiǎo shí hou}, "in childhood": {小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{玩|wán} (as a child I loved playing). It
contains {小时|xiǎo shí} but has nothing to do with hours.

## School: {小学|xiǎo xué}, {中学|zhōng xué}, {大学|dà xué}

| Stage | Pupil or student | Usual ages in mainland China |
|---|---|---|
| {小学|xiǎo xué} (primary school) | {小学生|xiǎo xué shēng} | about 6 to 12 |
| {中学|zhōng xué} (secondary school) | {中学生|zhōng xué shēng} | about 12 to 18 |
| {大学|dà xué} (university) | {大学生|dà xué shēng} | from about 18 |

{中学|zhōng xué} has two parts, {初中|chū zhōng} (junior secondary, usually three years) and {高中|gāo zhōng} (senior
secondary, three years). School is compulsory for nine years, primary school and junior
secondary. "To start school" is {上|shàng} + the school: {我|wǒ}{女儿|nǚ ér}{上|shàng}{小学|xiǎo xué}{了|le} (my daughter has started primary
school), with lesson 19's {上学|shàng xué} (to go to school).

## A few and a question: {少|shǎo} and {问题|wèn tí}

{少|shǎo} is "few, little", the opposite of {多|duō}. It's an adjective, so it describes with {很|hěn} and
can't stand straight before a noun:

{今天|jīn tiān}{超市|chāo shì}{里|lǐ}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}。 — There are very few people in the supermarket today. (×{少|shǎo}{人|rén})

{很|hěn}{少|shǎo} before a verb means "seldom": {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì} (I rarely watch TV). And as a verb {少|shǎo} is "to be
missing": {少|shǎo}{一个|yí gè}{人|rén} (one person is missing). It's the {少|shao} of {多少|duō shao}.

{问题|wèn tí} is a question you ask, and also a problem: {老师|lǎo shī}，{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí} (I have a question),
{问|wèn}{老师|lǎo shī}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí} (ask the teacher a question). The cheerful answer to a request is
{没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}！ — No problem!

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 题 (traditional 題) | topic; question | tí | 页 | 15 | {问题|wèn tí} |
| 候 | time, season; to wait | hòu (neutral in {时候|shí hou}) | 亻 | 10 | {时候|shí hou} |

### New radical: 页

**页, "head"** ({页|yè}): on its own it means "page" (HSK 3), but as a radical it was first a
drawing of a head, and characters with it are often about the head or the face. It always
stands on the right. Four characters of this track are filed under it: {题|tí} now, {颜|yán} (in
{颜色|yán sè}, colour) in HSK 2, and two in HSK 3.

- {题|tí} = {是|shì} (sound) + 页 (head). It first meant the forehead, the front of the head; then the
  front of a piece of writing, a title, a topic; now also a question in a test.
- {候|hòu} looks like {侯|hóu} (a surname) with one more stroke: the short vertical between 亻 and the
  right side. Without it, it's a different character.

Stroke order: in {题|tí}, write {是|shì} completely, including the long sweep along the bottom, then 页
above the sweep. In {候|hòu}, the order is 亻, the short vertical, then the right side from top to
bottom.

```trace
题候
```

=}

## Dialogue: what did you do yesterday?

{安娜|Ān nà} meets {王芳|Wáng Fāng} on Monday morning.

```dialogue
# {你|nǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}{了|le}？
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}{了|le}？
= Anna, where did you go yesterday?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{书店|shū diàn}{了|le}。{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{中文|Zhōng wén}{书|shū}。
= I went to the bookshop. I bought two Chinese books.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{看|kàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Have you read them?
安娜: {看|kàn}{了|le}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。{有些|yǒu xiē}{字|zì}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi}。
= I've read a bit. There are some characters I don't know.
王芳: {没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}，{你|nǐ}{可以|kě yǐ}{问|wèn}{我|wǒ}。
= No problem, you can ask me.
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}！{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？{你|nǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{了|le}？
= Thanks! And you? What did you do yesterday?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}，{没|méi}{出|chū}{去|qù}。
= I rested at home. I didn't go out.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Have you eaten?
王芳: {还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}。{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}！
= Not yet. Let's go and eat!
```

Notes: {有些|yǒu xiē}{字|zì}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi} puts the object first as the topic: "some characters, I don't know
(them)". {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi} has no {了|le}: it describes how the day was, a state rather than a single
completed action, and the {没|méi}{出|chū}{去|qù} (didn't go out: {出|chū}{去|qù} from lesson 21) after it says what didn't happen.

## Reading: Li Ming's story

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{今年|jīn nián}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}。{我|wǒ}{七|qī}{岁|suì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{上|shàng}{了|le}{小学|xiǎo xué}，{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}。{十三|shí sān}{岁|suì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{我|wǒ}{上|shàng}{了|le}{中学|zhōng xué}。{中学|zhōng xué}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}，{朋友|péng you}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。{去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{上|shàng}{了|le}{大学|dà xué}，{现在|xiàn zài}{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{学习|xué xí}{英文|Yīng wén}。{明年|míng nián}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{英国|Yīng guó}{学习|xué xí}。

({英文|Yīng wén}: English; {英国|Yīng guó}: the UK.)

Questions:

1. How old was Li Ming when he started primary school?
2. What did he love doing at secondary school?
3. What does he want to do next year?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

My name is Li Ming, and I'm twenty this year. I started primary school when I was seven, and I
really liked my teacher. When I was thirteen, I started secondary school. At secondary school I
loved singing, and I had lots of friends. Last year I started university, and now I'm a
university student. I study English at university. Next year I'd like to go to the UK to study.

1. Seven ({七|qī}{岁|suì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}). 2. Singing ({唱|chàng}{歌|gē}). 3. Go to the UK to study ({去|qù}{英国|Yīng guó}{学习|xué xí}).
</details>

The single events take {了|le} ({上|shàng}{了|le}{小学|xiǎo xué}, started primary school); what he liked and how things were
don't ({很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}, {很|hěn}{爱|ài}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}, {朋友|péng you}{很|hěn}{多|duō}).

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Have you eaten?
{还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}。
= Not yet.
{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。
= I bought a book.
{昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}。
= I didn't go yesterday.
{你|nǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}{了|le}？
= Where did you go yesterday?
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{小学生|xiǎo xué shēng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。
= When I was at primary school, I loved singing.
{没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}！
= No problem!
```


## Common mistakes

- ×{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}{了|le}。 The negative drops {了|le}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}.
- ×{昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 for "I didn't go yesterday". Something that didn't happen takes {没|méi}: {昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}.
- ×{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{书|shū}。 on its own. Give an amount ({买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}) or move {了|le} to the end ({我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{书|shū}{了|le}).
- ×{去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{了|le}{中学生|zhōng xué shēng}。 Past states need no {了|le}: the time word says when.
- Putting "when" at the end: ×{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}{我|wǒ}{小|xiǎo}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}。 The {的|de}{时候|shí hou} part comes first.
- ×{少|shǎo}{人|rén}, ×{少|shǎo}{朋友|péng you}. {少|shǎo} describes: {人|rén}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}, {朋友|péng you}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}.

## Key points

- {去年|qù nián}, {今年|jīn nián}, {明年|míng nián}: last, this, next year; time words go before the verb.
- Completed action: verb + {了|le} (+ amount + noun): {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}. Without an amount, {了|le} at the end:
  {我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}.
- Negative: {没|méi} / {没有|méi yǒu} + verb, no {了|le}. Not yet: {还|hái}{没|méi}…{呢|ne}.
- Questions: …{了|le}{吗|ma}？ / …{了|le}{没有|méi yǒu}？ Answers: {吃|chī}{了|le}。/ {没|méi}{吃|chī}。/ {还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}。
- {了|le} isn't a past tense: no {了|le} for past states, habits or likes.
- …{的|de}{时候|shí hou}: when…, always first. {时候|shí hou} (when) ≠ {时间|shí jiān} (time) ≠ {小时|xiǎo shí} (hour).
- School: {小学|xiǎo xué}, {中学|zhōng xué}, {大学|dà xué}; {上|shàng}{小学|xiǎo xué}: start primary school.

lessons.title: Morning in the park
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Walk into a city park in China early in the morning and it's anything but quiet. Before most
offices open, the paths and squares are full of people exercising, dancing, singing, chatting
and playing games, many of them retired. This honors lesson describes the most common of these
sights, gives you the words for them, and lets you use this module's grammar ({爱|ài}, {有的|yǒu de}…{有的|yǒu de}…,
{还|hái}, {了|le}) to talk about them. The new words here are glossed, not added to your reviews.

Not everyone does these things, of course, and not every park looks the same: what follows are
common sights in many Chinese cities, especially in big, old parks.

## The park: {公园|gōng yuán}

A park is a {公园|gōng yuán} ({公|gōng} as in {公司|gōng sī}, {园|yuán} "garden"). Many open very early, and the busiest
time is from dawn to about breakfast time, then again in the evening after dinner.

{早上|zǎo shang}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}，{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — At six in the morning, the park is full of people.

{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}，{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}。 — Some people sing, some dance,
and there are also people doing tai chi.

The people you see are often {退休|tuì xiū} (retired). For many of them the morning in the park is
exercise, a routine and a social life at once: the same groups meet in the same corner every day.

## Tai chi: {太极拳|tài jí quán}

{太极拳|tài jí quán}, tai chi, is a slow, flowing exercise: relaxed, circular movements of the whole body,
done with calm breathing and a quiet mind. It is also a martial art, practised alone, in groups or
in pairs (one partner-exercise is "pushing hands"). Groups often practise in rows behind a
leader, sometimes to recorded music.

According to UNESCO, which added Taijiquan to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of
Humanity in 2020, it began in the mid-seventeenth century in {温县|Wēn Xiàn} (Wenxian County), in {河南|Hé nán}
(Henan Province), and is now practised all over China by people of all ages. There are several
styles, named after the families or masters that passed them on.

"To do tai chi" is {打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}: {打|dǎ} (from {打电话|dǎ diàn huà}) is used for many activities with the hands.

{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}。 — My dad does tai chi every morning. ({每天|měi tiān}: every day, HSK 2)

## Square dancing: {广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ}

{广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ}, "square dance", is group dancing in a {广场|guǎng chǎng} (public square), a park or any open
space. The dancers are mostly middle-aged and retired women. They stand in rows, the most
practised at the front and beginners at the back, and follow simple routines to popular songs
played from a portable speaker. Groups meet in the early morning and in the evening after
dinner. ({跳舞|tiào wǔ}: to dance, HSK 2.)

{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{去|qù}{跳|tiào}{广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ}。 — In the evening my mum goes square dancing.

Its popularity has a side that neighbours notice: the music can be loud, and in some places
residents have complained about the noise; some groups now keep the volume down or keep to set
hours. For the dancers it's exercise and company. Many say they come for the friends as much as
for the dancing.

## Singing, games and shuttlecocks

In many parks you'll also hear groups singing together, sometimes with someone playing an
instrument, and see people playing cards, Chinese chess or other board games at stone tables, with
a small crowd watching.

A game you may not know is {踢|tī}{毽子|jiàn zi}, kicking a shuttlecock: a weighted disc with feathers that
players keep in the air with their feet, passing it around a circle without using their hands.
({踢|tī}: to kick; {毽子|jiàn zi}: the shuttlecock.)

## Kites: {放|fàng}{风筝|fēng zheng}

A kite is a {风筝|fēng zheng} ({风|fēng}, wind), and to fly one is {放|fàng}{风筝|fēng zheng} ({放|fàng}: to let go, to release). In spring
especially, open squares and parks fill with kites, from simple paper ones to long dragons
made of many sections.

The city of {潍坊|Wéi fāng} (Weifang) in {山东|Shān dōng} (Shandong Province) calls itself the kite capital of the
world. It has held an international kite festival in April since 1984.

{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{放|fàng}{风筝|fēng zheng}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go and fly a kite in the park on Sunday!

## Walking the birds: {遛|liù}{鸟|niǎo}

In Beijing parks in the morning you may see people, often older men, carrying a birdcage, some
of them covered with a cloth. They're taking their songbirds out: {遛|liù}{鸟|niǎo}, "walking the birds"
({鸟|niǎo}: bird). The owners swing the cage gently as they walk, then hang it from a branch so the
bird can sing with the others, and sit and chat nearby. Owners of the same kind of bird tend to
gather together. The custom goes back to imperial times.

{树|shù}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{鸟|niǎo}，{它们|tā men}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}{很|hěn}{好听|hǎo tīng}。 — There are lots of birds in the tree, and they sing
beautifully. ({树|shù}: tree, HSK 3)

## Writing with water: {地书|dì shū}

One of the most beautiful sights is {地书|dì shū}, "ground writing": people write large characters on
the paving stones with a long brush dipped in water instead of ink. The characters shine for a
few minutes, then dry and disappear, and the writer moves on. Some write poems they know by
heart; passers-by stop to read. The practice spread through Chinese parks from around the 1990s
(sources differ on how old it is). It's practice in calligraphy that costs nothing and leaves no
mark.

## A notice in the park

Parks put up notices like this one. Read it with the words you know:

> **{公园|gōng yuán}{早上|zǎo shang}{的|de}{活动|huó dòng}** (morning activities)
>
> {太极拳|tài jí quán}：{星期一|xīng qī yī}{到|dào}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}，{早上|zǎo shang}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}
>
> {唱|chàng}{歌|gē}：{星期六|xīng qī liù}{上午|shàng wǔ}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}
>
> {请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}{放|fàng}{风筝|fēng zheng}。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Morning activities in the park. Tai chi: Monday to Friday, 6:30 in the morning. Singing: Saturday,
9 a.m. Please don't fly kites here.
</details>

## Reading: Grandpa's morning

> {我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{今年|jīn nián}{七十|qī shí}{岁|suì}。{他|tā}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{五|wǔ}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}，{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}。{他|tā}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}，{也|yě}{爱|ài}{和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{说话|shuō huà}。{我|wǒ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{不|bú}{爱|ài}{打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}，{她|tā}{晚上|wǎn shang}{跳|tiào}{广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ}。{昨天|zuó tiān}{爷爷|yé ye}{没|méi}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}，{他|tā}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{冷|lěng}，{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}{了|le}{一|yì}{天|tiān}。

({爷爷|yé ye}: grandpa, father's father; {奶奶|nǎi nai}: grandma, father's mother. {和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{说话|shuō huà}: talk with friends.)

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

My grandpa is seventy this year. Every day he gets up at five in the morning and goes to the park
at six. He loves doing tai chi, and he loves talking with his friends. My grandma doesn't like tai
chi; she goes square dancing in the evening. Yesterday Grandpa didn't go to the park: he felt a
bit cold, and stayed at home and rested for the day.
</details>

## Words in this lesson (glossed, not for review)

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {公园|gōng yuán} | park |
| {退休|tuì xiū} | to retire; retired |
| {太极拳|tài jí quán} | tai chi; {打|dǎ}{太极拳|tài jí quán}: to do tai chi |
| {广场|guǎng chǎng} / {广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ} | public square / square dancing |
| {跳舞|tiào wǔ} | to dance (HSK 2) |
| {踢|tī}{毽子|jiàn zi} | to kick a shuttlecock |
| {风筝|fēng zheng} / {放|fàng}{风筝|fēng zheng} | kite / to fly a kite |
| {鸟|niǎo} / {遛|liù}{鸟|niǎo} | bird / to take a bird out for a walk |
| {地书|dì shū} | water calligraphy on the ground |
| {爷爷|yé ye} / {奶奶|nǎi nai} | grandpa / grandma (father's parents) |

lessons.title: Radicals and dictionaries
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've met a new radical or two in almost every lesson so far. This honors lesson steps back and
asks what radicals are actually for: how they hint at meaning, how dictionaries use them to put
thousands of characters in order, how many there are (it depends whom you ask), and how to look
up a character you can't read, on paper or on a phone. It ends with a fact about stroke order
that surprises many learners: mainland China and Taiwan don't always agree.

The words here are glossed, not added to your reviews: {部首|bù shǒu} (radical), {字典|zì diǎn} (a character
dictionary, HSK 3), {词典|cí diǎn} (a dictionary of words), {查|chá} (to look up, HSK 3), {笔画|bǐ huà} (stroke).

## What radicals do

{=

### A hint at the meaning

Most characters are built from a meaning part and a sound part (lesson 21: {病|bìng} = 疒 + {丙|bǐng}), and
the radical is usually the meaning part. Look at the characters you know, grouped by radical:

| Radical | Meaning | Characters you know |
|---|---|---|
| 讠 (言) | speech | {说|shuō} speak, {话|huà} words, {语|yǔ} language, {请|qǐng} please, {谁|shéi} who, {课|kè} lesson, {读|dú} read aloud, {认识|rèn shi} know |
| 口 | mouth | {吃|chī} eat, {喝|hē} drink, {唱|chàng} sing, {叫|jiào} call, {吗|ma}, {呢|ne}, {吧|ba} (spoken particles), {喂|wèi} hello |
| 亻 (人) | person | {你|nǐ}, {他|tā}, {们|men}, {住|zhù} live, {做|zuò} do, {休|xiū} rest |
| 女 | woman | {她|tā} she, {妈|mā} mum, {姐|jiě} older sister, {妹|mèi} younger sister, {奶|nǎi} milk |
| 氵 (水) | water | {汉|hàn} (first the name of a river), {没|méi} (first "to sink"), {漂|piào} (first "to float") |
| 艹 | grass, plants | {茶|chá} tea, {菜|cài} vegetables, {苹|píng} (in {苹果|píng guǒ}, apple) |
| 犭 (犬) | dog, animal | {狗|gǒu} dog, {猫|māo} cat |
| 忄 (心) | heart, mind | {忙|máng} busy |
| 目 | eye | {看|kàn} look, {睡|shuì} sleep (closing the eyes) |

The hint is often a good one: a character with 讠 is very likely about speaking, and one with 艹
about plants. But it's a hint, not a rule. {很|hěn} has 彳 "step", which has nothing to do with "very";
{都|dōu} and {那|nà} have 阝, a town or a mound; {们|men} is about people only because of 亻. Meanings
drift over three thousand years, and some radicals were chosen only because a dictionary had
to file the character somewhere.

### A filing system

The radical's other job is practical: it's where a dictionary files a character. Characters
aren't letters, so there's no alphabet to sort them by. Instead, a dictionary groups them under
their radicals, orders the radicals by their number of strokes, and within each radical orders
the characters by the number of strokes *outside* the radical.

That's why a dictionary sometimes has to choose. {爱|ài} is under 爫 in one dictionary and under {心|xīn}
in another (its traditional form {愛|ài} has 心 in the middle); {玩|wán} is under 王 or {玉|yù} (jade); {么|me} is
under 丿 or 厶. When a character isn't where you expect, try another part of it.

=}

## How many radicals are there?

It depends on the dictionary, and it has changed over time:

| Dictionary or list | Date | Radicals |
|---|---|---|
| {说文解字|Shuō wén jiě zì} (Explaining Graphs and Analysing Characters), the first dictionary organised by radical | Han dynasty, about 1,900 years ago | 540 |
| {字汇|Zì huì} (Zihui) | 1615 | 214 |
| {康熙字典|Kāng xī zì diǎn} (Kangxi Dictionary) | 1716 | 214, the "Kangxi radicals" |
| {汉字部首表|Hàn zì bù shǒu biǎo} (Table of Chinese Character Radicals), mainland standard GF 0011-2009 | 2009 | 201 main radicals, plus 100 side forms |

{=
The 214 Kangxi radicals, named after the famous 1716 dictionary, are still the system of many
dictionaries outside the mainland and of the radical charts you'll find in Unicode and in
learners' books. The mainland list of 2009 merges some of them and lists 100 side forms, such as
亻 (of 人), 氵 (of 水) and 讠 (of 言), under their main radicals. So "how many radicals are there?" has no
single answer: about two hundred, give or take, is the honest one.
=}

The app files each character under the radical its stroke data gives (from Make Me a Hanzi), which
mostly agrees with mainland dictionaries.

## Looking up a character by radical

{=

Suppose you meet {课|kè} and don't know it. With a paper dictionary:

1. *Find the radical* and count its strokes: 讠, 2 strokes.
2. *Find it in the radical index* ({部首|bù shǒu}{目录|mù lù}, list of radicals) under 2 strokes. It sends you to a
   page of the character index.
3. *Count the rest of the character*: {果|guǒ}, 8 strokes.
4. *Look under 讠 + 8 strokes* in the character index. {课|kè} is there, with the page number of its
   entry.

Practise counting on characters you know. The radical's strokes plus the rest always make the
total: {妈|mā} is 女 (3) + {马|mǎ} (3) = 6; {狗|gǒu} is 犭 (3) + {句|jù} (5) = 8; {院|yuàn} is 阝 (2) + {完|wán} (7) = 9; {病|bìng} is 疒 (5) +
{丙|bǐng} (5) = 10; {题|tí} is 页 (6) + {是|shì} (9) = 15.

Some dictionaries also have a *stroke-count index* for characters whose radical is hard to see,
and many have a separate list of characters that are hard to file under any radical.

=}

## Looking up by sound, by hand and by phone

- *By pinyin.* If you know how a character is said, an alphabetical index is fastest. The best-known
  mainland dictionary for characters, the {新华字典|Xīn huá zì diǎn} (Xinhua Dictionary), is arranged by pinyin,
  with a radical index for characters you can't say.
- *By handwriting.* Phone and computer keyboards for Chinese have a handwriting mode: you draw the
  character with your finger and choose it from a list of guesses. It works even if your drawing
  is rough, but it works best when you write the strokes in the right order and direction, which
  is one more reason to practise them.
- *By pinyin input.* Most Chinese is typed in pinyin: you type *pengyou* and choose {朋友|péng you} from the
  suggestions. This only helps when you know the word.
- *By camera.* Many dictionary apps can read characters from a photo of a sign or a page.

## Stroke order: mainland and Taiwan

Stroke order follows rules you learned in the pinyin course (top before bottom, left before right,
horizontal before vertical, outside before inside…), but for some characters different places
teach different orders. Mainland China and Taiwan each have an official standard, and they differ
in a number of characters and components. A few examples:

{=

| Character or part | Mainland order | Taiwan order |
|---|---|---|
| 艹 (grass, in {茶|chá}, {菜|cài}) | 3 strokes: horizontal, then two short verticals | 4 strokes: written as two halves |
| 忄 (in {忙|máng}) | left dot, right dot, vertical | left dot, vertical, right dot |
| {必|bì} (must, HSK 3) | the left-falling stroke before the last dot | the last dot before the left-falling stroke |
| 馬 (traditional for {马|mǎ}, horse) | the first horizontal before the vertical | the vertical first |

=}

Neither order is "wrong": each is right in its own school system, and the finished character looks
the same. This course, like the app's tracing pads, uses the *mainland order* (from the Make Me a
Hanzi stroke data) everywhere, also when the traditional switch shows Taiwan character forms. If
you later study in Taiwan or with a Taiwan textbook, expect to relearn a handful of characters.

## Practice

{=

Find the radical and count the strokes outside it. Answers below.

| Character | Radical | Strokes outside the radical |
|---|---|---|
| {读|dú} | ? | ? |
| {忙|máng} | ? | ? |
| {唱|chàng} | ? | ? |
| {给|gěi} | ? | ? |

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

{读|dú}: 讠 + 8 ({卖|mài}) = 10. {忙|máng}: 忄 + 3 ({亡|wáng}) = 6. {唱|chàng}: 口 + 8 ({昌|chāng}) = 11. {给|gěi}: 纟 + 6 ({合|hé}) = 9.
</details>

=}

## Reading: at the bookshop

> {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{一|yì}{本|běn}{字典|zì diǎn}。{书店|shū diàn}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}：{一|yì}{本|běn}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{很|hěn}{贵|guì}；{一|yì}{本|běn}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi}。{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{小|xiǎo}{的|de}。{有|yǒu}{一个|yí gè}{字|zì}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi}，{我|wǒ}{查|chá}{了|le}{字典|zì diǎn}：{它|tā}{的|de}{部首|bù shǒu}{是|shì}“{三点水|sān diǎn shuǐ}”，{是|shì}{水|shuǐ}{的|de}{意思|yì si}。

({意思|yì si}: meaning, HSK 2. {三点水|sān diǎn shuǐ}, "three-dot water", is the everyday name of the radical 氵.)

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

I wanted to buy a dictionary. The bookshop had two: one was big and expensive, the other small
and cheap. I bought the small one. There was a character I didn't know, so I looked it up: its
radical is 氵 ("three-dot water"), which means water.
</details>

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have met every kind of question HSK 1 uses, one at a time: {吗|ma} in lesson 1, {呢|ne} in
lesson 2, question words from {什么|shén me} to {怎么样|zěn me yàng}, A-not-A questions in lesson
15 and {吧|ba} in lesson 12. This lesson puts them side by side, so you can choose the right one
quickly, and shows how Chinese answers them. There are no new words: everything here is from
lessons 1–25 or the pinyin course.

The most useful thing to remember from this lesson: *a Chinese question keeps the word order of
the statement.* You don't move anything to the front, as English does with "Where are you
going?" You build the statement and then either add a particle at the end or put a question word
where the answer will go.

## The four ways to ask

| Kind | How it's built | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[Yes/no question]]** with {吗|ma} | statement + {吗|ma} | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？ | Are you a teacher? |
| A-not-A question | verb or adjective + {不|bù} + the same word | {你|nǐ}{去不去|qù bu qù}？ | Are you going (or not)? |
| **[[Question-word question]]** | a question word where the answer goes | {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ | Where are you going? |
| Particle question with {呢|ne} or {吧|ba} | a short phrase or a statement + {呢|ne} / {吧|ba} | {你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？ {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{安娜|Ān nà}{吧|ba}？ | And you? You're Anna, right? |

A question can only be one of these at a time. That gives the first rule of this lesson: *never
put {吗|ma} on a question that already has a question word or an A-not-A pair.*


## Yes/no questions with {吗|ma}

Add {吗|ma} to the end of any statement and it becomes a question that can be answered "yes" or
"no". Nothing else changes:

- {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 — He's a doctor. → {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}{吗|ma}？ — Is he a doctor?
- {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}。 → {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}{吗|ma}？ — Do you have an older brother?
- {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？ — Can you speak Chinese?
- {你|nǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{忙|máng}{吗|ma}？ — Are you busy today?
- {你|nǐ}{吃饭|chī fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you eaten?

### How to answer: repeat the verb

Chinese has no single word for "yes" or "no" that works everywhere. The usual answer repeats the
verb (or adjective) of the question, with {不|bù} or {没|méi} for "no":

| Question | Yes | No |
|---|---|---|
| {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？ | {去|qù}。 | {不去|bú qù}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{吗|ma}？ | {是|shì}。 | {不是|bú shì}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{手机|shǒu jī}{吗|ma}？ | {有|yǒu}。 | {没有|méi yǒu}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}{吗|ma}？ | {会|huì}。 | {不会|bú huì}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？ | {喜欢|xǐ huan}。 | {不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ | {买|mǎi}{了|le}。 | {没|méi}{买|mǎi}。 |

{有|yǒu} always takes {没|méi}: {没有|méi yǒu}, never {不|bù}{有|yǒu}. And a completed action (with
{了|le}) is denied with {没|méi} and no {了|le}, as in lesson 25. {对|duì} ("right") and
{是的|shì de} ("yes, that's so") are also common short answers, especially when you agree with
what the other person said.

In this lesson's dialogues, {王芳|Wáng Fāng} and {李明|Lǐ Míng} are Chinese students, and
{大卫|Dà wèi} (David), {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) and {马克|Mǎ kè} (Mark, new in "A new classmate") are
learners of Chinese with Chinese names. In "Where's my cup?" {小明|Xiǎo míng} (Xiaoming) is a child talking to his mother.

```dialogue
# Is this your phone?
王芳: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{吗|ma}？
= Is this your phone?
大卫: {不是|bú shì}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。
= No. My phone is here.
王芳: {是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}{的|de}{吗|ma}？
= Is it Li Ming's?
大卫: {是|shì}，{他|tā}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{很|hěn}{新|xīn}。
= Yes, his phone is very new.
```

### Answering a negative question

When the question is negative, {对|duì} agrees with *the sentence*, not with the fact:

- {你|nǐ}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？ — Don't you drink tea?
- {对|duì}，{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喝|hē}。 — Right, I don't. (English says "No, I don't".)

English speakers often want to start with "no" here, and a Chinese listener may hear that as
disagreeing. The safe answer repeats the verb: {不|bù}{喝|hē}。 (I don't) or {喝|hē}。 (I do), and you
can't go wrong.

## A-not-A questions

Say the verb or adjective, then {不|bù}, then the same word again. The {不|bu} in the middle is
said lightly, with the neutral tone. It's a neutral way of asking, a little more direct than
{吗|ma}:

- {你|nǐ}{去不去|qù bu qù}？ — Are you going (or not)?
- {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{贵不贵|guì bu guì}？ — Is this piece of clothing expensive?
- {你|nǐ}{是不是|shì bu shì}{老师|lǎo shī}？ — Are you a teacher (or not)?
- {你|nǐ}{有没有|yǒu mei yǒu}{钱|qián}？ — Do you have any money? ({有|yǒu} takes {没|méi} here too.)
- {你|nǐ}{喜欢不喜欢|xǐ huan bu xǐ huan}{猫|māo}？ — Do you like cats? People also say
  {喜不喜欢|xǐ bu xǐ huan}, with only the first syllable repeated.

Two things never go in an A-not-A question: {吗|ma} at the end, and {很|hěn} or another degree
adverb before the adjective. {这|zhè}{个|gè}{很|hěn}{贵不贵|guì bu guì}？ is wrong; ask
{这个|zhè ge}{贵不贵|guì bu guì}？ You answer it just like a {吗|ma} question: {贵|guì}。 or
{不贵|bú guì}。

```dialogue
# Going to the cinema
李明: {明天|míng tiān}{你|nǐ}{忙不忙|máng bu máng}？
= Are you busy tomorrow?
安娜: {不忙|bù máng}。{什么|shén me}{事|shì}？
= No. What's up?
李明: {我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{看电影|kàn diàn yǐng}，{你|nǐ}{去不去|qù bu qù}？
= We're going to see a film. Are you coming?
安娜: {去|qù}！{几点|jǐ diǎn}？
= Yes! What time?
李明: {下午|xià wǔ}{两点|liǎng diǎn}。
= Two in the afternoon.
```

## Question words stay where the answer goes

To ask for information, take the statement you expect as an answer and put a question word in the
place of the missing piece. No {吗|ma}, and no change of order:

- {他|tā}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。 → {他|tā}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}？ — Who is he?
- {你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{苹果|píng guǒ}。 → {你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you buying?
- {她|tā}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}。 → {她|tā}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}{工作|gōng zuò}？ — Where does she work?
- {我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。 → {你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}？ — What time is your class?

Here are all the question words of the level, with the place they usually take:

| Asks about | Question word | Example |
|---|---|---|
| a person | {谁|shéi} who | {谁|shéi}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}？ — Who's your teacher? |
| a thing | {什么|shén me} what | {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ — What's your name? |
| one of several | {哪|nǎ} + measure word, {哪个|nǎ ge}, {哪些|nǎ xiē} which | {你|nǐ}{要|yào}{哪个|nǎ ge}？ — Which one do you want? |
| a country | {哪国人|nǎ guó rén} | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪国人|nǎ guó rén}？ — Where are you from? |
| a place | {哪儿|nǎr}, {哪里|nǎ lǐ} where | {你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where do you live? |
| a small number | {几|jǐ} + measure word | {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几口人|jǐ kǒu rén}？ — How many people are in your family? |
| any number, a price | {多少|duō shao} | {这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much is this book? |
| age | {多大|duō dà}, {几岁|jǐ suì} (a child) | {你|nǐ}{女儿|nǚ ér}{几岁|jǐ suì}{了|le}？ — How old is your daughter? |
| a time | {几点|jǐ diǎn}, {什么时候|shén me shí hou} | {你|nǐ}{什么时候|shén me shí hou}{回家|huí jiā}？ — When are you going home? |
| a date or day | {几月几号|jǐ yuè jǐ hào}, {星期几|xīng qī jǐ} | {今天|jīn tiān}{星期几|xīng qī jǐ}？ — What day is it today? |
| a way of doing | {怎么|zěn me} + verb how | {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}？ — How do you get to school? |
| an opinion | {怎么样|zěn me yàng} how is it, how about | {这|zhè}{家|jiā}{饭店|fàn diàn}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ — What's this restaurant like? ({家|jiā} is the measure word for restaurants and shops) |

A few points from the table:

- {几|jǐ} expects a small number (under about ten) and always needs a measure word or a word like
  {点|diǎn}, {号|hào}, {岁|suì}: {几个|jǐ gè}{人|rén}, {几本|jǐ běn}{书|shū}. {多少|duō shao} is for
  any number and can go straight before a noun: {多少|duō shao}{人|rén}, {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}.
- {多大|duō dà} is the usual way to ask a young person's or an adult's age (for older people there
  are more respectful ways, which come at later levels); {几岁|jǐ suì} is for children.
- {怎么|zěn me} before a verb asks "how": {怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？ (how is it written?). When it
  sounds surprised, it means "how come": {你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{不|bù}{吃|chī}？ — How come you're not
  eating?
- {怎么样|zěn me yàng} comes at the end. After a suggestion it means "how about it?":
  {我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}，{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ — Let's go tomorrow. How about it?

To answer, put the information where the question word was, and drop the rest if it's obvious:

```dialogue
# A new classmate
安娜: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= Hi! What's your name?
马克: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{马克|Mǎ kè}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪国人|nǎ guó rén}？
= I'm Mark. Where are you from?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。
= I'm American.
马克: {你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where do you live?
安娜: {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= At the school. And you?
马克: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。
= I live at the school too.
```

{美国人|Měi guó rén} is "American", built like {中国人|Zhōng guó rén}.

## {呢|ne}: "and you?" and "where is…?"

{呢|ne} after a noun or a pronoun on its own makes a short question. Its meaning comes from what
was just said:

- After a statement it asks the same question about someone else: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}，
  {你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？ — I'm a student. And you?
- With no statement before it, it asks where something is: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{呢|ne}？ —
  Where's my phone? {妈妈|mā ma}{呢|ne}？ — Where's Mum?

{呢|ne} can also go at the end of a question-word question to make it softer or more thoughtful:
{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}{呢|ne}？ But it never goes on a yes/no question: that's {吗|ma}'s job. (The
{呢|ne} at the end of {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne} from lesson 10 isn't a question at all: it
marks an action in progress.)

```dialogue
# Where's my cup?
小明: {妈妈|mā ma}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{杯子|bēi zi}{呢|ne}？
= Mum, where's my cup?
妈妈: {在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。
= On the table.
小明: {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{没有|méi yǒu}。
= It isn't on the table.
妈妈: {那|nà}{在|zài}{椅子|yǐ zi}{上|shàng}{吧|ba}… {你|nǐ}{看|kàn}！
= Then it must be on the chair… Look!
```

## {吧|ba}: checking a guess

{吧|ba} at the end of a statement asks the listener to confirm what you already think is true, like
English "…, right?" or "…, isn't it?":

- {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{吧|ba}？ — You're Teacher Wang, aren't you?
- {你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}{吧|ba}？ — You must be busy.
- {这|zhè}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{吧|ba}？ — This is your book, isn't it?

Compare: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？ is an open question (I have no idea);
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}{吧|ba}？ means I think you are and want you to confirm it.
The answer is {对|duì}, {是|shì} or {是的|shì de} when the guess is right. You already know the other
{吧|ba}, for suggestions: {我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go! (A suggestion has no question
mark.)

```dialogue
# At the station
安娜: {您|nín}{好|hǎo}！{您|nín}{是|shì}{张|Zhāng}{老师|lǎo shī}{吧|ba}？
= Hello! You're Teacher Zhang, aren't you?
张老师: {对|duì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{安娜|Ān nà}{吧|ba}？
= That's right. And you must be Anna?
安娜: {是|shì}。{认识|rèn shi}{您|nín}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= Yes. Pleased to meet you.
张老师: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。{我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{吧|ba}。
= Pleased to meet you too. Let's take a taxi to the school.
```

{张|Zhāng} is a common surname, and {张老师|Zhāng lǎo shī} ("Teacher Zhang") is how students
address and talk about a teacher, whether a man or a woman. Anna uses {您|nín} because it's a
teacher she's meeting for the first time.

## Questions without a particle

In speech, a statement said with a rising voice works as a question, usually a surprised one:
{你|nǐ}{不去|bú qù}？ — You're not going? It's fine to understand, but in writing and in the exam,
questions use {吗|ma}, A-not-A or a question word.

## Tones and stress in questions

Chinese words keep their tones in a question. The voice doesn't rise on the last syllable the way
English does, because a rise would change the tone. Instead:

- the question word or the A-not-A pair carries the stress: in {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ it's
  {哪儿|nǎr}. Listen for it, and you know what is being asked;
- {吗|ma}, {呢|ne} and {吧|ba} are neutral-tone particles: short and light;
- the whole sentence can be a little higher, but each tone still has its shape.

Practise asking:

```speak
{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= What's your name?
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪国人|nǎ guó rén}？
= Where are you from?
{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where do you live?
{这个|zhè ge}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
= How much is this?
{现在|xiàn zài}{几点|jǐ diǎn}？
= What time is it now?
{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{来不来|lái bu lái}？
= Are you coming tomorrow?
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{吧|ba}？
= You're Wang Fang, aren't you?
```

## Common mistakes

- *Adding {吗|ma} to a question-word or A-not-A question.* {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}{吗|ma}？ isn't
  "Where are you going?" (it means "Are you going anywhere?", a use of {哪儿|nǎr} for HSK 3).
  {你|nǐ}{去不去|qù bu qù}{吗|ma}？ is simply wrong.
- *Moving the question word to the front*, as English does: {什么|shén me}{你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}？ is wrong;
  say {你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}？
- *{几|jǐ} without a measure word*: {几|jǐ}{书|shū} is wrong; say {几本|jǐ běn}{书|shū}.
- *{很|hěn} in an A-not-A question*: {你|nǐ}{很忙|hěn máng}{不忙|bù máng}？ is wrong; say
  {你|nǐ}{忙不忙|máng bu máng}？
- *Answering with {是|shì} for every "yes"*: {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？ is answered {去|qù}, not
  {是|shì}. {是|shì} answers only questions with {是|shì} in them (and checks with {吧|ba}).
- *{不|bù}{有|yǒu}*: always {没有|méi yǒu}, and {有没有|yǒu mei yǒu} in A-not-A.

## Key points

- Chinese questions keep statement word order. Add a particle, or put a question word where the
  answer goes.
- {吗|ma}: yes/no questions. A-not-A ({去不去|qù bu qù}): yes/no questions without {吗|ma}.
- Question words ({谁|shéi}, {什么|shén me}, {哪|nǎ}, {哪儿|nǎr}, {几|jǐ}, {多少|duō shao},
  {怎么|zěn me}, {怎么样|zěn me yàng}) never take {吗|ma}.
- {呢|ne}: "and you?" after a statement; "where is…?" on its own.
- {吧|ba}: "…, right?" when you expect "yes".
- Answer with the verb: {去|qù} / {不去|bú qù}, {有|yǒu} / {没有|méi yǒu}, {会|huì} / {不会|bú huì};
  {对|duì} agrees with what was said.

This lesson has no new words: its questions practise the words of lessons 1–25.

lessons.title: Reading signs, menus and name cards
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've read sentences written to show one point of grammar. Real Chinese around you looks
different: a sign over a door, a menu on a wall, a name card someone hands you, a price label in a
supermarket, a train timetable, a note left on a desk. These are exactly the texts HSK 1 expects
you to read, and they're short, so you can read them with the characters you already know.

This lesson gives you one of each, all written for this course, and the strategies that make them
easy. Read each text first with pinyin on, then turn pinyin off with the switch at the top of the
lesson and see how much you can still read. The character list in the Study tools box has every
character of the course with its pinyin and meaning.

## Strategies

1. *Look at the shape first.* A short line over a door is a sign. Two columns of words and
   numbers are a menu or a price list. A name in big characters with a phone number under it is a
   name card. A name at the top, a name and a date at the bottom: a note.
2. *Read the question before the text.* If it asks "how much", you're looking for numbers and
   {元|yuán} or {块|kuài}. If it asks "when", look for {点|diǎn}, {星期|xīng qī}, {号|hào},
   {上午|shàng wǔ}, {下午|xià wǔ}. Moving your eyes over a text to find one fact like this is
   **[[scanning]]**; reading it all quickly for the general idea is **[[skimming]]**. Skim first, then scan
   for the answer.
3. *Find the characters you know.* With pinyin off, the characters you've learned stand out
   even in a text full of new ones. On signs they're usually the key: {男|nán}, {女|nǚ},
   {请|qǐng}, {不要|bú yào}, {开|kāi}, {出|chū}.
4. *Use numbers and measure words.* Numbers are written in Arabic digits on signs, menus and
   timetables. A measure word tells you what kind of thing is counted: 10{个|gè} (ten pieces),
   2{本|běn} (two books), 1{杯|bēi} (a cup of…).
5. *Don't stop at new characters.* Skip them and keep going. The characters around them, or a
   component you know inside them, often tell you enough.


## Signs

Public signs are short: often two characters, sometimes a whole polite sentence with {请|qǐng}
(please) or {请不要|qǐng bú yào} (please don't). Some useful ones, with the words you haven't
learned glossed:

| Sign | Meaning | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| {出口|chū kǒu} | exit | doors, stations |
| {入口|rù kǒu} | entrance | doors, stations, parks |
| {男|nán} / {女|nǚ} | men / women | toilet doors |
| {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān} | toilets | in shops, restaurants, stations |
| {推|tuī} / {拉|lā} | push / pull | on doors |
| {出租车|chū zū chē} | taxis | at a taxi rank |
| {请不要|qǐng bú yào}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}{吃|chī}{东西|dōng xi} | please don't eat here | shops, museums |
| {请不要|qǐng bú yào}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} | please don't make phone calls | cinemas, hospitals |

{出口|chū kǒu} is {出|chū} (out) + {口|kǒu} (mouth, opening): an "out-opening". You know both
characters. {入|rù} (to enter) is new: it looks like {人|rén} (person), but in {入|rù} the right-hand stroke is
the long one and the short left stroke leans against it, so look carefully. {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān} is an HSK 2 word: "wash-hand room". {推|tuī} and {拉|lā}
both have the hand radical 扌 on the left, as in {打|dǎ} and {找|zhǎo}.

A shop's opening hours often look like this:

> {书店|shū diàn}
>
> {时间|shí jiān}：{上午|shàng wǔ}9:00—{下午|xià wǔ}6:00
>
> {星期一|xīng qī yī}{休息|xiū xi}

The bookshop opens 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and is closed on Mondays. {休息|xiū xi} (to rest) on a sign
means "closed". Times on signs are written in digits, often on the 24-hour clock (18:00), and the
dash means "from … to".

Check yourself: can you buy a book there on Monday afternoon? (No: it's closed on Mondays.)

## Menus

A menu ({菜单|cài dān}, "dish list") is a list of dishes and prices. The price is in {元|yuán}, the
written word; people say {块|kuài} when they read it out.

> {饭店|fàn diàn}{菜单|cài dān}
>
> | {菜|cài} | {元|yuán} |
> |---|---|
> | {饺子|jiǎo zi}（10{个|gè}） | 18 |
> | {包子|bāo zi}（1{个|gè}） | 3 |
> | {面条儿|miàn tiáor} | 15 |
> | {米饭|mǐ fàn} | 2 |
> | {鸡蛋|jī dàn}{面条儿|miàn tiáor} | 18 |
> | {茶|chá}（1{杯|bēi}） | 5 |
> | {水|shuǐ} | 2 |

A few things to notice:

- The measure word in brackets tells you how much you get for the price: ten dumplings for 18
  yuan, but buns are priced one by one.
- Menus often write noodles {面条|miàn tiáo}, without the erhua (*-r*) of {面条儿|miàn tiáor} that
  you hear in Beijing speech; it's the same word.
- Read 18{元|yuán} aloud as {十八块|shí bā kuài}, and 12.50{元|yuán} as {十二块五|shí èr kuài wǔ}: the
  number after the point is the tenths of a yuan, said after {块|kuài}.

Check yourself: you order dumplings, one bun and a cup of tea. How much is it? (18 + 3 + 5 = 26:
{二十六块|èr shí liù kuài}.)

## Name cards

A name card ({名片|míng piàn}) gives the name, the company or school, the job and the phone numbers.
The name is the biggest line; the surname comes first.

> {大明|Dà míng}{学校|xué xiào}
>
> {赵兰|Zhào Lán}
>
> {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}
>
> {电话|diàn huà}：010-0000 1234
>
> {手机|shǒu jī}：125 0000 5678

Zhao Lan teaches Chinese at a school called {大明|Dà míng} (the school and the numbers on this
card are made up). Phone numbers are read digit by digit, and 1 is said *yāo* in them, not
*yī*: 125 is *yāo èr wǔ*. The 010 at the start of the first number is the area code of
Beijing ({北京|Běi jīng}).

Check yourself: what is Zhao Lan's job? (She's a Chinese teacher: {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}.)

## Labels

Price labels in a supermarket ({超市|chāo shì}) give the name, the price and how much you get:

> | {苹果|píng guǒ} | 6.50{元|yuán}/{斤|jīn} |
> |---|---|
> | {牛奶|niú nǎi} | 4{元|yuán} |
> | {鸡蛋|jī dàn}（10{个|gè}） | 9.90{元|yuán} |

{斤|jīn} is a unit of weight used in Chinese shops and markets: half a kilo. 6.50{元|yuán}/{斤|jīn} is 6.50 yuan
for every half kilo, read {六块五|liù kuài wǔ}{一斤|yì jīn}. A label can also say {新|xīn} (new) on
a new product.

Check yourself: how much are ten eggs? ({九块九|jiǔ kuài jiǔ}, 9.90 yuan.)

## Timetables

Train timetables list the train, where it goes, when it leaves and when it arrives. On a train
timetable {开车|kāi chē} means "the train departs", and {到|dào} "arrives":

> {北京|Běi jīng} → {上海|Shàng hǎi}
>
> | {车次|chē cì} | {开车|kāi chē} | {到|dào} |
> |---|---|---|
> | G123 | 07:00 | 11:30 |
> | G456 | 08:00 | 12:40 |
> | G789 | 10:00 | 14:30 |

{车次|chē cì} is the train number; G marks a high-speed train. (The times are made up for this lesson.
Numbers like G123 are also real trains' numbers, so check a real timetable before you travel.)

Check yourself: you need to be in Shanghai ({上海|Shàng hǎi}) before 1 p.m. Which trains can you
take? (G123 or G456; G789 arrives at 14:30.) How long is the G123's journey? (Four and a half hours:
{四个半小时|sì gè bàn xiǎo shí}.)

## Notes

A note starts with the name of the person it's for and a colon, and ends with the writer's name
and the date. Here's a note a student left for a teacher:

> {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}：
>
> {您好|nín hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{下午|xià wǔ}{要|yào}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}，{不能|bù néng}{来|lái}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}。{明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{我|wǒ}{再|zài}{来|lái}{学校|xué xiào}。{对不起|duì bu qǐ}！
>
> {安娜|Ān nà}
>
> 11{月|yuè}16{日|rì}

1. Why can't Anna come to class?
2. Where is she going this afternoon?
3. When will she come back to school?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

Teacher Wang, hello! I'm ill today. This afternoon I have to go to the hospital to see a doctor,
so I can't come to class. I'll come to school again tomorrow morning. Sorry! Anna, 16 November.

1. She's ill ({生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}). 2. To the hospital ({医院|yī yuàn}). 3. Tomorrow morning
({明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}).

</details>

Notice the two {了|le}: {生病|shēng bìng}{了|le} (she has fallen ill: a change) and
{不能|bù néng}{来|lái}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le} (she can't come any more: the plan has changed). Notes
write the date with {日|rì}; in speech it's {号|hào}. Anna writes {您|nín} to her teacher.

## Dialogue: at the restaurant

{李明|Lǐ Míng} and {大卫|Dà wèi} are reading the menu above.

```dialogue
# What shall we eat?
大卫: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{字|zì}？
= What's this character?
李明: {饺子|jiǎo zi}{的|de}{饺|jiǎo}。{十个|shí gè}{十八块|shí bā kuài}。
= It's jiao, the jiao in jiaozi. Ten for eighteen kuai.
大卫: {不贵|bú guì}！{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= That's not expensive! I'll have dumplings. And you?
李明: {我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}。{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{什么|shén me}？
= I'll have noodles. What are you drinking?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。{一杯|yì bēi}{五块|wǔ kuài}，{对|duì}{吧|ba}？
= I'll have tea. Five kuai a cup, right?
李明: {对|duì}。{一共|yí gòng}{三十八块|sān shí bā kuài}。
= Right. Altogether it's thirty-eight kuai for us.
```

{一共|yí gòng} (altogether) is an HSK 2 word you'll hear every time you pay. 18 + 15 + 5 = 38: Li
Ming isn't having a drink.

## Common mistakes

- *Reading every character in order and translating as you go.* Look at the shape, read the
  question, then scan.
- *Mixing up {入|rù} and {人|rén}*, and {出口|chū kǒu} and {入口|rù kǒu}. {出|chū} is "out":
  remember {出租车|chū zū chē}, which you take to go *out*.
- *Reading prices in {元|yuán}.* It's correct, but people say {块|kuài}: 15{元|yuán} is
  {十五块|shí wǔ kuài}.
- *Saying 1 as* yī *in phone numbers.* Say *yāo*: 139 is *yāo sān jiǔ*.
- *Missing the measure word on a menu or a label*: 10{个|gè} or {斤|jīn} decides how much you get.

## Key points

- Signs, menus, name cards, labels, timetables and notes each have a shape: recognise it first.
- Skim for the gist, read the question, then scan for the fact. Numbers, measure words and the
  characters you know carry the answer.
- Prices are written in {元|yuán} and read in {块|kuài}; 12.50 is {十二块五|shí èr kuài wǔ}.
- On timetables {开车|kāi chē} is the departure, {到|dào} the arrival.
- A note: name + colon at the top; writer's name and date ({日|rì}) at the bottom.

This lesson has no new words. Its glossed sign words ({出口|chū kǒu}, {入口|rù kǒu}, {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān},
{推|tuī}, {拉|lā}) are worth recognising, but they aren't in your reviews.

lessons.title: Listening and talking
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 expects you to understand simple questions and answer them, to introduce yourself, and to
use the everyday polite phrases, and the HSK 1 exam has a listening part as well as a reading part
(lesson 30). This lesson
brings those skills together: how to listen when you don't catch every word, the questions people
ask a newcomer and how to answer them, a self-introduction you can adapt, and what to say when
you don't understand.

Play every dialogue and phrase in this lesson. Listen first with the words hidden ("Hide the
words" on a dialogue), then read along, then say the lines yourself. If your device has no
Chinese voice, read the lines aloud instead; the first lesson of the pinyin course explains how to
add one.

## How to listen

You won't catch every syllable, and you don't need to. Listen for the few words that carry the
meaning:

1. *The question word.* {谁|shéi}, {什么|shén me}, {哪儿|nǎr}, {几|jǐ}, {多少|duō shao},
   {怎么|zěn me} tell you what kind of answer is wanted. If you hear {几点|jǐ diǎn}, the answer is a
   time; if you hear {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}, a price.
2. *{吗|ma}, {呢|ne}, {吧|ba} and A-not-A at the end.* They tell you it's a question, and what kind
   (lesson 26).
3. *{不|bù} and {没|méi}.* One short syllable turns the meaning round: {我|wǒ}{去|qù} / {我|wǒ}{不去|bú qù}.
4. *Numbers, times and dates.* They're often what the question is about. Listen for {点|diǎn},
   {分|fēn}, {号|hào}, {星期|xīng qī}, {块|kuài}, {岁|suì} after the number.
5. *Time words at the start.* {昨天|zuó tiān}, {今天|jīn tiān}, {明天|míng tiān} come early in the
   sentence and tell you when it happens.

### Sounds that are easy to mix up

| These | Sound like | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|---|
| {四|sì} 4 and {十|shí} 10 | *sì* / *shí* | tone 4 falls, tone 2 rises; *sh* has the tongue curled back |
| {七|qī} 7 and {一|yī} 1 | *qī* / *yī* | in phone numbers 1 is *yāo*, so it can't be mistaken for 7 |
| {买|mǎi} and {卖|mài} | buy / sell | tone 3 dips low, tone 4 falls |
| {那儿|nàr} and {哪儿|nǎr} | there / where? | tone 4 is a statement, tone 3 a question |
| {他|tā}, {她|tā}, {它|tā} | he, she, it | they sound the same: the situation tells you |
| {在|zài} and {再|zài} | at / again | the same sound: {在|zài} comes before a place, {再|zài} before a verb |


## Questions people ask you

When you meet someone, the questions come in a familiar order. Here are the ones HSK 1 expects
you to understand, with a natural short answer for each. Short answers are normal: you don't need
to repeat the whole question.

| Question | Meaning | A short answer |
|---|---|---|
| {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ | What's your name? | {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪国人|nǎ guó rén}？ | Where are you from? | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{今年|jīn nián}{多大|duō dà}？ | How old are you? | {二十五岁|èr shí wǔ suì}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？ | What do you do? | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}{工作|gōng zuò}？ | Where do you work? | {在|zài}{一家|yì jiā}{公司|gōng sī}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ | Where do you live? | {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几口人|jǐ kǒu rén}？ | How many people are in your family? | {四口人|sì kǒu rén}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？ | Do you speak Chinese? | {会|huì}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？ | What do you like doing? | {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱歌|chàng gē}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{号|hào}{是|shì}{多少|duō shao}？ | What's your mobile number? | 139…, said digit by digit |

A few things to notice:

- {在|zài}{一家|yì jiā}{公司|gōng sī} uses {家|jiā} as the measure word for a company or a shop.
- A number is asked with {多少|duō shao}, not {什么|shén me}: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{号|hào}{是|shì}{多少|duō shao}？
- {会|huì}{一点儿|yì diǎnr} ("I can a little") is the modest, natural answer about a language,
  even when you speak it quite well.

It's polite to send the question back: {你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？

## Introducing yourself

Here's a self-introduction a learner might give on the first day of a Chinese class. Read it, then
answer the questions.

> {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}，{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。{我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}{二十八岁|èr shí bā suì}，{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{五口人|wǔ kǒu rén}：{爸爸|bà ba}、{妈妈|mā ma}、{姐姐|jiě jie}、{哥哥|gē ge}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{妈妈|mā ma}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看电影|kàn diàn yǐng}，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。{认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！

1. How old is Anna, and what does she do?
2. Who is in her family?
3. What does she like?

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

Hello, everyone! My name is Anna, and I'm American. I'm twenty-eight and I'm a university student.
There are five of us in my family: my dad, my mum, my older sister, my older brother and me. My dad is a doctor
and my mum is a teacher. I like watching films, and I also like eating dumplings. I can speak a
little Chinese. Nice to meet you all!

1. She's twenty-eight and a university student. 2. Her dad, her mum, her older sister, her older
brother and herself. 3. Watching films and eating dumplings.

</details>

{大家好|dà jiā hǎo} is how you greet a group. {认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng} ("knowing
everyone, I'm glad") ends an introduction to a group; to one person it's
{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}. The 、 between the family members is the Chinese
list comma.

### Your own introduction

Fill in the frame with your own details, then say it aloud, slowly at first. Use the speak block to
compare your pronunciation with the model.

| Say | Fill in |
|---|---|
| {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}… | your Chinese or your own name |
| {我|wǒ}{是|shì}…{人|rén}。 | your country: {中国|Zhōng guó}, {美国|Měi guó}, {英国|Yīng guó}… |
| {我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}…{岁|suì}。 | your age |
| {我|wǒ}{是|shì}… / {我|wǒ}{在|zài}…{工作|gōng zuò}。 | your job, or where you work or study |
| {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}…{口|kǒu}{人|rén}：… | your family |
| {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}…，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}…。 | two things you like |
| {认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！ | |

```speak
{大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！
= Hello, everyone!
{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}，{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}。
= My name is Anna, and I'm American.
{我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}{二十八岁|èr shí bā suì}。
= I'm twenty-eight.
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{五口人|wǔ kǒu rén}。
= There are five people in my family.
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看电影|kàn diàn yǐng}。
= I like watching films.
{认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！
= Nice to meet you all!
```

## Polite phrases

| Situation | You say | They answer |
|---|---|---|
| meeting | {你好|nǐ hǎo}！ / {您好|nín hǎo}！ | {你好|nǐ hǎo}！ |
| meeting a group | {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！ | |
| thanks | {谢谢|xiè xie}！ | {不客气|bú kè qi}。 |
| an apology | {对不起|duì bu qǐ}。 | {没关系|méi guān xi}。 |
| asking a stranger something | {请问|qǐng wèn}，… | |
| offering a seat or a drink | {请坐|qǐng zuò}。{请喝茶|qǐng hē chá}。 | {谢谢|xiè xie}。 |
| first meeting | {认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。 | {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。 |
| leaving | {再见|zài jiàn}！ / {明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！ | {再见|zài jiàn}！ |
| on the phone | {喂|wèi}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！ | |

Remember the tones that change: {不客气|bú kè qi} (bú before the 4th tone of *kè*),
{对不起|duì bu qǐ} (*bu* neutral), and {你好|nǐ hǎo}, written with two third tones but said *ní hǎo*.
{喂|wèi} is usually said *wéi* when you answer the phone.

## When you don't understand

Everyone who learns a language needs these. Say them early, before you lose the thread:

| You say | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}。 | Sorry, I didn't catch that (didn't hear). |
| {请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià}。 | Please say it again. |
| {请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{说|shuō}。 | Please speak a bit more slowly. |
| {你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{什么|shén me}？ | What did you say? (friendly, to people you know) |
| …{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{意思|yì si}？ | What does … mean? |
| {这个|zhè ge}{汉字|hàn zì}{怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？ | How do you write this character? |
| {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。 | I don't know. |
| {我|wǒ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 | I speak a little Chinese. |

{慢|màn} (slow) and {意思|yì si} (meaning) are HSK 2 words, but they're worth learning now.
{请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià} uses {再|zài} (again) before the verb and the softener
{一下|yí xià} after it. With a stranger, start with {对不起|duì bu qǐ} or {请问|qǐng wèn} to sound
polite.

```speak
{对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}。
= Sorry, I didn't catch that.
{请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià}。
= Please say it again.
{请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{说|shuō}。
= Please speak a bit more slowly.
{这个|zhè ge}{汉字|hàn zì}{怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？
= How do you write this character?
```

## Dialogue: on the first day

{马克|Mǎ kè} (Mark) meets {王芳|Wáng Fāng}, a Chinese student, at the school.

```dialogue
# On the first day
王芳: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{新|xīn}{同学|tóng xué}{吧|ba}？
= Hi! You're a new student, aren't you?
马克: {对|duì}。{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{马克|Mǎ kè}，{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}。
= That's right. I'm Mark, and I'm British.
王芳: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？
= I'm Wang Fang. Do you speak Chinese?
马克: {会|huì}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。{请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{说|shuō}。
= A little. Please speak a bit slowly.
王芳: {好|hǎo}。{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= OK. Where do you live?
马克: {对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}。{请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià}。
= Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again?
王芳: {你|nǐ}——{住|zhù}——{在|zài}——{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Where — do — you — live?
马克: {我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I live at the school. And you?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}，{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！
= I don't live at the school: my family lives here. Nice to meet you!
马克: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！
= Nice to meet you too!
```

## Answering on the phone

Lesson 10's phone language in a short call. {张|Zhāng} is a surname; {张老师|Zhāng lǎo shī} is
Teacher Zhang.

```dialogue
# A phone call
李明: {喂|wèi}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{请问|qǐng wèn}{张老师|Zhāng lǎo shī}{在|zài}{吗|ma}？
= Hello! Excuse me, is Teacher Zhang there?
张老师: {我|wǒ}{就是|jiù shì}。{请问|qǐng wèn}{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}？
= Speaking. May I ask who's calling?
李明: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。{张老师|Zhāng lǎo shī}，{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{不能|bù néng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}。
= It's Li Ming. Teacher Zhang, I'm ill today, so I can't come to class.
张老师: {没关系|méi guān xi}，{你|nǐ}{好好|hǎo hǎo}{休息|xiū xi}{吧|ba}。
= That's all right. Get some good rest.
李明: {谢谢|xiè xie}{老师|lǎo shī}！{再见|zài jiàn}！
= Thank you! Goodbye!
```

{我|wǒ}{就是|jiù shì} ("I'm the one") is how you say "Speaking" on the phone; {就|jiù} is an HSK 2 word.
{好好|hǎo hǎo}{休息|xiū xi} means "rest well". Students often address a teacher simply as
{老师|lǎo shī}.

## Common mistakes

- *Trying to catch every word.* Listen for the question word, the numbers and {不|bù} / {没|méi};
  ask again if you need to.
- *Answering {是|shì} to every question.* {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？ is answered
  {会|huì}, not {是|shì}.
- *Asking for a number with {什么|shén me}.* Phone numbers and room numbers take
  {多少|duō shao}.
- *{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng} at the end of a long friendship.* It's for a first
  meeting.
- *Staying silent when you're lost.* {请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià} keeps the conversation going.

## Key points

- Listen for the question word, {吗|ma} / {呢|ne} / {吧|ba}, {不|bù} / {没|méi}, numbers and time words.
- The newcomer's questions: name, country, age, job, home, family, languages, likes, phone number.
  Short answers are natural; send the question back with {你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
- A self-introduction: {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}… {认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！
- When you don't understand: {对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}。{请|qǐng}{再说|zài shuō}{一下|yí xià}。
  {请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{说|shuō}。

This lesson has no new words. {慢|màn}, {意思|yì si} and {就|jiù} are glossed HSK 2 words you'll
learn properly in HSK 2.

lessons.title: Grammar review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've now met all the grammar HSK 1 asks for. This lesson puts it in one place: the kinds of
sentence Chinese builds, the order words go in, measure words, {不|bù} and {没|méi}, and the two
{了|le} with {在|zài} / {正在|zhèng zài}. Each section is short and points back to the lesson that
taught it. The table at the end is the whole level on one page; the reference sheets in the Study
tools box have the details.

Chinese grammar at this level comes down to a few habits. Verbs never change. Words go in a fixed
order, with *when* and *where* before the verb. Numbers need measure words. And small particles at
the end of the sentence ({吗|ma}, {呢|ne}, {吧|ba}, {了|le}) change what the whole sentence does.


## Three kinds of predicate

The predicate is what a sentence says about its subject. In Chinese it can be a verb, an
adjective or, for a few kinds of information, a noun. {是|shì} is itself a verb: it links two
nouns, and it isn't needed before an adjective.

| Kind | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **[[verb predicate]]** | {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 — I drink tea. | the usual kind; the verb never changes for person or time |
| adjective predicate | {她|tā}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。 — She's busy. | no {是|shì}; a plain {很|hěn} usually comes before the adjective (lesson 15) |
| noun predicate | {今天|jīn tiān}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。 — Today is Monday. | dates, days, times, ages and prices; {是|shì} can be added, and {不是|bú shì} is needed in the negative (lessons 4 and 6) |

More noun predicates: {我|wǒ}{二十岁|èr shí suì}。 (I'm twenty.) {现在|xiàn zài}{八点|bā diǎn}。 (It's eight
now.) {这个|zhè ge}{五块|wǔ kuài}。 (This one is five kuai.) In the negative they need {不是|bú shì}:
{今天|jīn tiān}{不是|bú shì}{星期一|xīng qī yī}。

The most common mistake of English speakers is to use {是|shì} for "is" before an adjective:
{她|tā}{是|shì}{忙|máng} is wrong. {是|shì} links two nouns ({她|tā}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}); an adjective
is the predicate by itself.

## Sentence types by purpose

| **[[Sentence type]]** | Ends with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **[[statement]]** | 。 | {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 — He's a doctor. |
| question | ？ | {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}{吗|ma}？ — Is he a doctor? (all four kinds: lesson 26) |
| **[[imperative]]** (a request or an order) | 。 or ！ | {请坐|qǐng zuò}。 — Please sit down. {不要|bú yào}{说话|shuō huà}！ — Don't talk! |
| **[[exclamation]]** | ！ | {太好了|tài hǎo le}！ — Great! {这件|zhè jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{真|zhēn}{漂亮|piào liang}！ — This is really pretty! |

Requests are softened with {请|qǐng} before the verb, {一下|yí xià} after it ({请|qǐng}{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}),
or {吧|ba} at the end ({我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吧|ba}). "Don't" is {不要|bú yào} + verb. Exclamations use
{太|tài}…{了|le} and {真|zhēn}.

Some sentences have no subject at all, because none is needed: {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}！ (It's raining!)
{谢谢|xiè xie}！ {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 Chinese drops a subject that is obvious from the situation much more
often than English does: {去|qù}{吗|ma}？ (Are you going?) is a full question.

## Special sentences

| Sentence | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {是|shì} sentence | A {是|shì} B | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 Negative {不是|bú shì}. |
| {有|yǒu} sentence (having) | person {有|yǒu} thing | {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{两个|liǎng gè}{弟弟|dì di}。 Negative {没有|méi yǒu}. |
| existential sentence (there is) | place {有|yǒu} thing | {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一本|yì běn}{书|shū}。 |
| {在|zài} sentence (where it is) | thing {在|zài} place | {书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。 |
| serial-verb sentence | verb 1 + verb 2 | {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 {他|tā}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{上海|Shàng hǎi}。 |
| double-object sentence | verb + person + thing | {他|tā}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{一本|yì běn}{书|shū}。 {我|wǒ}{问|wèn}{老师|lǎo shī}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí}。 |

- {有|yǒu} or {在|zài}? Use {有|yǒu} to bring in something new ("there's a book on the table"), with
  {一本|yì běn}, {一个|yí gè}…; use {在|zài} for where a known thing is ("the book is on the table").
  See lesson 17 and the position words sheet.
- In a serial-verb sentence the verbs come in the order things happen: first going, then buying;
  first the way you travel ({坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}), then the going ({去|qù}{上海|Shàng hǎi}).
- In a double-object sentence the person comes before the thing: {给|gěi}{他|tā}{一本|yì běn}{书|shū}, never
  {给|gěi}{一本|yì běn}{书|shū}{他|tā}.

## Word order on one line

Almost every sentence of HSK 1 fits this line. Not every slot is filled, but the order never
changes:

| (time) | subject | (time) | adverbs | (place with {在|zài}) | verb | (object) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | {我|wǒ} | {明天|míng tiān} | {也|yě} | {在|zài}{家|jiā} | {休息|xiū xi} | |
| {明天|míng tiān} | {我|wǒ} | | {不|bú} | {在|zài}{家|jiā} | {吃|chī} | {饭|fàn} |
| | {我们|wǒ men} | {八点|bā diǎn} | {都|dōu} | {在|zài}{学校|xué xiào} | {上课|shàng kè} | |

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{也|yě}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}。 — I'm resting at home tomorrow too.
{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{不在|bú zài}{家|jiā}{吃饭|chī fàn}。 — Tomorrow I'm not eating at home.
{我们|wǒ men}{八点|bā diǎn}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{上课|shàng kè}。 — At eight we all have class at school.

Three rules hold it together:

1. *When and where come before the verb*, unlike English: not {我|wǒ}{休息|xiū xi}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{明天|míng tiān}.
   Big time before small time: {明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{八点|bā diǎn}.
2. *Adverbs go right before the verb* (or before {在|zài} + place): {也|yě}, {都|dōu}, {还|hái},
   {不|bù}, {很|hěn}, {再|zài}, {正在|zhèng zài}. Two together keep a fixed order: {也|yě}{都|dōu},
   never {都|dōu}{也|yě}. With {都|dōu} and {不|bù} the order changes the meaning:
   {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{不去|bú qù} (none of us is going), {我们|wǒ men}{不|bù}{都|dōu}{去|qù} (not all of
   us are going).
3. *How long goes after the verb*: {我|wǒ}{睡|shuì}{了|le}{八个|bā gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} (I slept for eight
   hours), but *when* goes before it: {我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào} (I go to bed at eight).

Questions keep the same order (lesson 26).

## Measure words

Between a number (or {这|zhè}, {那|nà}, {哪|nǎ}, {几|jǐ}) and a noun, Chinese needs a measure word.

| Measure word | For | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {个|gè} | people and most things; the safe default | {一个|yí gè}{人|rén}, {两个|liǎng gè}{苹果|píng guǒ} |
| {本|běn} | books | {三本|sān běn}{书|shū} |
| {件|jiàn} | clothes (tops, jackets), matters | {一件|yí jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}, {一件|yí jiàn}{事|shì} |
| {口|kǒu} | members of a family | {四口人|sì kǒu rén} |
| {只|zhī} | animals | {一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo} |
| {家|jiā} | shops, restaurants, companies | {一家|yì jiā}{饭店|fàn diàn} |
| {块|kuài} | money (kuai); pieces | {五块|wǔ kuài}{钱|qián} |
| {些|xiē} | an unstated number: some | {一些|yì xiē}{东西|dōng xi}, {这些|zhè xiē}{人|rén} |

Some nouns are measures themselves and take no measure word: {一天|yì tiān}, {两年|liǎng nián},
{十分钟|shí fēn zhōng}, {二十岁|èr shí suì}. But {小时|xiǎo shí} and {星期|xīng qī} take {个|gè}:
{两个|liǎng gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}, {一个|yí gè}{星期|xīng qī}.

Before a measure word, "two" is {两|liǎng}: {两个|liǎng gè}{人|rén}, {两点|liǎng diǎn}. Inside numbers and
when counting it's {二|èr}: {十二|shí èr}, {二十|èr shí}, {第二|dì èr}.

## {不|bù} or {没|méi}?

| Use {不|bù} | Use {没|méi} / {没有|méi yǒu} |
|---|---|
| now, habits and the future: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 {明天|míng tiān}{不去|bú qù}。 | with {有|yǒu}: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{哥哥|gē ge}。 |
| adjectives: {不贵|bú guì}, {不忙|bù máng} | an action that didn't happen: {昨天|zuó tiān}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}。 |
| {是|shì}, {会|huì}, {能|néng}, {想|xiǎng}, {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {知道|zhī dào}… | |

Two traps: there's no {不|bù}{有|yǒu}, and a {没|méi} sentence never has {了|le}:
{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}, not {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}{了|le}.

## {了|le}, {在|zài} and {正在|zhèng zài}

| What you want to say | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| something has changed (a new situation) | sentence + {了|le} | {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 {我|wǒ}{不去|bú qù}{了|le}。 (lesson 20) |
| an action is completed | verb + {了|le} (+ object) | {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一本|yì běn}{书|shū}。 (lesson 25) |
| it didn't happen | {没|méi} + verb, no {了|le} | {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}。 |
| did it happen? | …{了|le}{吗|ma}？ / …{了|le}{没有|méi yǒu}？ | {你|nǐ}{吃饭|chī fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ |
| an action is in progress | {在|zài} / {正在|zhèng zài} + verb (+ {呢|ne}) | {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}。 (lesson 10) |

{了|le} isn't a past tense. A past habit or a state has none: {去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{工作|gōng zuò}。
(Last year I worked in Beijing.) The le sheet in the Study tools box has more examples.

## Joining sentences: {和|hé}, {也|yě} and {还|hái}

Joining two ideas of the same kind is **[[coordination]]**. HSK 1 has three tools for it:

- {和|hé} joins nouns and pronouns, never two sentences: {爸爸|bà ba}{和|hé}{妈妈|mā ma},
  {我|wǒ}{和|hé}{你|nǐ}. "I eat and drink" is not {我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{和|hé}{喝|hē}.
- {也|yě} (also) before the second verb adds something of the same kind:
  {他|tā}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{也|yě}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}。 — He can speak Chinese and write
  characters too.
- {还|hái} (also, in addition) adds one more thing, often with {有|yǒu}:
  {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo}，{还有|hái yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 — I have a cat, and a dog as well.

Both {也|yě} and {还|hái} go before the verb, never at the start of the sentence like English "also".

## Reading: my week

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}，{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}，{现在|xiàn zài}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。{我|wǒ}{星期一|xīng qī yī}{到|dào}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}{上午|shàng wǔ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{下午|xià wǔ}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。{星期六|xīng qī liù}{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{去|qù}{看电影|kàn diàn yǐng}。{上|shàng}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{没|méi}{去|qù}{玩|wán}，{在|zài}{家|jiā}{睡|shuì}{了|le}{一天|yì tiān}。{今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！

1. What does David do on weekday afternoons?
2. What did he do last Sunday, and why?
3. Find a completed-action {了|le} and a change-of-state {了|le}.

<details>
<summary>Translation and answers</summary>

My name is David, I'm British, and I live in Beijing now. From Monday to Friday I study Chinese at
school in the mornings and go to work at a company in the afternoons. On Saturdays I go to the
cinema with friends. Last Sunday I was ill, so I didn't go out; I slept at home all day. Today I'm
better!

1. He works at a company. 2. He stayed at home and slept all day, because he was ill.
3. Completed action: {睡|shuì}{了|le}{一天|yì tiān}. Change of state: {生病|shēng bìng}{了|le} (he fell ill),
{好|hǎo}{了|le} (he's better now).

</details>

{上|shàng}{星期天|xīng qī tiān} is "last Sunday" ({上|shàng}, previous). Notice how much grammar the
text uses: a time before the verb, a place with {在|zài} before the verb, a serial verb
({去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}), {和|hé} joining nouns, {没|méi} without {了|le}, and both {了|le}.

## Dialogue: what are you doing?

```dialogue
# What are you doing?
安娜: {喂|wèi}，{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{呢|ne}？
= Hello, Li Ming, what are you doing?
李明: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{呢|ne}。{明天|míng tiān}{有|yǒu}{课|kè}。
= I'm writing characters. I have a class tomorrow.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{晚饭|wǎn fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Have you had dinner?
李明: {没有|méi yǒu}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{没有|méi yǒu}{菜|cài}{了|le}。
= No. There's no food left at home.
安娜: {我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{饭店|fàn diàn}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}！{学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}{有|yǒu}{一家|yì jiā}{饭店|fàn diàn}，{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。
= Let's go and eat dumplings at a restaurant! There's one outside the school; it's very good.
李明: {太好了|tài hǎo le}！{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Great! Where are you?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}。
= I'm outside the school.
李明: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{去|qù}。
= OK, I'm coming now.
```

Find in it: progressive {在|zài}…{呢|ne}, a question with {了|le}{吗|ma}, the answer {没有|méi yǒu}, a
change-of-state {了|le} ({没有|méi yǒu}{菜|cài}{了|le}: "there's no more food"), {吧|ba} for a
suggestion, an existential sentence ({学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}{有|yǒu}{一家|yì jiā}{饭店|fàn diàn}), an exclamation
and {在|zài} as a verb ({我|wǒ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}).

## The whole level on one page

| Point | Pattern | Example | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| A is B | A {是|shì} B / {不是|bú shì} | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 | 1 |
| yes/no question | … {吗|ma}？ | {你|nǐ}{忙|máng}{吗|ma}？ | 1 |
| name | {叫|jiào} + name | {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 | 1 |
