questions.stem: {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo}，___ {有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 Choose the word (I have a cat, and a dog as well).
questions.explanation: {还|hái} before the second verb adds one more thing: …，{还有|hái yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 {和|hé} joins nouns only ({一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo}{和|hé}{一只|yì zhī}{狗|gǒu}), never a new clause, and {都|dōu} means "all".

questions.stem: {他|tā}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，___ {会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}。 Choose the word (He can speak Chinese, and he can write characters too).
questions.explanation: {也|yě} (also) goes before the second verb: …，{也|yě}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}。 {和|hé} can't join two clauses, and English "and" tempts learners to use it here.

questions.stem: Which of these is an imperative (a request)?
questions.explanation: {请坐|qǐng zuò} (please sit down) asks someone to do something: an imperative, made polite with {请|qǐng}. The others are a question, a statement and an exclamation.

questions.stem:
Read the text.

{上|shàng}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{没|méi}{去|qù}{玩|wán}，{在|zài}{家|jiā}{睡|shuì}{了|le}{一天|yì tiān}。{今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{好|hǎo}{了|le}，{下午|xià wǔ}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。

Which is true?
choices: The writer went out last Sunday.
The writer is still ill today.
The writer is going to work this afternoon.
questions.explanation: {今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{好|hǎo}{了|le}，{下午|xià wǔ}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò} — I'm better today, and I'm going to work this afternoon. Last Sunday the writer was ill ({生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}), didn't go out ({没|méi}{去|qù}{玩|wán}) and slept all day.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Chinese.
questions.prompt: At eight o'clock we all have class at school.
questions.explanation: The order is (time) subject (time) adverb, place with {在|zài}, verb: {我们|wǒ men}{八点|bā diǎn}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{上课|shàng kè}。 {都|dōu} goes right before {在|zài} + place, and the time can also open the sentence.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Chinese.
questions.prompt: I slept for eight hours.
questions.explanation: How long something lasts goes after the verb: {我|wǒ}{睡|shuì}{了|le}{八个|bā gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 {小时|xiǎo shí} (hours) needs {个|gè}. {八点|bā diǎn} is a clock time (eight o'clock), which would go before the verb.

questions.stem: Type the measure word, in characters or pinyin: {两|liǎng}___ {人|rén} (two people)
questions.explanation: People take the general measure word {个|gè}: {两个|liǎng gè}{人|rén}. In a family, members are counted with {口|kǒu} ({我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{三口人|sān kǒu rén}), but "two people" in general is {两个|liǎng gè}{人|rén}.

questions.stem: Listen. Which is true?
choices: Not all of us are going.
questions.explanation: {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{不去|bú qù} — none of us is going ("all not going"). With the other order, {我们|wǒ men}{不|bù}{都|dōu}{去|qù}, it would be "not all of us are going".

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {两|liǎng}, two (before a measure word): the third tone. {二|èr}, two in numbers, has the fourth tone.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {没有|méi yǒu}, not have; did not: a rising second tone, then a third tone (2+3).

questions.stem: How many words does the new HSK 1 (HSK 3.0) cover?
questions.explanation: The 2025 syllabus of the new HSK gives level 1 300 words and 246 characters. 150 was the old HSK 1, 500 is level 1 of the 2021 standard, and 1,000 is the total by the end of the new HSK 3.

questions.stem: Which skills does the new HSK 1 test?
questions.explanation: HSK 1 has a listening part and a reading part (about 40 questions in about 40 minutes, as far as has been reported). There is no speaking test and no writing task at level 1; check the official site for the current format.

questions.stem: In the listening part, what's the best thing to do before each item is played?
choices: read the choices, so you know what to listen for
close your eyes and listen only
write down every word you hear
go back to the last item you missed
questions.explanation: The choices tell you what kind of answer you need: if they're times, listen for {点|diǎn}; if they're places, for {在|zài} and place words. Going back to a missed item makes you miss the next one too.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker doing?
questions.explanation: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{看书|kàn shū} — I'm reading. {在|zài} before the verb means the action is going on. Watching TV would be {看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}, and writing characters {写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}.

questions.stem: Listen. What time is it?
questions.explanation: {现在|xiàn zài}{十点|shí diǎn} — It's ten o'clock now. {十|shí} has a rising tone; {四|sì} (4) falls. Writing the number in the margin as you hear it helps.

questions.stem: Listen. How is he going to Shanghai?
questions.explanation: {他|tā}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{去|qù}{上海|Shàng hǎi} — He's going to Shanghai by plane. {坐|zuò} + vehicle comes before {去|qù}. A train is {火车|huǒ chē}, a taxi {出租车|chū zū chē}.

questions.stem: Listen. Which reply fits?
questions.explanation: {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Where are you going? The answer puts a place where {哪儿|nǎr} was: {去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}。 A time would answer {什么时候|shén me shí hou}？

questions.stem: Listen. When are they meeting?
questions.explanation: {我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{三点|sān diǎn}{见|jiàn} — See you tomorrow at three in the afternoon. The time goes big to small: day ({明天|míng tiān}), part of the day ({下午|xià wǔ}), hour ({三点|sān diǎn}).

questions.stem: Listen. How much is the second one?

audio.text: 这个苹果五块，那个三块。

questions.explanation: {这个|zhè ge}{苹果|píng guǒ}{五块|wǔ kuài}，{那个|nà ge}{三块|sān kuài} — This apple is five kuai, that one three. {这个|zhè ge} is "this one", {那个|nà ge} "that one".

questions.stem: Match each question to its answer.
questions.explanation: Each answer fills the place of the question word: {几点|jǐ diǎn} → a time, {哪儿|nǎr} → a place, {多少|duō shao}{钱|qián} → a price, {什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi} → a name. {三口人|sān kǒu rén} would answer {你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{几口人|jǐ kǒu rén}？

questions.stem: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}___？ Choose the word for the gap (an open question: Are you a teacher?).
questions.explanation: An open yes/no question takes {吗|ma}: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？ {吧|ba} would make it a guess ("you're a teacher, right?"), {呢|ne} doesn't make a yes/no question, and {的|de} doesn't end one.

questions.stem: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{两|liǎng}___ {书|shū}。 Choose the word for the gap.
questions.explanation: Books are counted with {本|běn}: {两本|liǎng běn}{书|shū}. Exam gaps often test measure words; {个|gè} is the general one but not used with {书|shū}.

questions.stem: {他|tā}{昨天|zuó tiān}___ {来|lái}。 Choose the word for the gap (He didn't come yesterday).
questions.explanation: {昨天|zuó tiān} points to the past, and an action that didn't happen takes {没|méi}: {他|tā}{昨天|zuó tiān}{没|méi}{来|lái}。 {不|bù}{来|lái} would be "won't come" or "doesn't come".

questions.stem:
Read the text.

{今天|jīn tiān}{星期六|xīng qī liù}，{天气|tiān qì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{姐姐|jiě jie}{上午|shàng wǔ}{去|qù}{超市|chāo shì}{买|mǎi}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}，{下午|xià wǔ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}。

When do they go to the supermarket?
questions.explanation: {今天|jīn tiān}{星期六|xīng qī liù} (today is Saturday) and {上午|shàng wǔ}{去|qù}{超市|chāo shì} (go to the supermarket in the morning). In the afternoon ({下午|xià wǔ}) they watch TV at home.

choices: eat at a restaurant with classmates
cook dinner at home for his mum
questions.explanation: {不|bù}{回家|huí jiā}{吃饭|chī fàn}{了|le} — I won't come home for dinner (a change of plan), and {我|wǒ}{和|hé}{同学|tóng xué}{去|qù}{饭店|fàn diàn} — I'm going to a restaurant with classmates. Read to the end: the {不|bù} at the start changes everything.

questions.stem: Where are you most likely to see this sign? {请不要|qǐng bú yào}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}
questions.explanation: {请不要|qǐng bú yào}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} — Please don't make phone calls. It's the kind of polite request you see in cinemas and hospitals. Labels, menus and timetables give prices and times.

questions.stem: Which word goes with a picture of a plane?
questions.explanation: {飞机|fēi jī} is a plane: {飞|fēi} (to fly) + {机|jī} (machine). {火车|huǒ chē} is a train, {出租车|chū zū chē} a taxi and {电脑|diàn nǎo} a computer. On the exam, word–picture items test words like these.

questions.stem: A picture shows a child asleep in bed. Which sentence matches it?
choices: {小朋友|xiǎo péng you}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
{小朋友|xiǎo péng you}{在|zài}{吃饭|chī fàn}。
{小朋友|xiǎo péng you}{没|méi}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
questions.explanation: {小朋友|xiǎo péng you}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào} — The child is sleeping. {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} is a friendly word for a child. The third sentence has the right verb but {没|méi} says the opposite, and the last one is about a teacher.

questions.stem: Build the question in Chinese.
questions.prompt: What time do you get up?
questions.explanation: The question word stands where the answer would be, before the verb like any time: {你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}？ ({我|wǒ}{七点|qī diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。) It takes no {吗|ma}.

questions.stem: Type "Saturday" in characters or pinyin: ___
questions.explanation: {星期六|xīng qī liù}: {星期|xīng qī} (week) + {六|liù} (six). The days from Monday to Saturday are numbered; Sunday is {星期天|xīng qī tiān} or {星期日|xīng qī rì}.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {起床|qǐ chuáng}, to get up: a third tone, then a rising second tone (3+2), as in {你|nǐ}{几点|jǐ diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}？

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {电视|diàn shì}, television: two falling fourth tones (4+4). The first falls from high to mid, the second from mid to low.

questions.stem: Read: "{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo}，{它|tā}{叫|jiào}{小白|Xiǎo Bái}。{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{两岁|liǎng suì}{了|le}，{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。" How old is {小白|Xiǎo Bái}?
questions.explanation: {小白|Xiǎo Bái}{两岁|liǎng suì}{了|le} — Little White is two (now). {两|liǎng} is "two" before a measure word such as {岁|suì}.

questions.stem: Read: "{白天|bái tiān}{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{上课|shàng kè}，{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。" What does Little White ({小白|Xiǎo Bái}, Tingting's cat) do in the daytime?
questions.explanation: {白天|bái tiān}{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{上课|shàng kè}，{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{睡觉|shuì jiào} — In the daytime Tingting goes to class, and Little White sleeps at home.

questions.stem: Read: "{每天|měi tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{回家|huí jiā}{的时候|de shí hou}，{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{都|dōu}{叫|jiào}：“{喵|miāo}！{喵|miāo}！”……{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}{晚上|wǎn shang}，{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{回家|huí jiā}{了|le}，{她|tā}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}“{喵|miāo}”。" ({喵|miāo}: miaow) How did Tingting know something was wrong?
choices: She didn't hear Little White's miaow.
questions.explanation: {她|tā}{没|méi}{听见|tīng jiàn}“{喵|miāo}” — she didn't hear a "miaow". Every other evening Little White called when Tingting came home. Li Ming only comes in when Tingting phones him.

questions.stem: Read: "“{小白|Xiǎo Bái}，{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？”……{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{找|zhǎo}{了|le}{一个|yí gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}，{没|méi}{看见|kàn jiàn}{小白|Xiǎo Bái}。" How long did Tingting look for Little White at home?
questions.explanation: {婷婷|Tíng tíng}{找|zhǎo}{了|le}{一个|yí gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} — Tingting looked for an hour. The duration comes after the verb and its {了|le}. Ten o'clock ({十点|shí diǎn}) is when she and Li Ming came back later.

questions.stem: What does Li Ming mean by {你|nǐ}{不要|bú yào}{哭|kū}？
questions.explanation: {不要|bú yào} + verb is "don't", and {哭|kū} (glossed in the story) is "to cry": {你|nǐ}{不要|bú yào}{哭|kū} — Don't cry. Then he says {我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{去|qù}{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}, I'm coming to your place now.

questions.stem: In the story, Tingting and Li Ming asked people at the supermarket and the restaurant: “{你们|nǐ men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{一只|yì zhī}{白|bái}{猫|māo}{了|le}{吗|ma}？” Nobody had seen it. What did everyone answer?
questions.explanation: {大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{说|shuō}：“{没|méi}{看见|kàn jiàn}。” — Everyone said they hadn't seen it. A completed action is denied with {没|méi} and no {了|le}; {不|bù} doesn't deny what has happened.

questions.stem: Read: "{在|zài}{外边|wài bian}，{李明|Lǐ Míng}{听见|tīng jiàn}：“{喵|miāo}——”……{他们|tā men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{车|chē}{下|xià}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo}：{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{和|hé}{一只|yì zhī}{小|xiǎo}{黑|hēi}{猫|māo}。" ({黑|hēi}: black) Where did they find Little White ({小白|Xiǎo Bái})?
questions.explanation: {他们|tā men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{车|chē}{下|xià}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo} — they saw two cats under a car, outside Tingting's home. Earlier Tingting had already looked under the table ({桌子|zhuō zi}{下|xià}).

questions.stem: The story ends: {现在|xiàn zài}，{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo}{了|le}。 What does the {了|le} show?
choices: {'Something has changed': 'now there are two cats.'}
It happened a long time ago.
questions.explanation: {了|le} at the end of the sentence is the change-of-state {了|le}: there used to be one cat, and now there are two. It isn't a past tense, and nobody bought anything: Little Black came home with Little White.

questions.stem: What does {雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{大|dà} mean?
questions.explanation: {雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{大|dà}, "the rain is big", is how Chinese says it's raining hard. A light rain is {雨|yǔ}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}.

questions.stem: Listen. What does Tingting say on the phone?
choices: Little White is asleep at home.
Little White isn't at home any more!
questions.explanation: {小白|Xiǎo Bái}{不在|bú zài}{家|jiā}{了|le} — Little White isn't at home any more. {不在|bú zài} says where it isn't, and the final {了|le} marks the change: it was at home before.

questions.stem: Listen. What are they asking?

audio.text: 你们看见一只白猫了吗？

choices: Have you seen a white cat?
Do you have a white cat?
questions.explanation: {你们|nǐ men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{一只|yì zhī}{白|bái}{猫|māo}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you seen a white cat? {看见|kàn jiàn} is "to see", {了|le}{吗|ma} asks whether it has happened, and {只|zhī} is the measure word for animals.

questions.stem: Read: "{他们|tā men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{车|chē}{下|xià}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo}：{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{和|hé}{一只|yì zhī}{小|xiǎo}{黑|hēi}{猫|māo}。……{现在|xiàn zài}，{婷婷|Tíng tíng}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo}{了|le}：{小白|Xiǎo Bái}{和|hé}{小黑|Xiǎo Hēi}。" ({黑|hēi}: black) {小黑|Xiǎo Hēi} is…
questions.explanation: {一只|yì zhī}{小|xiǎo}{黑|hēi}{猫|māo} is "a little black cat", and Tingting names it {小黑|Xiǎo Hēi}, Little Black, like {小白|Xiǎo Bái}, Little White.

questions.stem: {=On squared paper, how much space do {一|yī} (1 stroke) and {谢|xiè} (12 strokes) take?=}
choices: half a square and two squares
as much as their strokes need
questions.explanation: Every character takes one square, however many strokes it has. A simple character is drawn a little smaller, centred, never stretched to the edges; a complicated one fits its strokes into the same square.

questions.stem: What are the dashed lines of a {田字格|tián zì gé} for?
choices: They show where the radical goes.
They help you centre the character and place its parts.
They mark where each stroke starts.
questions.explanation: The dashed cross (and the diagonals in a {米字格|mǐ zì gé}) isn't part of the character: it's a guide for placing it in the middle of the square and for judging proportions.

questions.stem: In {国|guó}, which stroke is written last?
choices: the bottom stroke that closes the frame
questions.explanation: {=Enclosures are written outside first, then inside, then closed: left vertical, the top and right side in one stroke, the inside ({玉|yù}: four strokes and a dot), and the bottom stroke last. "Close the door" at the end.=}

questions.stem: In {这|zhè} and {边|biān}, which part is written last?
questions.explanation: {=The walking radical 辶 is written after the part it carries: in {这|zhè} you write {文|wén} first, then 辶. The same goes for {边|biān} and {还|hái}. Stroke order doesn't depend on the font.=}

questions.stem: How many strokes does {口|kǒu} have?
questions.explanation: {口|kǒu} has three strokes: the left side; the top and right side in one turning stroke; then the bottom. Drawing it as one loop is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Which character means "earth" (bottom horizontal longer than the top)?
questions.explanation: 土 (earth) has the longer horizontal at the bottom. 士 has the longer one on top: it's the 士 in {女士|nǚ shì}. 十 is {十|shí} (ten).

questions.stem: Which character is "cow" (the vertical goes through the top)?
questions.explanation: 牛 ({牛奶|niú nǎi}, milk) has a vertical stroke that sticks out above the top horizontal. In 午 ({中午|zhōng wǔ}, noon) it doesn't.

questions.stem: Which character means "to sell"?
questions.explanation: {=卖 ({卖|mài}, to sell) is 买 ({买|mǎi}, to buy) with 十 on top. A memory aid: to sell, you need something more (十) on top. The two words differ in sound only by the tone. (Traditional: 賣 and 買.)=}

questions.stem: Which typeface is the closest to handwriting, and the best model for your own writing?
questions.explanation: Kai ({楷体|kǎi tǐ}) follows brush writing in the regular style, so it shows how strokes start and end; it's the style of most textbooks. Song has thin horizontals and thick verticals; Hei has even strokes like a sans-serif font.

questions.stem: A typeface has thin horizontal strokes, thick vertical ones and little "serifs" at the ends. Which is it?
questions.explanation: That's Song ({宋体|sòng tǐ}), the usual typeface of printed books and newspapers. Hei ({黑体|hēi tǐ}) has no decorations and strokes of even thickness.

questions.stem: 忄, as in {忙|máng}, is the side form of which component?
questions.explanation: On the left, 心 (heart) becomes 忄: two dots and a vertical. At the bottom it keeps its shape: {想|xiǎng}, {您|nín}, {怎|zěn}, {息|xī}. 水 becomes 氵, and 人 becomes 亻.

questions.stem: {=With the traditional switch on, what do you see in place of the 讠 of {说|shuō} and {话|huà}?=}
questions.explanation: {=Simplified characters write the speech radical 言 as 讠 (2 strokes). Traditional characters keep the full 言 (7 strokes): 說, 話.=}

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker asking?
choices: how many strokes a character has
questions.explanation: {这个|zhè ge}{汉字|hàn zì}{怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}？ — How do you write this character? {怎么|zěn me} + verb asks how to do something, and the verb here is {写|xiě}, to write.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the teacher ask you to do?
questions.explanation: {请|qǐng}{写|xiě}{一下|yí xià}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi} — Please write your name. {一下|yí xià} after the verb makes the request softer.

glossary.definition: The official way of spelling Mandarin in the Latin alphabet, with tone marks over the vowels: {老师|lǎo shī}. This course shows it above every character; the Pinyin switch hides it.

The pitch pattern that is part of every Mandarin syllable and changes its meaning: first (high, level) ā, second (rising) á, third (low) ǎ, fourth (falling) à, and the neutral tone (unmarked). {妈|mā} is mother, {马|mǎ} is horse.
A short, light syllable with no tone of its own, written without a mark: the second syllable of {名字|míng zi}, {谢谢|xiè xie}, and particles such as {吗|ma}.

A change of tone caused by the next syllable. Two third tones: the first is said as a second ({你好|nǐ hǎo} sounds like ní hǎo), never written. {不|bù} and {一|yī} also change before a fourth tone; this course writes those changes: {不|bú}{是|shì}.
The consonant at the start of a Mandarin syllable: sh in shì, j in jiào. Some syllables have none (ài).
The rest of a syllable after the initial: the vowel and any -n, -ng or -r ending. In jiào the final is iao; the tone mark goes on the final.
A unit of Chinese writing: one syllable with a meaning, written in a square space. Most words are one or two characters: {人|rén} (person), {老师|lǎo shī} (teacher).
A smaller part that a character is built from. 好 has the components 女 and 子; 您 has 你 and 心.
The component a dictionary files a character under, often a hint at the meaning: 亻 (person) in {他|tā} and {你|nǐ}, 口 (mouth) in {叫|jiào}. Many radicals take a narrower form at the side: 人 becomes 亻.

The fixed order and direction in which the strokes of a character are written: top before bottom, left before right, horizontal before a vertical that crosses it, outside before inside, and a few more rules. This course uses mainland China's order.
A word that stands in for a noun or a name: {我|wǒ}, {你|nǐ}, {您|nín}, {他|tā}, {她|tā}. Chinese pronouns never change form: {我|wǒ} is both "I" and "me".
A word for a person, place, thing or idea: {老师|lǎo shī}, {中国|Zhōng guó}, {名字|míng zi}. Chinese nouns have no plural ending and no article ("a", "the").
A word for an action or a state: {是|shì} (to be), {叫|jiào} (to be called), {有|yǒu} (to have). Chinese verbs never change for person or tense.
A word that describes: {好|hǎo} (good), {大|dà} (big), {小|xiǎo} (small). In Chinese an adjective can be the predicate by itself, without {是|shì}, and usually takes {很|hěn}: {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
A word placed before a verb or adjective to say how, how much, when or whether: {很|hěn} (very), {不|bù} (not), {也|yě} (also), {都|dōu} (all). Chinese adverbs come before the verb, never after it.
Who or what a sentence is about, usually at the start: {我|wǒ} in {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}.

What the sentence says about the subject: {是|shì}{学生|xué sheng} in {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}, or {很|hěn}{好|hǎo} in {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}. In Chinese it can be a verb phrase, an adjective, or (for ages, dates and prices) a noun phrase.
A small word at the end of a sentence that makes it a question. {吗|ma} makes a yes-or-no question; {呢|ne} asks "and ...?" about a new topic. Both are in the neutral tone.
An ending that marks more than one. Chinese has one, {们|men}, used only for people: {我们|wǒ men} (we), {老师们|lǎo shī men} (teachers). It is never used after a number.
A word that must stand between a number (or {这|zhè}, {那|nà}, {几|jǐ}) and a noun: {三|sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}, three people. {个|gè} is the general one; others go with certain kinds of things.
A word or phrase that describes a noun. In Chinese it always comes before the noun, often joined by {的|de}: {我|wǒ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi} (my name), {中国|Zhōng guó}{老师|lǎo shī} (a Chinese teacher).

The particle {的|de} after a person shows whose something is, like English "'s": {老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}, the teacher's name. It is usually left out with family members and close ties: {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}, {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}.
A word for a number: {一|yī}, {十|shí}, {百|bǎi}, {千|qiān}, {两|liǎng}. Before a noun a numeral needs a measure word: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}.
A character that began as a drawing of a thing: {人|rén} (a person seen from the side), {日|rì} (the sun), {山|shān} (three peaks). Only a few hundred characters began this way.

A character made of a meaning part (usually the radical) and a sound part: {妈|mā} = 女 (woman) + {马|mǎ} (the sound ma). By common estimates most characters are of this kind; the sound part is a clue, not always the exact reading.

A noun that names a time: {今天|jīn tiān} (today), {星期一|xīng qī yī} (Monday), {八点|bā diǎn} (eight o'clock), {晚上|wǎn shang} (evening). It needs no word for "at" or "on", and it goes before the verb, after the subject or at the front: {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{工作|gōng zuò} or {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}. Several time words line up from the biggest unit to the smallest: {明天|míng tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七点|qī diǎn}.

A predicate made of a noun phrase alone, with no verb: {今天|jīn tiān}{星期一|xīng qī yī} (today is Monday), {现在|xiàn zài}{八点|bā diǎn} (it's eight now), {我|wǒ}{二十岁|èr shí suì} (I'm twenty). It is used for dates, days, times, ages and prices. The negative needs {是|shì}: {今天|jīn tiān}{不是|bú shì}{星期一|xīng qī yī}.

A number that gives a place in a series: first, second, third. In dates and months Chinese uses the plain number for this: {一号|yī hào} (the 1st), {二月|èr yuè} (February, "month two"), {星期三|xīng qī sān} (Wednesday, "week-day three"). Elsewhere it adds {第|dì}: {第一|dì yī} (first), lesson 14.

How long something lasts: {两个小时|liǎng gè xiǎo shí} (two hours), {十分钟|shí fēn zhōng} (ten minutes), {三天|sān tiān} (three days). A duration goes after the verb ({我|wǒ}{工作|gōng zuò}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}), while a point in time goes before it ({我|wǒ}{八点|bā diǎn}{工作|gōng zuò}). Chinese uses different words for the two: {两点|liǎng diǎn} (two o'clock) but {两个小时|liǎng gè xiǎo shí} (two hours).

A verb built from a verb and its own object, such as {睡觉|shuì jiào} ({睡|shuì} "sleep" + {觉|jiào} "a sleep"), {起床|qǐ chuáng} and {上班|shàng bān}. Because the object is already inside, no other object can follow it, and in some sentences other words go between the two parts ({睡|shuì}{八个小时|bā gè xiǎo shí}{的|de}{觉|jiào}). Dictionaries usually list them as one word.

Two or more verb phrases one after the other with the same subject and no word joining them, in the order the actions happen: {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi} (I go to the shop to buy things: going first, buying second). Time words and {不|bù} go before the first verb.

The way a verb shows how an action unfolds (going on, finished, newly begun) rather than when it happens. Chinese verbs have no tenses; aspect is shown with words such as {在|zài} or {正在|zhèng zài} before the verb and {呢|ne} at the end (going on), and with {了|le} for completion (lesson 25). Time words say when.

An action seen as going on at a given moment, like English "is doing". In Chinese: {在|zài} or {正在|zhèng zài} before the verb, often with {呢|ne} at the end: {他|tā}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne} (he's sleeping). With a time word it can be past or future: {昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{八点|bā diǎn}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} (I was on the phone at eight last night). The negative is {没在|méi zài} + verb.

A word or phrase that makes a request or an action sound smaller, lighter and more polite. {一下|yí xià} after a verb ({看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}, have a look; {等|děng}{一下|yí xià}, wait a moment) and {一点儿|yì diǎnr} ({喝|hē}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{水|shuǐ}) are the commonest; {吧|ba} at the end of a request softens it too.

A number, a measure word and a noun, in that order: {一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū} (a book), {两|liǎng}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu} (two pieces of clothing), {三|sān}{个|gè}{包子|bāo zi}. The measure word can't be left out; the noun can, when it is clear: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}.

A pointing word: {这|zhè} (this), {那|nà} (that) and the question {哪|nǎ} (which). Before a noun it takes a measure word, like a number: {这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}, {那|nà}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}; with {些|xiē} it makes a plural: {这些|zhè xiē}{书|shū}. With a number, the demonstrative comes first: {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū}.

A sentence whose predicate is an adjective, with no verb "to be": {衣服|yī fu}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang} (the clothes are pretty), {书|shū}{不|bú}{贵|guì}. Plain statements usually put {很|hěn} or another degree adverb before the adjective; a bare adjective suggests a contrast. {是|shì} + adjective is a mistake.

An adverb that says how much, placed right before an adjective (or a verb like {喜欢|xǐ huan}): {很|hěn} (very, often weak), {非常|fēi cháng} (extremely), {真|zhēn} (really!), {太|tài}…{了|le} (so, too), {不|bú}{太|tài} (not very).

A yes/no question made by saying a verb or adjective twice with {不|bu} (light) between: {贵|guì}{不|bu}{贵|guì}？ (is it expensive?), {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{不|bu}{去|qù}？ It takes no {吗|ma}. With {有|yǒu} the form is {有|yǒu}{没有|méi yǒu}. Two-syllable words are often shortened: {喜|xǐ}{不|bu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}？

A word for a position that goes after a noun and turns it into a place: {上|shàng} (on), {下|xià} (under), {里|lǐ} (in), {外|wài} (outside), {前|qián} (in front), {后|hòu} (behind), and their two-syllable forms with {边|biān}: {杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}, in the cup; {学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}, outside the school. English puts a preposition before the noun; Chinese puts the locative after it.

A word that names a place and can follow {在|zài}, {去|qù} or {到|dào} by itself: countries and cities ({中国|Zhōng guó}), buildings and institutions ({学校|xué xiào}, {家|jiā}), {这儿|zhèr} / {那儿|nàr} / {哪儿|nǎr}, and any noun + locative ({桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}). Ordinary things and people are not place words: {在|zài}{杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}, {在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}.

A sentence that says something exists somewhere: place + {有|yǒu} + thing, {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū} (there's a book on the table). The place comes first with no {在|zài}, and the thing is usually new to the listener; the negative is {没有|méi yǒu}. To say where a known thing is, use thing + {在|zài} + place instead.

A verb that goes before another verb and adds an idea such as ability, permission or wish: {会|huì} (know how to), {能|néng} (be able to), {可以|kě yǐ} (may), {想|xiǎng} (would like to), {要|yào} (want to, will). {不|bù} goes before the modal verb, and a short answer is the modal verb alone: {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{开车|kāi chē}{吗|ma}？ — {会|huì}。

The particle {了|le} at the end of a sentence, saying that a situation is new: something has started, stopped or changed, or the speaker has just noticed it. {下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le} (it's started raining), {天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le} (it's got cold), {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le} (I'm not going any more). It is not a past tense; compare completed-action 了, which follows a verb.

A sentence whose verb takes two objects: first the person, then the thing. In HSK 1 the verbs are {给|gěi} (give) and {问|wèn} (ask): {我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū} (I'll give you a book), {我|wǒ}{问|wèn}{老师|lǎo shī}{一个|yí gè}{问题|wèn tí} (I'll ask the teacher a question). With {给|gěi} the thing can't come first: ×{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{你|nǐ}.

A verb followed by a second verb or an adjective that says what the action led to. {看|kàn} (look) + {见|jiàn} (perceive) = {看见|kàn jiàn}, to see; {听|tīng} (listen) + {见|jiàn} = {听见|tīng jiàn}, to hear. HSK 2 adds many more.

The {了|le} that goes straight after a verb and says the action happened and is complete: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū} (I bought a book). It isn't a past tense: past states take no {了|le} ({去年|qù nián}{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}). The negative is {没|méi}({有|yǒu}) + verb, with no {了|le}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}. Compare the change-of-state {了|le} at the end of a sentence.

A question that can be answered "yes" or "no". Chinese makes one by adding {吗|ma} to a statement ({你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{吗|ma}？) or with an A-not-A pair ({你|nǐ}{去不去|qù bu qù}？), and answers it by repeating the verb: {去|qù} or {不去|bú qù}.

A question that asks for information with a question word such as {谁|shéi}, {什么|shén me}, {哪儿|nǎr}, {几|jǐ}, {多少|duō shao} or {怎么|zěn me}. In Chinese the question word stays where the answer goes ({你|nǐ}{去|qù}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{商店|shāng diàn}。), and the question takes no {吗|ma}.
Reading a whole text quickly for its general idea, without stopping on each word. A good first step with a sign, a note or a menu, before you read the question and scan for the answer.

Moving your eyes over a text to find one particular fact, such as a time, a price or a name, without reading everything. Numbers, measure words and the characters you know ({元|yuán}, {点|diǎn}, {星期|xīng qī}) are good things to scan for.
A predicate built on a verb, the most common kind of sentence: {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 Chinese verbs never change for person or time; {了|le}, {在|zài} and time words show when and how an action happens.

The job a sentence does: a statement (ending in 。), a question (？), an imperative (a request or an order) or an exclamation (！). Grammar books also sort sentences by their predicate: verb, adjective or noun.
A sentence that tells something, ending in a full stop 。: {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 Add {吗|ma} and it becomes a yes/no question.

A sentence that asks or tells someone to do something. Chinese uses the plain verb, softened with {请|qǐng} before it ({请坐|qǐng zuò}), {一下|yí xià} after it or {吧|ba} at the end; "don't" is {不要|bú yào} + verb.
A sentence that expresses a strong feeling, ending in ！: {太好了|tài hǎo le}！ {这件|zhè jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{真|zhēn}{漂亮|piào liang}！ At HSK 1 they are built with {太|tài}…{了|le} and {真|zhēn}.

Joining two words or clauses of the same kind. {和|hé} joins nouns ({爸爸|bà ba}{和|hé}{妈妈|mā ma}) but never clauses; two clauses are joined with {也|yě} or {还|hái} before the second verb: {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{猫|māo}，{还有|hái yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{狗|gǒu}。

The official test of Chinese for speakers of other languages ({汉语|Hàn yǔ}{水平|shuǐ píng}{考试|kǎo shì}). Its new version (often called HSK 3.0, syllabus in force from July 2026) has nine levels; level 1 covers 300 words and 246 characters and tests listening and reading.

Practice paper for characters ({田字格|tián zì gé}): each square is divided into four by a dashed cross, like the character {田|tián}, to help centre the character and judge its proportions. A {米字格|mǐ zì gé} adds the two diagonals.

references.title: The 246 characters of HSK 1
references.body:
Every character of the course in the order it is taught: the 21 of the pinyin course, then the 225 of this course. Pinyin gives the readings our words use (a character may have others). Radical is the one the stroke-order data (Make Me a Hanzi) gives, which is usually but not always the radical a dictionary files it under. Strokes follow mainland stroke order. ✎ marks the characters HSK expects you to write by hand at levels 1–2.

The list shows the simplified forms the course teaches, so it stays in simplified characters when the script switch is on Traditional; the Traditional column gives the form the switch shows ("same" when the two scripts write it alike).
